## Saṃyutta Nikāya
## Nidāna Vagga Aṭṭhakathā
## Namo Tassa Bhagavato Arahato Sammāsambuddhassa
## 1. Nidāna Saṃyutta
## 1. Buddha Vagga
## 1. Paṭiccasamuppāda Sutta Vaṇṇanā
The discourse beginning with "Evaṃ me sutaṃ" is the first discourse in the Nidāna Vagga, the Paṭiccasamuppāda Sutta. In this sutta, the sequential commentary on the words is as follows:

In the sentence "Tatra kho bhagavā bhikkhū āmantesi" (There the Blessed One addressed the monks), the word "tatra" indicates the place and time. This word "tatra" signifies "at the time the Blessed One was dwelling, at that time; and in the Jeta Grove where he was dwelling, in that Jeta Grove." Alternatively, it indicates a place and time suitable for the teaching to be delivered. Indeed, the Blessed One does not teach the Dhamma in an unsuitable place or at an unsuitable time. In this regard, the Udāna passage beginning with "Bāhiya, it is not the right time now" serves as evidence.

The word "kho" is a particle used merely for completing the sentence, for emphasis, or in the sense of the beginning of a time. The word "Bhagavā" indicates the person who is most revered in the world. The word "bhikkhū" refers to the persons suitable for listening to the discourse. Furthermore, the meaning should be understood here through such methods as: "He is a bhikkhu because he begs; he is a bhikkhu because he has undertaken the practice of wandering for alms."

"Āmantesi" means he called, he spoke, or he made them aware; this is the meaning here. In other contexts, it is also used in the sense of informing. As it is said: "Monks, I address you; monks, I inform you."
2:
"Monks, I address you; monks, I inform you." (The word 'āmantesi' is also used) in the sense of summoning. As it is said: "Come, monk, in my name address Sāriputta." The word "bhikkhavo" indicates the manner of informing. That word "bhikkhu," which indicates the manner of informing, is spoken because they are endowed with qualities such as the habit of begging. Experts in grammar consider that one is called a "bhikkhu" because he is endowed with the quality of having a habit of begging, or endowed with the quality of the nature of begging, or endowed with the quality of being proficient in begging. By using the word "bhikkhavo," which is established by their being endowed with qualities such as the habit of begging, the Buddha reveals the mode of livelihood practiced by those of both low and high birth, and thereby subdues both elation (due to pride) and dejection (due to poverty).

With this word "bhikkhavo," preceded by a glance from eyes and a heart softened by the expansion of compassion, he brings those monks before him. By expressing his desire to speak, he generates in them a desire to listen; and by that same sense of addressing them, he urges them to pay careful attention. For the success of the Dispensation depends on careful attention.

If it is asked why he addressed only the monks when other devas and humans were present: it is because they are the seniors, the best, the ones nearby, and the ones always present. Although the Blessed One's Dhamma teaching is common to all assemblies, the monks are the seniors because they were the first to arise; they are the best because, starting with the state of homelessness, they follow the Teacher's conduct and are the recipients of the entire Dispensation; they are the ones nearby because they are seated close to the Teacher; and they are the ones always present because they move in the Teacher's presence. Furthermore, they are like vessels for the Dhamma teaching because of their existence in practice according to the instruction. Especially, he addressed them in this way because this teaching was intended specifically for certain monks.

Why did the Blessed One, when teaching the Dhamma, first address the monks instead of teaching the Dhamma directly? It was for the purpose of generating mindfulness. Monks might be sitting there thinking of other things, or with distracted minds, or reflecting on Dhamma they already know, or practicing meditation. If the Dhamma were taught without addressing them, they might not be able to note, "For what reason, due to what condition, or because of what specific occurrence is this teaching given?" and thus they might grasp it wrongly or not grasp it at all. Therefore, for the purpose of generating mindfulness, the Blessed One first addresses them and only then teaches the Dhamma.

"Bhaddante" is a word of respect, or a response given to the Teacher. Furthermore, in this context, the Blessed One, saying "bhikkhavo," addresses the monks. Those monks, saying "bhaddante," respond to the Blessed One. Thus, the Blessed One speaks first with the word "bhikkhavo."
3:
They replied, "Venerable Sir." By addressing them as "Monks," He prompted a response, and they gave their response as "Venerable Sir." "Those monks" refers to the monks whom the Blessed One addressed. "Responded to the Blessed One" means they listened to the Blessed One's address, turned towards Him, paid attention, acknowledged, and accepted it. "The Blessed One said this" means the Blessed One spoke the entire Sutta that is now being explained. Thus ends the explanation of the meaning of the introduction (nidāna), which was spoken by the Venerable Ānanda, adorned with the time, place, speaker, and audience, for the purpose of easily understanding this Sutta, which is perfect in meaning and phrasing and indicative of the depth of the Buddhas' knowledge in teaching.

Now the opportunity has arrived to explain the Sutta taught by the Blessed One beginning with "Paṭiccasamuppādaṃ vo" and so forth. Since the explanation of this Sutta becomes clear only after examining the occasion of its delivery (nikkhepa), we shall first examine the occasion of the Sutta's delivery. There are four occasions for delivering a Sutta (nikkhepa): one's own inclination (attajjhāsaya), the inclination of others (parajjhāsaya), by way of questioning (pucchāvasika), and by way of an occasion arising (aṭṭhuppattika). Among these four, those Suttas which the Blessed One teaches solely by His own inclination without being requested by others—such as the Dasabala Sutta, Candūpama Sutta, Vīṇūpama Sutta, Sammappadhāna Sutta, Iddhipāda Sutta, Indriya Sutta, Bala Sutta, Bojjhaṅga Sutta, Maggaṅga Sutta, and so forth—are called "delivery by one's own inclination" (attajjhāsaya nikkhepa).

"The factors for the ripening of Rāhula's liberation are mature; what if I were to lead Rāhula further to the destruction of the taints (arahantship)?"—considering in this way the inclination, preference, mental disposition, aspiration, and capacity for enlightenment of others, those Suttas taught according to the inclination of others—such as the Cūḷarāhulovāda Sutta, Mahārāhulovāda Sutta, Dhammacakkappavattana Sutta, Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta, Āsīvisūpama Sutta, Dhātuvibhaṅga Sutta, and so forth—are called "delivery by the inclination of others" (parajjhāsaya nikkhepa).

Furthermore, the four assemblies, the four classes, Nāgas, Garuḍas, Gandhabbas, Asuras, Yakkhas, the Great Kings, devas of the Tāvatiṃsa realm and so forth, and Mahābrahmā approach the Blessed One and ask questions such as: "Venerable Sir, it is said, 'Factors of Enlightenment, Factors of Enlightenment'"; "Venerable Sir, it is said, 'Hindrances, Hindrances'"; "Venerable Sir, are these the five aggregates of clinging..."; "What is a person's best wealth in this world?" and so forth. When the Blessed One is thus asked...
4:
...those Suttas that were spoken, such as the Bojjhaṅga Saṃyutta and others, as well as the Devatā Saṃyutta, Māra Saṃyutta, Brahma Saṃyutta, Sakkapañha Sutta, Cūḷavedalla Sutta, Mahါvedalla Sutta, Sāmaññaphala Sutta, Āḷavaka Sutta, Suciloma Sutta, Kharaloma Sutta, and so forth—the delivery of these is called "delivery by way of questioning" (pucchāvasika nikkhepa).

Those Suttas, however, which were spoken on account of an occasion that had arisen—such as the Dhammadāyāda Sutta, Cūḷasīhanāda Sutta, Puttamaṃsūpama Sutta, Dārukkhandhūpama Sutta, Aggikkhandhūpama Sutta, Pheṇapiṇḍūpama Sutta, Pāricchattakūpama Sutta, and so forth—the delivery of these is called "delivery by way of an occasion arising" (aṭṭhuppattika nikkhepa).

Among these four types of delivery, the delivery of this Paṭiccasamuppāda Sutta is "delivery by the inclination of others" (parajjhāsaya nikkhepa). Indeed, the Blessed One delivered this Sutta according to the inclination (ajjhāsaya) of other individuals. According to the inclination of what kind of individuals? It was according to the inclination of those of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū). For there are four types of individuals: the one of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū), the one who understands through elaboration (vipañcitaññū), the one who needs guidance (neyya), and the one for whom the word is the maximum (padaparama). Among these four, the individual who attains the realization of the Dhamma (dhammābhisamaya) at the very moment a teaching is uttered is called an "ugghaṭitaññū" individual. The individual who attains the realization of the Dhamma only when the meaning of a briefly stated text is elaborated in detail is called a "vipañcitaññū" individual. The individual who attains the realization of the Dhamma gradually through study, questioning, wise attention (yoniso manasikāra), and by associating with, following, and attending to good friends is called a "neyya" individual. The individual who, even though he hears much, remembers much, and recites much, cannot attain the realization of the Dhamma in that very life is called a "padaparama" individual. Thus, among these four types of individuals, this Sutta was delivered according to the inclination of individuals of quick understanding (ugghaṭitaññū).

At that time, it is said that five hundred monks living in the countryside—all of whom lived alone, or in groups of two, three, four, or five, having similar dispositions, observers of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), possessing stirred-up energy, devoted to spiritual practice, and practitioners of insight (vipassanā)—approached the Blessed One in the evening. After paying homage, they sat surrounding Him, longing for the teaching as if being enveloped by a red woolen curtain, and aspiring for the teaching on the mode of conditions (paccayākāra), which is subtle, profound, and shows the emptiness of beings. According to their inclination, the Blessed One began (taught) this Sutta. Just as a skilled painter, upon obtaining a wall that has not yet been prepared, does not start painting the figures right away, but first prepares the wall with yellow clay, clay-paste, and so forth, and only then...
5:
(A painter) draws a figure on a prepared wall. If he obtains a wall that is already prepared, he does not repeat the work of preparing the wall; instead, after mixing the colors and taking a cloth or a brush, he simply draws the figure. In the same way, when the Blessed One meets a noble son who is a beginner and has not yet practiced insight (vipassanā), He does not immediately teach him the subtle and empty characteristics of insight, which are the proximate cause of the fruition of arahantship (arahattaphala). Instead, while establishing him in virtue (sīla), concentration (samādhi), and the right view of the ownership of kamma (kammassakatādiṭṭhi), He first teaches only the preliminary practice (pubbabhāgapatipadā). With reference to this, it was said:

"Monk, therefore, in this teaching, you should first purify the very beginning of wholesome states. What is the beginning of wholesome states? It is well-purified virtue and straight view (diṭṭhi). Monk, when your virtue is well-purified and your view is straight, then, depending upon virtue and established in virtue, you should develop the four foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna) in a threefold way. What are the four? Here, monk, dwell contemplating the body in the body internally, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, removing covetousness and displeasure in the world. Dwell contemplating the body in the body externally... [pe]... dwell contemplating the body in the body both internally and externally... [pe]... dwell contemplating dhammas in dhammas, ardent, clearly comprehending, and mindful, removing covetousness and displeasure in the world. Monk, when you develop these four foundations of mindfulness in this threefold way, depending upon virtue and established in virtue, then whether night or day comes to you, only growth in wholesome states is to be expected, not decline." (SN 5.369).

In this way, after teaching the preliminary preparation (parikamma) through a discourse on virtue to the noble son who is a beginner, He then teaches the subtle and empty characteristics of insight, which are the proximate cause of the fruition of arahantship.

However, when He meets a practitioner of insight who possesses pure virtue, has aroused energy, and is devoted to spiritual practice, He no longer teaches the preliminary practice to that person. Instead, He directly teaches the subtle and empty characteristics of insight, which are the proximate cause of the fruition of arahantship. These five hundred monks were those who had already purified and established themselves in the preliminary practice; they were like well-refined gold or a well-polished gem. For them, only the supramundane path (lokuttaramagga) had not yet arrived. Thus, for the purpose of their attaining that path, the Teacher, observing their inclinations, undertook (taught) this sutta.
7:
"Listen"—this word is shown (with the meanings of listening firmly, listening according to the command, and listening to the good Dhamma). "Pay attention" means to reflect. It has the meaning of "direct your mind well [to the object]." The intention is: "Listen with an undistracted mind; keep it in your heart."

Now, in this context, "Listen to that [Dhamma]" is the prevention of the distraction of the faculty of hearing (sotindriya). "Pay attention well" is the prevention of the distraction of the faculty of mind (manindriya) by engaging in firm application of attention. The former statement prevents the distorted grasping of the phrasing (vyañjana), and the latter prevents the distorted grasping of the meaning (attha). By the former, he engages [them] in hearing the Dhamma; by the latter, he engages [them] in the retention and investigation of the heard teachings. By the former, he shows: "This Dhamma is complete in phrasing, therefore it is worth hearing"; by the latter: "It is complete in meaning, therefore it is worth paying attention to." Alternatively, by connecting the word "well" (sādhukaṃ) with both phrases, it should be understood as: "Because this Dhamma is profound in its text and profound in its delivery, listen well. Because it is profound in its meaning and profound in its penetration, pay attention well."

"I will speak" means "I will teach the discourse." In this context of "Listen to that," it means that he will not only teach the promised discourse in brief, but will also speak it in detail. For these words express both brevity and detail. As the Elder Vaṅgīsa said: "He teaches in brief and speaks in detail; with a voice like a myna bird, he rouses inspiration."

When he had spoken thus, those monks, becoming enthusiastic, respectfully accepted the word of the Blessed One, saying, "Yes, Bhante."

Then the Blessed One said to those monks the entire sutta, beginning with: "And what, bhikkhus, is dependent origination?" In that text, the question "And what, bhikkhus, is dependent origination?" is a question asked out of a desire to teach (kathetukamyatā-pucchā). For there are five kinds of questions: (1) a question to illuminate what is not seen (adiṭṭhajotanā-pucchā), (2) a question to compare what is seen (diṭṭhasaṃsandanā-pucchā), (3) a question to cut off doubt (vimaticchedanā-pucchā), (4) a question for consent (anumati-pucchā), and (5) a question asked out of a desire to teach (kathetukamyatā-pucchā). What is their distinction?

What is the question to illuminate what is not seen (adiṭṭhajotanā-pucchā)? By nature, a characteristic is unknown, unseen, unweighed, unjudged, unmanifested, and unexplained. In order to know that characteristic...
8:
...for the sake of seeing, weighing, judging, manifesting, and explaining it, one asks a question. This is the question to illuminate what is not seen (adiṭṭhajotanā-pucchā).

What is the question to compare what is seen (diṭṭhasaṃsandanā-pucchā)? By nature, a characteristic is already known, seen, weighed, judged, manifested, and explained. That person asks a question for the sake of comparing it with other wise people. This is the question to compare what is seen (diṭṭhasaṃsandanā-pucchā).

What is the question to cut off doubt (vimaticchedanā-pucchā)? By nature, one has fallen into doubt, fallen into perplexity, and is of two minds: "Is it thus, or is it not thus? How is it?" That person asks a question for the sake of cutting off doubt. This is the question to cut off doubt (vimaticchedanā-pucchā).

What is the question for consent (anumati-pucchā)? The Blessed One asks a question to obtain the consent (agreement) of the monks: "What do you think, bhikkhus, is form permanent or impermanent?" "Impermanent, Bhante." "Is that which is impermanent suffering or happiness?" "Suffering, Bhante." "Is it fit to regard that which is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change as: 'This is mine, this I am, this is my self'?" "No, Bhante." This is the question for consent (anumati-pucchā).

What is the question asked out of a desire to teach (kathetukamyatā-pucchā)? The Blessed One asks a question because of his desire to teach the monks: "Bhikkhus, there are these four foundations of mindfulness. Which four?" This is the question asked out of a desire to teach (kathetukamyatā-pucchā).

Among those five kinds of questions, the first three do not exist for the Buddhas. Why? Because for the Buddhas, there is nothing—whether a conditioned thing (saṅkhata) within the three periods of time or an unconditioned thing (asaṅkhata) beyond the three periods of time—that is not seen, not illuminated, not weighed, not judged, not manifested, or not explained by their knowledge. Therefore, the question to illuminate what is not seen (adiṭṭhajotanā-pucchā) does not exist for the Buddhas. There is no need for the Blessed One to compare the Dhamma he has penetrated with his own knowledge with any other ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā. Therefore, the question to compare what is seen (diṭṭhasaṃsandanā-pucchā) does not exist for him. This Blessed One has no "how or why" (perplexity), has crossed over doubt, and has destroyed doubt regarding all phenomena. Therefore, the question to cut off doubt (vimaticchedanā-pucchā) does not exist for him. However, the remaining two kinds of questions do exist for the Blessed One. Among those two, this question should be understood as the question asked out of a desire to teach (kathetukamyatā-pucchā).

Now, wishing to analyze the mode of conditions (paccayākāra) asked about by that question, he said: "Bhikkhus, with ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be," and so forth. Here, for example, a person who endeavors, saying, "I will tell you about the father," ...
9:
Just as a person intending to speak of a father mentions the son first, saying "Tissa's father" or "Soṇa's father," in the same way, the Blessed One, intending to teach the conditions, taught the phenomena such as ignorance (avijjā) which are the causes of formations (saṅkhāra) and the like, by way of the method beginning with "With ignorance as condition, formations [arise]" (avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā), and thus also taught the dependently arisen (paccayuppanna) phenomena. However, at the end of the Āhāravagga, he began with both and taught both, saying, "Bhikkhus, I will teach you Dependent Origination and dependently arisen phenomena."

Now, in the Pali passages such as "avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā," ignorance is both ignorance and a condition; therefore, it is called "avijjāpaccaya" (ignorance-condition). The meaning should be understood in this way: "Because of that condition which is ignorance, formations come into being." This is a brief explanation here. For a detailed explanation, the discourse on Dependent Origination in forward order (anuloma paṭiccasamuppāda), complete in all its aspects, has already been stated in the Visuddhimagga; therefore, it should be understood as stated in that text.

In the discourse on the reverse order (paṭiloma), "avijjāya tveva" means "only through ignorance." "Asesavirāganirodhā" means through the remainderless cessation by way of the path called detachment (virāga). "Saṅkhāranirodho" means the cessation of formations by way of non-arising. To show that through the cessation of these formations, consciousness and the rest cease, and mind-and-body and the rest are indeed ceased, he said "with the cessation of formations, the cessation of consciousness" and so forth, and then said, "Thus is the cessation of this entire mass of suffering."

In that context, "kevalassa" means the whole, or the pure, or that which is devoid of beings, or that which is devoid of a self or soul (atta jīva). "Dukkhakkhandhassa" means of the mass of suffering. "Nirodho hoti" means non-arising occurs.

Thus, the Blessed One taught the discourse on the cycle of existence (vaṭṭa) through twelve factors in forward order, and then, reversing that very cycle, he taught the ending of the cycle (vivaṭṭa) through twelve factors in reverse order, reaching the peak of the teaching with Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, those five hundred individuals of quick understanding (ugghaṭitannū) who had practiced insight (vipassanā) realized the Four Noble Truths and were established in the fruit of Arahantship, like lotus flowers that have reached maturity and bloom upon being touched by the sun's rays.

"Idamavoca bhagavā" means the Blessed One spoke this entire sutta by way of the cycle and the ending of the cycle. "Attamanā te bhikkhū" means those five hundred Arahant monks were delighted in mind. "Bhagavato bhāsitaṃ abhinandun" means they rejoiced in the words of the Blessed One, who spoke with a Brahma-voice (brahmassara) that was as sweet as the call of the Karavīka bird, pleasant to the ear, and like an infusion of ambrosia to the hearts of the wise...
10: The monks delighted in and accepted the words of the Blessed One with joy. Therefore, it is said: "The monks, rejoicing with heads bowed, accepted the well-spoken and well-uttered words of the Such-like One, saying, 'Excellent, excellent!'" ## The Commentary on the First Paṭiccasamuppāda Sutta is finished. ## 2. Commentary on the Vibhaṅga Sutta In the second sutta, the origin of the sutta should be understood in the same manner as stated in the first sutta. The distinction here is that the first sutta was shown in brief for the sake of persons of quick intuition (ugghaṭitaññū), while this second sutta is shown in detail for the sake of persons who learn through expansion (vipañcitaññū). In this sutta, the four similes of the man carrying a creeper should be mentioned; these have already been stated in the Visuddhimagga. Just as a man carrying a creeper, seeing the tip of the creeper and searching for the root by following that tip, finds the root, cuts the creeper at the root, and takes it to use for his desired purpose; so too, the Blessed One, when teaching the detailed discourse, brings the teaching starting from aging and death (jarāmaraṇa), which is the tip of dependent origination, down to the term ignorance (avijjā), which is the root, and then concludes by teaching the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa). In that second sutta, this is the decision on the meaning of the detailed teaching on aging and death and so forth. In the explanation of aging and death, the term "tesaṃ tesaṃ" (of those and those) should be understood as a brief explanation common to many beings. If one were to teach for a whole day in this way, "the aging of Devadatta, the aging of Somadatta," one would never reach the end of beings. However, by these two words, there is no being who is not included. Therefore, it is said, "This is a brief explanation common to many beings." The term "tamhi tamhi" (in that and that [existence]) is an explanation common to many groups of beings by way of their destination (gati) and birth (jāti). The term "sattanikāye" (in the assembly of beings) is the demonstration of the specific nature of the assembly of beings indicated by the general explanation. Among the terms jarā, jīraṇatā, etc., "jarā" (aging) is the explanation of the nature (sabhāva). "jīraṇatā" (decaying) is the explanation of the mode (ākāra). The first three terms, such as "khaṇḍiccaṃ" (brokenness), are explanations of the function in the passing of time, such as the breaking of teeth, while the last two terms are explanations of the natural state. Because the nature is shown by this term "jarā", it is called the explanation of nature (sabhāvaniddesa). Because the mode is shown by the term "jīraṇatā", it is called the explanation of the mode (ākāraniddesa). By the term "khaṇḍiccaṃ", the function of the breaking of teeth and nails in the passing of time is shown. By the term "pāliccaṃ", the [graying] of hair and body hair...
11:
The term "Jarā" (old age) is a description of nature (sabhāvaniddesa). Because it is described by the term "jīraṇatā" (aging) in terms of its mode, this term is a description of its mode (ākāraniddesa). It is described by the term "khaṇḍicca" (brokenness) due to the function of causing the breaking of teeth and nails when time has passed; by the term "pālicca" (grayness) due to the function of causing the graying of hair and body hair; and by the term "valittacatā" (wrinkling of skin) due to the function of causing the flesh to wither and the skin to wrinkle. Therefore, these three terms beginning with "khaṇḍicca" are descriptions of the function (kiccaniddesa) that occurs when time has passed. Through these three, evident old age (pākaṭajarā), which becomes manifest by seeing these transformations, is shown.

Just as the path taken by water, wind, or fire becomes evident through the breaking of grass and trees or by burning, yet that path is not the water, wind, or fire itself; in the same way, the path taken by old age is very evident through modes such as the breaking of teeth and so on, and can be seen even with the eyes open, yet those breakages and so on are not old age itself. This is because old age is not a phenomenon cognizable by the eye (cakkhuviññeyya).

However, by the terms "āyuno saṃhāni" (decline of life) and "indriyānaṃ paripāko" (ripening of the faculties), the natural state (pakaṭi) is shown, which is called the exhaustion of life and the ripening of the faculties such as the eye, which become very manifest only when time has passed. Therefore, these last two terms should be understood as descriptions of the natural state (pakaṭiniddesa). Therein, because life declines for one who has reached old age, old age is called "āyuno saṃhāni" by way of metonymy (phalūpacāra), attributing the effect to the cause. The faculties such as the eye, which in youth were very clear and subtle, capable of easily grasping their respective objects, become ripened, disturbed, and unclear upon reaching old age, unable to grasp even their own gross objects. Therefore, old age is also called "indriyānaṃ paripāko" by way of metonymy.

All such described old age is of two kinds: evident old age (pākaṭajarā) and concealed old age (paṭicchannajarā). Therein, old age occurring in material phenomena (rūpadhamma) is called evident old age because the modes such as brokenness in teeth and so on are seen. However, old age occurring in immaterial phenomena (arūpadhamma) is called concealed old age because such transformations are not seen. Therein, the clearly seen modes such as brokenness are merely the easily cognizable appearance (vaṇṇa) of such teeth and so on. Having seen that appearance with the eye and reflecting with the mind-door (manodvāra), one knows old age, thinking, "These teeth have been afflicted by old age." This is like seeing a cow's head or similar objects tied at a place where there is water and thereby knowing the existence of water below.
12:
Furthermore, old age is again of two kinds: old age without interruption (avīcijarā) and old age with interruption (savīcijarā). Among these two, in gems, gold, silver, coral, the moon, the sun, and so on; in living beings during periods such as the ten-year stages; and in inanimate objects such as flowers, fruits, and sprouts, the distinctions in appearance and so on occurring at intervals are difficult to know; therefore, that old age is called avīcijarā (old age without interval). Apart from those, in other aforementioned things, the distinctions in appearance and so on occurring at intervals are easy to know; therefore, that old age should be understood as savīcijarā (old age with intervals). From here on, the terms such as "tesaṃ tesaṃ" should be understood in the same manner as previously stated. In the terms such as "cuti cavanatā", "cuti" is stated by way of the aggregates that have the nature of passing away, and it is a general term common to all one-constituent, four-constituent, and five-constituent aggregates. By the abstract term "cavanatā", the characteristic is shown. By the term "bhedo", the destruction (reaching the moment of dissolution) of the passing-away aggregates is shown. By the term "antaradhānaṃ", it is shown that the destroyed passing-away aggregates have no place of remaining by any means, just as not even a shard remains of a broken pot. "Maccu maraṇaṃ" is death known as maccu; by that term, [the Buddha] excludes death by extirpation (samucchedamaraṇa) and so on. "Kāla" (Time) means the end, and the making of that end is called "kālakiriyā". Thus, by that term, death is shown according to worldly convention (lokasammuti).

Now, to show it in the ultimate sense (paramattha), [the Buddha] said the words beginning with "khandhānaṃ bhedo" (the breaking up of the aggregates). In the ultimate sense, only the aggregates break up; no being as such dies. However, while the aggregates are breaking up, there is the conventional expression in the world that "a being is dying," and when they have broken up, that "he is dead." Here, the breaking up of the aggregates should be understood by way of the four-constituent and five-constituent existences. The laying down of the carcass should be understood by way of the one-constituent existence. The breaking up of the aggregates should be understood by way of the four-constituent existence, and the laying down of the carcass by way of the remaining two. Why? Because in both [types of] existence, the carcass called the material body (rūpakāya) is clearly present. Alternatively, since in the heavens such as the Cātumahārājikā, the aggregates simply break up and nothing is laid down, the breaking up of the aggregates should be understood by way of those devas. Since in the human realm and so on there is the laying down of the carcass, the laying down of the carcass should be understood by way of those humans. Here, the meaning should be understood such that death is called "kaḷevarassa nikkhepo" because it is the cause for laying down the carcass. Thus, taking both "this old age and this death" together, it is called "old age and death" (jarāmaraṇa).
13:
In the description of birth (jāti-niddesa), among the words such as "jāti" and "sañjāti," it is called "jāti" because of the sense of being born. That "jāti" is appropriate by way of beings whose sense bases (āyatana) are not yet complete. It is called "sañjāti" because of the sense of being born completely. That "sañjāti" is appropriate by way of beings whose sense bases are complete. It is called "okkanti" because of the sense of descending. That "okkanti" is appropriate by way of egg-born (aṇḍaja) and womb-born (jalābuja) beings. Indeed, those egg-born and womb-born beings take rebirth as if they were descending into and entering an egg-shell or a womb. It is called "abhinibbatti" because of the sense of distinct production. That "abhinibbatti" is appropriate by way of moisture-born (saṃsedaja) and spontaneously born (opapātika) beings. Indeed, those moisture-born and spontaneously born beings arise only by becoming manifest. This is first the conventional teaching (vohāra-desanā).

Now, the ultimate teaching (paramattha-desanā) will be shown. In the ultimate sense, only the aggregates (khandhā) become manifest; there is no "being." In the manifestation of those aggregates, by the word "khandhānaṃ," the inclusion of one aggregate in one-constituent existence (ekavokāra-bhava), four aggregates in four-constituent existence (catuvokāra-bhava), and five aggregates in five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava) should be understood. "Pātubhāvo" means arising (uppatti). In this Pali text "āyatanānaṃ," the inclusion by way of the sense bases arising in various existences should be understood. "Paṭilābho" is the manifestation within the continuity of the aggregates. Those sense bases are said to be "acquired" only when they become manifest. With the phrase, "Bhikkhus, this is called birth," He makes the conclusion of birth taught by way of convention and by way of the ultimate sense.

In the description of existence (bhava-niddesa), "kāmabhava" (sensual existence) is of two kinds: kamma-bhava (existence as action) and upapatti-bhava (existence as rebirth). Of these two, only the kamma that leads to the sensual realm is called kamma-bhava. Because that kamma is the cause of rebirth-existence in that sensual realm, it is called "bhava" (existence) by the name of its fruit, as in such Pali passages as "The arising of Buddhas is pleasant" and "The accumulation of evil is painful." Upapatti-bhava is the group of five clung-to aggregates (upādinnakkhandhā) produced by that kamma. That upapatti-bhava is called "bhava" because it occurs in that sensual realm. In every way, both this kamma and rebirth are called "kāmabhava" here. In the cases of fine-material existence (rūpabhava) and immaterial existence (arūpabhava), it should be understood in the same way.

In the description of clinging (upādāna-niddesa), among the words such as "kāmupādānaṃ," [beings] cling to the objects of sensuality (vatthu-kāma) by means of this defilement of sensuality (kilesa-kāma), or it (the defilement) itself clings to those objects; therefore, it is called kāmupādāna (clinging to sensuality). It is called kāmupādāna because it is both sensuality and clinging. Clinging (upādāna) means a firm grasping. Here, the prefix "upa" has the sense of "firmly," as in such words as upāyāsa (despair) and upakaṭṭha (near). This is a name for the lust (rāga) for the five cords of sensual pleasure. This is just a brief explanation here. In detail, it should be understood according to the method taught: "Therein, what is kāmupādāna? It is the sensual desire (kāmacchanda) for sensual pleasures."
14:
Likewise, that view is called diṭṭhi (view) and it is also called upādāna (clinging); thus it is called diṭṭhupādāna (clinging to views). Alternatively, it clings to views, or by means of this [clinging], they cling to views; thus it is called diṭṭhupādāna. In fact, a subsequent view clings to a preceding view, and by that [subsequent] view, they cling to the view. As it is said: "The self and the world are eternal; only this is true, everything else is futile," and so forth (M. Ni. 3.27). This term diṭṭhupādāna is a designation for all wrong views, excluding sīlabbatupādāna (clinging to rules and observances) and attavādupādāna (clinging to the doctrine of self). This is the summary here; for the detailed explanation, it should be understood in the manner stated (in Dh. Sa. 1221): "Therein, what is diṭṭhupādāna? There is no fruit of giving," and so forth.

Likewise, by means of this, they cling to rules and observances (sīlabbata), or it itself clings to that; or it is both sīlabbata and upādāna, thus it is called sīlabbatupādāna. Indeed, because of the adherence to the practices of cows and the observances of cows, etc., thinking "Purification comes through this," they themselves become clingings. This is the summary here; for the detailed explanation, it should be understood in the manner stated: "Therein, what is sīlabbatupādāna? The view of recluses and brahmins outside of this [Dispensation] that purification comes through rules and observances."

Now, they speak by means of this, thus it is vāda (doctrine); they cling by means of this, thus it is upādāna (clinging). What do they speak of or cling to? The self (attā). The doctrine of or clinging to the self is attavādupādāna. Or, because they cling to the mere doctrine of self as "self" by means of this [clinging], it is called attavādupādāna. This is a designation for the identity view (sakkāyadiṭṭhi) consisting of twenty bases. This is the summary here; for the detailed explanation, it should be understood in the manner stated: "Therein, what is attavādupādāna? Here, an uninstructed worldling who has no regard for the Noble Ones..."

In the description of craving (taṇhā), the names rūpa-taṇhā (craving for visible objects) ...pe... dhamma-taṇhā (craving for mental objects) are names given based on the object which is like a father, just as in the cases of "son of a merchant" or "son of a brahmin," where the name is given based on the father for the craving that arises through the impulsion process (javana-vīthi) at the eye-door and so forth. Here, craving that has a visible object as its object, or craving for a visible object, is rūpa-taṇhā. When that rūpa-taṇhā arises enjoying the visible object in the form of sensual lust, it is called kāma-taṇhā (craving for sensual pleasures). When it arises enjoying it in the form of lust accompanied by the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi) as "The visible object is permanent, stable, and eternal," it is called bhava-taṇhā (craving for existence). When it arises enjoying it in the form of lust accompanied by the annihilationist view (uccheda-diṭṭhi) as "The visible object is cut off, destroyed, and does not exist after death," it is called vibhava-taṇhā (craving for non-existence). Thus, rūpa-taṇhā is of three kinds. Just as rūpa-taṇhā is, so too are sadda-taṇhā (craving for sounds) and the others, each being of three kinds. Thus, there are eighteen varieties of craving (taṇhā-vicarita). There are eighteen such varieties regarding internal visible objects, etc., and eighteen regarding external visible objects, etc., making thirty-six. Thus, there are thirty-six in the past, thirty-six in the future,
15:
There are 36 modes of craving in the present; thus, there are 108 modes of craving (taṇhā-vicarita). Based on the five aggregates occurring within one's own continuity, there are 18 modes of craving dependent on internal forms, etc., such as "I am," "I am such," and so forth. Based on the five aggregates occurring in the continuity of others, there are 18 modes of craving dependent on external forms, etc., such as "By this I am," "By this I am such," and so forth. Thus, there are 36 modes. In this way, there are 108 modes of craving due to 36 in the past, 36 in the future, and 36 in the present. Furthermore, when summarized, there are six groups of craving (taṇhā-kāya) regarding the six objects such as visible forms, and there are also three types of craving such as craving for sense-pleasures (kāma-taṇhā).

Thus—

## The wise should understand the detailed exposition (niddesa) by way of its meaning,
## and also understand craving by way of its summary.

In the exposition of feeling (vedanā-niddesa), 'groups of feeling' (vedanā-kāya) refers to the collection of feelings. In the statement, 'feeling born of eye-contact... feeling born of mind-contact,' it is stated in the Vibhaṅga: "Feeling born of eye-contact may be wholesome, may be unwholesome, or may be indeterminate." Thus, for the wholesome, unwholesome, and indeterminate feelings arising at the eye-door, etc., the name is given based on the physical base (vatthu), which is like a mother, just as names like "Sāriputta" (son of Sārī) and "Mantāṇiputta" (son of Mantāṇī) are given based on the mother. The grammatical derivation (viggaha) here is: feeling that arises because of eye-contact is 'feeling born of eye-contact' (cakkhu-samphassaja-vedanā). This method applies in all cases. This is the comprehensive explanation here. However, by way of result (vipāka), feeling should be understood as being associated with the two eye-consciousnesses, the two mind-elements, and the three mind-consciousness-elements at the eye-door. This same method applies to the ear-door, etc. At the mind-door, it is only associated with the mind-consciousness-element.

In the exposition of contact (phassa-niddesa), 'eye-contact' (cakkhu-samphassa) means contact at the eye. This method applies in all cases. By the phrase 'eye-contact... body-contact,' the ten types of contact dependent on the five physical bases, which are wholesome results and unwholesome results, are spoken of. By the term 'mind-contact' (mano-samphassa), the contacts associated with the remaining 22 mundane resultant consciousnesses are meant.

In the exposition of the six sense bases (saḷāyatana-niddesa), what should be said regarding 'eye-base' (cakkhāyatana), etc., has already been stated in the exposition of the aggregates (khandha-niddesa) and the exposition of the bases (āyatana-niddesa) in the Visuddhimagga.
16:
In the exposition of mentality-and-materiality (nāmarūpa-niddesa), that which has the characteristic of bending [towards an object] is called mentality (nāma). That which has the characteristic of being deformed (ruppana) is called materiality (rūpa). In the analysis of mentality and materiality, the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha) is to be understood by the term 'feeling' (vedanā); the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha) by the term 'perception' (saññā); and the aggregate of formations (saṅkhārakkhandha) by the terms 'volition' (cetanā), 'contact' (phassa), and 'attention' (manasikāra). Although there are indeed other states included in the aggregate of formations besides volition, contact, and attention, the aggregate of formations is shown here by way of these three because they exist even in the weakest types of consciousness. In the phrase "cattāro ca mahābhūtā" (and the four great essentials), 'cattāro' is a numerical delimitation. 'Mahābhūtā' is a designation for earth, water, fire, and air. The reason why these elements are called 'great essentials' and all other methods of determination have already been stated in the exposition of the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha-niddesa) in the Visuddhimagga. In the phrase "catunnñca mahābhūtānaṃ upādāya," the term 'catunnaṃ' is a genitive case used in the sense of the accusative, meaning "the four great essentials." 'Upādāya' means having clung to, or having taken. Some teachers also say it means "dependent on." Here, the word 'vattamānaṃ' (existing) is an ellipsis (pāṭhasesa). Alternatively, the genitive case 'catunnaṃ mahābhūtānaṃ' is used in the sense of a group, and the meaning should be understood as "materiality existing dependent on the group of the four great essentials." Thus, in every way, the four great essentials such as earth, etc., and the twenty-three kinds of materiality mentioned in the Abhidhamma Pāḷi by way of divisions such as the eye-base (cakkhāyatana), etc., which exist dependent on the four great essentials—all that should be understood as 'materiality' (rūpa).

In the exposition of consciousness (viññāṇa-niddesa), 'eye-consciousness' (cakkhu-viññāṇa) is so called because it is consciousness in the eye, or consciousness born from the eye. The same applies to ear, nose, tongue, and body consciousness. As for the other, 'mind-consciousness' (mano-viññāṇa) is so called because the mind (mano) itself is the consciousness. This is a designation for the resultant consciousness of the three planes (tebhūmaka-vipāka-citta), excluding the ten-fold five-sense consciousness.

In the exposition of formations (saṅkhāra-niddesa), formation (saṅkhāra) has the characteristic of processing (abhisaṅkharaṇa). In its analysis, 'bodily formation' (kāyasaṅkhāra) is the formation proceeding from the body. This is a designation for the twenty bodily volitions (kāyasañcetanā), consisting of eight sense-sphere wholesome volitions and twelve unwholesome volitions, which proceed by way of producing bodily intimation (kāyaviññatti) at the bodily door. 'Verbal formation' (vacīsaṅkhāra) is the formation proceeding from speech. This is a designation for the twenty verbal volitions (vacīsañcetanā) which proceed by way of producing verbal intimation (vacīviññatti) at the verbal door. 'Mental formation' (cittasaṅkhāra) is the formation proceeding from the mind. This is a designation for the twenty-nine mental volitions (manosañcetanā) by way of mundane wholesome and unwholesome states, which proceed for one who sits in seclusion and thinks without producing movement at the bodily or verbal doors.
17:
In the exposition of ignorance (avijjāniddesa), "dukkhe aññāṇaṃ" means ignorance regarding the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca), and it is a synonym for delusion (moha). In the same way, it should be understood in phrases such as "dukkhasamudaye aññāṇaṃ" (ignorance regarding the origin of suffering). There, ignorance regarding the Truth of Suffering should be understood through four reasons: (1) inclusion within, (2) being the basis (vatthu), (3) being the object (ārammaṇa), and (4) concealment (paṭicchādana).

Indeed, because it is included within the Truth of Suffering, it is "included within" suffering. The Truth of Suffering is the "basis" (vatthu) for that ignorance by way of being a support-condition (nissaya-paccaya), and it is the "object" (ārammaṇa) by way of being an object-condition (ārammaṇa-paccaya). That ignorance "conceals" the Truth of Suffering by preventing the penetration (paṭivedha) of its true nature and by not allowing the occurrence of knowledge (ñāṇa) regarding this Truth of Suffering.

Ignorance regarding the Truth of the Origin of Suffering should be understood through three reasons: being the basis, being the object, and concealment. Ignorance regarding the Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path should be understood through only one reason: concealment. This is because ignorance conceals them by preventing the penetration of the true nature of the Truth of Cessation and the Truth of the Path, and by not allowing the occurrence of knowledge regarding those Truths. However, that ignorance is not "included within" those two Truths because it is not contained in them. Those two Truths are not the "basis" (vatthu) for that ignorance because they do not arise together (asahajāta). They are not the "object" (ārammaṇa) because ignorance does not arise taking them as objects. This is because the latter two Truths (Cessation and Path) are profound and difficult to see; thus, ignorance, which is like blindness, cannot occur there. The former two Truths (Suffering and Origin), however, are profound because their intrinsic nature is difficult to see; ignorance occurs there by way of perverted perception (vipallāsa-gāha).

Furthermore, by the term "dukkhe", ignorance is shown through inclusion, basis, object, and function (kicca). By the term "dukkhasamudaye", it is shown through basis, object, and function. By the term "dukkha-nirodhe dukkha-nirodha-gāminiyā paṭipadāya", it is shown through function. Without distinction, it should be understood that by the term "aññāṇa", ignorance is described by its intrinsic nature (sabhāva).

"Iti kho bhikkhave" means "Thus, O monks." "Nirodho hoti" means "non-arising (anuppāda) occurs." Alternatively, in this sutta, Nibbāna is taught by all the terms for "nirodha". Because various phenomena cease depending on Nibbāna, Nibbāna is called the "cessation" (nirodha) of those phenomena. Thus, the Blessed One, while teaching the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) with twelve terms in this sutta, concluded the teaching with the peak of Arahantship. At the conclusion of the teaching, five hundred monks were established in Arahantship.

## The Vibhaṅga Sutta, the second.
18:
## ၃။ ပဋိပဒါသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ

In the third sutta, "micchāpaṭipadā" (wrong practice) refers first to the practice that does not lead out of the round of suffering (aniyyanika-paṭipadā). One might ask: "There are meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) and imperturbable formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra) that have ignorance as their condition; how can these be wrong practice?" It is because they are the "head of the round" (vaṭṭasīsa). Any merit performed by yearning for the "round" (vaṭṭa) known as the three realms of existence—even the attainment of the five higher powers or the eight meditative attainments—all of that is wrong practice because it belongs to the side of the round and is the head of the round. However, any merit performed by yearning for Nibbāna, which is the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa)—even a gift of gruel as small as a ladleful or a gift of a handful of vegetables—all of that is right practice (sammāpaṭipadā) because it belongs to the side of cessation, depends on cessation, and has the quality of leading to cessation. Whether it be a small merit like a gift of a handful of vegetables or a great merit like the gift of Velāma, if it is wrongly placed by way of depending on the round and yearning for worldly prosperity (vaṭṭasampatti), it can only bring about the round and not the cessation of the round. But if it is correctly placed by way of the cessation of the round, yearning for Nibbāna with the thought, "May this gift of mine lead to the destruction of the taints (āsavakkhaya)," it is indeed capable of granting Arahantship, the knowledge of a Paccekabuddha, or Omniscient Knowledge; it does not end until it reaches Arahantship. Thus, it should be understood that wrong practice is taught by way of the forward order (anuloma) and right practice by way of the reverse order (paṭiloma).

In this sutta, one might ask: "The question was about practice, but Nibbāna was analyzed, and in the conclusion, practice was again mentioned. Nibbāna is not called 'practice'; that name belongs only to the four paths along with insight. Therefore, the analysis of terms (padabhājanī) does not agree with the question and the conclusion." It is not that it does not agree; it does agree. Why? Because the practice (the cause) is shown by way of the fruit (the result). In this sutta, the practice is shown by the fruit. The meaning here is: "That Nibbāna, called cessation, which is the fruit of a certain practice—'through the total fading away and cessation of ignorance, formations cease'—that practice, O monks, is called right practice." In this context, in the phrase "asesavirāganirodhā", "virāga" (fading away) is a synonym for "nirodha" (cessation); the meaning is "through total fading away, total cessation." Alternatively, this analysis of terms is stated to show the Path known as "virāga" through which total cessation occurs. In this way, the practice is analyzed along with its efficacy. Thus, in this sutta also, only the round and the cessation of the round are taught. The third sutta is finished.
19:
## 4. Commentary on the Vipassī Sutta

In the fourth sutta, the meaning of the word 'Vipassī' should be understood as follows. It is said that when worldly people look at an object, their eyes blink (quiver) because the kamma-born visual sensitivity (kammaja-cakkhu-pasāda) produced by meager wholesome kamma is weak. However, for that Bodhisatta, there was no such blinking. Because the kamma-born visual sensitivity produced by powerful wholesome kamma was strong, he looked with unblinking eyes, just like the Tāvatiṃsa devas. Therefore, the Blessed One taught: "Monks, because Prince Vipassī looked without blinking, the name 'Vipassī, Vipassī' arose for him." (D. Ni. 2.40). The meaning here is: he sees clearly because he is free from the darkness produced by blinking at intervals, or he is called Vipassī because he sees with open eyes. In this regard, although all Bodhisattas in their final existence do not blink because their kamma-born visual sensitivity produced by powerful kamma is strong, only this Bodhisatta Vipassī received his name for this reason.

Alternatively, he is called Vipassī because he sees by investigating and discerning. The meaning is that he sees after careful consideration. It is said that one day, while his father, King Bandhuma, was sitting in the place of judgment deciding cases, they brought the adorned Great Man (Vipassī) and placed him on the King's lap. While the King was fondling the prince on his lap, the ministers judged unfairly, making the rightful owner the non-owner and the non-owner the owner. At that time, the Bodhisatta made a sound of displeasure. The King said, "Investigate why he makes such a sound." Upon investigation, seeing no other reason, they thought, "It must be because the case was poorly decided," and they restored the rightful owner to his status. Wanting to test if the prince did this knowingly, they again made the owner a non-owner. Again, the Bodhisatta made the same sound. Then the King said, "The Great Man knows," and from then on, he judged cases with heedfulness. Therefore, the Blessed One taught: "Monks, because Prince Vipassī discerned and understood matters through the right method, the name 'Vipassī, Vipassī' arose for him even more exceedingly." (D. Ni. 2.41).

'Bhagavato' means one who is endowed with the six glories. 'Arahato' is a name arising from his qualities: because he has killed the enemies such as greed, etc.; or because he has destroyed the spokes of the wheel of saṃsāra; or because he is worthy of receiving the four requisites. 'Sammāsambuddhassa' is because he has rightly, through the proper cause and by his own personal effort, realized the Four Truths without distortion. Previously, the knowledge that arises in the four paths is called 'Sammāsambodhi'. In the word 'Bodhisattassa', 'Bodhi' means the knowledge of the path of Arahantship and the knowledge of omniscience. It means a being who possesses that knowledge, or a person who has that wisdom. Indeed, from the time of making the initial aspiration at the feet of the Buddhas, that being is only a wise person, not a fool. Therefore, he is called a Bodhisatta. Alternatively, just as a mature lotus (paduma) that has risen above the water will certainly bloom when touched by the sun's rays...
20:
Sammā-sambodhi refers to the knowledge that arises in the four paths; it occurs even before that path-knowledge arises. In the phrase "while still a Bodhisatta," 'Bodhi' means knowledge (the knowledge of the path of Arahantship and the knowledge of omniscience). A being who possesses Bodhi-knowledge is a Bodhisatta. It means one who has knowledge, one who has wisdom, a wise person (paṇḍita). Indeed, from the time of making the initial aspiration (abhinīhāra) at the feet of previous Buddhas, that being is only a wise person, not a blind fool; therefore, he is called a Bodhisatta.

Alternatively, just as a mature lotus (paduma) that has risen above the water is called a "lotus about to bloom" because it will certainly bloom when touched by the sun's rays; in the same way, because he has received the prophecy (byākaraṇa) in the presence of the Buddhas, he will certainly fulfill the perfections (pāramīs) without hindrance and awaken (become a Buddha). Thus, in the sense of a "being who will awaken," he is also called a Bodhisatta. Furthermore, there is that Bodhi known as the knowledge of the four paths; because he exists aspiring for that Bodhi, he is also called a Bodhisatta in the sense of a "being intensely devoted to Bodhi."

Thus, by the power of the name arising from his qualities, "while still a Bodhisatta." "Kicchaṃ" means suffering. "Āpanno" means has reached or fallen into. The meaning is: "Alas, this world of beings has fallen into suffering; how strange it is!" The phrase "passes away and is reborn" is taught by way of successive death and rebirth. "Nissaraṇa" means Nibbāna. Because that Nibbāna is the escape from the suffering of aging and death, it is called the "escape" (nissaraṇa) from that aging and death. "Kudāssu nāma" means "at what time?".

"Yoniso manasikāra" means wise attention, or attention by way of means and cause. "Ahu paññāya abhisamayo" means there was a breakthrough or realization of the cause of aging and death together with wisdom that comprehends the cause of aging and death; it was a perfect union. The meaning is that he saw: "Aging and death occur with birth as condition." Alternatively, through wise attention and wisdom, there was a breakthrough (abhisamayo). The meaning is that there was a penetration of the cause of aging and death, thus: "When there is birth, there is aging and death." This method should be understood in all places.

"Iti hidaṃ" means "thus this [meaning]." With the words "Samudayo samudayo" (origin, origin), he points out the arising (samudaya) of the formations (saṅkhāra), etc., collectively in eleven places. "Pubbe ananussutesu" means "with ignorance as condition, the arising of formations occurs." Thus, in things (dhammas) not heard before from others in this life, or in the four Noble Truths (the eye of knowledge arose). The terms 'eye' (cakkhu), etc., are merely synonyms for knowledge (ñāṇa). Here, knowledge itself is called 'eye' (cakkhu) in the sense of seeing; 'knowledge' (ñāṇa) in the sense of knowing; 'wisdom' (paññā) in the sense of understanding specifically; 'true knowledge' (vijjā) in the sense of penetration; and 'light' (āloka) in the sense of illuminating.
21:
It is said thus. This [knowledge] should be understood as being pointed out by the Blessed One as a mixture of mundane and supramundane regarding the Four Noble Truths. In the section on cessation (nirodhavāra) as well, the meaning should be understood in this very same way. The fourth sutta is finished.

## 5–10. Commentary on the Sikhī Sutta and Others

5–10. In the fifth sutta and those following, the meaning of the words "Sikhissa, bhikkhave" and so on should be understood without connecting them as "Sikhissapi, bhikkhave." Why? Because they were not taught in a single sitting. For the Blessed One taught these suttas in various places. However, although taught in various places, the meaning is the same in all of them.

Indeed, to all Bodhisattas seated upon the seat of enlightenment (bodhipallaṅka), no other recluse, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā tells them: "In the past, Bodhisattas attained Buddhahood by contemplating the mode of conditions (paccayākāra), which is Dependent Origination." For example, just as when it rains at the beginning of an aeon, subsequent rainwater flows along the same path taken by the previous water, so too do subsequent Bodhisattas follow the very path taken by those previous Buddhas. It is taught in the seven suttas in succession that all Bodhisattas, having emerged from the fourth jhāna of mindfulness of breathing (ānāpānasati), apply insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) to the mode of conditions (paccayākāra), and by contemplating that Dependent Origination in forward and reverse order (anuloma-paṭiloma), they attain Buddhahood; this is called "Buddha-Vipassanā."

## The First Chapter: The Buddha Chapter (Buddhavagga)

## 2. The Chapter on Nutriment (Āhāravagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Āhāra Sutta

In the first sutta of the Āhāra Vagga, "nutriments" (āhārā) means supporting conditions (paccayā). For conditions are called nutriments because they bring (āharanti) their own results. In the passages such as "of beings (bhūtānaṃ) or of those seeking birth (sambhavesīnaṃ)," "beings" (bhūta) means those who are born or produced. "Those seeking birth" (sambhavesī) means those who seek or search for birth (jāti) or production.

In this regard, among the four types of birth (yoni), egg-born (aṇḍaja) and womb-born (jalābuja) beings are called "those seeking birth" (sambhavesī) as long as they have not yet broken the eggshell or the caul (membrane). Once they have broken the eggshell or the caul and emerged outside, they are called "beings" (bhūta). Moisture-born (saṃsedaja) and spontaneously born (opapātika) beings are called "those seeking birth" (sambhavesī) at the moment of the first rebirth-linking consciousness. From the second moment of consciousness onwards, they are called "beings" (bhūta). Alternatively, they are called "those seeking birth" (sambhavesī) as long as they remain in the posture in which they were born and have not yet reached another posture. After reaching another posture, they are called "beings" (bhūta).

Furthermore, "beings" (bhūta) means those who are born and fully produced. Those Arahants who are of the nature of being already produced and will not...
22:
...be reborn are called by this name (adhivacana). Because they seek a new birth, they are called "those seeking birth" (sambhavesī). This name "sambhavesī" is the designation for worldlings (puthujjanas) and learners (sekhas) who, because their fetters of existence (bhavasaṃyojana) have not yet been abandoned, will seek birth in the future as well. Thus, in every way, all beings are included by these two terms. The word "vā" (or) here has the sense of conjunction (sampinḍana). Therefore, the meaning should be understood as "of both those who have become beings and those seeking birth."

"For maintenance" (ṭhitiyā) means for the purpose of staying. "For support" (anuggahāya) means for the purpose of assistance. This is merely a difference in phrasing; the meaning of both words is the same. Alternatively, "for maintenance" (ṭhitiyā) means for the non-interruption of the states (dhamma) that have arisen for various beings by way of continuous succession. "For support" (anuggahāya) means for the arising of states that have not yet arisen. Both of these [terms] should be seen as connected to both [types of beings] thus: "for the maintenance and support of beings, and for the maintenance and support of those seeking birth."

"Edible food" (kabaḷīkārāhāra) means nutriment that is to be made into a bolus and swallowed. This is a designation for the nutritive essence (ojā) residing in substances such as boiled rice, junket, and so on. "Whether gross or subtle" (oḷāriko vā sukhumo vā) means it is called gross due to the grossness of the physical substance, and subtle due to its subtleness. In terms of its intrinsic nature, however, edible food is only subtle because it is included within subtle matter (sukhumatā-rūpa). Its grossness or subtleness according to the physical substance should be understood by way of relative comparison.

Compared to the food of crocodiles, the food of peacocks is subtle. It is said that crocodiles swallow stones, and those stones melt once they reach their stomachs. Peacocks eat creatures such as snakes and scorpions. Compared to the food of peacocks, the food of hyenas (taraccha) is subtle. It is said that they eat horns and bones that have been discarded for three years; those [horns and bones] become as soft as tubers just by being moistened with their saliva. Compared to the food of hyenas, the food of elephants is subtle. They eat various tree branches and so on. Compared to the food of elephants, the food of animals such as gayals (gavaya), gokannas, and deer is subtle. It is said that they eat various leaves and so on that have no essence. Compared to their food, the food of cattle is subtle. They eat moist and dry grass. Compared to their food, the food of rabbits is subtle. Compared to the food of rabbits, the food of birds is subtle. Compared to the food of birds, the food of border-dwellers is subtle. Compared to the food of birds, the food of border-dwellers is subtle. Compared to the food of border-dwellers, the food of village headmen...
23:
Nutriment is subtle. The nutriment of border-dwellers is subtler than that of birds. The nutriment of village headmen is subtler than that of border-dwellers. The nutriment of kings and great ministers is subtler than that of village headmen. Even subtler than the nutriment of those kings and great ministers is the nutriment of a wheel-turning monarch. The nutriment of earth-dwelling devas is subtler than that of a wheel-turning monarch. The nutriment of the devas of the Realm of the Four Great Kings is subtler than that of the earth-dwelling devas. In this manner, the nutriments should be understood in detail up to the devas of the Realm of Controlling Devas' Creations (Paranimmitavasavatti). The nutriment of those devas reaches the ultimate limit of subtlety.

In this matter, in a coarse substance, the nutritive essence (ojā) is scant and weak; in a subtle substance, the nutritive essence is powerful. This is true: a person who drinks just a cup of gruel (yāgu) feels hungry again in a moment and wishes to eat something else. However, by consuming just a small measure (about a spoonful) of the finest clarified butter (sappi) and such, one has no desire to eat for the rest of the day. That substance can dispel the danger known as kamma-born heat (kammaja-tejo), but it is not able to sustain the material body (rūpakāya). The nutritive essence (ojā), however, can sustain the material body but cannot dispel the danger. Only when the substance and the nutritive essence are combined can they both dispel the danger and sustain the material body.

'Contact is the second' means that the six kinds of contact, such as eye-contact (cakkhu-samphassa), should be understood as the second nutriment among these four nutriments. Since this is merely the sequence of the teaching (desanā-naya), one should not search for a reason why it is specifically the second or the third. 'Mental volition' (manosañcetanā) refers to volition (cetanā) itself. 'Consciousness' (viññāṇa) refers to the mind (citta). Thus, in this context, the Blessed One showed the four nutriments by grouping them together as clung-to (upādiṇṇaka) and not clung-to (anupādiṇṇaka). Edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) can be both clung-to and not clung-to; likewise for contact and the others. Among them, clung-to edible food should be understood by way of frogs and such swallowed by snakes and the like. Frogs swallowed by snakes remain alive for a short time even after reaching the stomach. As long as those frogs remain in the category of the clung-to, they do not fulfill the function of nutriment. Only when they perish and remain in the category of the not clung-to do they fulfill the function of nutriment. Even at the time of perishing, they are still called clung-to nutriment. However, the teachers do not favor this view, and rejecting it in the Commentary itself, it is said: For these beings, whether they eat or not, there is what is called kamma-born nutritive essence (kammaja-ojā) that arises together with the rebirth-consciousness. That kamma-born nutritive essence sustains the continuity (santati) for up to seven days. This kamma-born nutritive essence itself should be understood as clung-to edible food. Furthermore, clung-to contact and the others should be understood by way of the resultants (vipāka) occurring in the three planes. Not clung-to contact and the others should be understood by way of the wholesome, unwholesome, and functional (kiriya) states occurring in the three planes. Supramundane (lokuttara) contacts are preached as nutriment by way of a figurative method. In this matter, an analytical teacher asks: 'If the meaning of support (paccaya) is the meaning of nutriment (āhāra), why are only these four taught when there are other conditions (paccaya) for beings?' The answer is: Because they are special causes for the continuity of the internal aggregates (attabhāva-khandha-santati). Edible food is the special cause for the material body (rūpakāya) of beings who consume edible food. Contact is the special cause for feeling (vedanā) in the mental body (nāmakāya). Mental volition is the special cause for consciousness (viññāṇa).
24:
This kamma-born nutritive essence (kammaja-ojā) arising with the rebirth-consciousness should be understood as clung-to (upādiṇṇaka) edible food. Furthermore, clung-to contact and the others should be understood by way of the resultants (vipāka) occurring in the three planes. Not clung-to contact and the others should be understood by way of the wholesome, unwholesome, and functional (kiriya) states occurring in the three planes. Supramundane (lokuttara) contacts should be understood as being taught as nutriment by way of a figurative method.

Regarding the teaching of these four nutriments, an analytical teacher asks: 'If the meaning of support (paccaya) is indeed the nature of nutriment (āhāra), then why are only these four things taught when there are other conditions besides contact and so forth for beings?' To provide the answer: These four things alone are taught because they are special causes for the continuity of the aggregates that constitute the individual (attabhāva). To clarify: Edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) is the special cause for the material body (rūpakāya) of beings who consume edible food. Contact (phassa) is the special cause for feeling (vedanā) in the mental body (nāmakāya). Mental volition (manosañcetanā) is the special cause for consciousness (viññāṇa). Consciousness (viññāṇa) is the special cause for mind-and-matter (nāmarūpa). The Blessed One taught thus: 'Bhikkhus, this body consisting of mind and matter has nutriment as its cause; it stands depending on nutriment; without nutriment, it cannot stand. Likewise, feeling stands due to the cause of contact; consciousness stands due to the cause of formations (saṅkhāra); mind-and-matter stands due to the cause of consciousness.'

Among these four nutriments, which state is called nutriment, and what does it bring? To answer: Edible food brings material qualities of which nutritive essence is the eighth (ojāṭṭhamaka-rūpa). The nutriment of contact brings the three kinds of feeling. The nutriment of mental volition brings the three kinds of existence (bhava). The nutriment of consciousness brings rebirth mind-and-matter.

How does it bring them? Edible food, as soon as it is placed in the mouth, produces eight material qualities. Specifically, when it is chewed fine by the teeth and swallowed, each and every grain of rice produces eight material qualities. Thus, edible food brings material qualities of which nutritive essence is the eighth. As for the nutriment of contact, when contact that produces pleasant feeling arises, it brings pleasant feeling. Contact that produces painful feeling brings painful feeling. Contact that produces neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling brings neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling. Thus, in every way, the nutriment of contact brings the three kinds of feeling.

Regarding the nutriment of mental volition, kamma that leads to the sense-sphere existence brings sense-sphere existence (kāmabhava). Kammas that lead to fine-material or immaterial existence bring those respective existences. Thus, in every way, the nutriment of mental volition brings the three kinds of existence.

The nutriment of consciousness is said to bring, by way of conditions such as conascence (sahajāta), the three mental aggregates associated with that rebirth-consciousness at the moment of rebirth, as well as the thirty kamma-born material qualities that arise by way of the three continuities. Thus, the nutriment of consciousness should be understood to bring rebirth mind-and-matter.

In this context, when it is said 'mental volition brings the three kinds of existence,' it refers only to wholesome and unwholesome volitions that are associated with the taints (sāsava).
25: When it is said, "Consciousness brings rebirth mentality-materiality," it refers specifically to rebirth-consciousness. More specifically, these states should be understood as "nutriments" (āhāra) because they bring along states that are associated with and originated by them. Among these four nutriments, edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) fulfills the function of nutriment by providing support. Contact (phassa) fulfills it by touching, mental volition (manosañcetanā) by striving, and consciousness (viññāṇa) by cognizing. How? Edible food, by supporting the physical body, enables the persistence of beings. This body, though born of kamma, being supported by edible food, can last for ten years, a hundred years, or as long as its life-span allows. For example, just as a child, though born of a mother, lasts a long time when nourished by a nurse with milk and so on; or just as a house supported by a prop lasts a long time. It has also been said: "Great King, just as a house about to lean and fall does not fall when supported by another piece of wood; even so, Great King, this body is sustained by nutriment and persists depending on nutriment." Thus, edible food fulfills the function of nutriment by providing support. Even while doing so, edible food is the condition for two types of material continuity: that which is originated by nutriment and that which is clung-to (upādiṇṇaka) [born of kamma]. It is a condition by way of maintaining kamma-born matter and by way of producing nutriment-originated matter. Contact, however, enables the persistence of beings by producing feelings such as pleasure through the mere touching of an object that is the basis for such feelings. Mental volition enables the persistence of beings because it accomplishes the root of existence through striving by way of wholesome and unwholesome kamma. Consciousness enables the persistence of beings by producing mentality-materiality through the act of cognizing. In these nutriments that fulfill their functions through support and so on, four dangers should be seen. They are: in edible food, attachment (nikanti) itself is the danger; in contact, approaching (upagamana) is the danger; in mental volition, striving (āyūhana) is the danger; and in consciousness, falling into (abhinipāta) is the danger. Why? In edible food...
26:
Beings, having developed attachment [to edible food] and being oppressed by cold and so on, for the sake of food, engage in arts such as finger-calculation (muddā) and arithmetic (gaṇanā), thereby undergoing immeasurable suffering. Some, even after having gone forth in this Dispensation, seek food through wrong livelihood (anesanā) such as practicing medicine, and thus become blameworthy in this present life. In the future life as well, as stated in the Lakkhaṇa Saṃyutta: "His outer robe (saṅghāṭi) also burns, blazes, and glows," they become ascetic-ghosts (samaṇapeta). For this reason, it should be understood that attachment itself is the danger in edible food.

Those who indulge in contact, being delighted by it, commit offenses against the wives and property of others that are guarded and protected. The owners of the property seize them along with the stolen goods, cut them into pieces, and discard them on a rubbish heap, or hand them over to the king. Then the king subjects them to various forms of torture. After the breakup of the body, they can only expect a miserable destination (duggati). Thus, all dangers, both in the present life and in the future life, which are rooted in the delight of contact, come upon them. For this reason, it should be understood that approaching itself is the danger in the nutriment of contact.

In the striving for wholesome and unwholesome kamma, all dangers occurring in the three realms of existence, which have that striving as their root, come upon them. For this reason, it should be understood that striving itself is the danger in the nutriment of mental volition.

Rebirth-consciousness also arises in whatever place it falls into, taking up rebirth mentality-materiality in that very place. When that mentality-materiality has arisen, all dangers arise because they are rooted in that mentality-materiality. For this reason, it should be understood that falling into [a new existence] itself is the danger in the nutriment of consciousness.

In the terms "originating from what" (kiṃnidāna) and so on, all terms such as nidāna are synonyms for "cause" (kāraṇa). A cause is called nidāna because it delivers the result, as if saying, "Here, take this." Because the result arises, is born, and originates from that cause, it is called samudaya, jāti, and pabhava. Here is the meaning of the terms: "What is the cause (nidāna) of these?" thus they are kiṃnidāna. "What is the origin (samudaya) of these?" thus they are kiṃသမုဒယာ. "What is the birth (jāti) of these?" thus they are kiṃjātika. "What is the source (pabhava) of these?" thus they are kiṃpabhava. Because craving (taṇhā) is the cause, origin, birth, and source of those nutriments in the sense already stated, the Blessed One said: "Craving is the cause" (taṇhānidāna) and so on.
27:
That cause is called origin (samudaya), birth (jāti), and source (pabhava). Therefore, the Blessed One said, "Having craving as their source," and so forth. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all instances.

In this context, regarding the statement "These four nutriments have craving as their source," it should be understood as the source by way of the craving that occurred in the past life for the nutriments known as the personality (attabhāva), starting from the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi). How is this to be understood? At the moment of rebirth-linking, for beings with complete sense bases, there is nutritive essence (ojā) produced within the kamma-born matter (kammaja-rūpa) by way of the seven continuities (santati); for other beings with incomplete sense bases, it exists by way of fewer continuities than those seven. This kamma-born nutritive essence is called edible food (kabalīkārāhāra) which is clung-to (upādiṇṇaka) and has craving as its source. Furthermore, the contact (phassa) and volition (cetanā) associated with the rebirth-linking consciousness, as well as the rebirth-linking consciousness (viññāṇa) itself—these states are called the clung-to nutriments of contact, mental volition, and consciousness, which have craving as their source. Thus, the nutriments occurring at the moment of rebirth-linking, which have past craving as their source, should be understood. Just as the nutriments occurring at the time of rebirth-linking are understood, so too should the nutriments occurring after that, starting from the moment of the first life-continuum consciousness (bhavaṅga), be understood.

Because the Blessed One knows not only the source of the nutriments, but also the source of the craving that is the cause of the nutriments, and the source of feeling (vedanā) and so forth which are the causes of that craving, He showed the round of suffering (vaṭṭa) and the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) by way of the method beginning with, "Monks, what is the source of this craving?" In this instance, the Blessed One gave a teaching directed toward the past and showed the round of suffering by way of the past. How? This personality (attabhāva) is taken by way of nutriment.

Craving (taṇhā) is the kamma that produces this personality. Feeling, contact, the six sense bases, name-and-form, and consciousness are mentioned to show the personality in which one stays and exerts kamma. Ignorance (avijjā) and formations (saṅkhāra) are mentioned to show the kamma that produces that personality.
