Thus, the personality is shown in two places, and the kamma that produces that personality is shown in two places. In this way, by showing both kamma and the result of kamma (vipāka) in brief, He gave a teaching directed toward the past and showed the round of suffering by way of the past.

In that regard, this teaching should not be regarded as incomplete because it does not show the future. Rather, it should be regarded as complete by way of the method (naya). For example, a man with vision, seeing a crocodile lying on the surface of the water and looking at its upper part, might see the neck; looking further down, the back; and at the end, the base of the tail. But when looking at the belly below, he might not see the tip of the tail in the water or the four limbs. He does not, on that account, conclude that "the crocodile is incomplete"; rather, he understands it as complete by way of the method. This meaning should be understood in the same way.
28:
The round of existence (vaṭṭa) occurring in the three planes is like a crocodile lying on the surface of the water. The practitioner (yogāvacara) is like a man with vision standing on the bank. The time when the crocodile is seen on the surface of the water by that man is like the time when this personality (attabhāva) is seen by the yogi by way of nutriment. The time when the neck and so forth are seen further up is like the time when the craving (taṇhā) that produces this personality is seen. The time when the back is seen is like the time when that personality, in which the kamma known as craving was performed, is seen by way of feeling (vedanā) and so forth. The time when the base of the tail is seen is like the time when ignorance (avijjā) and formations (saṅkhāra), which produce that personality, are seen. Just as when looking at the belly below, even though the tip of the tail and the four limbs are not seen, one does not conclude that "the crocodile is incomplete" but understands it as complete by way of the method; so too, wherever a link of the round of causal conditions (paccaya-vaṭṭa) does not appear directly in the Pāḷi text, one should not conclude that "the teaching is incomplete" but should understand it as complete by way of the method. Among those links of Dependent Origination, there is one connection (sandhi) between nutriment and craving, one between craving and feeling, and one between consciousness and formations. Thus, the round of existence is shown with three connections and four groups (saṅkhepa). The first discourse is finished.

## 2. Moḷiyaphaggunasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second discourse, the Blessed One concluded the teaching at this very point: "or for the assistance of those seeking birth (sambhavesīnaṃ)." Why? Because a person of wrong views was sitting there. In that assembly, a monk named Moḷiyaphagguna, who held wrong views, was sitting. Then the Teacher thought, "This monk will stand up and ask Me a question, and then I will answer him." Thus, He concluded the teaching to give an opportunity for questioning. In the name "Moḷiyaphagguna," the word "moḷi" refers to a topknot (cūḷā). As it is said:

"Having cut the topknot scented with excellent perfume,
The Bull of the Sakyas threw it into the sky;
With a magnificent jeweled basket, Vāsava,
The thousand-eyed one, received it upon his head."

That topknot was very large during his time as a layman. Because of that, the name "Moḷiyaphagguna" arose for him. Even when he had gone forth, they recognized him by that same name. The words "He said this" (etadavoca) connect the sequence of the teaching, as he asked: "Venerable Sir, who consumes the nutriment of consciousness?" The meaning of those words should be understood as: "Venerable Sir, what person eats or consumes this nutriment of consciousness?"
29:
He spoke the words, "He consumes the nutriment of consciousness." The meaning of those words is: "Venerable Sir, who is it that chews or consumes this nutriment of consciousness?"

Why does this monk ask only about this nutriment of consciousness without asking about the other three nutriments? It is because of the view, "I know." He sees people making large morsels and eating edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra), so he has the view that he knows that nutriment. Having seen creatures such as partridges, quails, peacocks, and chickens being sustained by the mother's touch, he has the view that "these creatures are sustained by the nutriment of contact (phassāhāra)." Turtles, in their season, come out of the great ocean, lay their eggs in the sand on the shore, cover them with sand, and return to the great ocean. Those eggs do not rot due to the power of the mother's constant mindfulness. He has the view that those young turtles are sustained by the nutriment of mental volition (manosañcetanāhāra). 

Although the Venerable Moliya Phagguna holds this view, he does not ask this question based on this view alone. Indeed, one who holds wrong views is like a madman. Just as a madman, holding a basket, goes into the middle of the street and picks up cow dung, stones, excrement, or pieces of food—whether pleasant or unpleasant—and puts them in his basket; in the same way, one who holds wrong views asks questions whether they are appropriate or inappropriate. He should not be rebuked with "Why do you ask this?" but rather, the wrong grasp should be prohibited at every point of questioning. Therefore, the Blessed One did not say to him, "Why do you ask this?" but said, "The question is not fit," etc., in order to release him from the view he had grasped.

In that context, "no kallo" means inappropriate. "I do not say [he] consumes" means "I do not say that any being or person consumes." If I were to say, "He consumes," then in that case, your question would be appropriate. "Venerable Sir, for what state is the nutriment of consciousness a condition?"—this question alone is appropriate to ask the Blessed One. If asked in this way, the appropriate explanation is: "The nutriment of consciousness is a condition for the production of renewed existence in the future." Here, "nutriment of consciousness" (viññāṇāhāra) refers to the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhicitta). "The production of renewed existence in the future" refers to the name-and-form (nāmarūpa) that arises together with that very consciousness. "When that has come to be, the six sense bases [arise]" means that when name-and-form, which is called the production of renewed existence, has arisen, the six sense bases (saḷāyatana) come to be.
30:
In the passage "With the six sense bases as condition, contact [arises]," the Blessed One stopped the teaching here, wishing to give an opportunity for further questions. For one who holds wrong views is unable to generate a new question; rather, he grasps only what has been explained and asks about it. Therefore, the Blessed One gave him the opportunity. The meaning of this should be understood in the same way as explained for all the terms. 

Why does he not ask, "Venerable Sir, who becomes?" Because one who holds wrong views has the belief that "a being is something that truly exists and is born"; therefore, he does not ask "this [state]" which would contradict his own view. Furthermore, because it has been stated in many places as "with this as condition, this [arises]; with this as condition, this [arises]," he has reached an understanding [that it is merely a matter of conditions], and for that reason also he does not ask. The Teacher, knowing that "even though this monk asks much, he is not satisfied and asks only empty questions," from this point [clinging as condition, existence] made the teaching continuous and taught it. The words "But from the six [sense bases]" were spoken because the teaching had reached that point; taking that very point, he wished to continue the discourse. In this sutta, there is one link (sandhi) between consciousness and name-and-form, one link between feeling and craving, and one link between existence and birth. The second sutta [commentary] ends.

## 3. Samaṇabrāhmaṇasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, "ascetics or brahmins" (samaṇā vā brāhmaṇā vā) refers to those ascetics and brahmins outside the Dispensation who are unable to penetrate the Truths. In the passages beginning with "they do not understand aging and death," they do not know aging and death in terms of the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca). They do not know the origin of aging and death in terms of the Truth of the Origin (samudayasacca), as in "birth together with craving is the origin of aging and death." They do not know the cessation of aging and death in terms of the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasacca). They do not know the practice [leading to cessation] in terms of the Truth of the Path (maggasacca). 

They do not know birth in terms of the Truth of Suffering. They do not know the origin of birth in terms of the Truth of the Origin, as in "existence together with craving is the origin of birth." In this way, by connecting the origin with craving, the meaning should be understood in terms of the Four Truths in all instances. In the phrase "the goal of asceticism or the goal of brahminhood" (sāmaññatthaṃ vā brahmaññatthaṃ vā), the Noble Path (ariyamagga) is called both "asceticism" (sāmañña) and "brahminhood" (brahmañña). In both terms, "goal" (attha) should be understood as the Noble Fruit (ariyaphala). Thus, in this sutta, the Blessed One taught the Four Truths in eleven instances. The third sutta [commentary] ends.
31:
## 4. Dutiya-samaṇabrāhmaṇa Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta (the Second Sutta on Recluses and Brahmins), the teaching is expanded and delivered starting with "What are these things?" and so forth. It is taught as "They do not know these things," etc., according to the disposition (ajjhāsaya) of those individuals who are capable of penetrating the Four Noble Truths. The rest is exactly the same as the previous sutta. The fourth sutta is finished.

## 5. Kaccānagotta Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta (the Kaccānagotta Sutta), regarding the words "Right view, right view," whatever correct vision wise devas and humans speak of in various instances, the inquirer asks by summarizing all that right vision (sammā-dassana) into two terms. "Dvayanissito" means depending on two parts (of wrong views). By the word "yebhuyyena" (mostly), the Teacher shows the general mass of people, excluding the Noble Ones (Ariyas). "Atthitaṃ" (existence) refers to eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi). "Natthitaṃ" (non-existence) refers to annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi). In the term "loka-samudaya" (the origin of the world), "world" refers to the world of formations (saṅkhāra-loka), and it means its arising. "Sammapaññāya passato" means for one who sees with the path-wisdom (magga-paññā) accompanied by insight (vipassanā). "Yā loke natthitā" means that while the phenomena of mind and matter (nāma-rūpa) that have arisen according to causes in the world of formations are continuously manifest, the view of annihilation (uccheda-diṭṭhi) that "they do not exist" might arise, but for such a person, that view no longer occurs. "Loka-nirodha" means the destruction of formations. "Yā loke atthitā" means that while the phenomena of mind and matter that are perishing every moment in the world of formations are manifest, the view of eternalism (sassata-diṭṭhi) that "they exist" might arise, but for such a person, that view no longer occurs.

Alternatively, "loka-samudaya" refers to forward dependent origination (anuloma-paṭiccasamuppāda), and "loka-nirodha" refers to reverse dependent origination (paṭiloma-paṭiccasamuppāda). For one who sees forward dependent origination, because the causes such as ignorance (avijjā) do not cease, one sees that the effects such as formations (saṅkhāra) do not cease; thus, the view of annihilation "they do not exist" cannot occur. For one who sees reverse dependent origination, because the causes cease, one sees that the effects cease; thus, the view of eternalism "they exist" cannot occur. This is how the meaning should be understood here.

"Upayupādānābhinivesavinibandho" means being firmly bound by engagement (upaya), clinging (upādāna), and insistence (abhinivesa). In that phrase, "upaya" is of two kinds: craving-engagement (taṇhupaya) and view-engagement (diṭṭhupaya). The same method applies to clinging (upādāna) and the rest. Because craving and view approach the phenomena of the three planes (tebhūmaka-dhamma) through such modes as "I" and "mine"...
32:
...they are called "upaya" (engagements). Because they firmly cling to and insist upon those phenomena of the three planes, they are called "upādāna" (clinging) and "abhinivesa" (insistence). The world is firmly bound by these craving and view through the power of being difficult to liberate. Therefore, He taught: "The world bound by engagement, clinging, and insistence."

"Tañcāyaṃ" means this noble disciple [does not approach] that clinging of craving and view. "Cetaso adhiṭṭhānaṃ" means being the foundation of the unwholesome mind. "Abhinivesānusayaṃ" means the phenomenon which is both an insistence and an underlying tendency. The unwholesome mind stands upon craving and view; those craving and view both insist upon and lie latent within that unwholesome mind. Therefore, the combination of those two—craving and view—is taught as "cetaso adhiṭṭhānaṃ" and "abhinivesānusayaṃ." "Na upeti" means one does not approach through craving such as "mine." "Na upādiyati" means one does not firmly grasp through craving and view. "Nādhiṭṭhāti" means one does not insist with the mind as "my self." "Dukkham-eva" means only the five aggregates of clinging. "Na kaṅkhati" means one does not doubt, thinking, "Only suffering (the aggregates) arises, only suffering ceases; there is no such thing as a 'being' other than these five aggregates of clinging." "Na vicikicchati" means one does not give rise to perplexity.

"Aparappaccayā" means not through the faith of another; it is not a matter of reaching conviction through someone else, but rather that the noble disciple has personal direct knowledge (attapaccakkha-ñāṇa) regarding this suffering. By the words "Ettāvatā kho Kaccāna sammādiṭṭhi hoti," He spoke of mixed right view (missaka-sammādiṭṭhi)—both mundane and supramundane—stating that right vision occurs to this extent by the abandoning of the perception of a "being" (satta-saññā). In the phrase "Ayameko anto," this wrong view that "everything exists" is the lowest phenomenon, the first censurable eternalism. In the phrase "Ayaṃ dutiyo," this wrong view called the view that "everything does not exist" is the second lowest phenomenon, the second censurable annihilationism. The rest of the terms here are clear. The fifth sutta is finished.

## 6. Dhammakathika Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, "nibbidāya" means for the sake of disenchantment. "Virāgāya" means for the sake of dispassion. "Nirodhāya" means for the sake of cessation. "Paṭipanno hoti" (is practicing) should be understood here as practicing from the time of undertaking virtue (sīla) until the attainment of the path of Arahantship. "Dhammānudhammapaṭipanno" means one has practiced the way that is in accordance with the supramundane Dhamma of Nibbāna. "Anudhammabhūtaṃ" means being of a nature suitable for Nibbāna. "Nibbidā virāgā nirodhā" means through disenchantment, dispassion, and cessation. "Anu-upādā vimutto" means being liberated without clinging to any conditioned phenomenon (saṅkhāra-dhamma) through the four types of clinging. "Diṭṭhadhammanibbānappatto" means one who has attained Nibbāna in this very life. "Alaṃ vacanāya" means it is worthy of being so called; it is fit, suitable, and appropriate.
33:
This is the meaning. Thus, in this Sutta, the question of the Dhamma-preacher is taught in one way. By two ways, specifying that Dhamma-preacher's question, the planes of the trainee (sekha) and the non-trainee (asekha) are shown. The commentary on the sixth Sutta is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Acelakassapa Sutta

In the seventh Sutta, "Acela Kassapa" means he was "Acela" (naked) by appearance and "Kassapa" by name. "Even from afar" means he saw the Blessed One approaching, surrounded by a large community of monks, from a distance. "To some region" means for some reason. "Opportunity" means the moment or time for answering questions. "Inside the house" (antaraghara): in the passage "I will not sit cross-legged inside the house," it refers to inside the residence. In the passage "I will go inside the house with downcast eyes," it refers to inside the village starting from the threshold. In this Sutta, this [second] meaning is intended. "Whenever you wish" means whatever desire you have to ask.

Why did the Blessed One, though wishing to speak, refuse up to three times? It was to generate respect (gārava). For those with wrong views, if taught quickly, they do not show respect, saying, "It is easy to approach and question the recluse Gotama; he speaks as soon as he is asked," and they do not believe his words. But when refused two or three times, they show respect, thinking, "It is difficult to approach and ask a question of the recluse Gotama." When he speaks after being requested three times, they are eager to listen and they believe. Thus, the Blessed One, knowing "This person will be eager to listen and will believe," had him request three times before speaking. Furthermore, just as a skilled physician cooking oil or molasses waits for the time of soft-cooking or hard-cooking and takes it off the fire without letting the time pass; so too, the Blessed One, waiting for the maturity of beings' wisdom (ñāṇa-paripāka), knowing "By this much time, this person's wisdom will reach maturity," had him request three times.

"Do not say so, Kassapa" means "Kassapa, do not speak like this." He shows that it is not proper to say "suffering is self-created" (sayaṃkataṃ dukkhaṃ), and that there is no such thing as a "self" (attā) that creates suffering. The same method applies to subsequent statements. "Arisen without cause" (adhiccasamuppannaṃ) means arisen by chance, without a cause. Why is it said "Being thus questioned"? It is said that this thought occurred to Acela Kassapa: "When this recluse Gotama is asked 'Is suffering self-created?' and so on, he says 'Do not say so.' When asked 'Is it non-existent?' he says 'It exists.' When asked 'Does the Venerable Gotama not know or see suffering?' he says 'I know.' Have I asked something incorrectly?"
34:
Starting from the beginning, wishing to purify his own question, Acela Kassapa spoke thus: "May the Blessed One, Bhante, teach me." Here, having developed respect for the Teacher, he does not say "Bho Gotama" but says "Bhagavā" (Blessed One).

The passage "The same person acts" and so on is spoken to refute the view that "suffering is self-created." Here, the word "sato" is a genitive case used in the sense of the locative; therefore, the meaning should be understood thus: Kassapa, when it is first held that "the same person acts, the same person experiences," then later this view arises that "suffering is self-created." Here, "suffering" (dukkha) refers to the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭa-dukkha). The phrase "Thus they say" is connected with the preceding word "ādi" (beginning) and the subsequent word "sassata" (eternal). "Shows, takes up" is the remaining part of the text here. This is what is meant: Speaking thus, from the very beginning, he shows the eternalist view (sassata-diṭṭhi), he takes up the eternalist view. Why? Because that vision of his leads to this; taking the doer and the feeler as one and the same, he arrives at this eternalism.

The passage "Another acts" and so on is spoken to refute the view that "suffering is created by another" (paraṃkataṃ dukkhaṃ). The phrase "ādi sato" should be brought in here as well. The meaning here is: Kassapa, when it is first held that "one person acts, another experiences," then later, for one who is oppressed and pierced by the feeling associated with the view of annihilation (uccheda-diṭṭhi) that "the doer is annihilated right here, and another experiences what he has done," this view arises that "suffering is created by another." The phrase "Thus they say" and so on should be applied in the same manner as previously stated. The application is: Speaking thus, from the very beginning, he shows annihilationism, he takes up annihilationism. Why? Because that vision of his leads to this; he arrives at this annihilationism.

"Those two extremes" means without approaching the two extremes known as eternalism and annihilationism (the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma; Kassapa, without approaching those two extremes), having abandoned them, without clinging to them, the Blessed One teaches the Dhamma by the middle; he teaches standing in the Middle Way (majjhima-paṭipadā). If it is asked, "Which Dhamma?"—it is: "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be" (avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā), and so on. For here, the effect is shown from the cause, and its cessation is shown by the cessation of the cause; there is no doer or feeler. Therefore, by this statement alone, the Blessed One refutes the other five types of wrong views. By not approaching the two extremes, he abandons the third view of "self-created and other-created." By the passage "With ignorance as condition, volitional formations come to be," it should be understood that he also abandons the view of causelessness (adhiccasamuppanna).
35:
Alternatively, it has been explained. By this much, the remaining questions (views) are rejected. By the phrase 'without approaching either extreme' (ubho ante anupagamma), the third question regarding the view of self-created or other-created is rejected. By the phrase 'with ignorance as condition, volitional formations arise' (avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā), it should be understood that both causeless origination (adhiccasamuppanna) and ignorance are rejected.

The word 'I might obtain' (labheyya) was spoken by Acela Kassapa, desiring the state of a monk in the presence of the Blessed One. Then, the Blessed One, referring to the probation (parivāsa) prescribed in the Vinaya Khandhaka for those who were formerly members of other sects, spoke the words beginning with 'Whoever, Kassapa, was formerly a member of another sect.' This refers to one who, while in the stage of a novice (sāmaṇera), undertakes and undergoes probation in this manner: 'Venerable Sir, I, named so-and-so, was formerly a member of another sect. I desire full ordination in this Dhamma and Vinaya. Venerable Sir, I request the Saṅgha for four months of probation.' In that context, the word 'going forth' (pabbajjā) is used for the sake of linguistic smoothness. In truth, one can obtain the going forth even without undergoing probation. However, one who desires full ordination (upasampadā) must undergo probation while fulfilling the eight duties, such as entering the village at the appropriate time. 'With satisfied minds' (āraddhacittā) means having a mind pleased by the fulfillment of the eight duties. This is a summary here; the details of this probation for members of other sects should be understood according to the method stated in the explanation of the Pabbajjā Khandhaka in the Samantapāsādikā, the Vinaya Commentary.

In this context, there is the reading 'api ca mayā.' In other texts, however, it is 'api ca metthā.' 'Diversity of persons is known' (puggala-vemattatā viditā) means the difference between individuals is known. It shows: 'It is clear to me that this person is worthy of probation, and this person is not worthy of probation.' Then Kassapa thought, 'How wonderful is the Buddha's Dispensation! In this Dispensation, they accept only what is suitable after testing and examining (as if rubbing and striking gold), and they reject what is unsuitable.' Having thought thus, his enthusiasm for becoming a monk became even stronger, and he spoke the words beginning with 'If, Venerable Sir.' Then the Blessed One, knowing his intense desire, considered that 'Kassapa is not worthy of (i.e., does not need) probation,' and addressed a certain monk: 'Go, monk, bathe Kassapa, give him the going forth, and bring him back.' That monk did as commanded, gave him the going forth, and came to the Blessed One. The Blessed One, sitting in the midst of the assembly, granted him full ordination. Therefore, it is said, 'Acela Kassapa obtained the going forth and the full ordination in the presence of the Blessed One.' The remaining words beginning with 'not long after full ordination' (acirūpasampanno) are just as stated in the commentary on the Brāhmaṇasaṃyutta. The seventh sutta is finished.
36:
## 8. Commentary on the Timbaruka Sutta
In the commentary on the eighth sutta, the Timbaruka Sutta, the phrase beginning with 'That feeling and the one who feels are the same' is spoken for the purpose of refuting the view that 'pleasure and pain are self-created' (sayaṅkataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ). In this sutta also, the word 'sato' is a genitive case used in the sense of the locative. The explanation of the meaning regarding that pleasure of feeling is: 'Timbaruka, if from the very beginning it is held that "that is the feeling, and he is the one who feels," then this view of "self-created pleasure and pain" arises.' If this is so, then feeling itself would be created by feeling. One who speaks thus admits the existence of this feeling even previously; he demonstrates the view of eternalism (sassata) and grasps the view of eternalism. Why? Because his vision reaches that eternalism; it approaches that eternalism. The Blessed One must have spoken this sutta with reference to the meaning previously taught; therefore, in the Commentary, the meaning of this sutta is shown only by connecting it to that meaning. 'I do not say so' means 'I do not say that "that is the feeling, and he is the one who feels."' It means 'I also do not say that "pleasure and pain are self-created."

The phrase beginning with 'The feeling is one thing, the one who feels is another' is spoken for the purpose of refuting the view that 'pleasure and pain are created by another' (paraṅkataṃ sukhadukkhaṃ). Here too, the connection of meaning is: 'Timbaruka, if from the very beginning it is held that "the feeling is one thing, the one who feels is another," then subsequently, the "actor-feeling" that existed in the first part is annihilated.' For one who is pierced by feeling associated with the view of annihilationism (uccheda-diṭṭhi) that arises thus—'another feels what was created by that actor-feeling'—this view of 'pleasure and pain are created by another' arises. One who speaks thus demonstrates annihilationism and grasps annihilationism, saying that the actor is annihilated and another has taken up rebirth. Why? Because his vision reaches that annihilationism; it approaches that annihilationism. Here too, these words are brought from the Commentary and connected. In this sutta, pleasure and pain known as feeling are discussed. And it is stated that such pleasure and pain should only be understood as resultant (vipāka) pleasure and pain. The eighth sutta is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta
In the commentary on the ninth sutta, the Bālapaṇḍita Sutta, 'avijjānīvaraṇassa' means for one who is hindered by ignorance. 'Thus this body has arisen' means this body has been produced precisely because of being hindered by ignorance and being associated with craving. 'And this body' refers to this body of the fool himself, which is possessed of consciousness. 'And external mind-and-matter' refers to the external bodies of others, which are possessed of consciousness. Of oneself and of others...
37:
This meaning should also be shown by way of the five aggregates and the six sense bases. 'Itthetaṃ dvayaṃ' means in this manner, this is the duality (consisting of the continuity of oneself and others). In the phrase 'dvayaṃ paṭicca phasso' (contact dependent on duality), although in other suttas contact such as eye-contact is spoken of in dependence on the duality of the eye and forms, etc., in this sutta, the internal and external bases are spoken of (comprehensively). This statement is called 'Mahādvaya' (the Great Duality) because it encompasses all internal and external bases. 'Saḷāyatanaṃ' refers to the six bases of contact, which are the causes of contact. 'Yehi phuṭṭho' means touched by the contact that has arisen due to those bases which are the causes. In the word 'aññatarena', the state of being 'one or another' should be understood by way of a complete sense base. 'Tatra' means in that [context] of the production of the bodies of the fool and the wise, etc. 'Ko adhippayāso' means what is the extraordinary exertion?

'Bhagavaṃmūlakā' means they are 'rooted in the Blessed One' because the Blessed One is the root-cause of those teachings. This is what is meant: "Venerable Sir, these teachings of ours originated in the past during the time of the Buddha Kassapa; after his parinibbāna, throughout the interval between Buddhas, no other recluse or brahmin was able to bring these teachings to light. Now, the Blessed One alone has brought these teachings to light for us. It is only by depending on the Blessed One that we know and penetrate these teachings." Thus it is said, "Venerable Sir, our teachings are rooted in the Blessed One." 'Bhagavaṃnettikā' means they are 'guided by the Blessed One' because the Blessed One is the leader, the discipliner, and the guide of the teachings, showing them by taking each name according to its nature. 'Bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā' means they 'have the Blessed One as their resort' because the teachings belonging to the four planes, upon coming into the range of the Knowledge of Omniscience, resort to the Blessed One. 'Paṭisarantī' means they converge. Alternatively, by the power of the penetration of the Blessed One seated at the Great Seat of Enlightenment, contact comes and asks, "Blessed One, what is my name?" [The Buddha replies,] "You are called contact (phassa) in the sense of touching [the object]." Feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness come and ask, "Blessed One, what is my name?" [The Buddha replies,] "You are called consciousness (viññāṇa) in the sense of cognizing [the object]." In this way, because the Blessed One takes each name of the teachings belonging to the four planes according to their nature, the Blessed One is the resort (convergence point) for the teachings; thus they are 'Bhagavaṃpaṭisaraṇā'. 'Bhagavantaṃyeva paṭibhātu' means let the meaning of this statement be clear to the Blessed One alone; it means "May the Blessed One himself explain it to us."

In the phrase 'sā ceva avijjā' (that same ignorance), although that ignorance and craving have ceased after instigating kamma and pulling forth rebirth, just as one says of the medicine drunk today, "I drink the same medicine as yesterday," or "I eat the same food," because of similarity, so too here, it is said 'that same ignorance, that same craving' because of similarity.
38: Brahmacariya means the holy life of the Path. Dukkhakkhayāya means for the sake of the destruction of the suffering of the round of rebirth. Kāyūpago hoti means one who goes to another body of rebirth. "The practice of this brahmacariya" means the practice of that holy life of the Path; this shows the distinction between the fool and the wise man. Thus, in this sutta, all worldlings (puthujjana) who still undergo rebirth are called "fools," and the Arahants who no longer undergo rebirth are called "wise men." As for Stream-enterers, Once-returners, and Non-returners, they should not be called either "wise men" or "fools," but in their association, they associate with the side of the wise. The ninth sutta is finished. ## 10. Commentary on the Paccaya Sutta In the tenth sutta, when saying, "Monks, I will teach you dependent origination and dependently arisen phenomena," the Teacher begins by teaching both the causal conditions (paccaya) and the natural phenomena arisen from conditions (paccayuppanna) in this sutta. "Whether Tathāgatas arise" means whether Tathāgatas arise or not, whether Buddhas have appeared or not, aging and death occur because of birth as a condition; birth alone is the condition for aging and death. "That element remains stable" means that the nature of that condition is stable; there is never a time when birth is not the condition for aging and death. By these two terms, "dhammaṭṭhitatā" and "dhammaniyāmatā", He also speaks only of the causal condition (paccaya). For dependently arisen phenomena stand because of the condition; therefore, the condition itself is called "dhammaṭṭhitatā" (the stability of the Dhamma). Because the condition regulates the phenomena, it is called "dhammaniyāmatā" (the fixedness of the Dhamma). "Idappaccayatā" means the conditions for these things like aging and death are called "idappaccaya" (this-conditionality); the state of being "idappaccaya" is itself "idappaccayatā". "That phenomenon" means that causal condition. "He fully awakens to it" means He fully awakens to it with knowledge. "He realizes it" means He arrives at it with knowledge. "He tells" means He speaks. "He teaches" means He shows. "He makes known" means He makes it understood. "He establishes" means He places it at the entrance of knowledge. "He opens" means He opens and shows it. "He analyzes" means He shows it by way of parts. "He makes it clear" means He makes it evident. "He also says, 'Behold!'" means He says, "Behold!" How? "Monks, because of birth as a condition, aging and death occur," and so forth. "Thus, monks" means in this way, monks. "That which therein" means that which is in those causal natures such as "because of birth as a condition, aging and death occur." The terms "tathatā" and so forth are just synonyms for the mode of conditions (paccayākāra), which is dependent origination. Because those various phenomena arise from those various conditions which are neither deficient nor excessive, it is called "tathatā" (suchness). Because when the conditions have come together, there is no absence of the phenomena arising from them even for a moment, it is called "avitathatā" (unfailingness).
39:
It is called *ananyathatā* (non-otherness) because other effects do not arise from the causes of a different effect. It is called *idappaccayatā* (specific conditionality) because it is the cause of aging and death, etc., or because it is a collection of causes. In this term *idappaccayatā*, the word-definition is: the causes of these [aging and death, etc.] are *idappaccaya*. These *idappaccaya* themselves are *idappaccayatā*. Alternatively, the collection of these *idappaccaya* is *idappaccayatā*. The characteristic [of the suffix -tā] here should be understood from the science of grammar.

'Impermanent' (*anicca*) means impermanent because of the sense of non-existence after having come to be. Here, 'impermanent' does not mean that aging and death are impermanent in the primary sense; rather, because aging and death occur to the aggregates which are impermanent by nature, they are called 'impermanent' [metaphorically]. The same method applies to terms like 'conditioned' (*saṅkhata*). Here, 'conditioned' means that which is made by the meeting and combining of causes. 'Dependently arisen' (*paṭiccasamuppanna*) means that which arises depending on causes. 'Subject to destruction' (*khayadhamma*) means having the nature of being destroyed. 'Subject to vanishing' (*vayadhamma*) means having the nature of disappearing. 'Subject to fading away' (*virāgadhamma*) means having the nature of dispassion. 'Subject to cessation' (*nirodadhamma*) means having the nature of ceasing. Regarding 'birth' (*jāti*), its impermanence should be understood in the same way as mentioned. Alternatively, because [the state of being born] is seen at the moment the functions of the producing causes are completed, the terms 'impermanent' etc. are suitable here in another sense. States such as 'existence' (*bhava*) also possess the nature of impermanence and so on.

'With right wisdom' (*sammapaññāya*) means with the wisdom of the path together with insight (*vipassanā*). 'The past' (*pubbanta*) means the preceding past time. In the phrases such as 'Was I in the past?', one doubts about one's own existence or non-existence in the past, based on the mode of eternalism (*sassata*) or the mode of fortuitous origination (*adhiccasamuppatti*). One should not ask 'For what reason does one doubt?'; for a foolish worldling, like a madman, acts in whatever way. 'What was I?'—based on caste, appearance, and rebirth, one doubts: 'Was I a king? Was I one of the brahmins, merchants, workers, householders, monastics, devas, or humans?' 'How was I?'—based on the shape and form of the body, one doubts: 'Was I tall? Was I one of those who are short, fair, dark, of medium size, or of immeasurable size?' Some teachers, however, say that based on the creation by a Supreme Lord (*Issara*), etc., one doubts regarding the cause: 'For what reason was I?' 'Having been what, what did I become?'—based on caste, etc., one doubts the sequence of one's own succession: 'Having been a king, did I become a brahmin? ... Having been a deva, did I become a human?' In all places, 'duration' (*addhāna*) is a term for time. 'The future' (*aparanta*) is the limit of the future to come. 'Shall I be? Shall I not be?'—based on the mode of eternalism and the mode of annihilationism (*uccheda*), one doubts about one's own existence or non-existence in the future. The remaining meanings here are just as previously mentioned.
40:
'Or the present duration' (*etarahi vā paccuppannaṃ addhānaṃ*) refers to taking the entire present time in this current life, starting from rebirth-linking until death. 'He will be a doubter regarding the internal' (*ajjhattaṃ kathaṃkathī bhavissati*) means he will have doubt and hesitation regarding his own five aggregates. 'Am I?'—he doubts the existence of his own self (*attā*). If one asks, 'Is such doubt appropriate?', what is the use of thinking whether it is appropriate or inappropriate here? Furthermore, they cite this story here: It is said that the son of a younger mother was bald, while the son of the elder mother was not. They shaved the head of the elder mother's son. When he woke up, he thought, 'Am I the son of the younger mother?' In the same way, the doubt 'Am I?' occurs. 'Am I not?'—he doubts the non-existence of his own self. In that doubt too, there is this story: It is said that a certain man, while catching fish, stayed in the water for a long time; thinking his cold thigh was a fish, he struck it. Another man, guarding a field near a cemetery, slept curled up out of fear; when he woke up, he thought his two knees were two ogres (*yakkha*) and struck them. In this way, the doubt 'Am I not?' occurs.

'What am I?'—even while being a king, he doubts his own state as a king. The same method applies to the rest, such as brahmins. While being a deva, there is no such thing as not knowing one's state as a deva; however, even that deva doubts in this way: 'Am I a deva with form or without form?' etc. If it is asked, 'Why do kings and others not know?', it is because their birth in those respective families is not personally evident to them. Also, householders like Potthalika perceive themselves as monastics. Monastics also perceive themselves as householders in such ways as 'Has my [monastic] act been disturbed?' etc. Humans also, like kings, have the perception of themselves as devas. 'How am I?' is just as previously mentioned. Specifically here, by grasping that there is a so-called 'soul' (*jīva*) within, and based on the shape and form of that soul, one doubts: 'Am I tall, short, square, hexagonal, octagonal, sixteen-sided, or some other kind?' This should be understood as the doubt 'How am I?'. As for the shape of the present body, there is no one who does not know it. 'Where has he come from? Where will he go?'—doubting the place of coming and the place of going of this individual existence (*attabhāva*), he doubts in this way. In this context, 'of the noble disciple' (*ariyasāvakassa*) refers to a Stream-enterer (*sotāpanna*). However, the other three [Once-returner, Non-returner, and Arahant] are also not excluded. The tenth sutta is finished.

## The Second Chapter: On Nutriment (Āhāra Vagga).
41:
## 1. Dasabalasutta-vaṇṇanā
## 3. Dasabalavagga
The first sutta of the Dasabala Chapter is merely a summary of the second sutta.

## 2. Dutiya-dasabalasutta-vaṇṇanā
The Blessed One taught the second sutta according to his own inclination. In that sutta, 'dasabalasamannāgato' means being endowed with the ten powers. Power (bala) is of two kinds: physical power (kāyabala) and knowledge power (ñāṇabala). Among these two, the physical power of the Tathāgata should be understood according to the lineage of elephants. Thus, the ancient teachers said:
'There are ten lineages of elephants: Kāḷāvaka, Gaṅgeyya, Paṇḍara, Tamba, Piṅgala, Gandha, Maṅgala, Hemavata, Uposatha, and Chaddanta.'

These are the ten elephant lineages. Among these ten, the Kāḷāvaka lineage should be regarded as the ordinary elephant lineage. The physical power of ten men is equal to the power of one Kāḷāvaka elephant. The power of ten Kāḷāvaka elephants is equal to the power of one Gaṅgeyya elephant. The power of ten Gaṅgeyya elephants is equal to the power of one Paṇḍara elephant. The power of ten Paṇḍara elephants is equal to the power of one Tamba elephant. The power of ten Tamba elephants is equal to the power of one Piṅgala elephant. The power of ten Piṅgala elephants is equal to the power of one Gandha elephant. The power of ten Gandha elephants is equal to the power of one Maṅgala elephant. The power of ten Maṅgala elephants is equal to the power of one Hemavata elephant. The power of ten Hemavata elephants is equal to the power of one Uposatha elephant. The power of ten Uposatha elephants is equal to the power of one Chaddanta elephant. The power of ten Chaddanta elephants is equal to the physical power of the Tathāgata. 

This power is also called Nārāyanasaṅghāta power. In terms of ordinary elephants, it is equal to the power of one thousand crores of elephants; in terms of men, it is equal to the power of ten thousand crores of men. This is the physical power (kāyabala) of the Tathāgata. However, in this context of 'dasabalasamannāgato', this physical power is not considered to be included. This is because this physical power is external and inferior, and it can also exist in animals such as lions. Based on this physical power, there can be no full understanding of suffering (dukkha-pariññā), abandoning of the origin (samudaya-pahāna), development of the path (magga-bhāvanā), or realization of the fruit (phala-sacchikiriyā). There is another ten-fold power of knowledge (ñāṇabala) which is characterized by being unshakable and supportive in ten areas. It is with reference to these ten powers of knowledge that 'dasabalasamannāgato' is said.
42:
What are those ten knowledge powers? They are knowing things as they really are, such as the possible and the impossible. Namely:
1. Knowing as it really is what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible.
2. Knowing as it really is the result of past, future, and present actions (kamma) undertaken, by way of their place and cause.
3. Knowing as it really is the practice leading to all destinations.
4. Knowing as it really is the world with its many and diverse elements.
5. Knowing as it really is the diverse inclinations of beings.
6. Knowing as it really is the state of the faculties (indriya) of other beings and persons, whether superior or inferior.
7. Knowing as it really is the defilement, cleansing, and emergence regarding the jhānas, liberations, concentrations, and attainments.
8. Knowing as it really is the recollection of past lives.
9. Knowing as it really is the passing away and rebirth of beings.
10. Knowing as it really is the knowledge of the destruction of the taints (āsava).

In the Abhidhamma, however:
"Here, the Tathāgata understands as it really is what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible. Since the Tathāgata understands as it really is what is possible as possible and what is impossible as impossible, this is a Tathāgata's power of the Tathāgata, by virtue of which the Tathāgata claims the peerless place (āsabha), roars his lion's roar in the assemblies, and sets in motion the Wheel of Brahma (Brahmacakka)."

These are explained in detail in such a manner. The explanation of their meaning is also stated in every aspect in the Vibhaṅga Commentary and in the Majjhima Commentary, the Papañcasūdanī. That meaning should be understood exactly as stated in those commentaries.

In the phrase "catūhi ca vesārajjehi" (and by the four intrepidities), vesārajja is the quality that is the opposite of fear or timidity. This name 'vesārajja' refers to the knowledge accompanied by joy that arises in the Blessed One when reviewing His state of fearlessness in four areas. In which four? In the grounds for accusation such as, "While you claim to be perfectly enlightened, these things are not fully understood by you."

In this regard, there is this Pali text:
"Monks, there are these four intrepidities of the Tathāgata... What are the four? 'While you claim to be perfectly enlightened, these things are not fully understood by you'—monks, I do not see any ground on which any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, or Brahmā, or anyone else in the world, could justly accuse me of this. Monks, seeing no such ground, I abide in safety, fearlessness, and intrepidity. 'While you claim to be one whose taints are destroyed, these taints are not destroyed'—..."
43:
I do not see any ground, monks, on which any ascetic, brahmin, deva, Māra, Brahmā, or anyone else in the world could, in accordance with the Dhamma, accuse me thus: 'While you claim to be a Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), you have not fully awakened to these things.' Monks, seeing no such ground, I abide in a state of security, fearlessness, and self-confidence. I do not see any ground on which anyone could accuse me thus: 'While you claim to be an Arahant who has destroyed all taints (āsava), these taints are not yet destroyed in you.' I do not see any ground on which anyone could accuse me thus: 'Those things which you have declared to be obstructive do not actually constitute an obstruction for one who indulges in them.' I do not see any ground on which anyone could accuse me thus: 'The Dhamma you have taught for a specific purpose does not lead the one who practices it to the complete destruction of suffering.' For these reasons, I abide in a state of self-confidence.

'Āsabhaṃ ṭhānaṃ' (The Supreme Station) means the noble station or the most excellent station. Alternatively, it means the station of former Buddhas. In another sense, a bull that is the leader of a hundred cows is called 'Usabha', and a leader of a thousand cows is called 'Vasabha'. A bull that is superior to all cattle, capable of enduring all dangers, pure white, inspiring confidence, capable of bearing heavy burdens, and unshakable even by a hundred thunderclaps is called 'Nisabha'. Here, 'Usabha' refers to that very 'Nisabha'. This is a synonymous term for it. 'Āsabhaṃ' means that which belongs to such a bull. 'Ṭhānaṃ' (Station) refers to standing firmly by pressing the earth with four feet. This knowledge of self-confidence (Vesārajja-ñāṇa) is called 'Āsabha' because it stands like the lordly bull Nisabha. Just as the bull called Nisabha, endowed with the strength of a bull, stands in an unshakable position by pressing the earth with its four feet, so too the Tathāgata, endowed with the ten powers (Dasabala), stands unshakably in the world with its devas, unperturbed by any enemy or adversary, by pressing the ground of the eight assemblies with the four feet of self-confidence. Standing thus, he claims that supreme station, attains it, does not reject it, and takes it upon himself. Therefore, it is said, 'He claims the supreme station' (Āsabhaṃ ဌာနံ ပဋိဇာနာတိ).

'In the assemblies' (Pariisāsu) refers to these eight assemblies: the assembly of nobles (khattiya), the assembly of brahmins, the assembly of householders, the assembly of ascetics, the assembly of the Four Great Kings, the assembly of the Tāvatiṃsa devas, the assembly of Māras, and the assembly of Brahmās. 'He roars the lion's roar' (Sīhanādaṃ nadati) means he utters a noble and fearless sound, or a sound similar to a lion's roar. This meaning should be understood through the Sīhanāda Sutta. Just as a lion is called 'Sīha' because of enduring (sahana) and striking (hanana), so too the Tathāgata is called 'Sīha' because he endures worldly conditions and strikes down the doctrines of others. The roar of such a Buddha-lion is called the 'lion's roar'. In this context, just as a lion, endowed with a lion's strength, roars fearlessly and without horripilation everywhere, so too the Tathāgata, endowed with the ten powers, roars the lion's roar in the eight assemblies, fearlessly and without horripilation, endowed with the grace of various teachings. Therefore, it is said, 'He roars the lion's roar in the assemblies'.

In the phrase 'He sets in motion the Supreme Wheel' (Brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti), 'Brahma' means highly praised or noble, and it is a name for the Wheel of Dhamma (Dhamma-cakka) which is pure from defilements. That Wheel of Dhamma is twofold: the knowledge of penetration (Paṭivedha-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of teaching (Desanā-ñāṇa). Between these two, the knowledge of penetration is produced by the power of wisdom and brings about one's own state of an Ariya (Noble One), while the knowledge of teaching is produced by the power of compassion and brings about the state of an Ariya for the disciples. Among these two knowledges, the knowledge of penetration is of two kinds: 'arising' (uppajjamāna) and 'arisen' (uppanna). To show this distinction, it is said 'Tatra'.
44:
Just as a lion roars the lion's roar, so too the Tathāgata-lion, endowed with the powers of a Tathāgata, being fearless and without horripilation in the eight assemblies, roars the lion's roar endowed with the grace of various teachings in the manner of 'Such is form,' and so forth. Therefore, it is said, 'He roars the lion's roar in the assemblies.'

In the phrase 'He sets in motion the Supreme Wheel' (Brahmacakkaṃ pavatteti), 'Brahma' means excellent or supreme; this is a designation for the pure Wheel of Dhamma. That Wheel of Dhamma is twofold: the knowledge of penetration (Paṭivedha-ñāṇa) and the knowledge of teaching (Desanā-ñāṇa). Of these, the knowledge of penetration, produced by wisdom, brings about one's own noble fruition; the knowledge of teaching, produced by compassion, brings about the noble fruition for the disciples. The knowledge of penetration is twofold: 'arising' (uppajjamāna) and 'arisen' (uppanna). It is called 'arising' from the time of the Great Renunciation until the path of Arahantship, and 'arisen' at the moment of fruition. Or, it is called 'arising' from the Tusita heaven until the path of Arahantship at the seat of the Great Enlightenment, and 'arisen' at the moment of fruition. Or, it is called 'arising' from the time at the feet of Dīpaṅkara Buddha until the path of Arahantship, and 'arisen' at the moment of fruition. The knowledge of teaching is also twofold: 'being set in motion' (pavattāmāna) and 'set in motion' (pavatta). It is called 'being set in motion' until the Venerable Aññāsi Koṇḍañña reached the path of Stream-entry, and 'set in motion' at the moment of fruition. Among these, the knowledge of penetration is supramundane (lokuttara), while the knowledge of teaching is mundane (lokiya). However, both of these are the personal (orasā) knowledge of the Buddhas, not shared with others.

Now, to show the roar he roars while endowed with this knowledge, he said 'Such is form' (iti rūpaṃ), etc. In that text, 'Such is form' means: this is form, form is only this much, there is no form beyond this; thus he taught the comprehensive grasping of form without remainder by way of its nature of being deformed (ruppana), its division into primary and derived form, and by way of characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause. By the phrase 'Such is the origin of form' (iti rūpassa samudayo), he taught the origin of form thus grasped. In that context, 'iti' means 'in this way the origin occurs.' Its detail should be understood thus: 'With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of form; with the arising of craving, with the arising of kamma, with the arising of nutriment, there is the arising of form; one who sees the characteristic of birth sees the arising of the aggregate of form.' Regarding the disappearance (atthaṅgama), the detail is: 'With the cessation of ignorance, there is the cessation of form... one who sees the characteristic of change sees the cessation of the aggregate of form.'

In the passages 'Such is feeling' (iti vedanā), etc., it means: this nature is called feeling, feeling is only this much, there is no feeling beyond this; this is perception; these are mental formations; this is consciousness, consciousness is only this much.
45:
Consciousness is only this much; there is no consciousness beyond this. The Blessed One taught the delimitation of feeling (vedanā), perception (saññā), mental formations (saṅkhāra), and consciousness (viññāṇa) without remainder, starting from the nature of experiencing, perceiving, constructing, and cognizing, as well as the varieties such as pleasant feeling, perception of forms, contact, and eye-consciousness, by way of characteristic, function, manifestation, and proximate cause. Furthermore, with the words 'Thus is the origin (samudaya) of feeling,' etc., He taught the origin of the feeling, perception, mental formations, and consciousness thus delimited. In that context, 'iti' means 'arising in this manner.' The detailed explanation of these things should be understood in the same way as stated for the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha): 'With the arising of ignorance, there is the arising of feeling' (Paṭisambhidāmagga 1.50). However, there is this distinction: for the three aggregates (feeling, perception, formations), one should not say 'with the arising of nutriment' but 'with the arising of contact'; for the aggregate of consciousness, one should say 'with the arising of name-and-form.' The term 'disappearance' (atthangama) should also be applied by way of those same factors like ignorance. This is a summary here. For the detailed analysis of arising and passing away (udayabbaya) in all its aspects, it has been taught in the Visuddhimagga.

'When this exists, that comes to be'—this is another 'Lion's Roar' (sīhanāda). Its meaning is: when this cause such as ignorance exists, this effect such as mental formations comes to be. 'With the arising of this, that arises' means: with the arising of this cause such as ignorance, this effect such as mental formations arises. 'When this does not exist, that does not come to be' means: when this cause such as ignorance does not exist, this effect such as mental formations does not come to be. 'With the cessation of this, that ceases' means: with the cessation of this cause such as ignorance, this effect such as mental formations ceases. Now, in order to show in detail how it arises and ceases, He said, 'With ignorance as condition, mental formations come to be,' and so on.

'Thus well-expounded' (svākkhāto) means well-spoken or taught by way of the analysis of the five aggregates, etc. 'Dhamma' refers to the five aggregates and the law of dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda). 'Uttāna' (open) means the Dhamma is not overturned but laid open (clear). 'Vivaṭa' (unveiled) means the Dhamma is kept open. 'Pakāsita' (manifested) means the Dhamma is illustrated and illuminated by the lamp of wisdom. 'Chinnapilotika' (free from shredded rags): 'pilotikā' refers to old cloth that is torn, broken, and stitched or knotted in various places. One who does not have such old cloth but wears a new cloth of eight or nine cubits is called 'chinnapilotika.' This Dhamma is also like that. In this Dhamma, there is no state of being torn, broken, stitched, or knotted by way of deceit (kohañña), etc. Alternatively, a small cloth is also called 'pilotikā'; one who does not have that small cloth but has a large cloth of eight or nine cubits is also 'chinnapilotika,' meaning 'one from whom shreds are gone.' This Dhamma is like that. For instance, just as a man who takes a cloth of four cubits...
46:
...and wears it is exhausted by pulling it here and there, so too, those who have gone forth in the teachings of outsiders (titthiyas) are exhausted as they speculate and analyze their own meager teachings, thinking, 'If it is thus, it will be so.' However, just as a man who wears a large cloth of eight or nine cubits can wrap it as he likes and is not exhausted, having no need to pull it to make it larger, so too, in this Dhamma, there is no need for speculation and repeated analysis. With the intention of saying, 'By various reasons, I alone have well-analyzed and well-detailed this Dhamma,' He said 'chinnapilotika' (the Dhamma free from shredded rags).

Furthermore, rubbish is also called 'pilotikā.' In this Dispensation (sāsana), 'monastic rubbish' (corrupt monks) cannot find a footing. Therefore, the Blessed One said:

'Expel the crow-like [monk],
Remove the monastic refuse,
Then blow away the husks—
Those who are not monks but think they are.
Having expelled those of evil desires,
Whose conduct and resort are evil,
Being pure, dwell with the pure, 
Ever mindful and alert.
Then, united and prudent,
You shall make an end of suffering.' (Aṅguttara Nikāya 8.10)

Because 'monastic rubbish' is cut off (removed), this Dhamma is called 'chinnapilotika.'

'Alam-eva' means it is truly fitting. 'Saddhāpabbajitena' means one who has gone forth out of faith. Regarding 'kulaputtena' (son of good family), there are two types: ācārakulaputta (son of good family by conduct) and jātikulaputta (son of good family by birth). Among them, one who goes forth from any family and fulfills the five groups of Dhamma such as virtue (sīla) is called an ācārakulaputta. One who goes forth from a family of high birth, like the noble youth Yasa, is called a jātikulaputta. Here, the ācārakulaputta is intended. If a jātikulaputta is also endowed with good conduct, he is indeed the best. For such a son of good family 'to arouse energy' (vīriyaṃ ārabhituṃ) means to exert energy endowed with four factors. Now, wishing to show those four factors of energy, He said, 'Let only my skin remain,' etc. Here, skin is one factor, sinews one, bones one, and flesh and blood one. One who undertakes this energy endowed with four factors should apply it in nine instances: before the meal, after the meal, in the first watch of the night, in the middle watch, in the last watch, while walking, while standing, while sitting, and while lying down.
47:
“Monks, the lazy person lives in suffering” means that in this Dispensation (Sāsana), the person who is lazy lives in suffering. Outside the Dispensation, however, the lazy person lives happily. ‘Vokiṇṇo’ means mixed (with unwholesome states). ‘Sadatthaṃ’ means the beautiful benefit or one’s own benefit, which refers specifically to the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala). ‘Parihāpeti’ means to diminish, or to fail to reach (the Fruit of Arahantship).

For a lazy person, the six sense-doors are unguarded, the three types of actions (body, speech, and mind) are impure, the morality with livelihood as the eighth (ājīvaṭṭhamaka-sīla) is not pure, and with a ruined livelihood, they become one who hangs around supporters. Such a person is like dust fallen into the eyes of their fellow practitioners, being an oppressor and living in suffering. They are “oppressors of couches and benches” (excessive sleepers) and like a pot of filth; they cannot grasp the Teacher’s intention and miss the rare opportunity. Even the alms-food of the country consumed by them is not of great fruit.

“Monks, the person who has aroused energy lives happily” means that only in this Dispensation does the energetic person live happily. Outside the Dispensation, however, the energetic person lives in suffering. ‘Pavivitto’ means being secluded and detached (from unwholesome states). ‘Sadatthaṃ paripūreti’ means reaching the Fruit of Arahantship. For the energetic person, the six sense-doors are well-guarded, the three types of actions are pure, and the morality with livelihood as the eighth is pure. Like cool eye-ointment or sandalwood applied to the body, they are pleasing to their fellow practitioners and live happily; they can grasp the Teacher’s intention.

Indeed, when the Teacher was addressed by the foster-mother Gotamī:
‘O Great Hero, live long! O Great Sage, remain for an aeon!’—
the Buddha rejected this, saying, ‘Gotamī, Tathāgatas should not be honored in this way.’ When she requested to know the proper way to honor him, he said:

‘See the disciples who have aroused energy, who are resolute,
Always firm in effort, and in harmony;
This (seeing) is the honoring of the Buddhas.’

Thus, the energetic person can grasp the Teacher’s intention and does not miss the rare opportunity. For them, the arising of a Buddha, the preaching of the Dhamma, and the good practice of the Saṅgha are fruitful and bring growth. Even the alms-food of the country consumed by them is of great fruit.
48:
Attaining the supreme Fruit of Arahantship is not possible through inferior faith, inferior energy, inferior mindfulness, inferior concentration, or inferior wisdom. Only through supreme faith and other qualities is the attainment of the supreme Fruit of Arahantship possible. “Maṇḍapeyya” is called ‘maṇḍa’ because of its clarity and ‘peyya’ because it is to be drunk. If one drinks liquor (or intoxicants) and falls down in the middle of the road, becoming unconscious and losing control even over one’s own clothes, such a thing should not be drunk even if it is clear. To show that “My Dispensation is both clear and worthy of being drunk,” the Buddha said ‘maṇḍapeyya’.

There are three kinds of clarity (maṇḍa): clarity of teaching (desanā-maṇḍa), clarity of recipients (paṭiggaha-maṇḍa), and clarity of the holy life (brahmacariya-maṇḍa). What is clarity of teaching? It is the explaining, making known, establishing, opening, analyzing, and making plain of the Four Noble Truths. Furthermore, it is the explaining and making plain of the four foundations of mindfulness... up to... the Noble Eightfold Path. This is called clarity of teaching. What is clarity of recipients? Monks, nuns, laymen, laywomen, devas, humans, and whoever else can understand the Dhamma are called clarity of recipients. What is clarity of the holy life? It is this very Noble Eightfold Path (from Right View to Right Concentration). Alternatively, the faculty of faith (saddhindriya) is the clarity of resolution (adhimokkha-maṇḍa). Discarding the dregs of faithlessness, one drinks the clarity of resolution of the faculty of faith—this is how the meaning should be understood here according to the method starting with ‘maṇḍapeyya’.

“The Teacher is present” is the statement of reason here. Because the Teacher is present, exert energy and drink this clarity of the Dispensation. When people drink medicinal essence outside in the absence of a doctor, they have doubts, not knowing the dosage, or whether it will cause vomiting or purging. But in the presence of a doctor, they drink without doubt, thinking, “The doctor will know.” Similarly, because our Teacher, the Lord of Dhamma, is present, exert energy and drink. To urge them to drink the essence of the Dispensation, he said, “Therefore, monks,” and so on. In that context, ‘saphala’ means having benefits (āniśaṃsa), and ‘saudraya’ means having growth.

Now, to point out the practice in accordance with the exhortation, he said, “For one’s own benefit, monks,” and so on. In that context, ‘attattha’ (one’s own benefit) refers to the Fruit of Arahantship. ‘Appamādena sampādetuṃ’ means to perform all tasks with diligence (heedfulness). ‘Parattha’ (others’ benefit) means causing the donors of the four requisites to obtain great fruit and benefit. The rest of the words are clear everywhere. The commentary on the second sutta ends.
49:
## 3. Upanisasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the third sutta, the Upanisa Sutta, regarding the words "jānato ahaṃ" and so forth, "jānato" means for one who knows (with the eye of wisdom). "Passato" means for one who sees (with the eye of wisdom). Although these two terms have the same meaning, they differ only in phrasing. Despite having the same meaning, the term "jānato" indicates the person by way of the characteristic of knowing in wisdom. This is because wisdom has the characteristic of knowing. The term "passato" indicates the person by way of the power of wisdom. Wisdom has the power of seeing. Just as a person with eyes sees forms with their eyes, a person endowed with wisdom sees the supramundane states opened by wisdom.

In the phrase "āsavānaṃ khayaṃ", the abandoning of taints, their non-arising, the state of their exhaustion, and their non-existence are also called "āsavakkhaya" (destruction of taints). Furthermore, it refers to the moment of dissolution (bhaṅga), as well as the Path, Fruition, and Nibbāna. In passages such as "āsavānaṃ khayā anāsavaṃ cetovimuttiṃ", the state of exhaustion of taints is called "āsavakkhaya". In the passage "yo āsavānaṃ khayo vayo bhedo paribhedo aniccatā antaradhānaံ", the moment of dissolution is called "āsavakkhaya".

In the verse: "For the trainee (sekkha) who is training, following the straight path, first knowledge arises in the destruction (of taints), and then immediately after, the final knowledge (aññā)," the Path is meant. Since that Path arises while exhausting and subsiding the taints, it is called "āsavānaṃ khaya". In the passage "āsavānaṃ khayā samaṇo hoti", the Fruition is meant. Since that Fruition arises when the taints have been exhausted, it is called "āsavānaṃ khaya".

In the verse: "His taints increase; he is far from the destruction of taints," Nibbāna is meant. Since the taints are exhausted depending on that Nibbāna, it is called "āsavānaṃ khaya". In this sutta, however, the Path and Fruition are intended. "No ajānato no apassato" means: "I do not say (the destruction of taints) is for one who does not know and does not see (with wisdom)." By this statement, those who claim purification through the round of rebirth (saṃsāra) alone, without knowing or seeing, are refuted. With the first two terms, the Buddha teaches the appropriate means (upāya), and with this term, He prohibits the inappropriate means.

Now, wishing to show for one who knows what the destruction of taints occurs, He begins the question: "Knowing what, monks...?" In that context, knowing is of many kinds. For instance, a certain monk skilled in crafts knows how to make an umbrella, or another knows how to make robes and so forth. For that monk who performs such tasks as a matter of duty...
50:
It should not be said that such knowing is not a proximate cause (padaṭṭhāna) for the path and fruition of the heavenly realms (meaning, such knowing is indeed a cause). However, for one who, having gone forth in the Dispensation, knows how to practice medicine and so forth, the taints only increase because of such knowing. Therefore, showing only that which, when known and seen, leads to the destruction of taints, He said: "This is form," and so forth. "Thus, monks, for one who knows" means for one who knows the rise and fall of the five aggregates in this way. "The destruction of taints occurs" means the occurrence of Arahattaphala, which receives the name "destruction of taints" because it is produced at the end of the taints.

Having thus concluded the teaching with the pinnacle of Arahatship, He now said: "Monks, for him that..." and so forth, to show the preliminary practice (pubbabhāgapatipadā) leading to the attainment of an Arahant. In that text, "knowledge of destruction in the destruction" refers to the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) that arises after the attainment of Arahattaphala, which is called the destruction of taints. Since that reviewing knowledge arises after the first occurrence of the destruction of taints known as Arahattaphala, it is called "knowledge in the destruction" (khaye ñāṇa). "Saupanisaṃ" means with a cause, with a condition. "Vimutti" refers to the liberation of Arahattaphala. That liberation is the condition that assists that reviewing knowledge by way of the decisive support condition (upanissaya-paccaya). In this way, the causal relationship should be understood in the subsequent states according to their availability.

"Virāga" (dispassion) refers to the Path. Since that Path arises while making the defilements fade away and exhausting them, it is called "virāga". "Nibbidā" (disenchantment) refers to the knowledge of disenchantment (nibbidā-ñāṇa). By this term, strong insight (balava-vipassanā) is shown. Strong insight is a designation for the four knowledges: knowledge of the appearance as fearful (bhayatūpaṭṭhāna-ñāṇa), knowledge of contemplation of danger (ādīnavānupassanā-ñāṇa), knowledge of the desire for deliverance (muñcitukamyatā-ñāṇa), and knowledge of equanimity about formations (saṅkhārupekkhā-ñāṇa). "Yathābhūtañāṇadassana" (knowledge and vision of things as they are) refers to the vision known as knowing according to reality. By this term, tender insight (taruṇa-vipassanā) is shown. Tender insight is the condition for strong insight. Tender insight is a designation for the four knowledges: knowledge of the delimitation of formations (saṅkhārapariccheda-ñāṇa), knowledge of the overcoming of doubt (kaṅkhāvitaraṇa-ñāṇa), knowledge of comprehension (sammasana-ñāṇa), and knowledge of what is and what is not the path (maggāmagga-ñāṇa). "Samādhi" (concentration) refers to the concentration of the basic jhāna (pādakajjhāna). That concentration is the condition for tender insight. "Sukha" (happiness) refers to the happiness in the preliminary stage of absorption (appanā). That happiness is the condition for the basic jhāna. "Passaddhi" (tranquility) refers to the subsiding of distress. That tranquility is the condition for the happiness in the preliminary stage of absorption. "Pīti" (rapture) refers to strong rapture. That rapture is the condition for the subsiding of distress. "Pāmojja" (joy) refers to weak rapture. That joy is the condition for strong rapture. "Saddhā" (faith) refers to faith that arises repeatedly. That faith is the condition for weak rapture. "Dukkha" (suffering) refers to the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha). That suffering is the condition for the faith that arises repeatedly. "Jāti" (birth) refers to that which is accompanied by change...
51:
The birth of the aggregates (khandhajāti) is the cause of the suffering of the round of rebirths (vaṭṭadukkha). 'Existence' (bhava) refers to the kamma-process of existence (kammabhava). (For that kamma-process of existence is the cause of birth which is subject to transformation.) In this manner, the remaining terms should also be understood.

'Thullaphusitaka' refers to large raindrops. In the passage mentioning mountain glens, clefts, and rivulets, a 'kandara' (mountain glen) is a place on a mountain carved out by water, which is called 'ka', or broken by water; it is also called a 'nitamba' (mountain slope) or a 'nadīkuñcha' (river bend). A 'padara' (cleft) is a fissure in the earth that opens when it has not rained for eight months. 'Sākhā' (rivulets) are small channels flowing into small pools (kusumbha). 'Kusobbha' refers to small puddles. 'Mahāsobbha' refers to large pools. 'Kunnadī' refers to small rivers. 'Mahānadī' refers to great rivers such as the Ganges and the Yamuna. Monks, in the same way, in the passages beginning with 'with ignorance as a proximate cause, volitional formations arise,' ignorance should be regarded as being like a mountain. Kamma-formations (abhisaṅkhāra) are like a rain cloud; the round of rebirths starting with consciousness is like the mountain glens and so forth; and liberation (vimutti/Nibbāna) is like the great ocean.

Just as when it rains on a mountain top, filling the mountain glens and so forth, and gradually filling the great ocean, in the same way, one should understand the raining of the cloud of kamma-formations upon the mountain top of ignorance. For the unlearned worldling, being ignorant due to ignorance and having desire through craving, exerts himself in wholesome and unwholesome kamma. That wholesome and unwholesome kamma is the cause of rebirth-linking consciousness. Rebirth-linking consciousness and so forth are the causes of mentality-materiality and so forth. Thus, just as the rain falling on the mountain top fills the glens and so forth until it reaches and stays in the great ocean, so too should it be understood as the time when the rain of kamma-formations falling on the mountain top of ignorance fills the round of rebirths starting with consciousness through a sequence of successive causes.

Although the words of the Buddha are not directly taken from this Sutta text, they should be understood as being included by virtue of the passage: 'Here, a Tathāgata arises in the world... he goes forth from the household life into homelessness.' The birth (conception) of that son of good family in his ancestral home is called 'birth subject to transformation,' which has the kamma-process of existence as its cause. That person, having come into the presence of the Buddhas or the disciples of the Buddhas, hears a Dhamma discourse that illustrates the faults of the round of rebirths and bears the three characteristics (tilakkhaṇa), and thus becomes oppressed by the power of the suffering of the round. In this way, for him, the birth of the aggregates (khandhajāti) which is subject to transformation becomes the cause of the suffering of the round. Being oppressed by the suffering of the round, he develops successive faith and goes forth from the household life into homelessness. In this way, for him, the suffering of the round is the cause of successive faith. Not being satisfied with mere ordination, during the period before completing five rains...
52:
That son of good family, taking dependence (nissaya) and fulfilling his duties and practices, masters the two codes of monastic rules (mātikā), learns the Vinaya procedures, and without having any doubts until reaching Arahantship, takes a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), lives in the forest, and exerts himself in objects such as the earth kasina. Based on that meditation subject, weak rapture (pīti) arises in him. At that time, gladness (pāmojja) based on faith arises, and that gladness supports strong rapture. Strong rapture supports the tranquility (passaddhi) of the heat of defilements; that tranquility supports the happiness (sukha) that precedes absorption (appanā); and that happiness supports the concentration of the foundational jhana (pādakajjhāna-samādhi). Having made the mind fit for insight through that concentration, he exerts himself with tender insight (taruṇa-vipassanā). Thus, the concentration of the foundational jhana supports tender insight; tender insight supports powerful insight; powerful insight supports the Path (magga); the Path supports liberation which is the Fruit (phala-vimutti); and liberation which is the Fruit supports reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇāñāṇa). In this way, just as the flow of rainwater gradually fills the great ocean, so should be understood the time when the Arahant who has destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava) remains having filled the ocean of liberation.
The third sutta is finished.

## 4. Aññatitthiyasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, 'pāvisi' means he entered for alms. Although the Venerable Sāriputta had not yet entered the city of Rājagaha, it is said thus because he had set out with the intention, 'I will enter for alms.' For example, a man who has set out to go to a village, though he has not yet reached it, is said to have 'gone to the village' when someone asks, 'Where is so-and-so?' 'Atippago' means that on that day, the Elder had set out at a very early time. Monks who set out very early tend to engage in proliferation (papañca) at the Bodhi terrace, the Cetiya terrace, or the place for putting on robes until the time for the alms round arrives. But the Elder, thinking, 'Until the time for the alms round, I will have a word or two with the wanderers,' the thought occurred to him: 'What if I were to go (to the wanderers)?' 'Paribbājakānaṃ ārāmo' means that the park was situated between the Southern Gate and the Veḷuvana Monastery. 'Idha' refers to these four doctrines. 'Kiṃvādī kimakkhāyī' means they ask, 'What does he say? What does he teach? What is the view of the ascetic Gotama in this matter?' 'Dhammassa cānudhammaṃ vyākareyyāma' means we would speak a reason that is in accordance with the reason stated by the Blessed Gotama. 'Sahadhammiko vādānu pāto' means that since there is a reason along with the reason stated by others, how could any reason deserving of censure by the wise come into the sequence of the ascetic Gotama's doctrine even in the slightest? This is what is meant: How could there be any ground for reproach in the doctrine of the ascetic Gotama in any way whatsoever?
53:
"They say, 'Suffering arises due to contact'" means they are speaking in this manner. "Therein" refers to those four views. "Indeed, for them, there is no [suffering] apart from contact" is a supporting statement that fulfills the admission that "that [suffering] also arises due to contact." Because there is no experience of suffering without contact, it should be understood that "that [suffering] also arises due to contact"; this is the intended meaning here.

"Excellent, excellent, Ānanda"—this word of praise was given to the Elder Sāriputta, but the Blessed One addressed it together with the Elder Ānanda. In the phrase "Ekamidāhaṃ," "idha" is merely a particle; it means "at one time." This was said to show: "Not only did Sāriputta enter Rājagaha, I also entered. Not only did this thought occur to Sāriputta, it also occurred to Me. And not only did such a conversation with the wanderers happen to Sāriputta, it has also happened to Me before."

"Wonderful, marvelous"—both of these terms express astonishment. Here is the word-definition: "Acchariya" is that which is worthy of a snap of the fingers. "Abbhuta" is that which has become extraordinary, never having happened before. "With a single word" means with this single phrase: "Suffering arises due to contact." By this phrase, the meaning of rejecting all [other] views is stated. "This very meaning" refers to this meaning of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda), that "suffering arises due to contact." "Let that very [meaning] be clear here" means let that very meaning be manifest here. Now, the Elder, wishing to show the depth of that meaning and its profound appearance through the discourse on Dependent Origination starting with aging and death, said, "Venerable Sir, if [they were to ask] me..." and so on. Taking the very term 'contact' (phassa) which was the root from which the talk arose, and wishing to show the cessation (vivaṭṭa), he said, "Only because of the six bases of contact..." and so on. The remaining words are clear. The explanation of the fourth sutta ends.

## 5. Bhūmijhasutta-vaṇṇanā
