25-26. In the fifth sutta, "Bhūmija" is the name of that Elder. The rest here should be understood in the same way as stated in the previous sutta. However, this is the distinction: because this pleasure and pain do not arise solely due to contact, but are also produced by what is done by the body, by speech, and by the mind; done by oneself, or by another; done consciously, or unconsciously. Therefore, to show other specific conditions for that pleasure and pain, He said, "Ānanda, when there is the body..." and so on. "Kāyasañcetanāhetu" means due to the volition (cetanā) arising at the body-door. The same method applies to verbal volition and mental volition. Here, at the body-door, one obtains 20 volitions by way of sense-sphere wholesome and unwholesome [states]. At the speech-door, likewise, one obtains 20 volitions. At the mind-door, one obtains 29 volitions: 9 unwholesome volitions and 17 sense-sphere and fine-material/immaterial sphere wholesome volitions. Thus, 69 volitions arise at the three doors. The Blessed One showed the resultant pleasure and pain which have those 69 volitions as their condition. The phrase "And due to ignorance..." is to show the cause of those volitions.
54:
By way of sense-sphere wholesome and unwholesome [states], twenty volitions are obtained at the body-door; likewise at the speech-door. At the mind-door, however, twenty-nine volitions are obtained along with nine unwholesome volitions and seventeen sense-sphere, fine-material, and immaterial-sphere wholesome volitions. Thus, there are a total of sixty-nine volitions at the three doors. The Blessed One showed the resultant pleasure and pain conditioned by those volitions. The phrase "And due to ignorance" was said to show that those volitions also have ignorance (avijjā) as their condition. Because one performs those bodily formations, verbal formations, and mental formations—which have the aforementioned distinctions of volition—by oneself with an unprompted (asaṅkhārika) mind without being urged by others, or performs them with a prompted (sasaṅkhārika) mind when urged by others. One performs them while knowing the action and the result, thinking, "If I do such an action, such a result of that action will occur." Or, like children who imitate their parents when they perform acts such as worshiping a stupa, one performs them knowing only the act itself but not knowing the result, [not thinking] "This will be the result of this action." Therefore, to show those distinctions of volition, He said, "Ānanda, that person either by himself conditions that bodily formation..." and so on.

"Ānanda, in these things" refers to the two hundred and seventy-six volitional states mentioned in the four instances such as "Ānanda, either by himself... that bodily formation." In these states, ignorance follows by way of decisive support (upanissaya). Indeed, all of them are included right here in the phrase "formations conditioned by ignorance" (avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā). Now, wishing to show the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa), He said, "But through the [fading away and cessation] of ignorance..." and so on. "That body does not exist" means when there is a body, internal pleasure and pain conditioned by bodily volition arise; that body no longer exists [for the Arahant]. The same method should be understood for speech and mind. Alternatively, "body" means the body of volition, "speech" is the speech of volition, and "mind" is just the karmic mind. Or, the body which is the door is called "body." The same method applies to speech and mind. An Arahant worships a stupa, recites the Dhamma, and attends to a meditation subject; yet, why is it said that for that Arahant, the body and so on do not exist? Because they do not produce results (avipākatta). Indeed, the action performed by an Arahant is neither wholesome nor unwholesome. Having no result, it stands merely as functional (kiriya). Therefore, it is said that for that Arahant, those [factors] such as the body do not exist.

In the phrases such as "That action is not a field," it is not a field in the sense of growth; it is not a site in the sense of a foundation; it is not a base (āyatana) in the sense of a condition; it is not a locus (adhikaraṇa) in the sense of a cause. Indeed, the internal [pleasure and pain] which have bodily volition as their root...
55:
Pleasure and pain may arise; because that volition (of body, speech, and mind) lacks these meanings such as growth (virūhana) and so on, it is not the field (khetta), nor the site (vatthu), nor the source (āyatana), nor the occasion (adhikaraṇa) for that pleasure and pain. In this sutta, among the states such as feeling, only pleasure and pain are spoken of, and that pleasure and pain is only feeling which is a resultant (vipāka). The fifth sutta is finished.

The sixth, the Upavāṇa Sutta, is clear in meaning. In this sutta, however, only the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha) is spoken of. The sixth sutta is finished.

## 7. Paccaya Sutta Vaṇṇanā

27-28. In the seventh sutta, taking the final term among the states taught in sequence (such as ignorance, etc.), it is said: "And what, bhikkhus, is aging and death?" and so on. "Thus he knows the cause" means he knows the cause in this manner by way of the Truth of Suffering (dukkha-sacca). The origination of the cause (paccaya-samudaya) and so on should also be understood only by way of the Truth of Origination (samudaya-sacca) and the others. "Possessed of vision" (diṭṭhisampanna) means being endowed with the Path-view (maggadiṭṭhi). "Possessed of seeing" (dassanasampanna) is just a synonym for that same term. "Has come to this true Dhamma" means he has come to the true Dhamma of the Path. "He sees" means he sees only the true Dhamma of the Path (through the knowledge of reviewing). "With trainee's knowledge" (sekkhena ñāṇena) means only with the Path-knowledge. "With trainee's true knowledge" (sekkhāya vijjāya) means only with the Path-wisdom. "Has entered the stream of Dhamma" means he has entered the stream of Dhamma (dhammasota) known as the Path. "Noble one" (ariya) means one who has transcended the level of a worldling. "One with penetrative wisdom" (nibbedhikapañño) means one endowed with wisdom that penetrates the Four Noble Truths. "Stands knocking at the door of the Deathless" means he stands having reached the Noble Path, which is the entry door to the Deathless called Nibbāna. The eighth sutta is clear in meaning. The seventh and eighth suttas are finished.

## 9. Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Sutta Vaṇṇanā

29-30. The ninth sutta was taught according to the inclination of the bhikkhus who recite the syllables and phrases (akkhara-bhāṇaka). For they are able to penetrate the meaning when it is spoken by adding the prefix 'pari'. The ninth sutta is finished.

In the tenth sutta, everything is clear. In these two suttas, only the penetration of the Four Noble Truths is spoken of. The tenth sutta is finished.

## The Third Chapter: Dasabala
56:
## 4. Kaḷārakhattiya Vagga
## 1. Bhūta Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the first sutta of the Kaḷārakhattiya Vagga, the Ajitapañha Sutta, 'ajitapañhe' means in the question asked by the youth Ajita. 'Saṅkhātadhammāse' refers to those who have the truths fully understood, weighed, and crossed over. 'Sekkhā' refers to the seven types of trainees. 'Puthu' is said in reference to those same seven trainees by way of common usage. 'Idha' means in this Dispensation (sāsana). 'Nipako' is called so because he is endowed with wisdom, which is called 'nepakka'; it is a request saying, "May you, who are wise, speak." 'Iriyaṃ' refers to occurrence, conduct, resort, dwelling, and practice. 'Mārisa' is an address to the Blessed One. "O Wise One, Dear Sir, please tell me the practice of the trainees and of the taintless Arahants who have fully understood the truths, as asked by me"—this is the summary of the meaning of the verse.

In the phrase 'tuṇhī ahosi' (he remained silent), why did he remain silent even though asked three times? Was he doubtful about the question, or was he doubtful about the [Buddha's] intention? He was not doubtful about the question, but only about the intention. This thought occurred to the Venerable Sāriputta: "The Teacher wishes me to explain the practice for reaching the Path of the trainees and non-trainees. And that practice can be explained by many means, such as by way of the aggregates, elements, sense bases, or dependent origination. How should I explain it so that I can capture the Teacher's intention?" Then the Teacher reflected: "Except for me, there is no other disciple who wanders taking the bowl who is equal to Sāriputta in wisdom. Yet this Sāriputta remains silent even though I have asked the question three times. Is he doubtful about the question, or is he doubtful about my intention?" Then, knowing that he was doubtful about the intention, and wishing to give a lead for answering the question, He said: "Sāriputta, do you see this that has come to be (bhūtaṃ)?"

In that text, 'bhūtaṃ' means what has arisen or been produced; it is a name for the five aggregates which are conditioned. Thus the Teacher gives a lead to the Elder, saying, "Sāriputta, speak on this question by way of the five aggregates." As soon as the lead was given, the way to answer the question appeared to the Elder in hundreds and thousands of methods, like the great ocean appearing as a single open expanse to a man standing on the shore. Then, wishing to answer it, he said: "Venerable Sir, this that has come to be, the five aggregates..." and so on. In that text, 'bhūtaṃ idaṃ' refers to these five aggregates that have been produced. 'Sammapaññāya passati' means he sees clearly with Path-wisdom together with insight (vipassanā). 'Paṭipanno hoti' means he is one who practices for the sake of the fruit of disenchantment (nibbidā) and so on, starting from virtue up to the Path of Arahatship.

Why was the phrase 'yadāhārasambhūtaṃ' (what has come to be from nutriment) spoken? Because the five aggregates exist depending on a cause, the Teacher said "this which is produced from nutriment..." wishing to show that cause as 'sambhava' (source). By this means, the Teacher also taught the practice of the trainees. 'Tadāhāranirodhā' means because of the cessation of those causes. Why was this spoken? Because the five aggregates cease due to the cessation of causal conditions, He said this wishing to show that cessation of conditions as 'āhāra-nirodha-sambhava'. By this means also, He taught the practice of the trainee. It should be understood that all terms such as 'nibbidā' (disenchantment) are words expressing the cause. 'Anupādāya' means liberation without clinging to any state at all through the four types of clinging, such as clinging to sensual pleasures. With the words "Sādhu, Sādhu," He expressed appreciation for the Elder's answer, and He Himself...
57:
He practices for the sake of the knowledge of disenchantment (*nibbidā-ñāṇa*) and so forth, up to the path of arahantship. Why was this statement, "This (five aggregates) is originated from nutriment," undertaken? This group of five aggregates exists dependent on nutriment (cause); therefore, this statement was undertaken to show those five aggregates by naming them "originated from nutriment" (*āhāra-sambhava*). In this way, by this method, the practice of the learners (*sekha*) is also spoken of.

"Due to the cessation of that nutriment" means due to the cessation of those nutriments (causes). Why was this statement undertaken? That group of five aggregates ceases due to the cessation of nutriment; therefore, this statement was undertaken to show those five aggregates by naming them "originated from the cessation of nutriment" (*āhāra-nirodha-sambhava*). In this way, by this method, the practice of the learner is also spoken of. It should be understood that all terms such as disenchantment (*nibbidā*) and so forth are words that express the cause. "One liberated without clinging" (*anupādā vimutto*) means being liberated without clinging to any phenomenon through the four types of clinging (*upādāna*). With the words "Sadhu, Sadhu," the Buddha expressed delight in the Elder's explanation, and wishing to explain it in the same way Himself, He spoke again starting with the words "This is true" (*bhūtamidaṃ*). The commentary on the first sutta ends.

## 2. Commentary on the Kaḷāra Sutta

In the second sutta, "Kaḷāra Khattiya" is the name of that Elder. His teeth were of an uneven shape; therefore, he was called "Kaḷāra." "One who returns to the lower" (*hīnāyāvatta*) means returning to the lower state of a householder. "Did not obtain relief" (*assāsamalattha*) means he certainly did not obtain relief, a refuge, or a foundation; it shows that he certainly did not obtain the three paths and the three fruits. If he had obtained those paths and fruits, he would not have renounced the training and returned to the lower life of a householder; this is the Elder's intention.

"Friend, I certainly do not doubt" means "Friend, I do not doubt whether I have reached relief (foundation) or not." For the Elder Sāriputta, the Knowledge of a Disciple's Perfection (*sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa*) is the foundation; therefore, that Elder does not doubt. By the words "But in the future, friend," he asks about the attainment of arahantship, saying, "In the future, has rebirth been destroyed for you, or has it not been destroyed?" By the words "Friend, I do not doubt," the Elder shows that he has no doubt regarding that attainment of arahantship.

"Approached where the Blessed One was" means he approached thinking, "I will report this matter I have heard to the Blessed One." "The highest knowledge was declared" means arahantship was declared. "Birth is exhausted"—the Elder Sāriputta did not directly declare it with these exact words. This Elder Kaḷāra Khattiya, being joyful and confident, presented and reported it using these phrases. "He addressed a certain monk"—hearing those words, the Teacher thought: "Sāriputta is wise and possesses deep wisdom. He would not declare it in such a way as reported by this monk for any reason. But even if briefly, the problem..."
58:
(Even if briefly), the problem will be answered. Thinking, "I will have that Sāriputta called and make him answer the problem," He addressed a certain monk.

"Sāriputta, if you..." Regarding this statement, the Blessed One thought, "This Sāriputta will not declare the highest knowledge (*aññā*) by his own nature. I will ask this question; while answering that question, he will declare the highest knowledge." Desiring him to declare the highest knowledge, He asked in this way. "Friend, what is the source of birth?" means "Friend, this thing called birth occurs because of a certain cause (namely, kamma-bhava); when that cause is exhausted, birth's cause being exhausted, the effect known as birth is exhausted." This is the meaning to be understood. Here too, although the Elder was without doubt regarding the question, he was uncertain about the Blessed One's intention. The Elder thought, "The highest knowledge (*aññā*) can be declared through many reasons such as the exhaustion of craving, the exhaustion of clinging, the exhaustion of becoming, the exhaustion of causes, and the exhaustion of defilements. How should I speak so that I may capture the Blessed One's intention?"

Although he was thus uncertain about the intention, he answered by way of dependent origination (*paṭiccasamuppāda*) without setting aside the question. The Teacher also wished him to answer specifically by way of dependent origination; therefore, while answering, the Elder captured the intention. At 그 moment, he knew, "I have captured the Teacher's intention." Then, the answering of the question appeared to the Elder through hundreds and thousands of methods. It should be understood that because the Blessed One asked the question further, He approved of that explanation.

Why was this statement, "How is it known by you?" undertaken? It was to make him utter a lion's roar (*sīhanāda*) in his own domain. It is heard that while the Vedanāpariggaha Sutta was being preached to the wanderer Dīghanakha at the entrance of the Sūkarakhata Cave, the Elder stood fanning the Teacher with a fan, and by discerning the three types of feelings, he attained the Knowledge of a Disciple's Perfection (*sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa*); this is the Elder's own domain. The Teacher asked this question intending that, standing in this domain of his, he would utter a lion's roar. "Impermanent" (*anicca*) means impermanent because of the nature of non-existence after having come to be. In the phrase "Whatever is impermanent, that is suffering," although pleasant feeling is pleasant while it persists and is suffering when it changes, and painful feeling is painful while it persists and is pleasant when it changes, and neither-painful-nor-pleasant feeling is pleasant when known and painful when not known—yet, by the extreme of changeability (*vipariṇāma*), all feelings are indeed called suffering. "It is known" means that because the three feelings are thus known as suffering, it shows that the craving that exists therein no longer persists.
59:
"Sādhu Sādhu" (Well done, well done) is an expression of delight in the Elder's discernment of feelings. Although the Elder did not explicitly state whether feelings are one, two, three, or four, he understood the classification of three feelings according to the method taught. Therefore, the Blessed One, delighting the Elder, spoke thus. The Blessed One spoke the word "dukkhasmiṃ" (in suffering) with this intention: "Sāriputta, the answer you gave, 'For this reason, craving does not persist in feelings,' is well-answered. However, by analyzing them as 'three feelings,' you have made it very elaborate. Even if you had answered 'in suffering,' it would still have been well-answered for you. This is because by merely knowing that whatever is felt is suffering, craving cannot persist in feelings."

"Kathaṃ vimokkhā" means "What kind of liberations?" or "By what kind of liberation did you declare the fruit of Arahantship?" "Ajjhattaṃ vimokkhā" means by internal liberation, by attaining the fruit of Arahantship through the grasping of internal formations (ajjhatta-saṅkhāra). In this regard, a group of four should be understood: focusing internally and emerging internally, focusing internally and emerging externally, focusing externally and emerging externally, and focusing externally and emerging internally. This is because by focusing internally, external phenomena should also be contemplated; and by focusing externally, internal phenomena should also be contemplated. Therefore, a certain monk applies his knowledge to internal formations, defines those formations, and then applies his knowledge externally. Having grasped external formations, he again applies his knowledge internally. While he is contemplating internal formations, the emergence of the Path (maggavuṭṭhāna) occurs. This is called "focusing internally and emerging internally." Another monk applies his knowledge to internal formations, defines them, and then applies his knowledge externally. While he is contemplating external formations, the emergence of the Path occurs. This is called "focusing internally and emerging externally." Another monk applies his knowledge to external formations, defines them, and then applies his knowledge internally. Having grasped internal formations, he again applies his knowledge externally. While he is contemplating external formations, the emergence of the Path occurs. This is called "focusing externally and emerging externally." Another monk applies his knowledge to external formations, defines them, and then applies his knowledge internally. While he is contemplating internal formations, the emergence of the Path occurs. This is called "focusing externally and emerging internally." Among these four, the Elder, wishing to show that "I reached Arahantship through the emergence of the Path while grasping and defining internal formations," said, "Friend, I (reached Arahantship) through internal liberation."
60:
"Sabbupādānakkhayā" means due to the destruction of all four types of clinging (upādāna). "Tathā sato viharāmi" means "I dwell endowed with mindfulness because of the destruction of those clingings." "Yathā sataṃ viharantaṃ" means "Me, who dwells endowed with mindfulness for such a reason." "Āsavā nānussavanti" means that the taints such as the taint of sensual desire (kāmāsava), which have the nature of flowing into, constantly leaking, and arising in the six sense bases and six sense objects—starting from the eye into forms—do not follow into the mental continuum, do not increase, and do not arise in me. "Attānañca nāvajānāmi" means not looking down upon or perceiving oneself as inferior. By this statement, the abandonment of inferiority conceit (omāna) is mentioned. When this occurs, wisdom becomes clear and decisive. "Samaṇena" means "by the Monk who is the Buddha." Among those four taints, I have no doubt regarding their specific nature, such as "Which is the taint of sensual desire? Which is the taint of existence? Which is the taint of views? Which is the taint of ignorance?" nor regarding their numerical classification as "the four taints." "Te me pahīnā" means "I do not doubt those taints; they have been abandoned by me," thus not allowing doubt to arise. The Blessed One said this, wishing to show His intention: "By answering in this way, you would have answered well; however, by saying words such as 'Friend, I have internal liberation,' you have made it very elaborate."

"Uṭṭhāyāsanā vihāraṃ pāvisi" means that He rose from the prepared noble Buddha-seat and entered the Great Fragrant Chamber (Mahāgandhakuṭi) within the monastery before the assembly of monks dispersed. Why? When Buddhas rise from their seats and enter the Fragrant Chamber before the discourse is finished and before the assembly has dispersed, they do so either to praise a person or to praise the Dhamma. In the case of entering to praise a person, the Teacher thought: "This summary (uddesa) taught by Me in brief and not yet analyzed in detail will be taken up by the monks who receive the Dhamma, and they will approach Ānanda or Kaccāyana to ask about it. Those Elders will explain it in accordance with My knowledge. Then, the monks who receive the Dhamma will ask Me again. At that time, I will praise those individuals, saying, 'Monks, it was well-spoken by Ānanda; it was well-spoken by Kaccāyana. If you were to ask Me the meaning of this, I would answer it in the same way.' Then, having developed respect for them, the monks will approach those Elders. Those Elders will also engage the monks in the meaning and the Dhamma. The monks thus engaged will fulfill the three trainings (sikkhā) and bring an end to suffering."
61:
Alternatively, the Blessed One had this thought: "When I have departed, this Sāriputta will perform a display of his own power by praising [me]. Then, I too shall praise him in the same way. Hearing my words of praise, the monks, being filled with respect, will consider that Sāriputta should be approached, his words should be listened to, and he should be trusted. That will lead to their long-term welfare and happiness." Thus, for the sake of praising the Dhamma, the Buddha, as he entered [the monastery], thought in the same way as he had thought in the Dhammadāyāda Sutta.

In that Dhammadāyāda Sutta, the Blessed One had this thought: "When I have entered the monastery, Sāriputta, sitting in this very assembly, will teach the Dhamma, censuring the heir to material things and praising the heir to the Dhamma. Thus, this teaching, taught with a single intention by both of us, will be supreme and weighty, like a stone parasol."

In this sutta, however, desiring to uplift and make Venerable Sāriputta known, he rose from his seat and entered the monastery for the sake of praising the person. In such instances, it should be understood that the Blessed One disappears from his very seat and enters the monastery by the speed of his mind. If he were to go by the movement of his body, the entire assembly would follow him; if that assembly were once dispersed, it would be difficult to reassemble. Therefore, the Blessed One entered with an invisible body by the speed of mind alone.

When the Blessed One had thus entered, Venerable Sāriputta, desiring to roar a lion's roar in accordance with the Blessed One's intention, addressed the monks regarding the Blessed One who had not long departed. "Pubbe appaṭisaṃviditaṃ" means that which I did not know or see before, thinking "he will ask this." "Paṭhamaṃ pañhaṃ" refers to this first question: "Friend Sāriputta, if they were to ask you, 'Friend Sāriputta, knowing how and seeing how do you declare the realization of the destruction of birth?'" "Dandhāyitattaṃ" means slowness or lack of quickness for the sake of knowing the Teacher's intention. "Paṭhamaṃ pañhaṃ anumodi" refers to the Blessed One's approval of the first answer when he asked the second question: "Friend Sāriputta, what is the cause of birth?"—thus approving the first answer given as "Friend, birth is caused by this."

"Etadahosi" means that when the Blessed One expressed approval, this thought occurred because the question became clear through hundreds and thousands of methods as if in a single open space. "Divasampāhaṃ bhagavato etamatthaṃ vyākareyyaṃ" means "I could explain this meaning to the Blessed One for the whole day."
62:
"If asked about the meaning of Dependent Origination (Paṭiccasamuppāda), I could answer for the whole day using different words and phrases (synonyms)," [Venerable Sāriputta said]. "Approached the Blessed One" means a thought occurred to that monk: "The Elder roars a great lion's roar; this is a good reason; I will report this to the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala)." Therefore, he approached the Blessed One.

"Monks, that dhamma-dhātu of Sāriputta..."—here, dhamma-dhātu is the disciple's perfection of knowledge (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa) capable of seeing the open nature of the causal condition (paccayākāra). The disciple's perfection of knowledge follows the way of omniscience (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa). Just as past, future, and present phenomena are clear to the Buddhas' omniscience, so the Elder's disciple-perfection-knowledge knows all phenomena within the scope of a disciple's knowledge. The commentary on the second sutta is finished.

## 3. Ñāṇavatthu Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, "Listen to that" means listen to that teaching on the bases of knowledge (ñāṇavatthu). Here, it should be understood that knowledge itself is the basis of knowledge. Regarding the four [knowledges] such as "knowledge of aging and death," the first knowledge involves four types: knowledge based on hearing (savanamaya-ñāṇa), contemplation (sammasana-ñāṇa), penetration (paṭivedha-ñāṇa), and reviewing (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa). The second is the same. The third and fourth, however, exclude contemplation (sammasana-ñāṇa) and thus consist of only three types. Indeed, there is no such thing as contemplation (sammasana) in supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma). The same method applies to the passages such as "knowledge of birth."

"By this Dhamma" means by the Four Noble Truths or by the Dhamma of path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). Among the terms such as "seen," "seen" means seen with the eye of knowledge; "known" means known by wisdom; "timeless" (akālika) means giving results immediately after penetration without the passage of even a little time; "attained" means reached; "plunged into" means thoroughly entered and distinguished by wisdom. "Applying the method to the past and future" means taking the method to the past and future through the way of "whoever they were," etc. Here, it is not possible to apply the method to the past and future by the Four Noble Truths or path-knowledge alone. It should be understood that the method is applied by the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇa-ñāṇa) that arises after the Four Noble Truths have been penetrated by path-knowledge. "They understood specifically" means they knew with higher knowledge. "As I know now" means just as I know now by the power of the Four Noble Truths. "Anvaye ñāṇaṃ" (inferential knowledge) is the knowledge that follows the Dhamma-knowledge; this is a name for reviewing knowledge. "Dhamme ñāṇaṃ" (knowledge of the Dhamma) is path-knowledge. In this sutta, the ground of the trainee (sekkha-bhūmi) of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) is taught. The commentary on the third sutta is finished.
63:
## 4. Dutiyañāṇavatthusutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, "sattasattari" refers to seven and seventy (seventy-seven). It is heard that those monks were reciters of the phrasing (byañjanabhāṇaka); when a teaching is delivered with an abundance of phrasing, they are able to penetrate the meaning. Therefore, the Buddha taught this sutta according to their inclination. "Dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa" refers to the knowledge regarding the mode of conditions (paccayākāra). Because the mode of conditions is the cause for the occurrence and stability of phenomena (dhamma), it is called "dhammaṭṭhiti." The knowledge that arises in this mode of conditions is called dhammaṭṭhiti-knowledge. This name is also a designation for that very knowledge which arises by way of the seventy-seven bases of knowledge. "Khayadhamma" means having the nature of reaching destruction. "Vayadhamma" means having the nature of reaching decay. "Virāgadhamma" means having the nature of dispassion. "Nirodhadhamma" means having the nature of cessation. Regarding "sattasattari," seventy-seven bases of knowledge are to be understood by applying seven aspects to each of the eleven factors, such as aging and death. In this sutta, insight (vipassanā) and counter-insight (paṭivipassanā) are taught. The fourth sutta ends.

## 5. Avijjāpaccayasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, the Blessed One stopped the teaching at this point with the words "samudayo hoti" (there is an origin). Why did He stop? It was to give an opportunity to one of wrong view. In the Buddha's assembly, there was a person of wrong view with a mind intent on criticism; the Buddha stopped the teaching to give him an opportunity, thinking, "He will ask a question, and then I shall answer him." "No kallo pañho" means an improper question, a poorly asked question. Is not the question "Venerable Sir, what is aging and death?" a well-asked question? Although it might be a well-asked question, just as when a lump of dung the size of an emblic myrobalan is placed on top of excellent food served in a golden bowl worth a hundred thousand, all that food becomes disgusting and must be discarded; in the same way, because of the lump of dung which is the phrase of the wrong view assuming the existence of a being (sattūpaladdhivāda)—namely, "For whom is this aging and death?"—this entire question becomes a bad question.

"Brahmacariyavāsa" means the living of the Noble Path. For one who holds the view "that life is that body," he assumes that "when life is cut off, the body is cut off; when the body is cut off, life is cut off." For one who assumes thus, that view is called annihilationism (ucchedadiṭṭhi) because it assumes that "the being is annihilated." If one were to assume that "only formations (saṅkhāra) arise and cease," that would be called right view (sammādiṭṭhi) within the Dispensation. This Noble Path, while causing the cessation of the round of existence (vaṭṭa) and utterly cutting off the round...
64:
(The Noble Path) arises. If that round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) were to cease in the continuity of one who holds the view of annihilation (ucchedadiṭṭhi) without the development of the path, then the development of the path would be useless. Therefore, it is said, "The holy life cannot be lived."

In the second method, for whoever holds the view "the soul (jīva) is one thing, the body (sarīra) is another," that person takes it thus: "The body perishes only in this life, but the soul does not perish; the soul goes as it pleases like a bird released from a cage." For one who takes it thus, that view is called eternalism (sassatadiṭṭhi) because it is held that "the soul goes from this world to the next world." This Noble Path also arises while causing the round of rebirth in the three planes (tebhūmakavaṭṭa) to cease. If even a single formation (saṅkhāra) were permanent (nicca), stable (dhuva), or eternal (sassata), the path, even if it arose, would not be able to stop the round of rebirth; thus, the development of the path would be useless. Therefore, it is said, "Monks, when there is the view that the soul is one thing and the body is another, the holy life cannot be lived."

All terms such as 'visūkāyika' (distortion) are merely synonyms for wrong view (micchādiṭṭhi). That wrong view is called 'visūkāyika' because it covers and blocks itself like a thorn against the penetration of right view (sammādiṭṭhi). It is called 'visevita' because it proceeds in opposition to right view without following it. It is called 'vipphandita' (agitation), which is a distorted trembling, because it sometimes grasps the view of annihilation and sometimes the view of eternalism. 'Tālāvatthukatāni' means they are made like a palm stump where leaves and buds cannot grow; furthermore, it means they are made like a palm tree with its head cut off because they do not grow again, or like the place where a palm tree has been uprooted along with its roots. 'Anabhāvaṅkatāni' means they are made to not arise again. The fifth sutta is finished.

## 6. Dutiya-avijjāpaccayasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the sixth sutta, regarding the words "Monks, if someone should say so," there was a person in that assembly who held a certain view and wished to ask a question; however, because he was not confident by nature, he was unable to stand up and ask the Dasabala (the Buddha). Therefore, knowing his inclination, the Teacher, wishing to ask and answer the question himself, spoke in this way. The sixth sutta is finished.
65:
## 7. Commentary on the Natumha Sutta
In the commentary on the seventh sutta, the Natumha Sutta, "na tumhākaṃ" (it is not yours) means that if there were a self (attā), there would be what is called "belonging to a self" (attaniya). Since the self itself does not exist, He said, "it is not yours." "Nor does it belong to others" means that "other" refers to the self of others; if that self existed, there would be what is called "belonging to others." Since that self also does not exist, He said, "nor does it belong to others."

"Monks, this is old kamma" means that this body is not merely old kamma itself, but rather it is a body that has arisen because of old kamma; therefore, it is spoken of in this way by designating it by its cause. The words beginning with "abhisaṅkhata" (constructed) are spoken because of their similarity to the past through the usage of the term "kamma." In this context, the meaning is: "abhisaṅkhata" should be understood as that which is conditioned by causes (paccaya). "Abhisañcetayita" (volitioned) should be understood as a state having volition (cetanā) as its cause or root. "Vedaniya" (to be felt) should be understood as the basis for experiencing feeling (vedanā). The seventh sutta is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Cetanā Sutta
In the commentary on the eighth sutta, the Cetanā Sutta, "Monks, what one intends (ceteti)" means what volition one brings about or sets in motion. "What one plans (pakappeti)" means what planning one constantly performs or sets in motion. "What lies latent (anuseti)" means what underlying tendency (anusaya) one causes to lie latent or sets in motion. Here, by the word "ceteti," wholesome and unwholesome volitions belonging to the three planes (tebhūmaka) are taken. By the word "pakappeti," the schemes of craving (taṇhā) and views (diṭṭhi) occurring in the eight types of consciousness accompanied by greed are taken. By the word "anuseti," the underlying tendency is taken by way of conascence (sahajāta) and decisive support (upanissaya) of the twelve volitions.

"This becomes an object" means (since the arising of kamma-consciousness cannot be prevented when the group of states such as volition exists) this group of states such as volition is the condition (paccaya). In this sutta, the condition itself is intended by the term "object" (ārammaṇa). "For the standing of consciousness" means for the purpose of the persistence of kamma-consciousness. "When there is an object" means when that condition exists. "It is a support for consciousness" means it is the station for that kamma-consciousness. When that kamma-consciousness is established, "when it grows" means when the root has been produced, being capable of pulling rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi) after having instigated kamma. "The production of renewed existence" means the specific arising known as renewed existence (punabbhava).
66:
"Monks, if one does not intend" (no ce ceteti)—by this, the moment of non-occurrence of volition belonging to the three planes is stated. "If one does not plan" (no ce pakappeti)—by this, the moment of non-occurrence of planning through craving and views (is stated). Nevertheless, "if it lies latent" (atha ce anuseti)—by this, the underlying tendency (anusaya) that has not yet been fully abandoned in the resultant (vipāka) consciousnesses of the three planes, in the small functional (paritta-kiriya) consciousnesses, and in matter (rūpa) is taken. "This is an object" means that when the underlying tendency exists, there is no state to prevent the arising of kamma-consciousness; therefore, this collection of underlying tendencies is indeed the condition (paccaya).

In the sentences beginning with "if one does not intend," in the first clause, wholesome and unwholesome volitions of the three planes are excluded. In the second clause, craving and views in the eight types of consciousness rooted in greed are excluded. In the third clause, the underlying tendency that lies latent without being fully abandoned in the aforementioned states is excluded.

Furthermore, to avoid confusion in this context, this fourfold set (catukka) should also be understood: "one intends, one plans, it lies latent"; "one intends, one does not plan, it lies latent"; "one does not intend, one does not plan, it lies latent"; and "one does not intend, one does not plan, it does not lie latent." Among these four, in the first method, the delimitation of states is shown. In the second method, by the word "intends," wholesome volitions of the three planes and four unwholesome volitions are taken. By the word "does not plan," craving and views in the eight types of consciousness rooted in greed are excluded. By the word "lies latent," the underlying tendency is taken by way of decisive support (upanissaya) in the wholesome states of the three planes, and by way of both conascence (sahajāta) and decisive support in the four unwholesome volitions. In the third method, by the word "does not intend," wholesome and unwholesome states of the three planes are excluded. By the word "does not plan," craving and views in the eight types of consciousness rooted in greed are excluded. By the word "lies latent," excluding what is mentioned in the Sutta text, the decisive support that is not yet fully abandoned in the wholesome, unwholesome, resultant, functional states of the three planes, and in matter, is taken. The fourth method is just like the previous one.

"When that [consciousness] is not established" means when that kamma-consciousness does not persist. "When it does not grow" means when the root or sprout capable of pulling rebirth-linking by instigating kamma has not been produced. What is taught here? It is appropriate to say that it teaches the function of the path of Arahantship (arahatta-magga), the completion of the task of an Arahant (khīṇāsava), or the nine supramundane states (lokuttara-dhamma). Among these states, there is one link (sandhi) between consciousness and future renewed existence, one between feeling and craving, and one between existence (bhava) and birth (jāti). The commentary on the eighth sutta is finished.
67:
## 9. Commentary on the Second Cetana Sutta
In the ninth sutta, it should be understood that there is one connection (sandhi) between consciousness and name-and-form, one connection between feeling and craving, and one connection between existence and birth. The ninth sutta is finished.

## 10. Commentary on the Third Cetana Sutta
In the tenth sutta, 'inclination' (nati) refers to craving (taṇhā). That craving is called 'inclination' because of its nature of inclining towards the six sense objects, such as forms, which have a pleasing nature. 'Coming and going' (āgatigati) refers to the occurrence of rebirth-consciousness in the object of kamma and so forth, which is called 'coming' (āgati). Alternatively, when one of the objects among kamma, the sign of kamma (kammanimitta), or the sign of destination (gatinimitta), which are called 'coming' (āgati), appears, it is the occurrence of resultant consciousness by way of rebirth in that object. 'Passing away and reappearing' (cutūpapāta) means that when there is a settling in the rebirth-object, which is the support for rebirth-consciousness in the manner already described, there is the passing away from this life known as 'death' (cuti) and the arising of rebirth in a new life known as 'reappearance' (upapāta); this is called 'passing away and reappearing'. Thus, in this sutta, only one connection of cause and effect is taught between craving, called 'inclination', and the destination (gati) of consciousness, called 'coming and going'. The tenth sutta is finished.

## The Fourth Chapter: Kaḷārakhattiyavagga

## 5. The Householder Chapter (Gahapativagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Sutta on the Five Fears and Enmities
In the first sutta of the Householder Chapter, 'whence' (yato) means 'at which time'. 'Fears and enmities' (bhayāni verāni) refers to the intentions of killing and so forth, which are called 'fears' because they are of a nature that is fearful and productive of enmity. In the phrase 'by the factors of stream-entry' (sotāpattiyangehi), there are two types of factors of stream-entry. Firstly, the factors that lead to the attainment of the path and fruit of stream-entry in the preliminary stage are: 'associating with superior persons, hearing the True Dhamma, wise attention, and practice in accordance with the Dhamma'; these are called factors of stream-entry as they appear in the texts.

The factors of a person who has reached and stands in the path and fruit of stream-entry through the virtues attained are also called the factors of a stream-enterer. This is a designation for unshakeable confidence in the Buddha and so forth. This is the meaning intended here. 'Noble' (ariya) means faultless and without reproach. 'Method' (ñāya) refers both to the knowledge that stands having known the conditionally arisen phenomena and to Dependent Origination itself. Therefore, it is said: 'The method is called Dependent Origination; the Noble Eightfold Path is also called the method.' 'By wisdom' (paññāya) means by insight wisdom that has arisen successively. 'Is well-seen' (sudiṭṭho hoti) means well-seen by way of vision through successive arisings.
68:
In the words beginning with 'one for whom hell is exhausted' (khīṇanirayo), because of the non-arising in that hell in the future, one who considers 'Hell is exhausted for me' is called 'one for whom hell is exhausted'. This method applies to all terms. 'Stream-enterer' (sotāpanno) means one who has entered the stream of the Path. 'Not subject to perdition' (avinipātadhammo) means one who does not have the nature of falling into the states of deprivation. 'Fixed' (niyato) means fixed by the assurance of righteousness known as the first Path. 'Destined for enlightenment' (sambodhiparāyano) means that enlightenment, known as the three higher paths, is my destination; it means one who will certainly awaken to that enlightenment.

'Because of the destruction of life' (pāṇātipātapaccayā) means due to the act of killing living beings. 'Fear and enmity' (bhayaṃ veraṃ) are the same in meaning. This enmity is of two kinds: external (bāhira) and internal (ajjhattika). For instance, if someone's father was killed by another, he thinks, 'It is said that my father was killed by this person; I too will kill him,' and he goes about carrying a sharpened weapon. The intention of enmity that has arisen within him is called 'external enmity' (bāhira-vera). On the other hand, the intention that arises in the other person, 'It is said that this person is going about to kill me; I will kill him first,' is called 'internal enmity' (ajjhattika-vera). Both of these are fears and enmities pertaining only to the present life (diṭṭhadhammika).

In the future life (samparāyika), however, the intention of a hell-warden who, seeing that person arisen in hell, thinks 'I will strike him' and takes up a blazing iron club, is called 'future external enmity'. And the intention that arises in that hell-being, 'This person is coming to strike me who am faultless; I will strike him first,' is called 'future internal enmity'. That external enmity is called 'personal enmity' (puggalavera) in the Commentary. 'Suffering and displeasure' (dukkhaṃ domanassaṃ) are also the same in meaning. Just as in the case of killing, the arising of enmity should be understood in the remaining terms in this manner: 'This person stole my property, committed misconduct with my wife, destroyed my interests by telling lies, or did such a thing while intoxicated with liquor.'

'By unshakeable confidence' (aveccappasādena) means by the unwavering confidence attained through the Path. 'By virtues dear to the Noble Ones' (ariyakantehi) refers to the five precepts. For those virtues are cherished and dear to the Noble Ones. Even when they have gone to another life, the Noble Ones do not abandon those virtues; therefore, they are called 'virtues dear to the Noble Ones'. Whatever else should be said here has already been stated in the 'Explanation of Recollections' (Anussatiniddesa) in the Visuddhimagga. The first sutta is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Second Pañcaverabhaya Sutta
In the second sutta, the only difference is that it was taught to the monks. The second sutta is finished.
69:
## 3. Dukkhasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third discourse, 'dukkhassa' means of the suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha). Regarding the word 'samudaya', there are two types of origin: momentary origin (khaṇikasamudaya) and causal origin (paccayasamudaya). A monk who sees the causal origin also sees the momentary origin; a monk who sees the momentary origin also sees the causal origin. 'Atthangama' (cessation) is also of two types: absolute cessation (accantatthangama) and cessation by breaking up (bhedatthangama). A monk who sees absolute cessation also sees cessation by breaking up; a monk who sees cessation by breaking up also sees absolute cessation. 'Desessāmi' means "I will teach the distinction between the arising and cessation, and the birth and breaking up of the suffering of the round; listen to that Dhamma."

'Paṭicca' means having made a condition by way of support and by way of object. 'Tiṇṇam saṅgati phasso' means contact arises because of the meeting of the three. 'Ayam kho bhikkhave dukkhassa samudayo' means "Monks, this is the arising of the suffering of the round." 'Atthangamo' means breaking up. In this way, the suffering of the round is broken and there is no further rebirth. The third discourse is finished.

## 4. Lokasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fourth discourse, 'lokassa' means of the world of formations (saṅkhāraloka). This is the distinction in this discourse. The fourth discourse is finished.

## 5. Ñātikasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the fifth discourse, 'ñātike' means in the village of the two relatives. 'Giñjakāvasathe' means in the great mansion made of bricks. 'Dhammapariyāyam' means the Dhamma reasoning. 'Upassuti' means a place where one can listen by approaching closely; it means a place where, upon reaching it, one can hear the voice of the Blessed One, and he was standing in that place.

It is said that the monk came to sweep the precinct of the Gandhakuti, but abandoning his work, he stood listening to the sound of the Blessed One's Dhamma. 'Addasā' means that at that time, the Blessed One was reflecting on the Law of Dependent Origination from the beginning, considering, "This arises because of this condition; this arises because of this condition," and it became a single expanse as far as the peak of existence (bhavagga). The Blessed One, having ceased his reflection, performed a verbal recitation and concluded the teaching according to the sequence. Then, while considering, "Did anyone hear this Dhamma discourse?", he saw that monk. Therefore, it is said, "The Blessed One saw him."
70:
"Assosi no" means "Assosi nu" (Did you hear?). Alternatively, "Assosi no" should be understood as "Did you hear us speaking?". In the words beginning with "uggaṇhāhi", the act of studying mentally while remaining silent after hearing is called "uggaṇhāti" (he learns). The act of studying verbally by connecting the sequence of words is called "pariyāpuṇāti" (he masters). The act of making it firm in the flow of the mind by studying in both these ways is called "dhāreti" (he bears in mind). "Atthasaṃhito" means having a meaning based on cause. "Ādibrahmacariyako" means because it is the foundation and beginning of the noble practice of the Path. Thus, in these three discourses—the third, fourth, and fifth—the Blessed One taught only the round (vaṭṭa) and the ending of the round (vivaṭṭa). The fifth discourse is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Aññatarabrāhmaṇa Sutta
In the sixth discourse, "aññataro" refers to a certain brahmin who is not well-known by name. The sixth discourse is finished.

## 7. Commentary on the Jāṇussoṇi Sutta
In the seventh discourse, "Jāṇussoṇi" is the name obtained by virtue of his rank; he was a great chaplain with a wealth of eighty crores. The seventh discourse is finished.

## 8. Commentary on the Lokāyatika Sutta
In the eighth discourse, "lokāyatiko" refers to one who has practiced the Lokāyata, which is a treatise on casuistry (vitanḍa). "Jeṭṭhametaṃ lokāyataṃ" means this view is the primary Lokāyata treatise. "Lokāyataṃ" should also be understood as that which is the cause of the world, the cause of the world of foolish worldlings; it is to be regarded as a view (diṭṭhigata) of limited nature that is mistakenly thought to be great and profound. "Ekattaṃ" is an inquiry: "Is it of a single nature, an eternal nature only?". "Puthuttaṃ" is an inquiry with reference to the view of annihilation (uccheda): "Is it of a diverse nature, different from the previous nature; having first come into being as a deva, human, etc., does it not exist afterwards?". Thus, in this eighth discourse, these two views—"Everything exists" and "Everything is a unity"—are to be known as eternalist views (sassatadiṭṭhi). These two views—"Everything does not exist" and "Everything is a plurality"—are to be known as annihilationist views (ucchedadiṭṭhi). The eighth discourse is finished.

## 9. Commentary on the Ariyasāvaka Sutta
In the ninth discourse, the phrase "kiṃ nu kho" is a demonstration of the manner in which doubt arises. "Samudayati" means it arises. The ninth discourse is finished.
71:
## 10. Dutiya-ariyasāvaka-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth discourse, both methods are taught together. The fact that the method taught in the ninth discourse is included in the tenth is the only distinction between the previous ninth discourse and the tenth; the rest of the meaning is exactly the same as what has been stated. The tenth discourse ends.

## Gahapati-vagga Pañcama

## 6. Dukkha-vagga

## 1. Parivīmaṃsana-sutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first discourse of the Dukkha-vagga, "parivīmaṃsamāno" means while investigating or reflecting. In the phrase "jarāmaraṇaṃ," if it is asked why the single factor of aging and death is taken by saying "anekavidhaṃ nānappakārakaṃ" (of various kinds and manifold), it is because when aging and death are taken, all suffering is already taken. For example, if a man is caught by his topknot, the whole man is captured; in the same way, when aging and death are taken, all suffering is indeed taken. Therefore, having shown all suffering like a man standing and saying, "This various and manifold suffering arises in the world," He took aging and death as if catching that man by his topknot.

"Jarāmaraṇanirodhasāruppagāminī" means the practice that leads to the cessation of aging and death, being similar to it in its state of being free from defilements and its purity. "Tathā paṭipanno ca hoti" means he practices in such a manner that he is said to be one who practices the way suitable for the cessation of aging and death; he is one who practices in that manner. "Anudhammacārī" means he practices or fulfills the practice that follows the Dhamma of Nibbāna. "Dukkhakkhayāya paṭipanno" means he is one who practices for the cessation of the suffering of aging and death, beginning with virtue (sīla). "Saṅkhāranirodhāya" means for the purpose of the cessation of the suffering of formations (saṅkhāra-dukkha). Up to this point, the teaching is spoken as far as Arahatship.

Now, although the teaching should be concluded after showing the reflection on the fruit of Arahatship (phala-paccavekkhaṇā) and the constant abiding (satata-vihāra), why does He take this discourse on the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa-kathā) starting with "avijjāgato"? It is taken to show the round of suffering (vaṭṭa-dukkha) that has been transcended by the Arahant. Furthermore, it should be understood that when the round is restarted and the cessation of the round is taught, there are beings present who can realize the truth, and He takes this based on the inclination of such beings. In that text, "avijjāgato" means...
72:
...one who has gone to ignorance, approached it, or is possessed of it. "Purisapuggala" means a person who is a man. With these two terms, the Buddha speaks a conventional discourse (sammuti-kathā). For the Buddhas, there are two types of discourse: conventional discourse and ultimate discourse (paramattha-kathā). Among them, speech such as "being, person, man, individual, Tissa, Nāga" is called conventional discourse. Speech such as "aggregates, elements, bases" is called ultimate discourse. Even when teaching the ultimate truth, they teach without abandoning the worldly convention (sammuti). Whether those Buddhas teach conventional discourse or ultimate discourse, they teach only the truth. Therefore, it was said:

"The Fully Enlightened One, the best of speakers, declared two truths:
Conventional truth and ultimate truth; a third is not found.
Conventional speech is true as a worldly designation;
Ultimate speech is true as the actual nature of phenomena."

"Puññaṃ ce saṅkhāraṃ" refers to meritorious formations (puññābhisaṅkhāra) which are divided into thirteen types of wholesome intentions (cetanā). "Abhisaṅkharoti" means he performs or constructs. "Puññūpagaṃ hoti viññāṇaṃ" means kamma-consciousness is associated with meritorious kamma, and resultant consciousness (vipāka-viññāṇa) is associated with meritorious results. "Apuññaṃ ce saṅkhāraṃ" means he performs demeritorious formations (apuññābhisaṅkhāra) divided into twelve types of unwholesome intentions. "Āneñjaṃ ce saṅkhāraṃ" refers to imperturbable formations (āneñjābhisaṅkhāra) divided into four types of formless wholesome intentions. "Āneñjūpagaṃ hoti viññāṇaṃ" means kamma-consciousness is associated with imperturbable kamma, and resultant consciousness is associated with imperturbable results. Here, because the three types of kamma-formations are taken, the twelve-linked dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) is already included. By this much, the round of existence (vaṭṭa) is shown.

Now, wishing to show the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa), He said "Yato kho bhikkhave," etc. Therein, "avijjā" is non-knowledge of the Four Noble Truths. "Vijjā" is the knowledge of the path of Arahatship (arahatta-magga-ñāṇa). Here, ignorance is first abandoned, and then knowledge arises. Just as darkness is dispelled by the lighting of a lamp in a night of fourfold darkness, so should the abandoning of ignorance through the arising of knowledge be understood. "Does not cling to anything in the world" means he does not take or misapprehend any phenomenon in the world of aggregates as "mine" and so on. "Being unattached, he is not agitated" means because he does not cling or take, he is not agitated by the agitation of craving or the agitation of fear; the meaning is that he does not crave and does not fear. "By himself alone" (paccattaññeva) means he attains Nibbāna by himself, through his own effort, and not through the power of another.
73:
Why is this statement 'If he feels a pleasant feeling' (so sukhaṃ ce vedanaṃ) initiated? It is initiated to show the 'constant abiding' (satatavihāra) of an Arahant after having shown his 'reviewing knowledge' (paccavekkhaṇāñāṇa). 'Not clung to' (anajjhosita) means not being seized by craving, having swallowed and finished with it. If that is so, why is painful feeling mentioned? Is there anyone who greatly delights in that painful feeling? Yes, there is. Indeed, only one who delights in pleasant feeling is said to delight in painful feeling. This is because when one encounters painful feeling, one longs for pleasant feeling, and also because pleasant feeling itself is 'suffering due to change' (vipariṇāmadukkha).

'Limited to the body' (kāyapariyantika) refers to the five-door feelings (pañcadvārika-vedanā) that occur as long as the physical body, consisting of the five doors, persists. 'Limited to life' (jīvitapariyantika) refers to the mind-door feelings (manodvārika-vedanā) that occur as long as life persists.

Between these two types of feelings, the five-door feeling arises after the mind-door feeling and ceases first. The mind-door feeling arises before the five-door feeling and ceases last. That mind-door feeling, at the moment of rebirth-linking (paṭisandhi), is established only in the heart-base (hadayavatthu). The five-door feeling, occurring during the course of existence (pavatti) by way of the five doors, is extremely powerful in the first stage of life, around the age of twenty, through the power of lust, hatred, and delusion. At the age of fifty, it remains stable without increasing or decreasing. From the age of sixty onwards, it declines, and at the age of eighty or ninety, it becomes weak. At that time, even when others say, 'We have sat and slept together for a long time,' beings tend to say, 'We do not remember.' Even regarding very distinct objects such as visible forms, they say, 'We do not see, we do not hear; we do not know whether a scent is good or bad, whether a taste is sweet or bitter, or whether something is rough or soft.' Thus, for them, the five-door feeling is broken and weak, and only the mind-door feeling continues to occur. That mind-door feeling also gradually declines and, at the time of death, occurs depending only on the edge of the heart-base. As long as this mind-door feeling occurs, the being is said to be alive. When that feeling no longer occurs, the being is said to be dead or ceased.

This meaning should be illustrated by the simile of a large reservoir (lake). For example, a man might construct a large reservoir equipped with five small water-inlets. At first, when it rains, water enters through those five inlets and fills the small hollows and pits within the reservoir. As it rains again and again, the water-inlets are filled, and the water stands covering an area of about half a gāvuta or half a league (yojana), overflowing from various places. Then, when the sluice gates are opened and work is done in the fields, the water flows out. When the crops are ripe, the water flows out and decreases to the point where one might say, 'Let us catch the fish.' The water then remains only in the small hollows and pits in various places. As long as that water remains in the small hollows, it is still referred to as 'there is water in the large reservoir.' But when...
74:
...thereafter, after a few days, the water remains only in the small hollows. As long as that water is in the hollows, it is reckoned as 'there is water in the large reservoir.' But when the water there is cut off, it is said, 'there is no water in the reservoir.' This comparison should be understood in this way:

The time when the water enters through the five channels and fills the hollows when it first rains is like the time when the mind-door feeling is established in the physical base at the first moment of rebirth-linking. The time when the five channels are filled by repeated rain is like the time of the occurrence of the five-door feeling during the course of existence. The overflowing of about half a gāvuta or half a league is like the state of extreme strength of that feeling through lust and so on in the first stage of life at the age of twenty. The time when the full reservoir remains as long as water does not yet exit the reservoir is like the time of the stability of that feeling until the age of fifty. The time when water exits when the sluice gates are opened and agricultural work is performed is like the decline of that feeling from the age of sixty onwards. The time when the water has dropped and a small amount of water remains in the water-channels is like the time of the weakness of the five-door feeling at the age of eighty or ninety. The time when water is established only in the small hollows is like the time of the occurrence of the mind-door feeling depending on the edge of the heart-base. The time when it is said 'there is water in the reservoir' even when there is only a little water in the hollows is like the time when it is said 'the being is alive' as long as that mind-door feeling occurs. Just as when the water in the hollows is cut off it is said 'there is no water in the reservoir,' so too when the mind-door feeling does not occur, it is said 'the being is dead.' It is with reference to this feeling that the Blessed One said, 'feeling a feeling that is at the end of life.'

'With the breaking up of the body' (kāyassa bhedā) means because of the destruction of the body. 'Beyond the exhaustion of life' (jīvitapariyādānā uddhaṃ) means after the end of life. 'Right here' (idheva) means occurring in this very existence without going to the next by way of rebirth. 'Will become cool' (sītībhavissanti) means they will reach a state of being extinguished, free from the vibrations and distress of the process of existence, having the nature of non-occurrence. 'Bodies' (sarīrāni) refers to the bodily remains (relics/bones). 'Will remain' (avasissanti) means they will be left behind.

'From the potter's kiln' (kumbhakārapāka) means from the place where the potter bakes the vessels. 'Should place' (paṭisiṣṣeyyā) means one should set down. 'Potsherds' (kapallāni) refers to the broken pieces of the pot that remain joined with the rim.
75:
"Avasisseyyuṃ" means "they would remain." In this phrase "Evameva kho," the following is a comparison and correlation between the simile and its meaning. The three planes of existence (bhava) should be understood as being like a burning potter's kiln. The practitioner (yogāvacara) should be understood as being like the potter. The knowledge of the Path of Arahantship (arahattamagga-ñāṇa) should be understood as being like the stick used to pull out the pots and vessels from within the kiln. The unconditioned ground of Nibbāna should be understood as being like the level ground. The time when the practitioner, having developed insight (vipassanā) and contemplating the sevenfold groups of materiality (rūpa-sattaka) and immateriality (arūpa-sattaka), finds the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) becoming familiar and clear, obtains suitable weather and other conditions, sits in a single seat, develops insight, reaches the supreme fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala), extracts himself from the four woeful states, and dwells in the unconditioned ground of Nibbāna by the power of Fruition attainment (phala-samāpatti), should be understood as being like the time when the hot pot is pulled out with the stick and placed on the level ground.

An Arahant, like the hot pot, does not attain Parinibbāna on the very day he reaches the Fruition of Arahantship; rather, he remains for fifty or sixty years, continuing the lineage of the Dispensation (sāsana), and then attains Parinibbāna through the Anupādisesa-nibbāna element because of the breaking up of the clung-to aggregates (upādiṇṇaka-khandha) upon the occurrence of the final consciousness (cuti-citta). At that time, just as the shards of the pot remain, only the deceased physical remains (sarīra) of that Arahant, which are no longer clung to (anupādiṇṇaka), are left behind. The statement "He knows that the remains are left behind" (sarīrāni avasissantīti pajānāti) is said for the purpose of attributing investigation to the Arahant.

"Viññāṇaṃ paññāyetha" means the rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa) would be known. "Sādhu sādhu"—He (the Buddha) expresses approval of the elders' explanation. "Evametaṃ" means that it is exactly as stated: if the three types of volitional formations (abhisaṅkhāra) are absent, the rebirth-linking consciousness will not be known, and so on. "Adhimuccatha" means "acquire the conviction (adhimokkha) known as decision." "Esevanto dukkhassa" means "this Nibbāna alone is the end of the suffering of the round; this Nibbāna alone is the limit of the suffering of the round." The first sutta is finished.

## 2. Upādāna Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, "upādāniyesu" means in those things belonging to the three planes (tebhūmaka) which are the causes of the four types of clinging (upādāna). "Assādānupassino" means for one who repeatedly contemplates gratification. "Tatra" means in that mass of fire. "Tadāဟာရော" (tadāhāro) means having that as its cause. The word "tadupādāno" is a synonym for that word "tadāhāro." In this simile "Evameva kho," the three planes of existence should be understood as being like a great mass of fire; the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) occurring in the three planes is also this very thing. The foolish worldling (bāla-puthujjana) attached to the round should be understood as being like the man tending the fire. Adding fuel such as dry grass and dry cow dung is like...
76:
...the foolish worldling performing wholesome and unwholesome kamma through the six doors by the power of craving (taṇhā) and so on, while repeatedly contemplating gratification. Just as the mass of fire grows by repeatedly adding fuel when the grass and cow dung are exhausted, so too the foolish worldling, by exerting effort and accumulating the aforementioned kamma, repeatedly brings about the suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha).

Regarding the phrase "He would not add dry grass from time to time," a certain person who desires his welfare might say: "My dear man, why do you exert yourself to bring wood and add dry grass and dry wood? Why do you fill baskets with dry cow dung and make this fire burn? Does any benefit come to you from increasing this mass of fire in this way?" Then he would reply: "My dear friend, tending the fire in this way is our family tradition. But what benefit could there be for me from this cause? There is no benefit at all. Indeed, while I am tending this fire, I do not get to bathe, eat, or sleep." Then the other would say: "My dear friend, what is the use of this useless burning of fire? Come, leave those bundles of grass and wood you have brought right here; they will burn out by themselves. As for you, there is a lotus pond with cool water in such-and-such a place; bathe there, adorn yourself with garlands and perfumes, dress and cloak yourself well, put on sandals, enter the city, ascend a noble palace, open the window, and sit looking out at the main street, appearing magnificent. While you sit there, concentrated and endowed with happiness, this fire will go out by itself as the fuel such as grass and wood is exhausted." That man would do so. And while he sits there in the palace, that fire would go out by itself due to the exhaustion of fuel. With reference to this meaning, the Buddha spoke the words beginning with "Na kālena kālaṃ."

In correlating this simile: the round of rebirth in the three planes (tebhūmaka-vaṭṭa) should be understood as being like a great mass of fire burning with forty cartloads of wood. The practitioner (yogāvacara) attached to the round should be understood as being like the man tending the fire. The Fully Enlightened Buddha should be understood as being like the wise man who desires his welfare. The time when the Tathāgata teaches the Vipassanā meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), saying, "Come, bhikkhu, be weary of the things of the three planes; in this way, you will be liberated from the suffering of the round," should be understood as being like the advice given by that man. The time when the practitioner accepts the advice, enters a secluded place, begins to develop Vipassanā meditation on the things of the three planes, and contemplates such things as his inclinations (āsaya) while staying in one place, should be understood as being like the time when that man, having practiced according to the instruction, sits in the palace.
77:
When a practitioner (yogi), having well-received the instruction of the Sugata (the Buddha), enters a secluded place and applies insight (vipassanā) to the phenomena of the three planes of existence, and gradually obtains suitable food and conditions, the time when he is established in the highest fruit of Arahantship while sitting in a single posture is (metaphorically) like the time when that man, dwelling in a palace, has his body well-washed and adorned with bathing and perfumes, and is endowed with peaceful happiness. The yogi, having well-washed the stains of defilements with the pure water of Path-knowledge in the pond of the Noble Path, wears the garment of moral shame and moral dread (hiri-ottappa), anoints himself with the perfume of virtue (sīla), adorns his person with the ornament of the fruit of Arahantship, wears the flower-garland of liberation (vimutti), puts on the sandals of the bases of power (iddhipāda), enters the city of Nibbāna, ascends the palace of the supramundane Dhamma, and while appearing magnificent on the great street of the foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), he dwells having entered the attainment of fruition (phala-samāpatti) with Nibbāna as the object. Furthermore, just as for that man dwelling in that palace, the great fire reaches a state where it cannot even be designated as existing due to the exhaustion of fuel such as grass, branches, and dry wood, so too should be understood the cessation of the great round of suffering when the Arahant, having remained for the duration of his life, attains Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu) upon the breaking up of the clusters of clinging (upādinnaka-khandha). The second Sutta is finished.

## 3. Saṃyojana Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the third Sutta, "saṃyojaniyesu" means in the causes of the ten fetters (saṃyojana). "Jhāyeyya" means it should burn. "Should pour oil, should apply the wick" means that for the sake of tending the lamp, one takes an oil vessel and a large lamp-dish and, staying constantly nearby, pours oil when the oil is exhausted and inserts a new wick when the wick is exhausted. The remaining meaning here, along with the comparison of the simile, should be understood in the same way as the previous method. The third Sutta is finished.

## 4. Dutiya Saṃyojana Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fourth Sutta, the simile is given first and the meaning is taught afterwards. The rest is exactly the same as that (the third Sutta). The fourth Sutta is finished.

## 5. Mahārukkha Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fifth Sutta, "they draw up the nutrients" means they send the earth-essence (pathavī-rasa) and water-essence (āpo-rasa) upwards. Because the nutrients are sent up, the essence remains like droplets on the tips of the sprouts of a tree a hundred cubits high. In this matter, the comparison with the simile is as follows: The round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) occurring in the three planes should be understood as the great tree. The sense bases (āyatana) should be understood as the roots. Just as nutrients are drawn up by the roots, the performing of karma through the six doors should be understood. Just as the great tree stands for a long time because it draws up nutrients, the foolish worldling (puthujjana) who relies on the round of rebirth stands in the cycle of saṃsāra, increasing the round of suffering continuously because of performing karma through the six doors.

"Kudālapitaka" means a hoe and a basket. "Should cut it into small and large pieces" means cutting it into parts and fragments. In this context of the discourse on the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭakathā), the comparison with the simile is: The round of rebirth in the three planes should be known as the great tree. The practitioner (yogāvacara) should be known as the man who wishes to destroy the tree. The knowledge of urgency (saṃvega-ñāṇa), which is the root of one who wishes to destroy the round of suffering, should be known as the hoe. Concentration (samādhi) should be known as the basket. Insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) that arises depending on concentration should be known as the axe that cuts the tree.
78:
The comparison with the simile is as follows: The round of rebirth (vaṭṭa) occurring in the three planes should be understood as the great tree. The sense bases (āyatana) should be understood as the roots. Just as nutrients are drawn up by the roots, the performing of karma through the six doors should be understood. Just as the great tree stands for a long time because it draws up nutrients, the foolish worldling who relies on the round of rebirth stands for a long time in saṃsāra by increasing the round of suffering through the performance of wholesome and unwholesome karma via the six doors.

Kudālapitaka means a hoe and a basket. Khaṇḍākhaṇḍikaṃ chindeyya means one should cut it into small and large pieces and fragments. In this matter, the comparison with the simile is: In this discourse on the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭakathā) as well, the round of rebirth in the three planes should be known as the great tree. The practitioner (yogāvacara) should be known as the man who wishes to destroy the tree. The knowledge of urgency (saṃvega-ñāṇa), which is the root of one who wishes to destroy the round of suffering, should be known as the hoe. Concentration (samādhi) should be known as the basket. Insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) that arises depending on concentration should be known as the axe that cuts the tree. The wisdom of the yogi who, having taken a meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna) from a teacher, applies his mind to it, should be known as the time of cutting the roots of the tree. Contemplating the four great elements (mahābhūta) in brief should be known as the time of cutting into pieces. Contemplating in detail the forty-two parts (koṭṭhāsa) should be known as the time of splitting the tree. Discerning mind and matter (nāmarūpa) by way of the derived matter (upādā-rūpa) and the consciousness that has the form-aggregate (rūpakkhandha) as its object should be known as the time of making it into fragments. Searching for the causes of that mind and matter should be known as the absolute cutting of the roots. Developing insight (vipassanā) in sequence, obtaining suitable conditions (sappāya), and when the meditation subject becomes clear, practicing the Dhamma of a monk while sitting in a single posture and reaching the highest fruit (the fruit of Arahantship) should be known as the time of drying it in the wind and sun and burning it with fire. Remaining for the duration of one's life before Parinibbāna, even on the very day of reaching the fruit of Arahantship, should be known as the time of making it into ashes. The cessation of the round of suffering of the Arahant who attains Parinibbāna through the Nibbāna element without remainder (anupādisesa-nibbānadhātu) due to the breaking up of the clusters of clinging (upādinnaka-khandha) should be known as the winnowing in the wind or the washing away in the river water. The fifth Sutta is finished.

## 6. Dutiya Mahārukkha Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the sixth Sutta as well, the Buddha taught the simile first and the meaning afterwards; this is the only difference. The sixth Sutta is finished.
79:
## 7. Taruṇarukkhasutta-vaṇṇanā

57-59. In the seventh sutta, "taruṇa" refers to a tree that has not yet borne fruit. "Palimajjeyya" means clearing away grass, rubbish, and so on. "Paṃsuṃ dadeyya" means removing hard and rough old soil and pouring in good fertile soil mixed with soft cow-dung powder. "Vuddhi" means that after growing, it obtains flowers at the time of flowering and fruit at the time of fruiting.

In this context, to compare the simile and the signified: The young tree is like the cycle of existence in the three realms (tebhūmaka-vaṭṭa). The man who tends the tree is like the worldling (puthujjana) who is dependent on the cycle. The sequential arising of roots, fruits, and branches is like the accumulation of wholesome and unwholesome kamma through the three doors. The growth of the tree is like the repeated occurrence of the cycle because the worldling accumulates kamma through the three doors. As for the cessation of the cycle (vivaṭṭa), it should be understood as stated in the fifth sutta. The eighth and ninth suttas have very clear meanings.

## 10. Nidānasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, "kurūsu viharati" means staying in the country called Kuru. It means that he made the market town of the Kurus named Kammāsadhamma his resort for alms. "Āyasmā" is a term used for a beloved and respected person. "Ānando" is the name of that elder. "Ekamantaṃ nisīdi" means that Venerable Ānanda, the Treasurer of the Dhamma, sat down while avoiding the six faults of sitting, facing the right knee-cap, entering within the six-colored rays of the Buddha, as if descending into clear lacquer essence, as if wrapping himself in a golden cloth, or as if entering the middle of a red woolen canopy. Therefore, it is said, "he sat down to one side (ekamantaṃ nisīdi)."

At what time and for what reason did this Venerable approach the Blessed One? It was in the evening for the purpose of asking a question about Dependent Origination (paccaya-ākāra). It is heard that on that day, Venerable Ānanda, like one placing a thousand-piece bundle of coins at every house-door for the sake of favoring families, wandered for alms in the market town of Kammāsadhamma. After returning from the almsround and performing his duties for the Teacher, when the Teacher entered the Fragrant Chamber (gandhakuṭi), he paid homage to the Teacher and went to his own place for the day's rest. After having his disciples perform their duties and when they had left, he swept the day-quarters, spread out his leather mat, cooled his hands and feet with water from a pitcher, and sat down cross-legged. Sitting thus, he entered the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala-samāpatti). After the determined time had elapsed, he emerged from the attainment and applied his knowledge to Dependent Origination. That Venerable Ānanda, starting from "with ignorance as condition, volitional formations (avijjāpaccayā saṅkhārā)" to the end...
80:
