Having cooled his hands and feet, he sat down cross-legged and entered the attainment of the fruit of stream-entry. Then, after emerging from the attainment according to the determined time, he applied his knowledge to the law of conditionality (paccaya-ākāra). That Venerable Ānanda contemplated the twelve-linked law of conditionality three times, proceeding from the beginning to the end, from the end to the beginning, from both ends to the middle, and from the middle to both ends. As he was contemplating in this way, the law of conditionality appeared to him as if it were very shallow and clear.

Then he thought: "This law of conditionality has been described by all Buddhas as being deep and having a deep appearance. However, to me, a disciple established in partial knowledge (padesañāṇa), it appears as if it were very shallow and clear. Does it appear shallow only to me, or does it appear so to others as well? I will inform the Teacher of the reason for it appearing to me in this way." Then, rising from his seat, he shook out his leather mat, took it, and approached the Blessed One in the evening. Therefore, it is said: "He approached in the evening for the purpose of asking a question about Dependent Origination."

In the passage "Yāva gambhီro," the word "yāva" is used in the sense of exceeding a measure. It means deep beyond measure, extremely deep. "Gambhīrā-vabhāso" means that it is indeed deep but appears so to knowledge. In fact, some water, like old water that has turned black due to the essence of rotten leaves, appears deep although it is shallow. Such water, though only knee-deep, appears as deep as a hundred fathoms. Some water, like clear water with the luster of gems, appears shallow although it is deep. Such water, though a hundred fathoms deep, appears to be only knee-deep. Some water, like water in a bowl or similar vessels, is both shallow and appears shallow. Some water, like the water of the great ocean at the foot of Mount Sineru, is both deep and appears deep. Thus, water alone receives four names. But in Dependent Origination, this is not the case. This Dependent Origination receives only one name: it is both deep and has a deep appearance. "Venerable Sir, although it is of such a nature, to me it appears as if it were very shallow. Venerable Sir, it is wonderful! It is marvelous!" Thus, expressing his wonder and having asked the question, he sat down in silence.
81:
Hearing the words of the Venerable Ānanda, the Blessed One thought: "Ānanda speaks of the question regarding the Buddha’s domain (Dependent Origination) as being very clear to him, as if he were stretching out his hand to grasp the peak of existence (Bhavagga), as if he were attempting to split Mount Sineru to extract its marrow, as if he wished to cross the great ocean without a boat, or as if he were attempting to turn over the earth to take its essence. Now, I shall explain to him the profound nature of this Dhamma." Thus, he spoke the words beginning with "Mā hevaṃ" (Do not say so).

In the phrase "Mā hevaṃ," the syllable "ha" is merely a particle; the meaning is "Do not speak thus." The Blessed One spoke these words, "Mā hevaṃ," both to encourage the Venerable Ānanda and to restrain (reprove) him. In that regard, the manner of encouraging him is: "Ānanda, you possess great wisdom and clear knowledge; therefore, to you, the profound Dependent Origination appears as if it were clear. However, it should not be regarded as clear to others. This Dhamma is indeed profound and has a profound appearance."

In this matter, the teachers provide four similes. It is said that there was a great wrestler who had been nourished with excellent food for six months, was well-trained in his art, and was experienced in lifting the wrestler's stone during festivals. While going to the battlefield, he saw a great wrestler's stone on the way that other wrestlers could not lift. He asked, "What is this?" When told, "It is the wrestler's stone," he said, "Bring it here." When they said, "We are unable to lift it," he went there himself, asked, "Where is the heavy part of this stone?" and lifting two stones with both hands, he threw them as if they were play-balls and went on his way. In that case, although the stone was light for the great wrestler, it should not be said that it is light for others as well. Like the great wrestler nourished with excellent food for six months, the Venerable Ānanda is one who has fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) for a hundred thousand aeons. Just as the stone is light for the great wrestler because of his great strength, so Dependent Origination may be said to be clear because of the Elder’s great wisdom; however, it should not be said to be clear for others.

In the great ocean, the great fish named Timi is two hundred yojanas long; the Timingala fish is three hundred yojanas long; the Timirapingala fish is five hundred yojanas long. These four types of great fish—Ānanda, Timinanda, Ajjhāroha, and Mahātimi—are each one thousand yojanas long. Among them, the simile is shown by means of the Timirapingala fish. It is said that when that great fish moves its right ear, the water trembles in an area of five hundred yojanas; the same occurs when it moves its left ear, its tail, or its head. When it moves both ears...
82:
...striking with its tail and moving its head to and fro, as it begins to play, the water in an area of seven or eight hundred yojanas boils like water placed in a vessel on a stove. In an area of about a hundred yojanas, the water is unable to cover its back. That great fish might say: "They say this great ocean is profound; where is its profundity? We do not even get enough water to cover our backs." In that simile, although the great ocean is shallow for the Timirapingala fish endowed with a massive body, it should not be said to be shallow for other small fish. In the same way, although Dependent Origination is clear for the Elder endowed with wisdom, it should not be said to be clear for others.

The King of Garuḍas (Suvaṇṇarājā) is one hundred and fifty yojanas in size. His right wing is fifty yojanas; likewise, his left wing is fifty yojanas. His tail-feathers are sixty yojanas; his neck is thirty yojanas; his face is nine yojanas; and his feet are twelve yojanas. When that King of Garuḍas begins to display the Garuḍa-wind, an area of seven or eight hundred yojanas is not enough for him. That King of Garuḍas might say: "They say this sky is infinite; where is its infinity? We do not even get enough space to spread the wind of our wings." In that simile, although the sky is small for the King of Garuḍas endowed with a massive body, it should not be said to be small for other small birds. In the same way, although Dependent Origination is clear for the Elder endowed with wisdom, it should not be said to be clear for others.

Rāhu, the lord of the Asuras (Asurinda), is four thousand eight hundred yojanas from the soles of his feet to the tips of his hair. The span between his two arms is one thousand two hundred yojanas; in thickness, it is six hundred yojanas. The palms of his hands and the soles of his feet are each three hundred yojanas; likewise, his face is three hundred yojanas. A finger-joint is fifty yojanas; likewise, the space between his eyebrows and his forehead are three hundred yojanas. His head is nine hundred yojanas. For that Rāhu Asurinda who has descended into the great ocean, the deep water reaches only to his knees. That Rāhu Asurinda might say: "They say this great ocean is very deep; where is its depth? We do not even get enough water to cover our knees." Just as the great ocean is shallow for Rāhu Asurinda endowed with a massive body, but should not be said to be shallow for others, in the same way, for the Elder endowed with wisdom, Dependent Origination...
83:
(To the wise Venerable Ānanda, Dependent Origination appeared shallow, but) it should not be said to be shallow for others. Intending this meaning, the Blessed One said, "Do not say so, Ānanda; do not say so, Ānanda."

To the Elder Ānanda, the profound Dependent Origination appeared as if it were shallow due to four reasons. What are the four? They are: the perfection of past supporting conditions (upaniṣṣaya), the constant residence and attendance upon the Teacher, the attainment of Stream-entry (Sotāpanna), and being a person of great learning (bahussuta).

One hundred thousand aeons ago from this present age, a Buddha named Padumuttara appeared in the world. His royal capital was Haṃsavatī; his father was King Ānanda, and his mother was Queen Sumedhā. The Bodhisatta was named Prince Uttara. On the day his son was born, he departed for the Great Renunciation, became a monk, practiced meditation, and in due course attained Omniscience. After uttering the solemn utterance beginning with "Aneka-jāti-saṃsāraṃ," he spent seven days at the Bodhi-throne and then extended his foot, thinking, "I shall place my foot on the ground." At that moment, the earth split open and a great lotus flower emerged. The outer petals of that lotus were ninety cubits, the filaments were thirty cubits, and the pericarp (kaṇṇikā) was twelve cubits. The pollen was as much as nine water-pots.

The Buddha was fifty-eight cubits in height. The span between his two arms was eighteen cubits, his forehead was five cubits, and his palms and soles were eleven cubits each. When he stepped on the twelve-cubit pericarp with his eleven-cubit foot, the pollen, amounting to nine water-pots, rose to a height of fifty-eight cubits and spread all around like scattered red arsenic powder. Based on this event, the Buddha became known by the name "Padumuttara." He had two chief disciples, Devila and Sujāta; two chief female disciples, Amitā and Asamā; and an attendant named Sumana. The Blessed One Padumuttara, to show favor to his father, resided in the capital Haṃsavatī, surrounded by a hundred thousand monks.

His younger brother was Prince Sumana. The Great King, his father, granted him a fief as a city ruler in a place one hundred and twenty yojanas away from Haṃsavatī. Occasionally, he would come to visit his father and the Buddha. Then one day, an uprising occurred in the border region. Prince Sumana sent a message to the King. The King replied, "My son, why did I place you there?" After quelling the threat of the thieves, the prince sent word, "Great King, the countryside is now peaceful." The King was pleased and said, "Let my son return quickly."
84:
Prince Sumana had about one thousand ministers. While on the journey, he consulted with them, saying, "If my father, being pleased with me, offers a boon, what should I take?" Then some ministers said, "Take elephants, take horses, take a province, or take the seven treasures."

Other ministers, however, said, "Since you are the sons of the lord of the earth, wealth is not difficult to obtain. Moreover, all wealth that is acquired must eventually be left behind. Only merit should be taken along. Therefore, when the Great King grants a boon, take the boon of being allowed to serve and attend upon the Blessed One Padumuttara for the three months of the rainy season."

The prince said, "You are indeed my good friends (kalyāṇamitta). Although I did not have such a desire to serve the Blessed One, you have given rise to this thought. Therefore, I shall do exactly as you say." He then went to the capital and paid homage to his father. The Great King embraced his son, kissed his head, and said, "My son, I grant you a boon." The prince replied, "Great King, I wish to serve and attend upon the Blessed One with the four requisites for the three months of the rainy season, so as to make my life meaningful. Please grant me this boon."

"My son, it is not possible to grant this boon; choose another," the King said. "Great King, kings do not speak with two tongues. Please grant me only this boon; I have no need for any other," he replied. "My son, the minds of the Buddhas are difficult to know. Even if I grant permission, what will happen if the Blessed One does not wish it?" the King said. "Very well, Great King, I shall find out the Blessed One's mind," the prince replied and went to the monastery.

At that time, the Blessed One had finished his meal and entered the Perfumed Chamber (Gandhakuṭi). The prince went to the monks who were gathered in the circular pavilion (maṇḍalamāḷa). The monks asked, "Prince, for what reason have you come?" "Venerable sirs, I have come to see the Blessed One. Please allow me to see the Blessed One," he replied. "Prince, we do not get to see the Teacher whenever we wish," they said. "Venerable sirs, which venerable one gets to see him whenever he wishes?" he asked. "Prince, the Elder Sumana gets to see him whenever he wishes," they replied.

The prince asked, "Venerable sirs, where is that Elder?" After inquiring about the Elder's residence, he went there, paid homage, and said, "Venerable sir, I wish to see the Blessed One. Please allow me to see the Blessed One." The Elder said, "Come, Prince," and taking him along, he had him wait in the precinct of the Perfumed Chamber and then ascended to the Perfumed Chamber himself. Then the Blessed One asked, "Sumana, for what reason have you come?" "Venerable sir, the prince has arrived to see the Blessed One," he replied. "In that case, monk, prepare a seat," the Blessed One said. The Elder prepared a seat, and the Blessed One sat on the prepared seat.

The prince paid homage to the Blessed One and engaged in polite conversation. "Prince, when did you arrive?" the Buddha asked. "Venerable sir, I have been here since the time you entered the Perfumed Chamber. The monks said, 'We do not get to see the Blessed One whenever we wish,' and sent me to the Elder. The Elder, however, allowed me to see you with just a single word. Venerable sir, the Elder..."
85:
"I think [Elder Sumana] is beloved in your Dispensation," the Prince said. "Yes, Prince, this monk is beloved in my Dispensation," the Buddha replied. "Venerable Sir, by doing what does one become beloved in the Dispensation of the Buddhas?" he asked. "Prince, by giving gifts, undertaking virtue, and performing the Uposatha observance, one becomes beloved," the Buddha replied.

"Venerable Sir, I too wish to be beloved in the Buddha's Dispensation like Elder Sumana. Please accept my invitation for the three-month rains retreat," he requested. The Blessed One, considering whether there would be benefit in going and seeing that there would be, said, "Prince, the Tathāgatas delight in secluded dwellings." The Prince replied, "I understand, Blessed One; I understand, Sugata," and said, "Venerable Sir, I will go ahead and have a monastery built. When I send word, please come with a hundred thousand monks." Having received the promise, he went to his father and said, "Great King, the Blessed One has given me his promise. When I send word, please send the Blessed One to me." Having paid homage to his father, he departed.

He had a monastery built at every league (yojana) along the two-hundred-league journey. Upon reaching his city, while searching for a site for a monastery, he saw the garden of a householder named Sobhana. He bought it for a hundred thousand and spent another hundred thousand to build the monastery. There, he had a Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) built for the Blessed One, and huts, caves, and pavilions for the remaining monks to stay in by night and day. Having completed the surrounding wall and the gate-tower, he sent word to his father: "My task is finished; please send the Teacher."

The King, after offering a meal to the Blessed One, said, "Blessed One, Sumana's task is finished; he awaits your arrival." The Blessed One, surrounded by a hundred thousand monks, traveled, staying at the monasteries located at every league. Hearing that "The Teacher is coming," the Prince went out for a league to meet him. Honoring him with perfumes and flowers, he led him to the monastery and said:

"The garden named Sobhana, bought by me for a hundred thousand,
And built for a hundred thousand—
Accept it, O Great Sage!"

Thus, he dedicated the monastery. On the day of entering the rains retreat, having given gifts, he called his children, wife, and ministers and said, "The Teacher has come to us from a distant place. Buddhas are those who honor the Dhamma, not material gifts. Therefore, during these three months, I will wear only two robes, undertake the ten precepts, and stay right here in this monastery. You all should give gifts to the hundred thousand monks in this manner throughout the three months."
86:
"I will stay right here in this monastery. You all should provide alms to the hundred thousand Arahants in this same manner for the three months," he said.

Staying in a place similar to where Elder Sumana resided, the Prince observed all the major and minor duties the Elder performed for the Blessed One. He thought, "This Elder is certainly very beloved in this position. It is fitting to aspire for this very office." As the Pavāraṇā ceremony approached, he entered the village and gave a great alms-giving for seven days. On the seventh day, placing sets of triple robes at the feet of the hundred thousand monks, he paid homage to the Blessed One and said, "Venerable Sir, whatever merit I have performed, starting from the building of monasteries at every league along the way, I have done so not desiring the prosperity of Sakka, Māra, or Brahmā, but desiring only the position of a Buddha's attendant. Therefore, may I also become the attendant of a Buddha in the future, just like Elder Sumana." He then prostrated himself with the fivefold touching. The Blessed One, considering, "The aspiration of this clansman is great; will it be fulfilled or not?" saw that "In the future, a hundred thousand aeons from now, a Buddha named Gotama will arise. He will be the attendant of that very Buddha." He then said:

"May all that you wish and aspire for be fulfilled;
May all your intentions be completed, like the moon on the fifteenth day."

Hearing this prophecy, the Prince thought, "The words of the Buddhas are never twofold," and from the very next day, he acted as if he were constantly following behind the Blessed One, carrying his bowl and robes. In that Buddha's lifetime, he gave gifts for a hundred thousand years and was reborn in heaven. During the time of Kassapa Buddha, he offered his upper robe to an Elder walking for alms so that the Elder could hold his bowl, and thus performed an act of worship. Being reborn again in heaven and passing away from there, he became the King of Bārāṇasī. He built leaf-huts for eight Paccekabuddhas, provided them with jeweled bowl-stands, and attended to them with the four requisites for ten thousand years. These are his well-known deeds.

Giving gifts for a hundred thousand aeons, he was reborn in the Tusita heaven together with our Bodhisatta. Passing away from there, he took conception in the house of Amitodana the Sakyan. In due course, after the Great Renunciation and the attainment of Supreme Enlightenment, when the Blessed One first came to Kapilavatthu and was departing from there, he followed along with princes such as Bhaddiya when the princes were ordaining as the Blessed One's retinue, and he went forth in the presence of the Blessed One. Not long after, having heard a Dhamma discourse from the Venerable Puṇṇa, son of Mantāṇī, he was established in the fruit of Stream-entry. Thus, the Venerable Ānanda was one possessed of prior supporting conditions. This is the account of the Venerable Ānanda's perfection of prior supporting conditions.
87:
When the princes were ordaining to have attendants, Ānanda set out together with princes such as Bhaddiya and others, and having ordained in the presence of the Blessed One, not long after, he heard the Dhamma in the presence of the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta and was established in the fruit of Stream-entry (sotāpatti-phala). Thus, this Venerable Ānanda was possessed of past supporting conditions (upanissaya); because of being possessed of such past supporting conditions, even the profound Dependent Origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) appeared to him as if it were shallow.

'Titthavāsa' refers to the acts of learning, listening, questioning, and bearing in mind in the presence of teachers. That 'titthavāsa' was extremely pure for the Elder. For that reason also, this profound Dependent Origination appeared to him as if it were shallow. Furthermore, for Stream-enterers, the law of conditionality (paccayākāra) tends to appear as if it were shallow, and this Venerable Ānanda was a Stream-enterer. For those of great learning (bahussuta), just as when a lamp is lit in a chamber of four cubits, the couches and stools are clear, so too the distinction of mind and matter (nāmarūpa-pariccheda) is clear; and this Venerable Ānanda was the foremost among those of great learning. Thus, due to the state of being of great learning as well, the profound law of conditionality appeared to him as if it were shallow.

Dependent Origination is profound through four kinds of depth (gambhīratā). That profundity has been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. All that profundity appeared to the Elder as if it were shallow. Therefore, the Blessed One, wishing to encourage the Venerable Ānanda, spoke the words beginning with "Mā hevaṃ" (Do not say so). The meaning here is: Ānanda, you possess great wisdom and clear knowledge; therefore, the profound Dependent Origination appears to you as if it were shallow. Therefore, do not say, "Does this appear as if it were shallow only to me, or to others as well?"

In the words said as "apasadento" (reproving), this is the meaning: Ānanda, do not say such words as, "Yet, it appears to me as if it were very shallow." If this Dependent Origination appears to you as if it were very shallow, why did you not become a Stream-enterer by your own nature? Was it not only by standing on the method given by me that you penetrated the path of Stream-entry? Ānanda, if only this Nibbāna is profound and the law of conditionality has become shallow, then why do you not realize the fruit of Once-returning (sakadāgāmi-phala) by utterly destroying these four defilements: the coarse fetter of sensual lust, the fetter of ill-will, the coarse underlying tendency of sensual lust, and the underlying tendency of ill-will? Why do you not realize the fruit of Non-returning (anāgāmi-phala) by utterly destroying those same four defilements in their subtle stage?
88:
Why do you not realize the fruit of Arahantship by utterly destroying the five fetters such as lust for form (rūparāga) and these eight defilements: the underlying tendency of conceit (mānānusaya), the underlying tendency of lust for existence (bhavarāgānusaya), and the underlying tendency of ignorance (avijjānusaya)? Or else, why do you not penetrate the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvaka-pāramī-ñāṇa) like the Venerable Sāriputta and the Venerable Moggallāna, who fulfilled perfections for one incalculable (asankheyya) and a hundred thousand aeons? Why do you not penetrate the knowledge of Paccekabuddha-enlightenment (paccekabodhi-ñāṇa) like the Paccekabuddhas who fulfilled perfections for two incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons? If this Dependent Origination appears to you as shallow in every way, then why do you not realize Omniscient knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) like the Buddhas who fulfilled perfections for four, eight, or sixteen incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons? Do you have no desire for these special attainments? See how much you have erred! While standing in the limited knowledge of a disciple (sāvaka-padesa-ñāṇa), you say of the extremely profound law of conditionality, "It appears to me as if it were shallow." These words of yours are contrary to the discourse of the Buddhas. It is not fitting for a monk like you to intend to speak words contrary to the discourse of the Buddhas.

Ānanda, while I was striving to penetrate this law of conditionality, did not four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons pass? For the sake of penetrating this Dhamma, there is no gift I have not given, no perfection I have not fulfilled. While I was destroying the forces of Māra, reflecting, "Today I shall penetrate the law of conditionality," this great earth did not tremble even two inches for me. Likewise, it did not tremble when I achieved the knowledge of past lives (pubbenivāsa-ñāṇa) in the first watch, or the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) in the middle watch. However, in the powerful dawn of the last watch, as soon as I saw that "Ignorance is a condition for volitional formations" (avijjā saṅkhārānaṃ paccayo) in nine ways, the ten-thousandfold world system, like a bronze bowl struck with an iron rod, letting out hundreds and thousands of sounds, trembled violently like a drop of water on a wind-blown lotus leaf. Ānanda, thus this Dependent Origination is profound and has a profound appearance. Ānanda, because of not knowing this Dhamma through full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā), and not penetrating it through full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā) and full understanding by abandonment (pahāna-pariññā), beings become entangled like a tangled ball of thread. For example, a weaver's ball of thread that is poorly kept and bitten by mice becomes tangled here and there, so that it is difficult to join end to end or root to root, thinking, "This is the end, this is the root." In the same way, beings stumble and are confused and entangled in this law of conditionality.
89:
(Beings) are unable to straighten the law of Dependent Origination. In that analogy, although a ball of thread might be straightened by one's own effort, with the exception of the two types of Bodhisattas (the Paccekabodhisatta and the Mahābodhisatta), there is no other being who is capable of straightening Dependent Origination by their own nature. Just as a tangled ball of thread, even when sprayed with sour rice gruel and combed with a brush, remains knotted and tangled in various places, so too these beings, stumbling in the conditions and unable to straighten them, become knotted and tangled like a ball of thread through the power of the sixty-two types of wrong views. Whoever relies on wrong views, all of them are simply unable to straighten the conditions.

'Kulāgaṇṭhikajāta' refers to a weaver's ball of thread sprayed with silk-solution (or rice-washing water) that is so tangled that the beginning and the end cannot be known; this is called 'kulāgaṇṭhika'. 'Kulā' refers to a small bird, and some teachers say that the nest of that small bird is also called 'kulāgaṇṭhika'. In both cases, the difficulty of aligning end with end and beginning with beginning should be understood according to the previous method.

'Muñjapabbajabhūta' means they have become like Muñja grass and Babbaja grass. Just as a rope made by twisting those grasses, when it has rotted, makes it difficult to distinguish the end and the beginning (and although that grass might be straightened by one's own effort, no being other than the two types of Bodhisattas can straighten Dependent Origination by their own nature). This multitude of beings, unable to straighten the conditions, becomes knotted through the power of wrong views and cannot transcend the states of deprivation (apāya), the bad destination (duggati), the downfall (vinipāta), and the round of rebirths (saṃsāra).

In that context, 'apāya' refers to hell, the animal realm, the realm of hungry ghosts (peta), and the host of asuras. It is called 'apāya' because of the absence of 'aya', which means prosperity or growth. It is called 'duggati' because it is the destination of suffering. It is called 'vinipāta' because it is a falling away from the sum of happiness. The remaining term 'saṃsāra' refers to the continuous and uninterrupted occurrence of the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), and sense bases (āyatana).

Unable to transcend that entire round of rebirths, repeatedly taking up death and rebirth, from death to rebirth and from rebirth to death, they must revolve in the three states of existence, the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings, like a ship tossed by a storm in the great ocean, or like an ox yoked to a mill. In this way, the Blessed One spoke this sutta wishing to admonish and discipline Venerable Ānanda. The remaining words in this sutta are to be understood according to the method already mentioned. This marks the end of the commentary on the tenth sutta. The Chapter on Suffering (Dukkha Vagga) is finished. The meaning of the first sutta of the Great Chapter (Mahā Vagga) should be understood by the following method. 'Assutavā' refers to a worldling who lacks inquiry, hearing, and decision regarding the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, foundations of mindfulness, and so forth. Of the many various...
90:
...nor can they transcend the misery of the states of deprivation. Indeed, taking up death and rebirth repeatedly in this manner, from death to rebirth and from rebirth to death, they simply revolve in the three states of existence, the four modes of birth, the five destinations, the seven stations of consciousness, and the nine abodes of beings, like a ship tossed by a storm in the great ocean, or like an ox yoked to a mill. Thus, the Blessed One spoke all this wishing to admonish and discipline Venerable Ānanda. The rest is exactly as already stated. The tenth sutta is finished.

## 6. The Chapter on Suffering (Dukkha Vagga)

## 7. The Great Chapter (Mahā Vagga)

## 1. Commentary on the Assutavā Sutta

In the first sutta of the Great Chapter, 'assutavā' refers to one who is devoid of learning, inquiry, and decision regarding the aggregates, elements, sense bases, dependent origination, foundations of mindfulness, and so forth. 'Puthujjana' (worldling) is so called because of the reasons such as generating many various defilements and so on. For it has been said: "They are called worldlings (puthujjana) because they generate many (puthu) defilements (kilesa)"; this should be expanded in detail. Alternatively, one is called a worldling because of being included among the many people who have exceeded the count, who have turned their backs on the Noble Dhamma, and who behave with low conduct. Or, a worldling is a person who is distinct and separate from the Noble Ones who are endowed with virtues such as morality and learning.

Thus, by these two terms 'assutavā puthujjana'—
"Two types of worldlings were spoken of by the Buddha, the Kinsman of the Sun: the blind worldling (andha-puthujjana) and the virtuous worldling (kalyāṇa-puthujjana)"—
of these two types of worldlings, the blind worldling is meant here.

By the word 'imasmiṃ' (in this), he shows the body that is present and evident. 'Cātumahābhūtikasmim' means in the body produced by the four great elements, consisting of the four great elements. 'Nibbindeyya' means one should become disenchanted. 'Virajjeyya' means one should not be attached (become dispassionate). 'Vimucceyya' means one should desire to be liberated. 'Ācaya' means accumulation or growth. 'Apacaya' means diminution or loss. 'Ādāna' means arising through rebirth. 'Nikkhepana' means the breaking up of the aggregates (death).

Therefore, 'tasmā' means because these four—growth, loss, birth, and breaking up—are evident; for that reason is the meaning. In this way, the Blessed One, regarding the body consisting of the four great elements...
91:
(The Blessed One) made the physical form (rūpa) appear as something unsuitable for grasping and made the mental (nāma) appear as something suitable for grasping. Why? Because for those monks, the attachment to rūpa was strong and excessive. Therefore, to show them the nature of rūpa as something to be defined and grasped, and to lead them away (from the grasp of craving, etc.) and establish them in nāma, He spoke thus.

All terms beginning with "citta" are merely names for the mind-base (manāyatana). That manāyatana is called "citta" because it is conditioned (citta), because it has diverse (citta) objects of experience, and because it is diverse through the power of associated mental states. It is called "mano" in the sense of thinking (manana). It is called "viññāṇa" in the sense of cognizing (vijānana) the object. "Nālaṃ" means not being capable. "Ajjhositaṃ" means swallowed and seized completely by craving. "Mamāyitaṃ" means cherished and taken as "this is mine" through the attachment of craving. "Parāmaṭṭhaṃ" means misapprehended and taken through the repeated wrong touch of views (diṭṭhi). "This is mine" is the grasp of craving; by this, the 108 modes of craving are included. "This I am" is the grasp of conceit (māna); by this, the nine types of conceit are included. "This is my self" is the grasp of views; by this, the sixty-two types of wrong views are included. Therefore, "tasmā" means because it has been grasped in this way for a long time, one is not capable of becoming weary of it.

Why did He say, "Monks, it is better..."? First, the Blessed One made rūpa appear unsuitable for grasping and nāma appear suitable. Then, knowing that "the attachment of those monks has left rūpa and gone to nāma," He began this teaching to remove that attachment. In that Pali, "attato upagaccheyya" means one should take it as self. "Bhiyyopi" means even beyond a hundred years. Why did the Blessed One say this? Is there any rūpa that lasts beyond a hundred years? Does not the rūpa that exists in the first stage of life fail to reach the middle stage? Does not the rūpa of the middle stage fail to reach the last stage? Does not the rūpa of the morning fail to reach the evening? Does not the rūpa of the evening fail to reach the first watch of the night? Does not the rūpa of the first watch fail to reach the middle watch? Does not the rūpa of the middle watch fail to reach the last watch? Likewise, the rūpa that exists in walking does not reach standing; the rūpa in standing does not reach sitting; the rūpa in sitting does not reach lying down. Even within a single posture, the rūpa in lifting the foot does not reach the stretching forward; the rūpa in stretching forward does not reach the moving across; the rūpa in moving across does not reach the letting down; the rūpa in letting down does not reach the placing on the ground; the rūpa in placing on the ground does not reach the pressing down. In each and every stage, being limited and segmented, the formations (saṅkhāra) break apart, crackling like sesame seeds thrown into a hot earthen pan, do they not? This destruction of rūpa is indeed true. For example, just as a lamp flame perishes right where it is without passing beyond its respective wick-section, yet is said to have burned all night by way of continuity...
92:
...it is called a lamp. Similarly, here too, by way of continuity, this physical body is shown by the Blessed One as if it were long-lasting.

"Rattiyā ca divasassa ca" means in the night and in the day. This compound is in the locative sense. "One arises, another ceases" means that the mind which arises and ceases at night is different from the mind which arises and ceases during the day. One should not take the meaning as "one arises, and another that has never arisen before ceases." This sentence "rattiyā ca divasassa ca" was spoken by the Blessed One by way of continuity, taking a shorter continuity than the previously mentioned continuity of rūpa. In reality, there is no single mind that can last for a whole night or a whole day. Even in a single finger-snap, many hundreds of thousands of crores of minds arise. This is also stated in the Milindapañha:

"Great King, if one were to count the grains of a hundred vāha of rice, fifty vāha (cūḷavāha), seven ambaṇa, and two tumba, and set aside one grain for each mind that occurs in a single finger-snap, those grains would be exhausted and used up."

"Pavana" means in a great forest. By the words "it lets go of that branch and grabs another, it lets go of that and grabs another," it does not mean that the monkey descends to the ground because it fails to find a branch to grab. Rather, it shows the meaning that while wandering in that great forest, it moves only by grabbing various branches.

"In the same way"—here, the comparison should be understood thus: The forest of sense objects (ārammaṇa) should be known like the great forest. The mind arising in the forest of sense objects is like the monkey wandering in that forest. The attachment to the object is like the grabbing of the branch. Just as that monkey wandering in the forest lets go of one branch and grabs another, so too this mind wandering in the forest of sense objects sometimes arises grabbing a visual object, sometimes one of the sounds, etc., sometimes a past object, sometimes a future or a present object; likewise, sometimes an internal object and sometimes an external object. It cannot be said that the monkey wandering in the forest sits on the ground because it cannot find a branch; similarly, a single...
93:
Just as one sits only after grasping a tree branch, similarly, the mind wandering in the forest of sense objects cannot be said to arise without obtaining a single supporting object; it should be understood that it arises only by grasping a single type of object. By this much, the Blessed One led [the mind] out from materiality and established attachment in the immaterial; then led it out from the immaterial and established it in materiality.

Now, desiring to lead it out from both [materiality and immateriality], he began the teaching: "In that case, monks, the well-taught noble disciple..." This meaning should be illustrated by the simile of snake venom. The circumstances are as follows: A man was bitten by a cobra. Then, a skilled physician came to remove the venom, gave him an emetic, and recited the mantra "Garuda below, Naga above," causing the venom to rise upward. Knowing that the venom had risen as far as the eyes, the physician thought, "I will not let it rise further; I will keep it only at the site of the bite." He then recited the mantra "Garuda above, Naga below," blew into the ear, struck with a stick, brought the venom down, and kept it only at the site of the bite. Knowing that the venom was stationed there, he neutralized the venom by applying an antidote, bathed the man, said, "May you be happy," and went his way.

In this simile, the presence of venom in the body of the person bitten by the snake is like the period of excessive attachment to materiality (rūpa) by these monks. The skilled physician is like the Tathāgata. The time of raising the venom upward by reciting the mantra is like the time when the Tathāgata led the monks' attachment out from materiality and established it in the immaterial (arūpa). Preventing the venom that had risen to the eyes from going further and bringing it down again by the power of the mantra to the site of the bite is like the time when the Teacher led the monks' attachment out from the immaterial and established it in materiality. The neutralizing of the venom at the site of the bite with an antidote should be understood as the time of beginning this teaching to lead out attachment from both [materiality and immateriality]. In that teaching, by the words "is disenchanted, lust fades away," the Path (Magga) is taught. By the words "through the fading of lust, he is liberated," the Fruit (Phala) is taught. By the words "when liberated..." and so on, Reviewing knowledge (Paccavekkhaṇā) is taught. The first sutta is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Second Assutavā Sutta
In the second sutta, "sukhavedaniyaṃ" means the cause of pleasant feeling. "Phassaṃ" means eye-contact and so on. If it is asked, "Does eye-contact not fail to be a cause for pleasant feeling?"—it is not a cause by way of conascence condition (sahajāta-paccaya), but it is a cause for the feeling arising in the impulsion (javana) by way of strong dependence condition (upanissaya-paccaya). It should be understood that [the Buddha] said, "the cause of pleasant feeling," referring to this state of strong dependence. In the case of ear-contact and so on, the remaining meaning is the same. "Tatra" means arising in that contact. "Tassāruppaṃ" means the state of being a mental phenomenon (arūpa) of that contact. In the terms "dukkhavedaniya" and so on, the meaning should be understood in the same way as already stated. "Saṅghaṭṭana" means impact or collision. "Usmā" is the state of heat. In the phrase "tatra abhinibbattati," it should not be taken as a flame coming out. That phrase is merely a synonym for the word "usma," which has the meaning of the state of heat. In that simile, "manthanaṃ" refers to the two fire-sticks, the lower and the upper. Among those two, the physical base (vatthu) such as the eye should be understood as the lower fire-stick. The sense object (ārammaṇa) such as a visual form should be understood as the upper fire-stick. Contact (phassa) should be understood as the friction of the lower and upper fire-sticks. Feeling (vedanā) should be understood as the heat.
94:
arises; referring to that [strong dependence condition], I have spoken this word [that it is the cause of pleasant feeling]. In the case of ear-contact and so on, it should be understood in this very way. "Tajja" means appropriate to that contact, meaning its immaterial nature. The terms "dukkhavedaniya" and so on should be understood only by the method already stated. "Saṅghaṭṭana-samodhāna" means by impact and by collision, meaning the combination of impact. "Usmā" is the state of heat. In the phrase "tejo abhinibbattati" (fire arises), it should not be taken as sparks of fire coming out; rather, this is a synonym for the word "usma," which means the state of heat. In that simile, "dvinnaṃ kaṭṭhānaṃ" means of the two fire-sticks. Among those two, the physical base (vatthu) should be understood as the lower fire-stick, the sense object (ārammaṇa) as the upper fire-stick, contact (phassa) as the friction of the fire-sticks, and feeling (vedanā) as the heat. The second sutta [commentary] is finished.

## 3. Commentary on the Puttamaṃsūpama Sutta
In the third sutta, the words "Monks, there are these four nutriments" and so on are just as already stated. However, since this sutta was delivered due to a specific occasion (atthuppatti), I will provide the word-by-word commentary in this sutta only after showing that occasion. For what reason was this sutta delivered? It was delivered because of gain, honor, and renown (lābhasakkāra). Great gain and honor arose for the Blessed One, as is the case for one who has accumulated the perfections of giving (dāna-pāramī) fulfilled over four incalculables. Just as a great double-cloud rising in all directions and raining heavily causes a great flood, all the perfections of the Blessed One, as if combining to say, "We shall give fruit in this final existence," produced a great flood of gain and honor. From here and there, kshatriyas, brahmins, and others, holding food, drinks, vehicles, clothes, flowers, perfumes, and ointments in their hands, came and searched for the Blessed One, asking, "Where is the Buddha? Where is the Blessed One? Where is the God of gods, the Bull among men, the Lion among men?" Even when they brought requisites by the hundreds of carts, they could not find an opportunity to donate, and so they stood with their cart-poles touching cart-pole for a distance of a gāvuta all around, and they followed him on his travels, like the Brahmin Andhakavinda and others. All this should be understood according to the method mentioned in the Khandhaka of the Vinaya and in various suttas.

As it was for the Blessed One, so it was for the Saṅgha of monks. It is said: "At that time the Blessed One was honored, revered, respected, worshipped, and esteemed, a recipient of robes, alms-food, lodgings, and medicinal requisites for the sick. The Saṅgha of monks was also honored... [pe]... requisites."
95:
Likewise, He said: "Cunda, among whatever Saṅgha or group has arisen in the world at this time, I, Cunda, do not see even a single other group that has reached the pinnacle of gains and the pinnacle of fame as this Saṅgha of bhikkhus." (Dī. Ni. 3.176).

The gains and offerings that arose for the Blessed One and the Saṅgha became united and were as immeasurable as the flow of water from two great rivers. Then, the Teacher, having gone into seclusion, reflected: "Such great gains and offerings also arose for the Buddhas of the past, and will also arise for the Buddhas of the future. Can the bhikkhus, being endowed with mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña) regarding the discernment of food, remain indifferent and free from desire and lust while consuming food, or can they not?"

He saw some newly ordained sons of good family consuming food without reflection. Seeing this, He thought: "While I was fulfilling the perfections (pāramīs) for four incalculables and a hundred thousand aeons, I did not fulfill them for the sake of requisites such as robes; rather, I fulfilled them for the sake of the supreme fruit, Arahantship. These bhikkhus, too, when ordaining in my presence, did not ordain for the sake of requisites such as robes; they ordained only for the sake of Arahantship. Yet now, they are regarding what is essence-less as essence, and are pursuing only what is unbeneficial as beneficial." Thus, spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega) arose in Him.

Then He thought: "If it were possible to prescribe a fifth Pārājika, the consumption of food without reflection should be prescribed as the fifth Pārājika. However, it is not possible to do so, because the use of food is something that living beings must constantly do. Therefore, I shall set forth a mirror of Dhamma, a restraint, and a boundary, such that when it is taught, they will regard it as seriously as a fifth Pārājika. By reflecting on that boundary again and again, bhikkhus of the future will consume the four requisites only after reflecting upon them." Due to this special circumstance, He delivered this Puttamamsa Sutta, which uses the simile of the son's flesh. In that Sutta, the meaning of the words beginning with "Bhikkhus, there are these four nutriments" is just as stated previously.

Having explained the four nutriments in detail, He now said, "Bhikkhus, how should the nutriment of edible food be regarded?" and so forth, in order to show the danger in those nutriments. In that Pali, "jāyampatikā" means a wife and a husband. "Parittaṃ sambalaṃ" means a small amount of travel provisions, such as a portion of cooked rice or powdered grain. "Kantāramaggaṃ" means a road that is a wilderness, or a road within a wilderness. A wilderness (kantāra) is of five types: a robber-infested wilderness, a wild-beast-infested wilderness, a non-human-infested wilderness, a waterless wilderness, and a foodless wilderness. Among these, if there is danger from thieves on a journey...
96:
...it is a robber-infested wilderness. Where there is danger from wild beasts such as lions and leopards, it is a wild-beast-infested wilderness. Where there is danger due to non-humans such as powerful female ogres (yakkhiṇī), it is a non-human-infested wilderness. Where there is no water for drinking or bathing, it is a waterless wilderness. Where there is no food or edibles, even as little as roots or tubers, it is called a foodless wilderness. If all these five types of danger are present, it is simply a wilderness. There are types of wilderness that can be crossed in one, two, or three days, but those are not intended here. What is intended here is a wilderness of a hundred leagues (yojanas) that is waterless and foodless. They would travel on such a wilderness road. Thinking, 'After crossing this wilderness, we shall live happily in a country free from danger under a righteous king,' they would set out on that journey, being oppressed by the fear of famine, disease, and the king.

'Ekaputtako' means an only son who is carried, who is worthy of compassion, and whose body is very tender. 'Vallūrañca soṇḍikañca' means taking meat from the fleshy parts to make dried meat, and taking meat from the parts near the bones and tendons to make meat on skewers. 'Paṭipiseyyuṃ' means they would cut and crush. 'Kahaṃ ekaputtaka' is the manner of their lamentation.

Here, the brief explanation of the meaning from the beginning, based on the actual facts, is as follows: It is said that a husband and wife, taking their son and a small amount of provisions, entered a wilderness road a hundred leagues long. When they had traveled about fifty leagues, their provisions were exhausted, and being oppressed by hunger and thirst, they sat down in the sparse shade of a tree. Then the husband said to the wife: 'Dear, within fifty leagues of this place, there is no village or town. Therefore, the many tasks that must be done by men, such as farming and cattle-rearing, I can no longer do. Come, kill me, eat half of the meat, and make the other half into provisions to cross the wilderness with our son.' Again, she said to him: 'Lord, the many tasks that must be done by women, such as spinning thread, I can no longer do. Come, kill me, eat half of the meat, and make the other half into provisions to cross the wilderness with our son.' Again, he said to her: 'Dear, if the mother dies, it is certain that both will die. Indeed, a tender young boy cannot survive without his mother. If we live, we can have another son. Now, let us kill the son, take his meat, and cross the wilderness.' Then the mother said to the son: 'Dear son, go to your father.' The son went to the father. Then the father said: 'I have endured immeasurable suffering through farming, cattle-rearing, and so forth, thinking I would support my son. I am not able to kill my son. You yourself kill your son.' And he said, 'Dear son, go back to your mother.' The son went to the mother. Then the mother, although she longed for her son, said: 'I, through the practice of the cow-vow, the dog-vow, and the worship of deities...'
97:
He cannot survive apart from his mother. If we survive, we shall have another child. Come now, let us kill our little son, take his flesh, and cross the desert. Then the mother said to the little son, "Dear son, go to your father." He went. Then the father of the little son said, "I have experienced immeasurable suffering through plowing, cattle-rearing, and so forth, thinking, 'I shall raise my little son.' I am not able to kill my son; you yourself kill your son," and said, "Dear son, go to your mother." He went. Then his mother also said, "In my longing for a son, I first experienced immeasurable suffering through the cow-vow, the dog-vow, and supplicating deities. What need is there to mention the suffering of carrying him in the womb for ten months? I am not able to kill my little son," and said, "Dear son, go only to your father." Thus, while the little son was going between the two parents, he died. Seeing him dead, the parents lamented, and as previously mentioned, took the flesh and proceeded on their journey while eating it.

For those parents, that nutriment of their son's flesh was repulsive for nine reasons; it was not for play, nor for intoxication, nor for adornment, nor for beautification, but solely for the purpose of crossing the desert. By what nine reasons was it repulsive? It was because it was the flesh of one's own species, the flesh of a relative, the flesh of a son, the flesh of a dear son, tender flesh, raw flesh, unusable flesh, it lacked salt, and it lacked seasoning. Thus, while eating that son's flesh which was repulsive for nine reasons, they did not eat with a lustful or greedy mind, but remained in a state of equanimity, consuming it without desire or lust. They did not remove the flesh attached to the bones, tendons, and skin to select only the thick, choice pieces of meat, but ate only the flesh that came to their hands. They did not eat as much as they desired until their throats were full, but ate only a little each day, just enough to sustain themselves. They did not eat with a sense of stinginess toward each other, but ate with a pure mind free from the stain of selfishness. They did not eat in a state of delusion, thinking, 'We are eating venison or peacock meat,' but ate while knowing it was the flesh of their dear son. They did not eat with a wish, thinking, 'Oh, how good it would be if we could eat such son's flesh again,' but ate while being beyond such wishing. They did not store it, thinking, 'We will eat this much in the desert and mix the remainder with salt and sour fruit to eat after crossing the desert.' At the end of the desert journey, thinking, 'The public will see it,' they buried it in the ground.
98:
(The couple) also cremated the remaining flesh with fire. They did not act with conceit or vanity, thinking, "No one else gets to eat such flesh of a son as we do," but ate having subdued conceit and vanity. They did not eat with disparagement, thinking, "What shall we do with this meat that has no salt, no sourness, and a foul smell?" but ate having transcended disparagement. They did not look down on or argue with each other, saying, "This is your portion, this is my portion; this is your son, this is my son." Rather, they ate in harmony and with joy. Seeing this kind of consumption free from desire and lust, the Teacher, wishing to allow that same principle for the Saṅgha of bhikkhus, said, "What do you think, bhikkhus? Would they eat that food for play?" and so forth. In that passage, the terms such as "davāya vā" (for play) are explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga. "Kantārassa" refers to the remainder of the desert journey that had been crossed.

"Evameva kho" (Even so) means that by way of the nine repulsive aspects, it should be regarded as similar to the flesh of a dear son. What are the nine? They are the repulsiveness of going for alms, and so forth. One consumes the nutriment of edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) while reflecting on the repulsiveness of going for alms, the repulsiveness of seeking food, and the repulsiveness of consumption, the place of storage, the stomach, the digested and undigested food, the smearing, and the secretion. These aspects, such as the repulsiveness of going (gamanapāṭikulyatā), are explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga in the section on the perception of the repulsiveness of food (āhārepāṭikulyasaññā). Thus, by way of these nine repulsive aspects, nutriment should be consumed by making it like the simile of the son's flesh.

Just as those parents, while eating the repulsive flesh of their dear son, did not eat with lust or greed, but remained in equanimity and consumed it without desire or lust, even so, one should consume food by making it a consumption free from desire and lust. Just as those parents did not remove the flesh attached to the bones, tendons, and skin to select only the thick, choice pieces of meat, but ate only what came to their hands, even so, one should not push away dry rice or poor-quality curry with the back of the hand. Without showing a preference like a quail or a hen, and without selecting only the best food mixed with butter or meat from here and there, one should consume food in order (sapadāna), like a lion.

Just as those parents did not eat as much as they desired until their throats were full, but ate only a little each day to sustain themselves, even so, one should not eat until the stomach is stuffed like certain brahmins such as Āharahatthaka. Instead, one should consume food like the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, leaving space for four or five mouthfuls. It is heard that for forty-five years, after eating his meal, the Venerable Sāriputta never once experienced the sourness of indigestion, nor did he consume other nutriment, and he uttered a brave lion's roar. He spoke this verse: "One should drink water after leaving space for four or five mouthfuls; this is sufficient for the comfortable living of a bhikkhu with a mind directed toward Nibbāna." Those parents ate without stinginess toward each other.
99:
Otherwise, one should consume food like the General of the Dhamma, Venerable Sāriputta, leaving space for about four or five mouthfuls. While he lived for forty-five rains retreats (vassa), it is said that he uttered this lion's roar: "I have never once consumed food after a meal in a way that would cause sour eructation (indigestion)," and he spoke this verse:

"One should stop eating when there are four or five mouthfuls left and drink water instead. This is sufficient for the comfortable living of a bhikkhu who is resolute and has directed his mind toward Nibbāna." (Thag 983)

Just as that couple ate without being stingy toward each other, but ate with a pure heart free from the stain of stinginess, so too, upon receiving almsfood, one should consume it while established in the principles of cordiality (sāraṇīyadhamma), thinking: "I will give all of this to whoever will accept it; I will give half to whoever will accept half; if there is any remainder after they have taken, I will consume it myself."

Just as they did not eat in delusion, thinking, "We are eating some other kind of meat, such as venison or peacock meat," but ate while knowing it was the flesh of their beloved son, so too, upon receiving almsfood, one should consume it by abandoning delusion, without giving rise to the deluded perception of self, thinking, "I eat, I consume." One should reflect: "The nutriment of edible food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) does not know, 'I am nourishing this body made of the four great elements,' nor does the body know, 'The nutriment of edible food is nourishing me.'" One should also consume it without delusion through the power of mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña).

Just as that couple did not eat with a wish, thinking, "Oh, if only we could eat such flesh of our son again," but ate having transcended such wishing, so too, upon receiving choice food, one should not have a wish such as, "Oh, if only I could receive such food again tomorrow or the day after." Nor, upon receiving coarse food, should one grieve, thinking, "Today I did not receive choice food as I did yesterday." Instead, one should consume it without craving, recollecting this instruction:

"I do not grieve over the past, nor do I long for the future. I sustain myself with what is present; therefore, my complexion is bright." (Jātaka 2.22.90)

Recollecting this advice, one should consume food thinking, "I will sustain myself only with what is present."

Just as that couple did not make a hoard, thinking, "Having eaten this much in the difficult journey (wilderness), we will eat the remainder mixed with salt and sour fruits after crossing the wilderness,"
100:
but at the end of the difficult journey, thinking, "The public might see," they buried [the remains of their son's flesh] in the ground or burned it with fire. Similarly:

"Having obtained food, drink, snacks, and also robes, one should not make a hoard, nor should one be anxious if one does not obtain them." (Sn 930)

A bhikkhu who repeatedly recollects this instruction should, among the four requisites, take only as much as is necessary for his sustenance from whatever he receives, and give the rest to his fellow practitioners (sabrahmacārī). Avoiding hoarding, he should consume it.

Just as that couple did not feel pride or arrogance, thinking, "No one else can get such flesh of a son to eat as we do," but ate with pride and arrogance subdued, so too, upon receiving choice food, one should not feel pride or arrogance, thinking, "I am one who receives robes, almsfood, and so on." One should consume it only after reflecting, "This monkhood is not for the sake of robes and so on, but this monkhood is for the sake of the fruit of Arahantship (arahattaphala)," thus subduing pride and arrogance.

Just as that couple did not eat while disparaging the meat, saying, "What is the use of this meat which has no salt, no sourness, and a bad smell?" but ate having transcended disparagement, so too, upon receiving almsfood, one should not disparage the food, saying, "What is the use of this coarse and tasteless almsfood, which is like food for horses or cattle? Throw it into the dog's trough!" Nor should one disparage the donor, saying, "Who will eat this food? Give it to the crows and dogs!" Instead, one should consume it while repeatedly recollecting this instruction:

"Wandering with bowl in hand, he should behave like a mute, though he is not mute. He should not disparage a small gift, nor should he despise the donor." (Sn 718)

Just as that couple did not look down on each other, saying, "This is your portion, this is my portion; this is your son, this is my son," but ate in harmony and with joy, so too, upon receiving almsfood—unlike some bhikkhus who say, "Who would give to the likes of you, who wander about aimlessly, stumbling over thresholds? Even your own mother would not think of giving to you. But we..."
101:
Indeed, thinking, "We obtain exquisite robes and other requisites wherever we go," he disdains his virtuous fellow practitioners. With reference to such disdain, it is said:

"Monks, that monk, overcome and his mind obsessed by those gains, offerings, and fame, disdains other virtuous monks. Monks, for that misguided man, that disdain leads to his harm and suffering for a long time."

Thus, without disdaining anyone, one should partake [of requisites] in harmony and with joy together with all one's fellow practitioners.

Regarding the term 'pariññāte' (comprehended), it means to be fully understood through these three types of full understanding: full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā), full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā), and full understanding as abandoning (pahāna-pariññā). How is it fully understood? In this Teaching, a monk understands: "This so-called nutriment consisting of solid food (kabaḷīkārāhāra), by way of its physical basis, is matter with nutritive essence as the eighth (ojaṭṭhamakarūpa). Where does this nutritive-essence-octad strike? It strikes at the tongue-sensitivity (jivhāpasāda). On what does the tongue-sensitivity depend? It depends on the four great elements (mahābhūta)." Thus, he understands that the nutritive-essence-octad, the tongue-sensitivity, and the four great elements which are the cause of that tongue-sensitivity, are called the aggregate of matter (rūpakkhandha). For one who discerns that aggregate of matter, the four mental aggregates (nāmakkhandha) arise, consisting of states with contact as the fifth (phassapañcamaka). Thus, he understands that all these five aggregates are, in brief, merely mind and matter (nāmarūpa).

That monk, having defined those states by their own characteristic (or characteristic of function), and seeking their cause, sees dependent origination (paṭiccasamuppāda) in forward and backward order. To this extent, because he has seen mind and matter together with its causes as they really are, starting with the nutriment consisting of solid food, the nutriment consisting of solid food is said to be fully understood by the full understanding of the known (ñāta-pariññā). That monk then applies the three characteristics—impermanence, suffering, and non-self—to that very mind and matter together with its causes, and contemplates them by means of the seven contemplations (anupassanā). To this extent, it is said to be fully understood by the full understanding by investigation (tīraṇa-pariññā), which is the knowledge consisting of the penetration of the three characteristics. When it is fully understood by the Path of Non-returning (anāgāmimagga), which abandons sensual desire (chandarāga) in that very mind and matter, it is said to be fully understood by the full understanding as abandoning (pahāna-pariññā).

Regarding 'pañcakāmaguṇiko', it means that lust originating from the five strands of sensual pleasure is fully understood. In this context, there are three types of full understanding: single comprehension (eka-pariññā), total comprehension (sabba-pariññā), and root comprehension (mūla-pariññā). What is single comprehension? A monk who fully understands the single craving for tastes (rasataṇhā) at the tongue-door has already fully understood the lust originating from the five strands of sensual pleasure. Why? Because that very craving arises there. For that same craving, when it arises at the eye-door...
102:
...craving arising at the eye-door is called lust for forms (rūparāga). Craving arising at the ear-door and so forth are called lust for sounds (saddarāga) and so on. Thus, just as when a thief is plundering on five roads, if that thief is caught on one road and his head is cut off, all five roads become safe; similarly, when the craving for tastes (rasataṇhā) at the tongue-door is fully understood, the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure is already fully understood. This is called 'single comprehension' (eka-pariññā).

What is total comprehension (sabba-pariññā)? Lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure can occur even in a single bowl of almsfood placed in the bowl. How? First, lust for forms (rūparāga) arises in one who looks at the pure color of the almsfood. When hot ghee is poured onto that food, a 'paṭapaṭa' sound arises; likewise, when eating such crunchy food, a 'murumuru' sound arises, and lust for sounds (saddarāga) arises in one who relishes that sound. Lust for smells (gandharāga) arises in one who relishes the scent infused with cumin (jīraka) and so on. Lust for tastes (rasarāga) arises due to the delicious flavor. Lust for tangibles (phoṭṭhabbarāga) arises in one who relishes the touch of the soft food. Thus, if one partakes of this food without lust and attachment, having discerned it with mindfulness and clear comprehension (sati-sampajañña), then all that lust is already fully understood. This is called 'total comprehension' (sabba-pariññā).

What is root comprehension (mūla-pariññā)? The nutriment consisting of solid food (kabaḷīkārāhāra) is the root of the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure. Why? Because that lust arises only when that nutriment exists. It is said that during the Brāhmaṇatissa famine, for twelve years, husbands and wives did not even have the thought of looking at each other with lustful minds. Why? Because of the scarcity of food. But when the danger subsided, the island of Tambapaṇṇi (Sri Lanka), which is a hundred yojanas in extent, became continuous with the auspicious celebrations of the birth of children. Thus, when the nutriment, which is the root, is fully understood, the lust for the five strands of sensual pleasure is already fully understood. This is called 'root comprehension' (mūla-pariññā).

Regarding "That fetter does not exist," it means it does not exist because it has been abandoned in the sense of being abandoned along with that lust. Thus, this teaching was spoken up to the Path of Non-returning. However, the meaning of "Do not stop with just this much" is that one should develop insight (vipassanā) into the five aggregates by way of these forms and so forth, and the teaching should be given up to Arahantship.

## The First Nutriment (is finished).

Regarding the second nutriment (nutriment of contact), the Buddha gave the simile of the flayed cow. Why did He take the example of a cow flayed from its hooves to the base of its horns, red like the color of a Palāsa flower, instead of using examples like elephants, horses, or oxen? It is because He wished to show the state of being unable to endure painful feelings. Just as that cow, though having a noble body, cannot endure painful feelings, the Buddha brought this simile to show the meaning that the nutriment of contact (phassāhāra) is extremely vulnerable. "Those that dwell depending on a wall" refers to creatures such as spiders, snakes, and mice that depend on stone walls and so forth. "Those that dwell depending on a tree" refers to Uccalinga insects. "Those that dwell depending on water" refers to aquatic creatures such as crocodiles. "Those that dwell depending on the sky" refers to creatures such as gnats, mosquitoes, and hawks. These creatures would devour [the flayed cow].
103:
In the explanation of the second nutriment (contact as nutriment), 'a flayed cow' refers to a cow whose skin has been stripped from its entire body, from the hooves to the base of the horns, appearing like a cluster of Kiṃsuka flowers. Why is the simile of a flayed cow used instead of other animals like elephants, horses, or oxen? It is to illustrate the inability to endure. Just as a woman (represented by the cow) is unable to endure or tolerate the painful feelings that arise, so too is the nutriment of contact shown to be very weak and feeble; thus, this appropriate simile was brought forth.

'Wall' refers to any kind of wall, such as a stone wall. 'Creatures that depend on the wall' include spiders, snakes, mice, and so on. 'Creatures that depend on trees' include stinging insects (uccāliṅga) and the like. 'Creatures that depend on water' include fish, crocodiles, and so on. 'Creatures that depend on the sky' include gadflies, mosquitoes, crows, hawks, and so on. 'Would eat' means they would pluck and eat the flesh. Just as that cow, seeing the danger of being bitten by creatures depending on those various places like walls and trees, has no desire for respect or honor, nor for the stroking of its back, the massaging of its body, or warm water; in the same way, a monk, clearly seeing the danger of being bitten by the 'pests' of defilements rooted in the nutriment of contact, has no more desire for contact belonging to the three realms.

'Monks, when the nutriment of contact is fully understood' means it is fully understood through the three types of full understanding (pariññā). In this context of the nutriment of contact, there are also three types of full understanding. Among those three: seeing name-and-form together with its causes exactly as they are—such as 'contact is the aggregate of mental formations (saṅkhārakkhandha), the feeling associated with that contact is the aggregate of feeling (vedanākkhandha), perception is the aggregate of perception (saññākkhandha), consciousness is the aggregate of consciousness (viññāṇakkhandha), and the physical base and objects of these four mental aggregates are the aggregate of form (rūpakkhandha)'—is called 'full understanding of the known' (ñātapariññā). Applying the three marks of existence to those very same phenomena of name-and-form and investigating them as impermanent and so on by way of the seven contemplations is called 'full understanding by investigation' (tīraṇapariññā). The Path of Arahantship, which uproots desire and lust (chandarāga) for those same phenomena of name-and-form, is called 'full understanding by abandonment' (pahānapariññā). 'The three feelings' means that when the nutriment of contact is fully understood through these three types of full understanding, the three feelings are also already fully understood, because they are rooted in and associated with that contact. Thus, the teaching by way of the nutriment of contact is spoken up to the fruit of Arahantship. The second nutriment is finished.

In the third nutriment, 'aṅgārakāsu' means a pit of glowing coals. The word 'kāsu' can mean either a heap or a pit.
104:
'Other hell-beings, weeping and with scorched bodies, fall into the pit of glowing coals. O Mātali, the divine charioteer, seeing these beings, fear seizes me; therefore, I ask you.' (Jātaka 2.22.462).

In this context, 'kāsu' is said to mean a heap. In the passage, 'O charioteer, why do you dig a pit so hurriedly?' (Jātaka 2.22.3), it means a pit. In this Sutta (the Āhāra Sutta) as well, it is this 'pit' that is intended. 'Sādhikaporisa' means more than a man's height, about five cubits in measure. By the phrase 'without flames, without smoke,' the Buddha shows the intense heat of that pit of glowing coals. For when there are flames or smoke, wind arises and the heat is not so great; in their absence, because there is no wind, the heat is extremely intense. 'Ārakā vassa' means it should be far away.

In the phrase 'evam eva kho' (even so), the comparison between the simile and the thing signified is as follows: The round of rebirth in the three realms (tebhūmakavaṭṭa) should be seen as the pit of glowing coals. The foolish worldling (bālaputhujjana) attached to the round should be seen as the man who wants to live. Wholesome and unwholesome kamma should be seen as the two strong men. The time of the worldling's accumulation of kamma should be seen as the time of seizing that man by his arms and dragging him toward the pit of glowing coals. For kamma, when being accumulated, is said to drag along rebirth-linking. The suffering of the round caused by kamma should be understood like the suffering caused by the pit of glowing coals.

'Fully understood' means fully understood through the three types of full understanding. The application of full understanding here should be understood in the same manner as stated for contact. 'The three cravings'—namely, sensual craving (kāma-taṇhā), craving for existence (bhava-taṇhā), and craving for non-existence (vibhava-taṇhā)—become fully understood. Why? Because mental volition (manosañcetanā) is rooted in craving. Indeed, when the cause is not abandoned, the result cannot be abandoned. Thus, the teaching by way of the nutriment of mental volition is also spoken up to Arahantship. The third nutriment is finished.

In the fourth nutriment, 'āgucārī' means a wrongdoer or a criminal. By the question 'How is that man?', it asks: what is the condition of that man, does he survive or not? 'Even so, O King, he still lives' means he lives now just as he did before.
105:
In this passage 'Evameva kho', this comparison and analogy should be understood. Kamma should be seen as the King. The foolish worldling (bāla-puthujjana) who relies on the round of rebirths should be seen as the man who commits an offense disliked by the King. Rebirth-linking consciousness (paṭisandhi-viññāṇa) should be seen as the three hundred spears. The time when the King of Kamma seizes the worldling who relies on the round and casts them into rebirth should be understood as the time when the King orders the offender, 'Strike him with three hundred spears.' In that analogy, although rebirth-linking consciousness is like the three hundred spears, in truth, there is no suffering in the spears themselves; there is only suffering rooted in the wounds inflicted by the spears. Similarly, there is no suffering in rebirth-linking itself; however, when rebirth-linking is given, the resultant suffering (vipāka-dukkha) that occurs during the course of existence (pavatti) is like the suffering caused by the wounds from the spears.

'Pariññāta' means when it is fully understood through the three types of full understanding (pariññā). In this fourth nutriment as well, the application of full understanding should be understood in the same way as stated in the section on the nutriment of contact (phassāhāra). 'Nāmarūpa' refers to mentality-materiality caused by consciousness. When consciousness is fully understood, that mentality-materiality is also fully understood, because it is rooted in and arises together with it. Thus, the teaching has been delivered up to the fruit of Arahantship (arahatta-phala) by way of the nutriment of consciousness (viññāṇāhāra). The fourth nutriment is finished. The commentary on the third sutta is finished.

## 4. Atthirāga Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, terms such as 'rāga' are merely names for greed (lobha). That same greed is called lust (rāga) by way of attachment, delight (nandī) by way of rejoicing, and craving (taṇhā) by way of desiring. 'Viññāṇa established and growing there' (patiṭṭhitaṃ tattha viññāṇaṃ virūḷhaṃ) means it is established and increased by being capable of impelling kamma and pulling towards rebirth-linking. In the word 'yattha', the locative case is used in the sense of 'in the round of rebirths in the three planes' (tebhūmaka-vaṭṭa). Alternatively, this locative case should be understood as applying to every place or to each preceding term. The phrase 'there is the growth of formations there' (atthi tattha saṅkhārānaṃ vuddhi) is spoken with reference to the formations that are the causes of the future round for one established in this round of results (vipāka-vaṭṭa). 'Where there is the production of renewed existence in the future' (yattha atthi āyatiṃ punabbhavābhinibbatti) means in whatever place there is the production of renewed existence in the future.

In this passage 'Evameva kho', this comparison and analogy should be understood. Kamma along with its attendants should be understood as like a dyer or a painter. The round of rebirths in the three planes should be understood as like a wooden board, a wall, or a cloth. Just as dyers or painters produce a figure on a clean board and so on, similarly, kamma along with its attendants produces form (rūpa) in the various states of existence. In that process, just as a figure produced by an unskilled painter is ill-formed and unpleasant, similarly, when performing some kamma with a mind dissociated from knowledge...
106:
...some person performs kamma with a mind dissociated from knowledge. When that kamma produces form, it does not give the perfection of the eyes and so on, but produces a form that is ugly, ill-formed, and unpleasant even to the parents. However, just as a figure produced by a skilled painter is beautiful, well-formed, and pleasant, similarly, when some person performs kamma with a mind associated with knowledge, that kamma, when producing form, gives the perfection of the eyes and so on, and produces a form that is beautiful, well-formed, and as if decorated and prepared.

Here, it should be understood that there is one link (sandhi) between nutriment and mentality-materiality by grouping nutriment together with consciousness; one link between mentality-materiality and formations by grouping the sequence of results together with mentality-materiality; and one link between formations and future existence.

'Kūṭāgāra' is a house (pavilion) made by installing a single peak. 'Kūṭāgāra-sālā' is a hall made by installing two peaks. In the phrase 'Even so indeed' (evameva kho), the kamma of one whose taints are destroyed (khīṇāsava) should be understood as being like a sunbeam. Although the sunbeam exists, it is called 'unestablished' (appatiṭṭha) because it has no place to land; similarly, the kamma of an Arahant is said to be 'unestablished' because it lacks the nature of producing results. Although such an Arahant has a body and so on, the kamma performed with those is not called wholesome or unwholesome; it remains merely functional (kiriya) and is without result (avipāka). Thus, the kamma of that Arahant is called 'unestablished' because it is non-existent. The fourth sutta is finished.

## 5. Nagara Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, in the phrase 'When there is mentality-materiality, there is consciousness', it could have been said 'When there are formations, there is consciousness' and 'When there is ignorance, there are formations', but neither was said. Why? Because ignorance and formations belong to the (past) existence and do not fit with this insight (vipassanā). This is because the Great Being (Mahāpurisa) applied his mind only by way of the present five-constituent existence (pañcavokāra-bhava).

Is it not impossible to become a Buddha without seeing ignorance and formations? True, it is impossible.
