However, those ignorance and formations have already been seen by way of existence, grasping, and craving. Therefore, for example, a man chasing an iguana, seeing it enter a hole, would go down, dig the place where it entered, catch the iguana, and leave; he would not dig the other parts.
107:
Why does he not dig? Because there is no other being. Similarly, the Great Being (Bodhisatta), while sitting upon the throne of enlightenment (Bodhipallaṅka), like a man following a monitor lizard, searched from the perspective of aging and death, thinking, 'Because of this, this comes to be.' When he saw the cause of name-and-form (nāmarūpa) and searched further for the cause of that name-and-form, he saw only consciousness (viññāṇa). At that moment, he turned back his insight (vipassanā), realizing, 'The scope of investigation by way of the five-constituent existence (pañcavokārabhava) is only this much.' Although the two factors of ignorance (avijjā) and formations (saṅkhāra) existed, like the undug portion of an empty pit, he did not take them as separate objects for investigation because they had already been grasped in the lower stages of insight.

'Paccaudāvattati' means it turns back. Which consciousness turns back here? Both rebirth-consciousness (paṭisandhiviññāṇa) and insight-consciousness (vipassanāviññāṇa). Among them, rebirth-consciousness turns back from the cause, and insight-consciousness turns back from the object. Both do not transcend name-and-form; they do not go beyond name-and-form. Within this extent, such as in the phrases 'it may be born' or 'it may arise,' consciousness is the cause of name-and-form, and name-and-form is the cause of consciousness; since both are mutual causes, only by this much does birth or rebirth occur. Beyond this, what else could be born or arise? Is it not indeed only this consciousness and name-and-form that are born and arise?

Thus, having shown the five factors along with the successive deaths and rebirths, and wishing to assign the meaning already stated by the word 'ettāvatā' (by this much), he said, 'With name-and-form as condition, consciousness comes to be; with consciousness as condition, name-and-form comes to be.' Then, to show the future aging and death which has its root in name-and-form arising from consciousness by way of the forward dependent origination (anuloma-paccayākāra), he said, 'With name-and-form as condition, the six sense bases (saḷāyatana) come to be,' and so forth.

'Añjasa' is merely a synonym for the path (magga). 'Uddhāpavanta' means being endowed with a city wall called 'uddhāpa' because it rises high upwards. 'Ramaṇီya' (delightful) means being delightful due to the abundance of various goods within the four surrounding gates. 'Māpehi' means 'cause the people to be sent and dwell there.' 'Māpeyya' means 'he should cause them to dwell.' In establishing the city, he first sent eighteen crores of people and asked, 'Is it full?' When told, 'It is not yet full,' he should send another five families. When asked again and told, 'It is not yet full,' he should send another fifty-five families. When asked again and told, 'It is not yet full,' he should send another...
108:
...he should send another thirty families. When asked again and told, 'It is not yet full,' he should send another thousand families. When asked again and told, 'It is not yet full,' he should send another eleven thousand families. When asked again and told, 'It is not yet full,' he should send another eighty-four thousand families.

When asked once more, 'Is it full?' they would reply, 'Great King, what are you saying? The city is vast and cannot be crowded; it is impossible to fill it by sending families in this manner. Instead, have the drum beaten and proclaim the city's virtues and the protection the people will receive, saying: Our city is endowed with such and such prosperity; let those who wish to live there go as they please, and they shall receive such and such protection.' The king would do so. Then, hearing of the city's virtues and the protection to be gained, people would gather from all directions and fill the city. That city would later become prosperous and flourishing. Referring to such prosperity, the Buddha said, 'That city later became prosperous and flourishing,' and so forth.

In that text, 'Iddha' means prosperous and having abundant food. 'Phီta' means blooming with all kinds of wealth. 'Bāhujañña' means known by many, or for the benefit of many people. There is also a variant reading 'Bahujana.' 'Ākiṇṇamanussa' means crowded with people, filled without gaps. 'Vuḍḍhivepullappatta' means reaching growth and abundance, reaching the state of being noble and extensive; it means it became the foremost city in the ten thousand world-systems.

In the phrase 'Evameva kho' (Even so), this is the comparison of the simile: The Bodhisatta, who fulfilled the perfections (pāramīs) starting from the feet of the Buddha Dīpaṅkara, should be understood as the man wandering in the great forest. The Great Being's seeing of the eightfold insight path (vipassanāmagga) in the preliminary stage while sitting sequentially at the Bodhi tree should be understood as that man's seeing of the path followed by people of old. The Great Being's seeing of the supramundane path (lokuttaramagga) at the end of practicing higher insight should be understood as that man's seeing of the highway later while following the single-track path. The Tathāgata's seeing of the city of Nibbāna should be understood as that man's seeing of the city ahead while traveling by that path. In this simile, however, the outside of the city was seen by others and inhabited by others, but the city of Nibbāna was seen by the Teacher himself and inhabited by himself. The Tathāgata's time of seeing the four paths (maggas) should be understood as that man's time of seeing the four gates. The Tathāgata's time of entering Nibbāna through the four paths should be understood as that man's time of entering the city through the four gates. Just as that man discerned the goods in the city...
109:
The time of entering Nibbāna through the four paths should be understood as the time when that man determines the goods within the city; it is the time when the Tathāgata determines more than fifty wholesome states through His knowledge of reviewing (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa). The time of looking for families to build houses in the city is like the time when the Buddha, arising from the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti), surveys beings to be tamed (veneyya). The time when the King, requested by that man, sees a great householder is like the time when the Buddha, requested by the Great Brahmā, sees the Elder Aññāsi Koṇḍañña. The time when the King summons the great householder and sends him saying, "Live in the city," is like the time when the Buddha, after a meal, travels eighteen yojanas, enters Isipatana near Bārāṇasī on the full moon day of Āsāḷha, and preaches the Dhamma to the Elder, making him a "body-witness" (kāyasakkhi).

The time when the great householder takes eighteen crores of men and dwells in the city is like the time when the Buddha sets the Wheel of Dhamma in motion, and the Elder Koṇḍañña, along with eighteen crores of Brahmās, is established in the fruit of stream-entry (sotāpattiphala). Thus, the great city of Nibbāna was first established with households. Then, when asked, "Is the city full?" and the answer was "Not yet," just as families from five up to eighty-four thousand were sent, so the Buddha, from the fifth day onwards, preached the Anattalakkhaṇa Sutta and other discourses, causing a multitude of beings to descend into the Noble Path and sending them to the great city of Nibbāna: starting with the group of five (pañcavaggiya), fifty-five young men led by Yasa, thirty Bhaddavaggiya princes, one thousand former matted-hair ascetics (jaṭilas), one hundred and ten thousand brahmins and householders led by King Bimbisāra, and eighty-four thousand beings during the appreciation (anumodanā) of the Tirokuṭṭa Sutta.

Thereafter, as the city was still not full despite such sending, just as one would beat a drum to announce the city's virtues and the benefits of protection for the families, so should be understood the proclamation by Dhamma-preachers for eight days a month in various places, announcing the virtues of Nibbāna and the benefits of escaping the wilderness of birth (jātikantāra) for those who have reached Nibbāna. After that, just as people coming from all directions gather in the city, so should be understood the gathering in Nibbāna of countless young men of good family who, having heard the Dhamma-talk in various places, depart from those places, beginning with ordination and practicing the path in accordance with the supramundane Dhamma.

## Puraṇāṃ magganti ariyam aṭṭhaṅgikaṃ maggaṃ.

This Noble Path is called "anuppannamaggi" (the path not previously arisen) in the Pavāraṇā Sutta because it had not yet appeared. In this sutta, however, it is called "purāṇamagga" (the ancient path) because it is not [currently] being used.

## Brahmacariyanti sikkhattayasaṅgahaṃ sakalasāsanaṃ.

## Iddhanti

Iddha means being endowed with the bliss of jhāna.
110:
Being endowed with the bliss of jhāna is called "iddha". Being prosperous and increased by the factor of rapture (pīti) is called "subhikkha". "Phīta" means being blossomed with the ornaments of direct knowledge (abhiññā). Being widespread is called "vitthārika". Being known by many people is called "bāhujañña". "Yāva devamanussehi suppakāsitaṃ" means that within the world of space (okāsaloka) as far as it is defined by the gods and humans within the ten thousand world-systems, it has been well-expounded and well-taught by the Tathāgata. The explanation of the fifth sutta ends.

## 6. Sammasasuttavaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, it says "āmantesi" (he addressed). Why did he address them? Because the Dhamma teaching that is subtle and demonstrates the Three Marks of Existence (tilakkhaṇa) appeared to the Buddha. To elaborate, the people in that Kammasadhamma district had the supporting conditions (upanissaya) to attain the Noble Dhamma; they were wise. It is said that the food there was soft and rich; for those who consume such food, wisdom increases. They were capable of penetrating the profound Dhamma-talk that demonstrates the Three Marks of Existence. Because of the fulfillment of such internal and external factors, the Buddha preached there in that market town of Kammasadhamma other profound suttas such as the Mahāsatipaṭṭhāna Suttas in the Dīgha and Majjhima Nikāyas, the Mahānidāna Sutta, the Āneñjasappāya Sutta, and the Cūḷanidāna Sutta in the Saṃyutta Nikāya. "Sammasatha no" means asking "Do you contemplate and reflect?" "Antaraṃ sammasanti" refers to investigating and reflecting on the causes of the conditioned phenomena within one's own continuity (paccayasammasana). That monk could not please the Buddha's mind (could not follow His intention). This is because he did not answer according to the Buddha's wish to have him answer by way of the mode of conditions (paccayākāra), but instead answered by way of the thirty-two parts of the body (dvattiṃsākāra), and thus failed to grasp the [Buddha's] intention.

"Etadavoca" (he said this) was made because the discourse had not yet reached its proper sequence (anusandhi); he said this to bring the discourse to its proper sequence. "Tenahānanda suṇātha" (Therefore, Ānanda, listen) is a term in the Buddha's word of the Tipiṭaka that is unmixed and does not exist in this manner anywhere else. "Upadhinidānaṃ" means having the acquisition of the aggregates (khandhupadhi) as a cause. Here, "upadhi" refers to the group of the five aggregates. "Uppajjati" means it arises. "Nivisati" means it stays by way of repeated occurrence.

"Yaṃ kho loke piyarūpaṃ sātarūpaṃ" refers to whatever in the world is of a lovable nature and a pleasant nature. In the phrases "cakkhuṃ loke" etc., the meaning should be understood as follows: To elaborate—beings in the world who are attached to the eye etc. as "mine," being established in prosperity, regard their own eyes as being like a jeweled lion-window opened in a golden mansion, because of the clarity of the five sensitivities (pasāda) through observing the reflection in mirrors etc. They regard the ear as being like a silver tube or a decorated ear-ornament (pāmaṅgasutta). They regard the nose as being like a rounded ball of vermilion. They regard the tongue, which produces soft and sweet sounds, as being like the surface of a red blanket. They regard their body as being like a sal-tree trunk or a golden door-post. They think of their own mind as being noble, unlike the minds of others. "Niccato addakkhuṃ" means they see it as permanent. The same applies to the remaining terms such as pleasure (sukha) and self (atta). Such people cannot be liberated from the entire suffering of the round (vaṭṭadukkha). "Dakkhantī" means they will see. The term "apānīyakaṃse" is the name of a small drinking cup. Because water is drunk from that cup, it is called "apānīya". Since it is both a small cup and made of bronze (kaṃsa), the two words are combined to be called "apānīyakaṃsa".
111:
People, following the way of taking signs of appearance in mirrors and such, regard their own eyes—which are especially clear with the fivefold sensitivity (pasāda)—as a ruby-lion window opened in a golden mansion. They regard the ear as a silver tube or like a bundle of elephant-ear ornaments. They regard the nose, called ghāna, as a ball of orpiment (haritāla) that has been rounded and placed. They regard the tongue, which produces soft, sweet, and delicious tastes, as a red woolen carpet. They regard the body as a sal-tree trunk or a golden archway. They regard their own mind as noble and unlike the minds of others.

'Niccato addakkhuṃ' means they see it as permanent. The same method applies to the remaining terms like pleasure (sukha) and self (atta). 'Na parimuccanti dukkhasmā' means they are not liberated from the entire suffering of the round (vaṭṭa-dukkha). 'Dakkhanti' means they will see. 'Āpānīyakaṃsa' is the name of a small drinking cup. Because they drink water from it, it is called 'āpānīya'. Because it is both a drinking vessel and made of bronze (kaṃsa), it is called 'āpānīyakaṃsa'. It is the name for a small cup for liquor. Because of the words 'endowed with color' etc., this refers to the poisoned liquor contained in the bronze cup. 'Ghammābhitatto' means greatly tormented by heat. 'Ghammapareto' means touched or overcome by heat. To the one who drinks, that poisoned liquor will be pleasing due to its perfection of color etc., or it will remain after spreading through the whole body and producing joy and satisfaction. 'Appaṭisaṅkhā' means without reflection.

In the phrase 'Evameva kho', the comparison should be understood thus: The attractive and pleasant sense object in the world should be seen as the drinking cup (āpānīyakaṃsa). The worldling (puthujjana) dependent on the round of suffering should be seen as the man tormented by heat. The person who invites with the attractive and pleasant sense object should be seen as the man inviting with the poisoned liquor. The spiritual friend (kalyāṇamitta) such as a teacher or preceptor should be seen as the man who informs about the benefits (color etc.) and the danger of death in the poisoned liquor. Just as the man who was asked informs the heat-tormented man of the qualities and dangers in the drinking cup, so the teacher or preceptor tells the monk about the gratification (assāda) and the escape (nissaraṇa) regarding the five cords of sensual pleasure.

In that simile, although the qualities and dangers of the poisoned liquor are told, that thirsty and tormented man, having a strong urge for the perfection of color and scent, thinks, 'If I must die, I will know it later,' and drinks it hastily without reflection, meeting death or death-like suffering. Similarly, a monk [is told] that the gratification in the five cords of sensual pleasure is merely the joy that arises through seeing etc., but the danger is manifold and of various kinds in this life and the next, and that sensual pleasures provide little gratification but much suffering and despair. Although he is exhorted by teachers and preceptors to 'practice the ascetic way, guard the doors of the senses, be moderate in eating, and be devoted to wakefulness,' his mind is bound to gratification. Thinking, 'If such dangers occur, I will know it later,' he acts disrespectfully toward his teachers and preceptors, abandons his studies and duties, speaks of worldly matters, and desiring to enjoy sensual pleasures, he disavows the training and returns to the lower life of a layman. Then, practicing misconduct, he is caught as a thief while committing housebreaking etc., and being presented to the king, he undergoes punishment such as the amputation of hands and feet in this very life, and in the next life, he experiences great suffering in the four woeful states. 'Pānīyena vā vinetuṃ' means to remove with cool water or with buttermilk...
112:
"...they have much despair." Having thus spoken of the benefits and dangers, the teachers and preceptors exhort: "Practice the ascetic way, be one who guards the doors of the senses, be moderate in eating, and be constantly devoted to wakefulness." Yet, with a mind bound to gratification, he thinks, "If there be such dangers as mentioned, I will know later." Disrespecting the teachers and preceptors, abandoning the study, inquiry, and duties, and speaking of worldly gain, he disavows the training and returns to the low life because of his desire to enjoy sensual pleasures. Then, fulfilling misconduct, when he commits crimes like housebreaking and burglary, he is caught with the cry "This is a thief!" and shown to the king. He undergoes suffering like the amputation of hands and feet in this very life and experiences great suffering in the four woeful states in the future life.

"Pānīyena vā vinetuṃ" means removing with cool water. "Dadhimandakena" means with just the clear part of curds (whey). "Bhaṭṭhaloṇikāya" means with salted flour-water. "Loṇasovīrakena" means with the medicine called loṇasovīraka made by adding various grains, fruits, sprouts, and branches.

The comparison here is: The practitioner (yogāvacara) staying in the round of suffering should be seen as the man tormented by the sun's heat. Just as that man, reflecting, abandons the poisoned liquor cup and removes his thirst with water etc., so the monk, abiding in the advice of his teachers and preceptors, guarding the six sense doors, and gradually developing insight (vipassanā), attains the fruit of Arahatship. The four paths (magga) should be understood as the four drinks like cool water. Just as one drinks one of those four and removes the thirst for liquor and goes happily wherever he wishes, so the Arahant drinks the beverage of the four paths, removes craving (taṇhā), and goes to the region of Nibbāna where he has never been before. The sixth sutta is finished.

## 7. Naḷakalāpīsuttavaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, why is it asked, "Friend, how is it?" It is asked to know the disposition of the Elder Sāriputta, thinking, "If asked thus, how will he answer?" Alternatively, it is asked with the intention that "In the past, the two chief disciples settled this question; monks in the future will also know it." The phrase "Now we..." was said by the Elder (Mahākoṭṭhika) regarding that Name-and-Form for which Consciousness is a condition; that very Name-and-Form is for Consciousness...
113:
It is said because it is called a condition (paccaya). In this sutta, however, the simile of the bundle of reeds is brought forth to show the weakness of consciousness (viññāṇa) and name-and-form (nāmarūpa), without bringing in similes such as a bundle of iron.

In the passage 'cessation occurs,' the teaching is given by way of the five-constituent existence (pañcavokārabhavo) which has arisen from conditions. 'By thirty-six reasons' means by thirty-six causes, taking three types for each of the twelve factors previously answered. Herein, the first is the quality of a Dhamma speaker (dhammakathika), the second is practice (paṭipatti), and the third is the fruit of practice (paṭipattiphala). Among those three, the perfection of the teaching is stated by the first method, the plane of the trainee (sekkhabhūmi) by the second, and the plane of one beyond training (asekkhabhūmi) by the third. The seventh sutta [commentary] is finished.

## 8. Kosambisutta-vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, regarding the term 'aññatreva' (apart from): a certain person, believing the words of another, accepts it as 'what this person says is true.' Another person, while sitting and reflecting, takes a liking to a certain reason; he accepts it through preference (ruci), thinking 'this reason exists.' One person accepts it through oral tradition (anussava), thinking 'there has been such a tradition for a long time; this is true.' To another person, while reflecting, a certain reason appears in the mind; he accepts it through reasoned reflection (ākāraparivitakka), thinking 'this reason exists.' To another person, while reflecting, a certain view (diṭṭhi) arises; he likes that reason while pondering it with that view; he accepts it through acceptance of a view after pondering (diṭṭhinijjhānakkhanti), thinking 'this reason exists.' The Elder, however, rejecting these five reasons and wishing to ask about the state of having penetrated through direct knowledge, said, 'Friend Musila, apart from faith...' and so on. In that passage, 'aññatreva' means setting aside reasons such as faith, meaning without these reasons. 'Cessation of existence is Nibbāna' means the cessation of the five aggregates is Nibbāna.

'He remained silent' means that although the Elder was an Arahant, he remained silent without saying 'I am an Arahant' or 'I am not.' Why did the venerable Nārada say this to the venerable Paviṭṭha? It is said that he thought: 'This question, "Cessation of existence is Nibbāna," should be known even by trainees (sekhas). This Elder, however, is making this Elder [Musila] stand on the plane of one beyond training (asekkha). I will make this point known.' Thinking thus, he spoke these words.
114:
'Sammappaññāya sudiṭṭhaṃ' means well seen with insight knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa) and path knowledge (magga-ñāṇa). Saying 'I am not an Arahant' shows that he is not yet an Arahant because he stands in the Path of Non-Returning (anāgāmimagga). The knowledge that 'cessation of existence is Nibbāna' which he has now is the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa) that reviews Nibbāna among the nineteen types of reviewing knowledge. 'Udapāno' refers to a drinking well about thirty cubits deep. 'Udakavārako' refers to a water-dipping vessel (or a water-pot). 'Udakanti hi kho ñāṇaṃ assa' is like the knowledge 'this is water' that arises in a person standing by the well and looking in. 'Na ca kāyena phusitvā' means being unable to draw the water and touch or experience it with the body. A Non-returner's seeing of Nibbāna is like seeing water in a well. A Non-returner is like a man oppressed and parched by the heat of the sun. The Path of Arahantship (Arahattamagga) is like the water-dipping vessel. Just as a man oppressed by the sun sees water in a well, so too a Non-returner knows through reviewing knowledge that 'there is still the time of attaining the Fruit of Arahantship above.' However, just as that man cannot draw the water and touch it with his body because he lacks a water-dipping vessel, so too a Non-returner cannot yet sit having attained the Fruit of Arahantship (Arahattaphala-samāpatti) by making Nibbāna the object, because he does not yet possess the Path of Arahantship. The eighth sutta [commentary] is finished.

## 9. Upayantisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, 'upayanto' means rising upwards at the time of the water's increase. 'Mahānadiyo' refers to great rivers such as the Ganges and Yamuna. 'Upayāpeti' means causes to reach the top, causes to increase, or fills; this is the meaning. 'Avijjā upayantī' means ignorance rising upwards and being able to be a condition for formations (saṅkhāras). 'Saṅkhāre upayāpeti' means it causes formations to reach the top or to increase. The meaning should be understood thus in all terms. 'Apayanto' means receding or decreasing. 'Avijjā apayantī' means ignorance receding or decreasing and thus being unable to be a condition for formations above; this is the meaning. 'Saṅkhāre apayāpeti' means causing formations to recede. This method applies to all terms. The ninth sutta [commentary] is finished.

## 10. Susimasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, 'garukato' means being highly esteemed in the mind by all devas and humans, like a stone umbrella. 'Mānito' means being cherished in the mind. 'Pūjito' means being worshipped (with the four requisites).
115: He is honored with the four requisites. 'Apacita' means being respected by performing acts of humility. Upon seeing the Buddha, people descend from the backs of elephants and so forth, clear the path, lower their upper robes from their shoulders, rise from their seats, and pay homage. Because of these actions, the Buddha is said to be respected (apacita). Susima is a wise wanderer of that name, skilled in the branches of the Vedas. Regarding the words 'Come here,' it is said that they had this thought: 'The ascetic Gotama did not reach the pinnacle of gains because of his birth or lineage. Rather, this ascetic Gotama is superior to poets; being an excellent poet, he composes texts for his disciples. Those disciples learn those texts and, sitting near their supporters, speak words of conversation, words of appreciation (anumodanā), and chanting in intonation (sarabhañña), and so forth. Those supporters, being devoted, bring offerings and gains. If we also knew even a little of the texts known by the ascetic Gotama, we could incorporate our own doctrines into those texts and preach to the supporters. By doing so, we would receive even more gains than those monks. Who can ordain in the presence of the ascetic Gotama and learn quickly?' Having thought thus, they saw that 'Susima is capable' and approached him, speaking in this manner. Why did he approach the Venerable Ānanda? It is said that Susima had this thought: 'To whom should I go to obtain this Dhamma quickly?' Then he thought: 'The ascetic Gotama is highly revered, possessing great majesty, and is constantly devoted to his practices; it is not easy to approach him at an improper time. Many others, such as kings and so forth, also approach the ascetic Gotama, so it is not easy to approach him at those times either. Among his disciples, the Venerable Sāriputta is of great wisdom and is appointed as the foremost in the field of insight (vipassanā). The Venerable Mahāmoggallāna is appointed as the foremost in the field of concentration (samādhi). The Venerable Mahākassapa is foremost among those who uphold the dhutanga practices, the Venerable Anuruddha among those with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), the Venerable Puṇṇa Mantāṇiputta among the Dhamma preachers, and the Venerable Upāli is appointed as the foremost among the bearers of the Vinaya. This Venerable Ānanda, however, is very learned, a bearer of the Tipiṭaka, and the Teacher repeats to him the Dhamma preached in various places; he is appointed as the foremost in five categories, is the recipient of eight boons, and is endowed with four wonderful and marvelous qualities. If I go near this Venerable Ānanda, I will be able to obtain the Dhamma quickly.' Therefore, he approached the place where the Venerable Ānanda was.
116: In the phrase 'approached where the Blessed One was,' why did the Venerable Ānanda not ordain him himself but instead approach the Blessed One? It is said that he had this thought: 'This Susima wanders about claiming "I am a teacher" in a separate sectarian doctrine; after ordaining, he might strive to cause loss of gains to the Dispensation. I do not know his true intention, but the Teacher will know.' Therefore, taking Susima with him, he approached where the Blessed One was. Regarding the words 'In that case, Ānanda, ordain Susima,' it is said that the Teacher thought: 'This wanderer travels about claiming "I am a teacher" in a sectarian doctrine, yet now he says, "I wish to lead the holy life of the Path in this Dispensation." Is he devoted to me, or to my disciples, or is he devoted to the Dhamma talk of myself or my disciples?' Then, realizing that there was no devotion in Susima's mind toward any of these, He thought: 'This person wishes to ordain thinking "I will steal the Dhamma in the Dispensation of the Buddha." Thus, his coming is impure; how will the attainment of Arahantship be accomplished?' Upon investigating, He saw: 'Although he ordains with the intent to steal the Dhamma, within a few days he will strive and attain Arahantship.' Knowing this, He said, 'In that case, Ānanda, ordain Susima.' 'Final knowledge has been declared' means that those monks, having taken a meditation subject from the Teacher and residing for the three months of the rainy season, strove and exerted themselves within that very period and attained Arahantship. Those monks thought, 'We shall inform the Teacher of the special quality we have attained,' and after the Pavāraṇā ceremony, they put away their bedding and seats, came to the Teacher, and reported the special quality they had attained. This statement is made in reference to that reporting. 'Aññā' is a name for Arahantship. 'Byākatā' means reported or declared. 'He heard' means that Susima, being attentive, went to the places where those various monks stayed, wishing to hear their various conversations. In the phrase 'approached those monks,' why did he approach? It is said that upon hearing that news, he had this thought: 'What is called "Aññā" (Final Knowledge) must be the most supreme essence in this Dispensation, like a "teacher's fist" (ācariya-muṭṭhi); I will know it by asking.' Therefore, he approached. 'Anekavihitaṃ' means of many kinds. 'Iddhividhaṃ' means the categories of psychic power. 'Āvibhāvaṃ tirobhāvaṃ' refers to asking whether one can perform invisibility after taking manifestation, and manifestation after taking invisibility. 'Tirokuṭṭaṃ' means outside of a wall.
117:
In the other two terms as well, the method is the same. "Ummujjanimujjanti" means emerging and submerging. "Pallaṅkena" means by sitting cross-legged. "Kamatha" is a question asking whether they are able to sit or to go. "Pakkhi sakuṇo" means a winged bird. This is a brief explanation here; however, in detail, the account of this psychic power (iddhividha) and the explanations of the divine ear (dibbasota) and so forth that follow should be understood according to the method stated in the Visuddhimagga.

"Santā vimokkhā" (peaceful liberations) refers to the formless liberations (āruppa-vimokkha) which are peaceful due to the tranquility of the jhāna factors and the tranquility of the object. "Kāyena phusitvā" (touching with the body) means touching or attaining with the mental body (nāmakāya). By the words, "Friend, we are those liberated by wisdom," they show: "Friend, we are dry-insight practitioners (sukkhavipassaka) who, without the basis of jhāna, are liberated from defilements through wisdom alone." Why did they say, "Friend Susīma, whether you wish to know or not"? It is said that they thought: "We will not be able to answer by taking up the inclination of this Susīma; however, if he asks the Buddha, he will become free from doubt." "Dhammaṭṭhitiñāṇa" (knowledge of the stability of Dhamma) refers to insight-knowledge (vipassanā-ñāṇa), which arises first. "Nibbāne ñāṇa" (knowledge of Nibbāna) refers to the Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa) that occurs at the end of the practice of insight; that knowledge arises later. Therefore, the Blessed One spoke in this way.

Why was the statement beginning with "Whether you wish to know" spoken? It is to show the arising of such Path-knowledge even without concentration (samādhi). This is what is meant: Susīma, neither the Path nor the Fruit is a result of concentration, nor an advantage of concentration, nor a completion by concentration; rather, it is a result of insight, an advantage of insight, and a completion by insight. Therefore, whether you know or not, indeed, the knowledge of the stability of Dhamma comes first, and the knowledge of Nibbāna comes later.

Now, knowing his potential for penetration (paṭivedhabhabba), and wishing to teach the Dhamma in three rounds (teparivaṭṭa), the Buddha said, "Susīma, what do you think? Is form permanent or impermanent?" and so forth. At the end of that teaching in three rounds, the Elder attained Arahantship. Now, posing a question to him, the Buddha said, "Susīma, do you see that aging and death occur with birth as condition?" and so forth. Why did he begin with "But, Susīma..."? It was to make manifest the state of the dry-insight monks who do not possess jhāna. The meaning here is: Susīma, not only are you a dry-insight practitioner without jhāna, but these monks are also such dry-insight practitioners. In all other parts, the meaning is clear. The tenth sutta is finished.

## 7. Mahāvagga
118:
## 1. Commentary on Jarāmaraṇa Sutta and others
## 8. Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Vagga
71-72. In the Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Vagga, eleven discourses are taught by making each term, such as aging and death (jarāmaraṇa), a separate discourse. These eleven discourses have meanings that are clear.

## The eighth, Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Vagga, is finished.
## 9. Antarapeyyālaṃ
## 1. Commentary on Satthu Sutta and others
Following this Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Vagga, the twelve discourses proceeding in the manner of "The Teacher should be sought" are called the Antarapeyyāla Vagga. All those twelve discourses were also spoken in connection with the inclinations of the individuals to be led (veneyya) who are capable of understanding the Four Noble Truths in various ways. In that text, "Satthā" (Teacher) refers to either the Buddha or a disciple, depending on whom one relies to obtain Path-knowledge (magga-ñāṇa); this person who is the decisive support for Path-knowledge is called the Teacher, and that Teacher should be sought. "Sikkhā should be practiced" means the threefold training of higher virtue (adhisīla), higher mind (adhicitta), and higher wisdom (adhipaññā) should be practiced. Among the terms such as yoga, "yoga" means application in meditation (bhāvanā). "Chanda" means the wholesome desire to act. "Ussoḷhī" means excessive energy capable of enduring all obstacles to meditation. "Appaṭivānī" means unfaltering effort. "Ātappa" means only the energy that burns up defilements. "Sātacca" means the act of meditation performed continuously. "Sati" (Mindfulness) means the mindfulness that grasps the Four Noble Truths by way of aging and death, etc. "Sampajañña" (Clear comprehension) means the knowledge that is similar to that mindfulness. "Appamāda" (Heedfulness) means non-negligence in the cultivation of the Four Noble Truths. The remaining meaning is clear in all terms.

## The ninth, Antarapeyyāla Vagga, is finished.
## The Commentary on Nidāna Saṃyutta is finished.
119:
## 2. Abhisamayasamyutta
## 1. Nakhasikhāsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the Abhisamayasamyutta, "nakhasikhā" refers to the tip of the fingernail that is free from flesh. Although the tip of a fingernail is large for worldly beings, for the Blessed One, it is as delicate as the tip of a red lotus petal. If one asks how dust could stay on this fingernail tip, it is because it stayed there by the power of [the Buddha's] resolve (adhiṭṭhāna). Desiring to make the meaning known, the Blessed One caused it to stay on that fingernail tip by the power of resolve. "Sati maṃ kalaṃ" means taking the dust of the great earth, dividing it into a hundred parts, and taking one of those parts. In subsequent suttas, the method should be understood in this same way. "Abhisametāvino" refers to those who remain having realized the Noble Truths through the wisdom of the path.

The phrase "considering the mass of suffering that has been exhausted," mentioned first, means that one should place [this thought] near one's knowledge and investigate it, [realizing] that "this exhausted suffering alone is indeed much more." Here, what is meant by "former suffering" (purima-dukkha)? It is the suffering that has been exhausted. What is the suffering that has been exhausted? It is the suffering that would have arisen because the first path had not been developed. Considering what? It should be understood that all the suffering that would have arisen anywhere, starting from the eighth rebirth and including the planes of misery within the seven existences, has been exhausted. "Sattakkhattuṃ" means seven times or in seven existences. "Paramatā" shows that these seven existences are the ultimate limit for that person. "Mahatthiyo" refers to one who accomplishes a great benefit. This is the commentary on the first sutta.

## 2. Pokkharaṇīsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, "pokkharaṇī" means a pond. "Ubbedhena" means by depth. "Samatittikā" means level with the bank. "Kākapeyyā" refers to a state where a crow standing on the bank can drink by lowering its beak normally. This is the commentary on the second sutta.

## 3. Sambhejja-udakasutta-ādi-vaṇṇanā
76-77. In the third sutta, "yatthimā" means "in the place where these rivers meet." "Saṃsandanti" means they flow together after meeting. "Samenti" means they meet. "Dve vā tīṇi vā" means two or three. "Udakaphusitāni" refers to drops of water. "Sambhejja-udakaṃ" is the water at the place where it joins with other rivers. The fourth sutta has a clear meaning. These are the commentaries on the third and fourth suttas.
120:
## 5. Pathavīsutta-ādi-vaṇṇanā
78-84. In the fifth sutta, "mahāpathaviyā" means having taken from the great earth within the universe. "Kolaṭṭhimattiyo" are earth clods the size of jujube seeds. "Guḷikā" refers to balls of fine clay. "Upanikkhipeyya" means one should place them in one spot. In the sixth sutta and others, the meaning should be understood according to the method already stated. At the end, however, it means that the entire attainment of qualities by those outside the Dispensation (ascetics and brahmins of other sects) does not reach even a hundredth, a thousandth, or a hundred-thousandth part of the qualities attained through the first path. This is the commentary on the fifth sutta and others.

## The Commentary on the Abhisamayasamyutta is Finished.
The commentary on the Abhisamayasamyutta is concluded.
121:
## 3. Dhātusamyutta
## 1. Nānattavagga
## 1. Dhātunānattasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the Dhātusamyutta, "dhātunānatta" (diversity of elements) refers to the diverse nature of states that have received the name "elements" (dhātu) because of their intrinsic nature, which is defined as being non-soul and empty. Among the terms such as "cakkhudhātu" (eye element), eye-sensitivity is the eye element; the form-object is the form element; and the consciousness that has eye-sensitivity as its basis is the eye-consciousness element. Ear-sensitivity is the ear element; the sound-object is the sound element; and the consciousness that has ear-sensitivity as its basis is the ear-consciousness element. Nose-sensitivity is the nose element; the odor-object is the odor element; and the consciousness that has nose-sensitivity as its basis is the nose-consciousness element. Tongue-sensitivity is the tongue element; the taste-object is the taste element; and the consciousness that has tongue-sensitivity as its basis is the tongue-consciousness element. Body-sensitivity is the body element; the tangible-object is the tangible element; and the consciousness that has body-sensitivity as its basis is the body-consciousness element. The three types of mind element are called the mind element (manodhātu). The three aggregates beginning with feeling (vedanā), subtle forms, and Nibbāna are called the dhamma element (dhammadhātu). All mind-consciousness is called the mind-consciousness element (manoviññāṇadhātu). Among these elements, sixteen elements belong to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara); the last two (the mind element and the mind-consciousness element) are included in the four planes. This is the commentary on the first sutta.

## 2. Phassanānattasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, "uppajjati phassanānattaṃ" means that contact of diverse natures arises. Therein, eye-contact and so on are associated with eye-consciousness and so on. Mind-contact is associated with the first javana in the mind-door. Therefore, in the Pali "manodhātuṃ paṭicca," the meaning should be understood as: the contact associated with the first javana arises depending on the functional mind-consciousness element called mind-door adverting (manodvārāvajjana). This is the commentary on the second sutta.

## 3. Nophassanānattasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, regarding the phrase "no manosamphassaṃ paṭicca uppajjati manodhātu," the meaning should be noted as: the functional mind-consciousness element called adverting (āvajjana) does not arise depending on the contact associated with the first javana in the mind-door. This is the commentary on the third sutta.
122:
## 4. Commentary on the Vedanānānatta Sutta
In the fourth sutta, regarding the phrase "feeling born of eye-contact" (cakkhusamphassajā vedanā), although it could refer to all feelings occurring at that door starting from the receiving mind-element (sampaṭicchana-manodhātu), it is stated that it is appropriate to take only the immediately following receiving feeling (sampaṭicchana-vedanā) for the sake of ease of presentation. Regarding "dependent on mind-contact" (manosamphassaṃ paṭicca), this means that the first impulsion (javana) feeling arises dependent on the advertence-contact (āvajjanasamphassa) at the mind-door, and the second impulsion feeling arises dependent on the first impulsion-contact. The fourth sutta ends.

## 5. Commentary on the Dutiya-vedanānānatta Sutta
In the fifth sutta, the methods mentioned in the third and fourth suttas are taught together. Thus, in the four suttas starting from the second, the term "mind-element" (manodhātu) is not taken as the [usual] mind-element (comprising five-door advertence and receiving), but specifically as mind-door advertence (manodvārāvajjana). All these suttas were taught in various ways according to the inclinations (ajjhāsaya) of those capable of understanding. The same method applies to the suttas following this. The fifth sutta ends.

## 6. Commentary on the Bāhiradhātunānatta Sutta
In the sixth sutta, the five elements (visible form, etc.) belong to the sense sphere (kāmāvacara), while the dhamma-element (dhammadhātu) belongs to the four planes (catubhūmika). The sixth sutta ends.

## 7. Commentary on the Saññānānatta Sutta
In the seventh sutta, "form-element" (rūpadhātu) refers to a visible object based on things like one's own or another's cloth or turban that has come into range. "Perception of form" (rūpasaññā) is the perception associated with eye-consciousness. "Thought of form" (rūpasaṅkappa) is the thought associated with the three consciousnesses starting with receiving (sampaṭicchana). "Desire for form" (rūpacchanda) is desire in the sense of wanting the visible object. "Fever for form" (rūpapariḷāha) is fever in the sense of burning for the visible object. "Search for form" (rūpapariyesanā) is the searching to obtain that visible object by calling companions who have seen or enjoyed it when the fever arises. Here, perception, thought, and desire can be obtained in a single impulsion-process (javana-vāra) or in different impulsion-processes; however, fever and search can only be obtained in different impulsion-processes. In the phrase "Thus, bhikkhus, there is diversity of elements" (Evaṃ kho, bhikkhave, dhātunānattaṃ), the meaning should be understood in this way: dependent on elements of diverse natures such as form, perceptions of diverse natures such as the perception of form arise. The seventh sutta ends.
123:
## 8. Commentary on the No-pariyesanānānatta Sutta
In the eighth sutta, the statement "fever for mental objects does not arise dependent on the search for mental objects" (no dhammapariyesanaṃ paṭicca uppajjati dhammapariḷāho) differs [from the previous sutta] only in its negation. The eighth sutta ends.

## 9. Commentary on the Bāhiraphassanānatta Sutta etc.
93-94. In the ninth sutta, "perception of form arises" means perception arises in the object of the kind already described. "Thought of form" is the thought associated with the three consciousnesses in that same object. "Contact with form" (rūpasamphassa) is the contact that touches that same object. "Feeling" (vedanā) is the feeling that experiences that same object. Desire and the rest are as previously described. "Gain of form" (rūpalābha) refers to the object together with craving that is obtained after searching. This is first the all-inclusive method (sabbasaṅgāhika-naya) stated by way of the arising of all states in a single object.

Another method is the one mixed with a guest object (āgantukārammaṇa). These four states—perception of form, thought of form, contact, and feeling—occur in the constant object (nibaddhārammaṇa) that is regularly used. A constant object appears as something desired, lovely, pleasing, and dear. A guest object, however, even if similar to something else, stands by agitating [the mind].

Regarding this agitation, there is this story: It is said that a minister's son, surrounded by villagers, was performing his duties in the middle of a village. At that time, his female lay devotee (upāsikā), having gone to the river and bathed, was returning home adorned and surrounded by a group of nurses. Seeing her from afar, the perception arose in him, "She must be a guest woman," and he sent a man, saying, "Go, fellow, find out who she is." The man went, saw her, and upon returning, reported the truth when asked. In this way, a guest object agitates [the mind]. The desire that arises for that object is called "desire for form." The fever that arises based on that same object is called "fever for form." Searching for that object by taking companions is called "search for form." The object together with craving obtained after searching is called "gain of form."

However, the Elder Cūḷatissa, a resident of Uruvaḷḷi village, said: "Although the Blessed One placed contact and feeling in the middle of the text, if the text is reordered: perception arising in the object of the kind described is perception of form; thought in that same object is thought of form; desire in that visible object is desire for form; fever in that visible object is fever for form; searching in that visible object is search for form; the object together with craving obtained after searching is gain of form. Contact in the object thus obtained is contact, and experiencing it is feeling. These two states, rūpasamphassa and rūpasamphassajā, are [explained] in another section (avibhūta-vāra)."
124:
Desire arising in that object is called desire for form (rūpacchanda). The burning (fever) arising in that object is called the fever for form (rūpapariḷāha). The seeking in that object is called the search for form (rūpapariyesanā). The object obtained through seeking, together with craving, is called the gain of form (rūpalābha). Contact in the object thus obtained is called contact (phassa), and experiencing it is called feeling (vedanā). It is said: "These two things, contact with form and feeling born of contact with form, are obtained." Other teachers also accept what is called the unmanifest stage (avibhūtavāra). An object may be surrounded by curtains or walls, or covered by grass, leaves, and so on. For one who looks at it, thinking, "I have seen half of the object; I will look at it well," the perception arising in that object is called perception of form (rūpasaññā). Thoughts and so on arising in that very object should be known as thoughts of form (rūpasaṅkappa) and so forth. Here too, perception, thought, contact, feeling, and desire are obtained in a single javana cycle as well as in various javana cycles. However, fever, search, and gain are obtained only in various javana cycles. The tenth sutta is clear in meaning. Thus, the ninth and tenth suttas [are finished].

## First Chapter: Nānatta Vagga

## 2. Second Chapter

## 1. Commentary on the Satta Dhatu Sutta

In the first sutta of the second chapter, "element of radiance" (ābhādhātu) means the element of light (ālokadhātu). This is the name for light itself, for the jhāna arising from the preliminary work (parikamma) on the light-kasina, and for the jhāna together with its object. "Element of beauty" (subhadhātu) refers to the jhāna together with its object by way of the jhāna arising in the beauty-kasina (subhakasina). The sphere of infinite space itself is the element of the sphere of infinite space (ākāsānañcāyatana-dhātu). The cessation of perception and feeling itself is the element of the cessation of perception and feeling (saññāvedayitanirodha-dhātu). Thus, the Blessed One, while staying in that assembly, wishing to give an opportunity to a monk skilled in connecting the sequence of teachings (anusandhi) who desired to ask a question, concluded the discourse.

In the phrase "dependent on darkness" (andhakāraṃ paṭicca), darkness is delimited by light, and light by darkness. For that light is made manifest by darkness. Therefore, He said, "Dependent on darkness, (light) is manifested." In the phrase "dependent on foulness" (asubhaṃ paṭicca), the same method applies. Foulness is delimited by beauty, and beauty by foulness. When there is foulness, beauty is manifested; therefore, He spoke thus. "Dependent on form" (rūpaṃ paṭicca) means dependent on the fine-material sphere attainments (rūpāvacara-samāpatti). When there is a fine-material sphere attainment, the attainment of the sphere of infinite space...
125:
...comes to be, or there is the transcending of form; therefore, He spoke thus. In the case of the element of the sphere of infinite consciousness and so forth, this same method should be understood as the way of knowing. "Dependent on cessation" (nirodhaṃ paṭicca) means dependent on the non-occurrence (cessation) of the four [mental] aggregates. For it is only by depending on the cessation of the aggregates that the attainment of cessation (nirodhasamāpatti) is manifested, not by depending on the occurrence of the aggregates; therefore, He spoke thus. In this context (of cessation, etc.), it should be understood that the cessation of the four aggregates itself is the attainment of cessation.

In the phrase "How is the attainment to be reached?" (kathaṃ samāpatti pattabbā), it should be understood as: "What kind of attainments are they, and having become what kind of attainments are they to be reached?" In the phrase "The attainment of perception is to be reached" (saññāsamāpatti pattabbā), they are to be reached by becoming attainments of perception through the existence of manifest perception. In the phrase "The attainment of the remainder of formations is to be reached" (saṅkhārāvasesasamāpatti pattabbā), they are to be reached by becoming attainments of the remainder of formations because of the remaining of subtle formations. In the phrase "The attainment of cessation is to be reached" (nirodhasamāpatti pattabbā), the meaning is that the cessation of the four aggregates itself, having become the attainment of cessation, is to be reached. The first sutta [is finished].

## 2. Commentary on the Sanidāna Sutta

In the second sutta, the word "with a cause" (sanidānaṃ) is an adverbial neuter term (bhāvanā-napuṃsaka); the meaning is that it arises having a cause, having a condition. In the phrase "Dependent on the sensual element, O monks" (kāmadhātuṃ bhikkhave paṭicca), the sensual element refers to sensual thought (kāmavitakka), to the states of the sensual sphere (kāmāvacara-dhamma), and specifically to all unwholesome states. The Blessed One taught thus: "Therein, what is the sensual element? It is the thought, reflection, intention, absorption, fixed absorption, directing of the mind, and wrong intention associated with sensuality; this is called the sensual element. From the Avīci hell below as the limit, to the Paranimmitavasavattī devas above as the interior, the aggregates, elements, bases, forms, feelings, perceptions, formations, and consciousness that wander within this range and are included in this limit; this is called the sensual element. All unwholesome states are also called the sensual element" (taught in the Vibhaṅga).

In this sutta, there are two types of explanation: the all-inclusive (sabbasaṅgāhika) explanation and the distinct (asambhinna) explanation. How? By the term "sensual element," the element of ill-will (byāpādadhātu) and the element of cruelty (vihiṃsādhātu) are also included; therefore, this explanation is called "all-inclusive." However, since those two elements (ill-will and cruelty) are mentioned separately, only the remaining states are called the "sensual element"; therefore, this explanation is called "distinct." In this context of the Pali, the distinct explanation should be taken. Dependent on this sensual element, either by way of the object or by way of association, what is called sensual perception (kāmasaññā) arises.
126:
In the phrase 'dependent on sensual perception' (kāmasaññāṃ paṭicca), what is called sensual thought (kāmasaṅkappa) arises depending on sensual perception by way of association (sampayoga) or by way of decisive support (upanissaya). In this same manner, the meaning should be understood in all phrases. 'In three ways' (tīhi ṭhānehi) means by three causes. 'Practices wrongly' (micchā paṭipajjati) means practicing an improper path, a path that does not lead to liberation.

In the phrase 'the element of ill-will, monks' (byāpādadhātuṃ, bhikkhave), both the thought of ill-will and ill-will itself are called the element of ill-will. As it is said: 'Therein, what is the element of ill-will? The thinking, the thought... [pe]... associated with ill-will; this is called the element of ill-will. The resentment, the opposition, the anger, the intense anger... [pe]... the state of being displeased of the mind towards the ten grounds of resentment; this is called the element of ill-will.' Depending on this element of ill-will by way of conascence-condition (sahajātapaccaya) and so forth, what is called the perception of ill-will arises. The rest should be understood in the same way as the previous method.

In the phrase 'the element of cruelty, monks' (vihiṃsādhātuṃ, bhikkhave), both the thought of cruelty and cruelty itself are called the element of cruelty. As it is said: 'Therein, what is the element of cruelty? The thinking, the thought... [pe]... associated with cruelty; this is called the element of cruelty. Here, someone harms beings with the hand, or with a clod, or with a stick, or with a sword, or with a rope, or with any other weapon. Such harming, harassing, hurting, injuring, annoying, and killing of others; this is called the element of cruelty.' Depending on this element of cruelty by way of conascence-condition and so forth, what is called the perception of cruelty arises. Here too, the rest should be understood in the same way as the previous method.

'In a thicket of grass' (tiṇadāye) means in a forest dense with grass. 'Misfortune and ruin' (anaya-byasanaṃ) means lack of growth and destruction. In this passage 'Even so' (evameva kho), the object should be regarded like a dry grass thicket, unwholesome perception like a grass torch, and these beings like small insects depending on grass and wood. Just as when a grass torch is placed in a dry grass thicket, if one does not quickly strive to extinguish it, those insects meet with misfortune and ruin; even so, whatever recluses or brahmins...
127:
...or do not abandon an arisen unwholesome perception by way of abandonment by suppression (vikkhambhana-pahāna), abandonment by substitution of opposites (tadaṅga-pahāna), or abandonment by eradication (samuccheda-pahāna), they live in suffering.

'Gone to disharmony' (visamagataṃ) refers to unwholesome perception that follows disharmonious states such as lust (rāga) and so forth. 'Does not abandon quickly' means not abandoning swiftly by way of suppression and so forth. 'Does not dispel' means not removing. 'Does not bring to an end' means not making it disappear without remainder, even to the extent of its breaking up (bhaṅga). 'Does not bring to non-existence' means not making it reach the state of not arising again. In this way, the negative particle 'na' (not) should be applied to all phrases. 'To be expected' (pāṭikaṅkhā) means what is to be expected or desired.

'Monks, the element of renunciation' (nekkhamma-dhātuṃ, bhikkhave): in this passage, both the thought of renunciation and all wholesome states (kusala dhamma) are called the element of renunciation. The Blessed One said: 'Therein, what is the element of renunciation? The thinking, the thought... [pe]... right intention (sammā-saṅkappa) associated with renunciation; this is called the element of renunciation.'

In this matter of the element of renunciation, there are two ways of explanation. By taking the element of renunciation, the other two elements (non-ill-will and non-cruelty) are also included because they are comprised within wholesome states; this explanation is 'all-inclusive' (sabbasaṅgāhika). However, those two elements should be shown separately; therefore, excluding those two, all remaining wholesome states are called the element of renunciation; this explanation is 'unmixed' (asambhinna). Depending on this element of renunciation by way of conascence-condition (sahajāta-paccaya) and so forth, what is called the perception of renunciation arises. Depending on perception and so forth, thought and so forth arise accordingly.

'Monks, the element of non-ill-will' (abyāpāda-dhātuṃ, bhikkhave): in this passage, both the thought of non-ill-will and non-ill-will itself are called the element of non-ill-will. The Blessed One said: 'Therein, what is the element of non-ill-will? The thinking... [pe]... associated with non-ill-will; this is called the element of non-ill-will. The loving-kindness (mettā), the act of loving, the state of loving, the liberation of mind through loving-kindness towards beings; this is called the element of non-ill-will.' Depending on this element of non-ill-will, in the same way as previously mentioned, what is called the perception of non-ill-will arises.

'Monks, the element of non-cruelty' (avihiṃsā-dhātuṃ, bhikkhave): in this passage also, both the thought of non-cruelty and compassion (karuṇā) are called the element of non-cruelty. As to how the Blessed One taught...
128:
In that context, what is the element of non-cruelty (avihiṃsādhātu)? Reflection (vitakka) associated with non-cruelty... and so on... this phenomenon is called the element of non-cruelty. There is compassion (karuṇā) towards beings, the act of compassionating, the state of being compassionate, and the deliverance of mind (cetovimutti) through the power of compassion; this phenomenon is called the element of non-cruelty.

Dependent on this element of non-cruelty, in the manner already described, what is called the perception of non-cruelty (avihiṃsāsaññā) arises. The remaining meaning should be understood in the same way as described for all terms. The second sutta [ends].

## 3. Giñjakāvasathasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, starting from the phrase 'dhātuṃ, bhikkhave,' the [Buddha] shows that disposition (ajjhāsaya) is the 'element' (dhātu). 'Perception arises' (uppajjati saññā) means that dependent on disposition, perception arises, view arises, and reflection arises. In this sutta as well, thinking 'The monk Kaccāna will ask a question,' the Buddha concluded the teaching with only this much to give Kaccāna the opportunity. 'Among those not rightly self-awakened' (asammāsambuddhesu) refers to the six teachers such as Pūraṇa Kassapa. 'Rightly self-awakened' (sammāsambuddhā) means [they claim], 'We are rightly self-awakened.' By the phrase 'Dependent on what is it known?' (kiṃ paṭicca paññāyati), He asks about the views that have arisen in those teachers, [meaning] 'When what phenomenon exists does this occur?' He is also asking about the views of the disciples of the sectarians (titthiya) that have arisen thus: 'These [teachers] are rightly self-awakened,' even though they are not.

Now, because that wrong view occurs dependent on their element of ignorance (avijjādhātu), and the element of ignorance is a great element, He said 'Great indeed is this...' (mahatī kho esā) and so on, wishing to show the arising of that view dependent on a great element. 'Dependent on an inferior element, Kaccāna' (hīnaṃ, kaccāna, dhātuṃ paṭicca) means dependent on an inferior disposition. 'Aspiration' (paṇidhi) is the establishing of the mind. That aspiration (paṇidhi) arises in one who desires the state of a woman or the state of an animal such as a monkey. 'An inferior person' (hīno puggalo) means any person in whom these inferior states such as [inferior] perception and reflection arise is called an inferior person. 'Inferior speech' (hīna vācā) means whatever speech he has is also inferior. 'He points out the inferior' (hīnaṃ ācikkhati) means that even when he explains, he explains only what is inferior, and even when he teaches, he teaches only what is inferior; thus all terms should be applied.

'Arising' (upapatti) is of two kinds: arising as acquisition (paṭilābha-upapatti) and arising as rebirth (nibbattī-upapatti). Arising as rebirth should be understood by way of birth in low families and so on. Arising as acquisition should be understood by way of the inferior triad (hīna-tika) at the moment of the arising of consciousness. How? For him, birth in the five low families is called inferior rebirth (hīna-nibbattī); birth in the families of traders or farmers is called middle (majjhima); birth in the families of nobles or brahmins is called superior (paṇīta). As for the twelve types of unwholesome consciousness...
129:
...due to the acquisition of the twelve types of unwholesome consciousness, it is called inferior acquisition (hīna-paṭilābha). Due to the acquisition of phenomena belonging to the three planes, it is called middle acquisition (majjhima-paṭilābha). Due to the acquisition of the nine supramundane phenomena, it is called superior acquisition (paṇīta-paṭilābha). In this context of the Pāḷi, however, only rebirth (nibbattī) is intended. The third sutta ends.

## 4. Hīnādhimuttikasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, 'they associate' (saṃsandanti) means they come together with similar desires. 'They meet' (samenti) means they reach a state of similarity, becoming continuous (connected in mind). 'Those of low inclinations' (hīnādhimuttikā) are those with inferior dispositions. 'Those of good inclinations' (kalyāṇādhimuttikā) are those with good dispositions. The fourth sutta ends.

## 5. Caṅkamasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, 'Do you see?' (passatha no) means 'Behold.' 'All these indeed' (sabbē kho ēte) refers to the Elder Sāriputta, whom the Blessed One placed in the foremost position (etadagga), saying: 'Monks, among my monk disciples of great wisdom, Sāriputta is the foremost.' Thus, only those of great wisdom surround the Elder Sāriputta, thinking, 'We will ask deep questions concerning the analysis of the aggregates (khandha), elements (dhātu), bases (āyatana), foundations of mindfulness (satipaṭṭhāna), and the factors of enlightenment (bodhipakkhiya-dhamma), as well as those marked by the three characteristics.' And he answers every question asked, as if spreading out the earth, as if extracting sand from the foot of Mount Sineru, as if splitting the world-mountain, as if lifting Mount Sineru, as if expanding the sky, and as if making the moon and sun appear. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'Monks, all these monks are of great wisdom.'

The Blessed One also placed the Elder Mahā Moggallāna in the foremost position among those with psychic powers, saying: 'Monks, among my monk disciples with psychic powers, Mahā Moggallāna is the foremost.' Thus, only those with psychic powers surround the Elder Mahā Moggallāna, thinking, 'We will ask about the preliminary work (parikamma), the benefits (ānisaṃsa), the resolution (adhiṭṭhāna), and the transformation (vikubbana) of psychic powers.' That Elder also answers every question asked in the manner already described. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'Monks, all these monks are of great psychic power.'

The Blessed One also placed the Elder Mahā Kassapa in the foremost position among those who teach the ascetic practices (dhutavādā), saying: 'Monks, among my monk disciples who teach the ascetic practices, Mahā Kassapa is the foremost.' Thus, only those who teach the ascetic practices surround the Elder Mahā Kassapa, thinking, 'We will ask about the requirements of the ascetic practices (dhutaṅga), the benefits, the combination, the resolution, and the breach [of the practices].' That Elder also explains every question asked in the same way. Therefore, the Blessed One said, 'Monks, all these monks are teachers of the ascetic practices.'
130:
The Blessed One placed the Elder Anuruddha in the foremost position (etadagga) among those possessing the divine eye, saying: "Monks, among my disciple monks who possess the divine eye, this Anuruddha is the foremost." For this reason, only those who possessed the divine eye surrounded that Elder, thinking, "We shall ask about the preliminary practice (parikamma), the benefits (ānisaṃsa), and the defilements (upakkilesa) of the divine eye." The Elder also answered every question they asked in that very manner. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, all these monks are possessors of the divine eye."

The Blessed One also placed the Elder Puṇṇa in the foremost position among the Dhamma speakers, saying: "Monks, among my disciple monks who are Dhamma speakers, this Puṇṇa, son of the brahmin lady Mantāṇī, is the foremost." For this reason, only the Dhamma speakers surrounded that Elder, thinking, "We shall ask about various aspects of Dhamma discourse, such as its brevity, detail, depth, clarity, and its varied nature." The Elder also taught them various methods of Dhamma discourse, saying: "Friends, a Dhamma speaker should praise the assembly at the beginning, explain the nature of emptiness (suññatā) in the middle, and reach the pinnacle by means of the Four Noble Truths at the end." Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, all these monks are Dhamma speakers."

The Blessed One also placed the Elder Upāli in the foremost position among the bearers of the Vinaya, saying: "Monks, among my disciple monks who are bearers of the Vinaya, this Upāli is the foremost." For this reason, only the bearers of the Vinaya surrounded that Elder, thinking, "We shall ask about heavy and light offenses, curable and incurable offenses, and what constitutes an offense or non-offense." The Elder also answered every question they asked in that very manner. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, all these monks are bearers of the Vinaya."

The Blessed One also placed the Elder Ānanda in the foremost position among those of great learning, saying: "Monks, among my disciple monks who are of great learning, this Ānanda is the foremost." For this reason, only those of great learning surrounded that Elder, thinking, "We shall ask about the ten kinds of understanding of syllables, the circumstances of an event's origin, the connection of meanings, and the sequence of what comes before and after." The Elder also explained everything to them, saying: "This passage should be recited thus; this meaning should be taken thus." Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, all these monks are of great learning."

Devadatta, however, was one of evil desires and was overcome by those desires; therefore, only those of evil desires surrounded Devadatta, thinking, "We shall ask about the ways of winning over families and various forms of hypocrisy." Devadatta also explained those various methods to them. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "Monks, all these monks are of evil desires."
131:
Why did those Elders pace back and forth near the Blessed One? It was to provide protection, thinking, "Devadatta has a corrupt mind toward the Teacher and might even attempt to do him harm." Then why did Devadatta pace back and forth? It was to conceal the fault he had committed, thinking, "This Devadatta is not a wrongdoer; if he were a wrongdoer, he would not come here." Is Devadatta actually capable of harming the Blessed One, or is there a need for the Blessed One to be protected? There is not. Therefore, the Blessed One said: "It is impossible, Ānanda, it cannot happen, that a Tathāgata should attain final Nibbāna through the effort of another." The monks, however, came out of reverence for the Teacher. For that reason, the Blessed One spoke thus and had them dismissed, saying: "Ānanda, dismiss the Saṅgha of monks."

## 6. Sagātha Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the sixth sutta, the phrase "dung associates and meets with dung" means that even if it is located on the other side of the ocean, in another country, or on the other side of the universe, it associates and meets without any difference in color, smell, or taste; it is identical and indistinguishable. The same principle applies to the remaining substances like urine, etc. This unpleasant simile is brought in to show the similarity in nature of those with low dispositions. The superior simile of milk and so on is brought in to show the similarity in nature of those with good dispositions.

"Association" (saṃsagga) arises from the moisture of craving based on seeing, hearing, and so forth. "A forest has arisen" (vanatho jāto) means the forest of defilements has emerged. "It is cut off by non-association" (asaṃsaggena chijjati) means it is severed by not seeing or associating, such as not standing or sitting together. "One who lives well" (sādhujīvī) refers to one who lives a pure life. "Should live together" (sahāvase) means one should dwell in companionship. The sixth sutta ends.

## 7. Assaddhasaṃsandana Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the commentary on the seventh sutta, regarding the words "the faithless with the faithless" and so forth, individuals who lack faith in the Buddha, Dhamma, or Saṅgha, and who are devoid of the essence and flavor of faith, are identical and indistinguishable in their lack of faith, even if one stands on this shore of the ocean and the others stand on the far shore. Likewise, shameless persons (ahirika) who have broken the boundaries of moral shame associate with the shameless; those who are reckless (anottappa), not fearing the commission of evil, associate with the reckless; those of little learning (appassuta), devoid of heard knowledge, associate with those of little learning; the lazy (kusīta) associate with the lazy; those who are muddled in mindfulness (muṭṭhassatī) and are like a piece of meat dropped from a meal associate with the muddled; and those who are unwise (duppañña) because they lack the wisdom to distinguish birth and so forth associate with the unwise. "Endowed with" (sampannā) refers to those who are possessed of mindfulness and are diligent in tasks such as worshipping at a stupa.
132:
Lazy persons associate with lazy persons; unmindful persons associate with unmindful persons, who are like foxes that have been cast away with rice and meat; unwise persons, being devoid of wisdom that distinguishes the aggregates and so forth, associate with such unwise persons; those endowed with faith, who are devoted to tasks such as worshipping at a shrine, associate with those who have faith; those with a sense of shame, who are modest, associate with those who have a sense of shame; those with dread of wrongdoing, who fear evil, associate with those who have dread of wrongdoing; those who are very learned, who remember what they have heard, who preserve the scriptures, who protect the tradition, and who safeguard the lineage, associate with those who are very learned; those who have aroused energy, who possess complete effort, associate with those who have aroused energy; those with established mindfulness, who possess mindfulness that encompasses all tasks, associate with those with established mindfulness; and wise persons, even if they stay far away, associate and harmonize through that attainment of wisdom with those who possess great wisdom and diamond-like knowledge. The seventh sutta is finished.

## 8-12. Commentary on the Assaddhamūlaka Sutta and others

102-106. In these five suttas, starting from the eighth, those very same qualities such as lack of faith are taught by way of triads (tikas). Among those five suttas, in the eighth sutta, five triads are taught by way of the dark side (kaṇhapakkha) and the bright side (sukkapakkha), having lack of faith and so forth as their root. In the ninth sutta, four triads having lack of shame (ahirika) as their root; in the tenth sutta, three triads having lack of dread (anottappa) as their root; in the eleventh sutta, two triads having little learning (appassuta) as their root; and in the twelfth sutta, one triad having laziness (kusīta) as its root are taught. Thus, in all five suttas, there are fifteen triads. Teachers also refer to these fifteen triads as suttas. This is called the Tika-peyyāla (the repetitive series of triads). These are the eighth and following suttas.

## The Second Vagga is finished.

## 3. Kammapathavagga

## 1-2. Commentary on the Asamāhitasutta and others

107-108. In the suttas following this second vagga, the first sutta is taught by way of the group of five terms starting with lack of faith; likewise, the second sutta is also taught. Specifically, in the first sutta, the term 'unconcentrated' (asamāhita) is the fourth term; in the second sutta, the term 'immoral' (dussīla) is the fourth term. When taught in this manner, these suttas are taught according to the inclinations (ajjhāsaya) of those persons who are capable of realizing the Four Noble Truths. Here, 'unconcentrated' refers to those devoid of access concentration (upacāra-samādhi) and absorption concentration (appanā-samādhi). 'Immoral' refers to those without virtue. The first and second suttas are finished.
133:
## 3-5. Commentary on the Pañcasikkhāpadasutta and others

109-111. The third sutta is taught by way of the five courses of action (kammapatha), the fourth by way of the seven courses of action, and the fifth by way of the ten courses of action, according to the inclinations of those capable of realizing the Four Noble Truths. Among those suttas, in the third sutta, "surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhāyino" means they drink with the intention of negligence (pamāda-cetanā) caused by the intoxicant known as surā and meraya; that cause is called "surāmerayamajjappamāda"; because they stand in that state of negligence from intoxicants, they are called "surāmerayamajjappamādaṭṭhāyino." This is the meaning of the term that is not common to other terms in this sutta.

In the fifth sutta, they are called "pāṇātipātino" because they kill living beings; it means those who kill living beings. They are called "adinnādāyino" because they take what is not given, the property of others; it means those who steal the property of others. They are called "kāmesumicchācārino" because they behave wrongly in sensual objects with defiled lust. They are called "musāvādino" because they speak what is not true; it means those who speak empty or false words that destroy the welfare of others. Those who have speech that destroys the affection of others are called "pisuṇavācā." Those who have harsh speech that cuts the heart are called "pharusavācā." They are called "samphappalāpino" because they speak useless and frivolous words. They are called "abhijjhāluno" because they plan with the desire to look at others' wealth and property; it means those who have a nature of coveting others' property. Those who have a ruined and rotten mind are called "byāpannacittā." Those who have views that are perverted, base, and blamed by the wise are called "micchādiṭṭhikā"; it means those endowed with an un-emancipating view (aniyyānika-diṭṭhi) that is included in the courses of action, having such bases as "there is no result of giving," and included in the state of wrongness (micchatta). Those who have views that are not perverted, beautiful, and praised by the wise are called "sammādiṭṭhikā"; it means those endowed with the view of the ownership of deeds (kammassakatā-diṭṭhi) included in the courses of action, such as "there is a result of giving," and with the view of the Path (magga-diṭṭhi) included in the state of rightness (sammatta). This is merely the word-by-word commentary on the terms that are not clear in this fifth sutta.

There is a ten-fold meaning on the dark side (kaṇhapakkha) for them: pāṇātipāta, adinnādāna, kāmesumicchācāra, musāvāda, pisuṇavācā, pharusavācā, samphappalāpa, abhijjhā, byāpāda, and micchādiṭṭhi. Among those ten, the killing of living beings is called "pāṇātipāta"; it means the killing or harming of living beings.

In this context, "pāṇa" (life) refers to a "being" in conventional terms, but in the ultimate sense, it is the life faculty (jīvitindriya). The volition to kill (vadhaka-cetanā) occurring in either the door of body or the door of speech, which originates the effort to cut off the life faculty while perceiving that being as a living being, is called "pāṇātipāta."

That pāṇātipāta is of little blame in the case of small beings among those devoid of virtue such as animals, and of great blame in the case of beings with large bodies. Why is that?
134:
The offense is great because of the magnitude of the effort (payoga), or because of the magnitude of the object (vatthu) even if the effort is equal. Among beings such as humans who possess virtue, the offense is small if the being has little virtue and great if the being has great virtue. If the body and virtue are equal, it should be understood that the offense is small if the defilements and the effort are weak, and great if they are intense.

The five factors of that killing (pāṇātipāta) are: a living being, the perception of a living being, the intent to kill, the effort, and death resulting from that effort. The six types of effort are: personal effort (sāhattika), command (āṇattika), missiles/archery (nissaggiya), permanent/stationary (thāvara), magical arts (vijjāmaya), and psychic power (iddhimaya). If this meaning were expanded, it would be too extensive; therefore, we will not elaborate on the determination of these efforts and other such determinations. Those who desire [more detail] should consult and take from the Vinaya Commentary named Samantapāsādikā.

Taking the property of another that is not given is called 'adinnādāna'. It means carrying away, stealing, or pilfering another's property. In this context, 'not given' (adinna) refers to property possessed by another, where the owner, in doing as they wish with it, is not liable to punishment or blame. The intention to steal, which originates the effort to take that property while perceiving it as another's property, is called 'adinnādāna'. That stealing is a small offense regarding the inferior property of another and a great offense regarding the superior property of another. Why? Because of the superiority of the object.
