When the objects are equal, the offense is great regarding the property of those with superior virtue, and compared to those with superior virtue, the offense is small regarding the property of those with lesser virtue.

The five factors of that stealing are: property of another, perception of it as another's property, the intent to steal, the effort, and the carrying away by that effort. The efforts are the same six, starting with personal effort. These efforts occur through the modes of theft such as: theft by deception (theyyāvahāra), theft by force (pasayhāvahāra), theft by concealment (paṭicchannāvahāra), theft by stratagem (parikappāvahāra), and theft by changing marks (kusāvahāra). This is a brief summary here; the detailed explanation is stated in the Samantapāsādikā Commentary.

In the phrase 'kāmesumicchācāra', 'kāmesu' means in sexual misconduct. 'Micchācāra' is an entirely blameworthy, base conduct. By characteristic, the intention to transgress against a prohibited person (agamanīyaṭṭhāna) occurring through the body-door with the desire for unrighteous conduct is sexual misconduct. In that context, the prohibited persons for men are first: a woman protected by her mother, a woman protected by her father, a woman protected by both parents, a woman protected by her brother, a woman protected by her sister...
135:
...a woman protected by relatives, a woman protected by clan, a woman protected by Dhamma, a woman betrothed from the womb (sārakkhā), and a woman under penalty (saparidaṇḍā). These are the ten starting with 'mother-protected'. Then there are ten starting with 'bought with wealth' (dhanakkītā): a wife bought with wealth, a wife who lives together by choice, a wife who lives together for wealth, a wife who lives together for a garment, a wife married by dipping hands in a water bowl, a wife who lives together after lowering the head-load, a wife who is both a slave and a wife, a wife who is both a worker and a wife, a wife captured in war, and a wife for a moment. Thus, there are twenty types of women. Among these women, for the twelve types—the two (betrothed and under penalty) and the ten starting with 'bought with wealth'—men other than their own husbands are prohibited persons (agamanīyaṭṭhāna).

That sexual misconduct is a small offense regarding a prohibited person devoid of virtues such as morality (sīla), and a great offense regarding a prohibited person endowed with virtues such as morality. There are four factors (sambhāra) of that sexual misconduct: a prohibited object (agamanīyavatthu), the intent to associate with that object, the effort of association, and the acceptance of the union of the organs (maggena maggapatipatti). There is only one type of effort: personal effort (sāhattika).

In the term 'musāvāda', 'musā' refers to a vocal or bodily effort that destroys the welfare of one who is intended to be deceived. Alternatively, the intention that originates a bodily or vocal effort which causes another to be deceived, with the intent to deceive, is called 'musāvāda'. Another way: 'musā' is an untrue, false matter. 'Vāda' is making that matter known as true and real. By characteristic, the intention that originates the communication of an untrue matter as true, by one who wishes to make another perceive it as true, is 'musāvāda'.

That false speech is a small offense if the welfare it destroys is small, and a great offense if the welfare is great. Also, for laypeople, false speech such as saying 'I have none' because of not wanting to give one's own property is a small offense; false speech spoken as a witness to destroy welfare is a great offense. For monastics, if they obtain a little oil or ghee and say, with the intent to joke, 'Today in the village, I think a river of oil is flowing,' such speech in the manner of hyperbole is a small offense; but for those who say 'I saw' what they did not see, it is a great offense.

The four factors of that false speech are: an untrue matter, the intent to deceive, the corresponding effort, and the understanding of that meaning by another. There is only one type of effort: personal effort. That effort should be understood as performing an act of deceiving another by body, by something connected to the body, or by speech. If another understands that meaning through that act, at the very moment of the intention that originates the act, it is bound by the kamma of false speech.

In the terms such as 'pisuṇavācā' (slander), the meaning should be understood thus: the speech by which one speaks to someone, making oneself dear to that person's heart and making another person distant...
136:
Slanderous speech (Pisuṇavācā). That speech by which one makes oneself or another harsh, or that speech which is itself harsh, neither pleasant to the ear nor reaching the heart—this speech is called harsh speech (Pharusavācā). That speech by which one speaks useless, frivolous talk—that speech is called frivolous talk (Samphappalāpa). The volition which is the root cause of these, such as slanderous speech, also receives the name 'slanderous speech' and so on. In this context of the courses of action (kamma-patha), it is only that volition which is intended.

Among those [vocal misconducts], the volition that originates bodily or vocal effort, either for the purpose of dividing others or out of a desire to be loved by others, by one with a defiled mind, is called slanderous speech (Pisuṇavācā). That slanderous speech is of little blame if the person whose division is caused has few virtues, and of great blame if that person has great virtues. The four factors (sambhāra) of that slanderous speech are: there must be another to be divided; the aim of dividing them with the thought, 'These people will be divided from each other, they will be separated,' or the desire to be loved with the thought, 'I will be loved and trusted'; the corresponding effort; and the other person's understanding of that meaning.

The purely harsh volition that originates bodily or vocal effort which cuts the heart of another is called harsh speech (Pharusavācā). To clarify this harsh speech, this story should be known: It is said that a certain boy went to the forest, disregarding his mother's words. The mother, unable to make him turn back, cursed him, saying, 'May a fierce wild buffalo chase you!' Then, in the forest, a buffalo indeed rose up against him. The boy made an act of truth (sacca-kiriya), saying, 'May the words spoken by my mother's mouth not happen; may only the wish she conceived in her heart happen!' The buffalo stood still as if bound right there. Thus, even if it is an effort that causes pain to the heart, it is not harsh speech if the mind is soft. For parents sometimes say to their children, 'May thieves cut you into pieces!' yet they do not wish even a lotus petal to fall upon them. Teachers and preceptors also sometimes say to their pupils, 'Why do these shameless and fearless ones wander about? Drive them out!' Yet they only desire for those pupils the attainment of learning and realization. Just as it is not harsh speech when the mind is soft, so too it is not non-harsh speech simply because the words are soft. The words of one who wishes to kill, saying, 'Let this person sleep peacefully,' are not non-harsh speech. Because of the harshness of the mind, such speech is indeed harsh speech. That harsh speech is of little blame if the person it is directed towards has few virtues, and of great blame if that person has great virtues. The three factors (sambhāra) of that harsh speech are: another to be scolded; an angry mind; and the act of scolding.
137:
Unwholesome volition which makes known what is useless and which originates from bodily or vocal effort is called frivolous talk (Samphappalāpa). This frivolous talk is of little blame if practiced little, and of great blame if practiced much. The factors (sambhāra) of that frivolous talk are two: being intent on useless stories such as the Bharata war or the abduction of Sītā, and the speaking of such talk.

It is called covetousness (Abhijjhā) because it covets. It means it occurs by being directed towards another's property and bending towards it. That covetousness has the characteristic of coveting another's property in this way: 'O, may this be mine!' Like stealing (adinnādāna), it has both little blame and great blame. The factors of that covetousness are two: another's property and bending it towards oneself. Even if greed arises regarding another's property, it does not yet constitute a breach of the course of action (kamma-patha) as long as one does not bend it towards oneself, thinking, 'O, may this be mine!'

It is called ill-will (Byāpāda) because it destroys welfare and happiness. That ill-will has the characteristic of mental malice for the destruction of others. Like harsh speech (pharusavācā), it has both little blame and great blame. The factors of that ill-will are two: another being and the thought of that being's destruction. Even if anger arises regarding another being, it does not yet constitute a breach of the course of action (kamma-patha) as long as one does not think of that person's destruction, thinking, 'O, may this being be cut off, may he perish!'

It is called wrong view (Micchādiṭṭhi) because it sees wrongly, without grasping according to reality. That wrong view has the characteristic of perverted seeing in such ways as 'There is no result of giving,' etc. Like frivolous talk (samphappalāpa), it has both little blame and great blame. Furthermore, non-fixed wrong view (aniyata-micchādiṭṭhi) is of little blame, while fixed wrong view (niyata-micchādiṭṭhi) is of great blame. The factors of that wrong view are two: the perversion of the manner in which the object is grasped, and the appearance of it to the person according to the way he grasps it.

The decision regarding these ten unwholesome courses of action (akusala-kamma-patha) should be known by five aspects: (1) by nature (dhamma), (2) by category (koṭṭhāsa), (3) by object (ārammaṇa), (4) by feeling (vedanā), and (5) by root (mūla). Among these five, by nature: in these courses of action, seven are only the mental factor of volition (cetanā), while the three beginning with covetousness (abhijjhā) are states associated with volition. By category: the seven in order and wrong view—these eight are only courses of action, not roots. Covetousness and ill-will are both courses of action and roots. For when covetousness reaches the state of a root, it is the unwholesome root of greed (lobha); ill-will is the unwholesome root of hatred (dosa).

By object: killing (pāṇātipāta) has formations (saṅkhāra) as its object because it takes the life faculty as its object. Stealing (adinnādāna) takes either a being or formations as its object. Sexual misconduct (micchācāra) is...
138:
Sexual misconduct has only formations as its object through the power of the tangible object; however, some teachers say it also has beings as its object. False speech has either beings or formations as its object. Slanderous speech is the same. Harsh speech has only beings as its object. Frivolous talk has either beings or formations as its object through the power of what is seen, heard, sensed, or cognized. Covetousness is the same. Ill-will has only beings as its object. Wrong view has formations as its object through the power of the things belonging to the three planes (tebhūmaka-dhamma).

In terms of feeling: Killing involves painful feeling. Indeed, even though kings might smile when seeing a thief and say, "Go and kill him," their decisive volition (sanniṭṭhāpaka-cetanā) is associated only with painful feeling. Stealing can involve all three feelings. Sexual misconduct involves two feelings: pleasant and neutral; however, in the decisive mind, neutral feeling does not occur. False speech involves three feelings. Slanderous speech is the same. Harsh speech involves painful feeling. Frivolous talk involves three feelings. Covetousness involves two feelings: pleasant and neutral. Wrong view is the same. Ill-will involves painful feeling.

In terms of roots: Killing has two roots: hatred and delusion. Stealing has two roots: either hatred and delusion, or greed and delusion. Sexual misconduct has two roots: greed and delusion. False speech has two roots: either hatred and delusion, or greed and delusion. Slanderous speech and frivolous talk are the same. Harsh speech has two roots: hatred and delusion. Covetousness has only one root: delusion. Ill-will is the same. Wrong view has two roots: greed and delusion.

In the phrases such as "abstaining from killing," the terms like "killing" have the meanings already stated. The abstinence by which people are called "those who abstain" is of three kinds: abstinence from what is encountered (sampatta-virati), abstinence by undertaking (samādāna-virati), and abstinence by eradication (samuccheda-virati). Among these, abstinence from what is encountered should be understood as the abstinence arising in those who have not undertaken the precepts, but who, reflecting on their own birth, age, learning, etc., think, "It is not proper for people like us to do such a thing," and thus do not transgress against an object that is encountered. This is like the case of the lay follower Cakkana in the island of Sīhaḷadīpa. It is said that when he was young, his mother fell ill. The physician said, "It is necessary to get fresh rabbit meat." Then Cakkana's brother sent him, saying, "Go, dear, and wander through the fields." He went there. At that time, a rabbit had come to eat the young sprouts. Seeing him, it ran swiftly but got caught in a creeper and cried out, "Kiri, kiri!"
139:
(The rabbit) made a sound. Cakkana went toward that sound, caught the rabbit, and thought, "I will make medicine for my mother." Then he reflected, "It is not proper for me to deprive another of life for the sake of my mother's life." Then he released it, saying, "Go to the forest and enjoy grass and water with the other rabbits." When asked by his brother, "Dear, did you get a rabbit?" he told him what had happened. His brother then scolded him. Cakkana went to his mother and made an asseveration of truth, saying, "Since I was born, I do not recall ever intentionally depriving a living being of life." Immediately, his mother was cured of her illness.

Abstinence by undertaking should be understood as the abstinence arising in those who have undertaken the precepts and who, in the undertaking of the precepts and beyond that, do not transgress against an object even at the cost of their own lives. This is like the case of the lay follower living on Mount Uttaravaḍḍhamāna. It is said that he undertook the precepts from Elder Piṅgala-Buddharakkhita, a resident of Ambariya Monastery, and was plowing his field. Then his ox was lost. While searching for it, he climbed Mount Uttaravaḍḍhamāna, where a large python caught him. He thought, "I will cut off its head with this sharp billhook." Then he reflected, "It is not proper for me to break the precept after having taken it from a venerable teacher." Having thought this up to three times, he resolved, "I will sacrifice my life, but not the precept," and threw the sharp-handled billhook he was carrying on his shoulder into the forest. Immediately, the great beast released him and went away.

Abstinence by eradication should be understood as the abstinence associated with the Noble Path. From the moment of its arising, even the thought "I will kill a living being" does not occur to Noble Ones.

Just as for the unwholesome, the decision regarding these wholesome courses of action should also be understood by five aspects: by nature (dhammato), by portion (koṭṭhāsato), by object (ārammaṇato), by feeling (vedanato), and by root (mūlato). Therein, "by nature" means that in these wholesome courses of action, in sequence, the seven volitions are applicable, and the abstinences are also applicable. The final three are only those associated with volition.

"By portion" means that, in sequence, the seven are only courses of action, not roots. The final three are both courses of action and roots. For non-covetousness, having reached the state of a root...
140:
Non-greed is a wholesome root; non-ill will, which is non-hatred, is a wholesome root; right view, which is non-delusion, is a wholesome root. Regarding 'by way of object' (ārammaṇato), the objects of killing and so forth are indeed the objects of those [abstinences]. This is because abstinence (virati) occurs only in relation to the object to be transgressed. Just as the Noble Path, with Nibbāna as its object, abandons the defilements, it should be understood that these courses of action (kammapatha), with the life faculty and so forth as their objects, abandon the immoralities (dussīlya) such as killing and so forth.

Regarding 'by way of feeling' (vedanāto), all [wholesome courses of action] are accompanied by either pleasant feeling or neutral feeling (majjhatta-vedanā). This is because, upon reaching the wholesome, there is no such thing as painful feeling.

Regarding 'by way of root' (mūlato), for one who abstains from the seven [bodily and verbal actions] in sequence with a consciousness associated with knowledge (ñāṇasampayutta), there are three roots by way of non-greed, non-hatred, and non-delusion. For one who abstains with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge (ñāṇavippayutta), there are two roots. Non-covetousness (anabhijjhā), for one who abstains with a consciousness associated with knowledge, has two roots (by way of non-hatred and non-delusion); for one who abstains with a consciousness dissociated from knowledge, it has one root. This is because non-greed cannot be its own root. The same method applies to non-ill will. Right view has only two roots by way of non-greed and non-hatred. The same method applies to the third sutta and so forth.

## 6. Aṭṭhaṅgikasutta-vaṇṇanā
The sixth sutta is taught according to the inclinations of those who can be enlightened by way of the eight path factors. The explanation of the sixth sutta is finished.

## 7. Dasangasutta-vaṇṇanā
The seventh sutta [is taught] by way of the ten wrongnesses and the ten rightnesses. In that sutta, 'micchāñāṇino' means those endowed with wrong reviewing (paccavekkhaṇā). 'Micchāvimuttino' means those who possess a liberation that does not lead out [of saṃsāra], holding it to be a wholesome liberation. 'Sammāñāṇino' means those with right reviewing. 'Sammāvimuttino' means those endowed with the liberation of the fruit (phala-vimutti) which leads out [of saṃsāra]. The explanation of the seventh sutta is finished.

## The Third Chapter: Courses of Action (Kammapathavagga).
141:
## 4. The Fourth Chapter (Catuttha Vagga)

## 1. Catudhātusutta-vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the fourth chapter, the earth element (pathavī-dhātu) is the element that is the foundation for co-nascent states. The water element (āpo-dhātu) is the element that binds co-nascent states. The fire element (tejo-dhātu) is the element that matures co-nascent states. The air element (vāyo-dhātu) is the element that supports co-nascent states. This is a brief explanation in this sutta. In detail, however, these elements should be explained by way of the twenty parts (koṭṭhāsa) and so forth. The explanation of the first sutta is finished.

## 2. Pubbesambodhasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second sutta, 'this is the gratification of the earth element' (ayaṃ pathavīdhātuyā assādo) refers to the gratification (assāda) that arises depending on this earth element. The gratification depending on the earth element should be understood by way of a person who, raising their body and stretching their stomach, says, 'Strive so that I can insert my finger here,' or stretching their hand, says, 'Strive so that I can bend this hand.'

In the terms 'anicca' and so forth, they are impermanent (anicca) in the sense of non-existence after having come to be. They are suffering (dukkha) in the sense of being oppressive. They are subject to change (vipariṇāmadhamma) in the sense of departing from their own nature. 'This is the danger of the earth element' (ayaṃ pathavīdhātuyā ādīnavo) means that the very manner in which the earth element is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change is the danger (ādīnava) of the earth element. 'The removal of desire and lust, the abandoning of desire and lust' (chandarāgavinayo chandarāgap pahānaṃ) means that upon reaching Nibbāna, desire and lust for the earth element are removed and abandoned; therefore, Nibbāna is the escape (nissaraṇa) from that earth element.

'This is the gratification of the water element' (ayaṃ āpodhātuyā assādo) refers to the gratification that arises depending on this water element. The gratification depending on the water element should be understood by way of a person who, seeing another afflicted by the water element, thinks: 'From the time this person lies down, they are constantly going back and forth to the place of urination; even if they do a small task, their sweat-soaked clothes reach a state where they must be wrung out; even if they just speak words of appreciation (anumodanā), they must take up a fan. As for us, we lie down in the evening and rise early in the morning; our body is like a jar full of beans; even when performing heavy tasks, not even a bit of sweat arises in us; even when preaching the Dhamma like a thunderclap, there is not even a sign of heat in our body.'
142:
The gratification (assāda) of this fire element (tejo-dhātu) refers to the gratification that arises depending on this fire element. This gratification based on the fire element should be understood through the experience of those who, seeing people with cold digestion, think: 'These people, having swallowed only a small amount of gruel, rice, or snacks, sit with stiff bellies and search for a charcoal brazier throughout the three watches of the night; even if just a drop of water falls on their bodies, they cover themselves with a charcoal brazier and lie down. We, however, chew even very tough meat or cakes, eat rice until our bellies are full, and at that very moment, all the food dissolves like a ball of foam; even when it rains for seven days, there is not even a hint of cold or heat in our bodies.'

The gratification of this air element (vāyo-dhātu) refers to the gratification that arises depending on this air element. This gratification based on the air element should be understood through the experience of those who, seeing others who are fearful of wind, think: 'When these people perform even a minor task or speak even a few words of appreciation (anumodanā), the wind pierces their bodies; having traveled a distance of only a gāvuta, their hands and feet sink, their backs ache, and being constantly oppressed by stomach-wind, head-wind, ear-wind, and so on, they spend their time preparing wind-remedies such as oil and molasses. We, however, even when performing great tasks, or preaching the Dhamma throughout the three watches of the night, or traveling ten yojanas in a single day, do not experience even a slight sinking of hands and feet or any back pain.' Elements functioning in this way are called gratification (assāda).

'Abbhaññāsiṃ' means 'I have known with superior knowledge.' 'Anuttaraṃ sammāsambodhiṃ' means the unsurpassed, most excellent, and rightly self-awakened enlightenment (bodhi), or it means the praised and beautiful enlightenment. 'Bodhi' can refer to the tree, the path, omniscience (sabbaññutaññāṇa), or Nibbāna. In contexts such as 'He was first fully enlightened at the foot of the Bodhi tree' and 'Between the Bodhi tree and Gayā,' the tree is called Bodhi. In the context 'Bodhi is said to be the knowledge in the four paths,' it refers to the path. In the context 'The Buddha of great wisdom reaches Bodhi,' it refers to omniscience. In the context 'Having reached the deathless, unconditioned Bodhi,' it refers to Nibbāna. In this sutta, however, the Lord's Path of Arahatship (arahattamagga) is intended.
143:
Does the Arahattamagga of disciples constitute Unsurpassed Enlightenment (anuttara bodhi) or not? It does not. Why? Because it does not bestow all virtuous qualities. For some of those disciples, the Arahattamagga gives only the fruit of Arahatship (arahattaphala); for some, the three true knowledges (vijjā); for some, the six higher powers (abhiññā); for some, the four analytical insights (paṭisambhidā); and for some, the knowledge of a disciple's perfection (sāvakapāramīñāṇa). To Paccekabuddhas, it gives only the knowledge of private enlightenment (paccekabodhiñāṇa). To the Buddhas, however, it gives the fulfillment of all virtuous qualities, just as the consecration (abhiseka) of a king gives the state of sovereignty over the whole world. Therefore, no one else possesses Unsurpassed Enlightenment.

'Abhisambuddho' means 'I have realized'; he acknowledges, 'I am fully enlightened, I have reached and penetrated [the truth].' 'Knowledge and vision arose in me' (ñāṇañca pana me dassanaṃ udapādi) means the reviewing knowledge (paccavekkhaṇañāṇa) capable of seeing the attained qualities arose in me. 'My liberation (vimutti) is unshakable (akuppā)' means the knowledge arose that 'This, my liberation of the fruit of Arahatship, is of an unshakable nature.' In this statement, unshakability should be understood in two ways: by way of cause and by way of object. It is unshakable by way of cause because the defilements, being utterly cut off by the four paths, do not return again; and it is unshakable by way of object because it occurs by taking the unshakable Dhamma, Nibbāna, as its object. 'Antimā' means the last (birth). 'Now there is no more renewed existence' means that now there is no other existence hereafter.

In this sutta, the Four Noble Truths are taught. How? Gratification (assāda) in the four elements is the Truth of Origin (samudayasacca); danger (ādīnava) is the Truth of Suffering (dukkhasacca); escape (nissaraṇa) is the Truth of Cessation (nirodhasacca); and the path that knows cessation in detail is the Truth of the Path (maggasacca). It is also appropriate to explain it in detail. Here, the pleasure and joy that arise dependent on the earth element are the gratification (assāda) of the earth element; penetrating it through abandonment is the Truth of Origin. That the earth element is impermanent, suffering, and subject to change is the danger (ādīnava) of the earth element; penetrating it through full understanding is the Truth of Suffering. The removal and abandonment of desire and lust for the earth element is the escape (nissaraṇa) from the earth element; penetrating it through realization is the Truth of Cessation. Right view (diṭṭhi), intention (saṅkappa), speech (vācā), action (kammanta), livelihood (ājīva), effort (vāyāma), mindfulness (sati), and concentration (samādhi) regarding these three points are the Truth of the Path, which is penetration through development (bhāvanā). The second sutta ends.

## 3. Acariṃsutta-vaṇṇanā
In the third sutta, 'acariṃ' means 'I wandered' with the movement of knowledge, or 'I experienced.' 'Yāvatā' means 'as far as.' The third sutta ends.
144:
## 4. Commentary on the Noce-idaṃ Sutta

In the fourth sutta, the words beginning with 'nissaṭā' (escaped) should be understood in conjunction with the preceding negation (the letter 'na') as: 'they have not escaped, they are not detached, they are not released, they do not dwell with a boundless mind.' In the second method, 'vimariyādikatena' means with a mind that has been made boundless. There are two kinds of boundaries (mariyādā): the boundary of defilements (kilesa) and the boundary of the round of rebirth (vaṭṭa). Among these, if for a certain person half of the defilements are abandoned and half are not, or half of the round is abandoned and half is not, that person's mind can be said to be boundless with respect to the abandoned defilements or round, but it cannot be said to be boundless with respect to the unabandoned defilements or round. However, in this sutta, because both have been abandoned, it is said 'with a boundless mind.' The meaning is: with a mind that stands without making a boundary, a mind that has transcended the boundary. Thus, in all three of these suttas, only the Four Noble Truths are taught. The fourth sutta is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Ekantadu-kkha Sutta

In the fifth sutta, 'ekantadu-kkhā' means they are purely suffering, like an extremely hot state. 'Dukkhānupatitā' means followed by suffering. 'Dukkhāvakkantā' means plunged into or overcome by suffering. 'Sukhā' means being the causal condition for pleasant feeling. In this way, the meaning should be understood in all terms. In this sutta, the characteristic of suffering (dukkhalakkhaṇa) is taught. The fifth sutta is finished.

## 6–10. Commentary on the Abhinanda Sutta, etc.

119–123. In the sixth and seventh suttas, the cessation of the round (vivaṭṭa) is taught. In the final three suttas, only the Four Noble Truths are taught. The suttas beginning with the sixth are finished.

145:
## 4. Anamatagga-saṃyutta
## 1. The First Chapter
## 1. Commentary on the Tiṇakaṭṭha Sutta

In the first sutta of the Anamatagga-saṃyutta, 'anamatagga' means having a beginning that cannot be known by following it. Because the beginning is not known even after searching with knowledge for a hundred or a thousand years, it is called 'amatagga'; because the beginning is not evident, it is called 'aviditagga.' It is not possible to know the beginning of this saṃsāra as starting from this time or that time; the meaning is that it has a prior limit and a subsequent limit that are not delimited. Saṃsāra is the uninterrupted succession of the aggregates (khandha) and so on. 'The prior limit is not evident' means that the preceding boundary is not seen. Just as the prior limit of this saṃsāra cannot be known by any point, likewise the subsequent limit cannot be known; beings merely wander in the middle of saṃsāra.

'It would reach exhaustion'—this statement is made because the simile is small. In non-Buddhist texts, the meaning is often meager while the simile is grand. When it is said, 'This ox is like an elephant, the pig is like an ox, this pond is like the ocean,' those pigs or ponds do not actually have the proportions of an elephant or the ocean. In the Buddha's Dispensation, however, the simile is small but the meaning is extremely vast. Although in the Pāḷi text only the single continent of Jambudīpa is taken as a simile, the grass, wood, and so on of hundreds, thousands, or hundreds of thousands of such Jambudīpa continents could be exhausted by that method of cutting and laying them down, yet the successive mothers of a single man would not reach exhaustion.

'You have experienced suffering' means that you have undergone pain and distress. 'Tibba' (intense) is a synonym for that same suffering. 'Byasana' (ruin) refers to various kinds of ruin, such as the ruin of relatives. 'Kaṭasī' refers to a cemetery or the earth. That earth has increased through the disposal of the bodies of those who die again and again. 'It is fitting' means it is appropriate. The first sutta is finished.

## 2. Commentary on the Pathavī Sutta

In the second sutta, 'mahāpathavī' refers to the great earth ending at the edge of the universe. 'Should place' means breaking that earth and making it into pellets as taught, and placing them in a suitable spot. The second sutta is finished.
146:
## 3. Assu Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, the word "kandantānaṃ" means those who are weeping and wailing with sound. "Passannaṃ" refers to the tears that are flowing down. "Catūsu mahāsamuddesu" refers to the four great oceans that are demarcated by the rays of Mount Sineru. Indeed, the eastern side of Mount Sineru is made of silver, the southern side of emerald (maṇi), the western side of crystal, and the northern side of gold.

The silver and emerald rays emerging from the eastern and southern sides unite and, traveling over the surface of the great ocean, remain after striking the Cakkavāḷa mountain. Similarly, the emerald and crystal rays emerging from the southern and western sides, the crystal and gold rays emerging from the western and northern sides, and the gold and silver rays emerging from the northern and eastern sides unite and, traveling over the surface of the great ocean, remain after striking the Cakkavāḷa mountain. Between these rays lie the four great oceans. It is with reference to these oceans that it was said, "in the four great oceans."

In the words beginning with "ñātibyasanaṃ," the term "byasana" means particularly exhaustion or destruction. The destruction of relatives is called ñātibyasana; the destruction of wealth and possessions is called bhogabyasana. As for disease (rogo), it is called byasana because it personally destroys health; therefore, since disease itself is a form of ruin, it is called rogabyasana. The commentary on the third sutta is finished.

## 4. Khīra Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fourth sutta, "mātuthaññaṃ" refers to the mother's milk of a human mother with the same name. For these beings, when they are born as earthworms, ants, and so forth, or as fish, turtles, and so forth, or among the various species of birds, there is no such thing as mother's milk. However, when they are born as goats, deer, buffaloes, and so forth, there is mother's milk. Likewise, it exists when they are born among humans.

In that regard, when born in those states such as goats or humans, without taking into account the births in the wombs of mothers with various names such as "Devī, Sumanā, Tissā," it should be understood that the milk drunk while being born in the womb of a mother with the single name "Tissā" alone throughout many lives is more than the water in the four great oceans. The commentary on the fourth sutta is finished.

## 5. Pabbata Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the fifth sutta, regarding the phrase "sakkā pana bhante," it is said that the monk thought: "The Teacher says that because of the extreme length of the beginningless saṃsāra, it is 'not easy, not easy' (to give a simile).
147:
...How can it not be shown? Would it be possible to have a simile made?" Therefore, he asked, "Venerable Sir, is it possible?" "Kāsikena" refers to an extremely delicate cloth from the Kāsī country, woven with thread spun by taking three cotton strands together. If one were to ask how much would be worn away by rubbing with that cloth, the answer is that an amount about the size of a mustard seed would be worn away. The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.

## 6. Sāsapa Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the sixth sutta, "āyasaṃ nagaraṃ" refers to a city surrounded by a wall made of iron; it should not be understood as being crowded inside with palaces of a single story and so forth made of iron. The commentary on the sixth sutta is finished.

## 7. Sāvaka Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, "anussareyyuṃ" means that if one disciple recalls one hundred thousand eons, another disciple with the six higher powers (saḷābhiñña) recalls another hundred thousand from where the first stopped, and another recalls yet another hundred thousand; in this way, four disciples would successively recall four hundred thousand eons. The commentary on the seventh sutta is finished.

## 8-9. Gaṅgā Sutta Vaṇṇanā

131-132. In the eighth sutta, "yā etasmiṃ antare vālikā" refers to the accumulation of sand within the distance of five hundred yojanas in length. In the ninth sutta, there is nothing further to be said. The commentaries on the eighth and ninth suttas are finished.

## 10. Puggala Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, all three terms beginning with "aṭṭhikaṅkalo" are synonyms for a heap of bones. For these beings, the period without bones is much longer than the period with bones. For those who have become creatures such as earthworms, there are no bones at all; however, for those who have become creatures such as fish and turtles, bones are very numerous. Therefore, without taking the period of no bones and the period of many bones, one should take only the period of having a moderate amount of bones. "Uttaro Gijjhakūṭassa" means situated to the north of Vulture Peak. "Magadhānaṃ Giribbaje" means situated in Giribbaja (the city of Rājagaha) of the Magadha country, which is surrounded by five mountains. The remaining words are clear in all places. The commentary on the tenth sutta is finished.

In the first sutta of the second chapter, 'wretched' (duggata) means poor and miserable. 'Deformed' (durūpeta) means endowed with hands and feet of ugly shape. The first sutta ends.

## 2. Commentary on the Sukhita Sutta
In the second sutta, 'prosperous' (sukhita) means endowed with happiness, having great wealth and great possessions. 'Well-adorned' (susajjita) means decorated and prepared, mounted on the back of an elephant, and having a large retinue. The second sutta ends.

## 3. Commentary on the Tiṃsamatta Sutta
In the third sutta, 'Pāveyyakā' means those living in the region of Pāvā. In the phrases 'all were forest-dwellers' (sabbe āraññikā) and so forth, their state as forest-dwellers and so forth should be understood by way of their undertaking of ascetic practices (dhutaṅga).

'All were possessed of fetters' (sabbe sasaṃyojanā) means all of them were with bonds; some were Stream-enterers, some were Once-returners, and some were Non-returners. Among them, there were no worldlings (puthujjana) or Arahants (khīṇāsava). In the words 'of cattle' (gunnaṃ) and so forth, among colors such as white and black, only the time of each individual color should be taken. 'Highwaymen' (pāripanthakā) means robbers who stand on the path and strike travelers. 'Adulterers' (pāradārikā) means those who fall into the conduct of transgressing with others' wives. The third sutta ends.

## 4-9. Commentary on the Mātu Sutta and others
137-142. In the fourth sutta and others, the meaning should be understood by way of the fixity of gender (liṅganiyama) and the fixity of the world-system (cakkavāḷaniyama). Because there is a time when men become women and a time when women become men, there is no fixity of gender here. Beings from this world-system wander to other world-systems, and from other world-systems, they run into this world-system. In such cases, wishing to show only that one has been a mother during the time of being a woman in this world-system, He said, 'There is no being who has not been a mother before.' The same method applies to 'There is no being who has not been a father before' and so forth. The fourth to the ninth suttas end.
149:
## 10. Vepullapabbattasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, by the words "Bhūtapubbaṃ" (Once upon a time), the Buddha brings forth and shows an account from the past. "Samaññā udapādi" means that a designation or name arose. The Buddha spoke these words with reference to those who have passed away. The phrase "They climb in four days" is said with reference to those of medium strength. "Aggaṃ" means noble or supreme. "Bhaddayugaṃ" means an excellent pair. By the words "They climb in three days," it is meant that in the interval between two Buddhas, the earth rose by one league (yojana), and thus that mountain became three leagues in height.

"Appaṃ vā bhiyyo" (a little more or less) means slightly exceeding a hundred years by ten or twenty years. Furthermore, there is no one who lives exactly a hundred years; at the highest limit, they live for sixty or eighty years. Those who die before reaching a hundred years, at the age of five or ten years and so on, are indeed numerous. Here, the statement that the Blessed Kakusandha appeared during the time when the lifespan was forty thousand years, and the Blessed Koṇāgamana appeared during the time when the lifespan was thirty thousand years, is made to appear as if it were a gradual decline. However, it should be understood that it did not decline directly in this way, but rather that the lifespan increased and then declined again.

How is this so? The Blessed Kakusandha appeared in this very Bhadda Kappa during the time when the lifespan was forty thousand years. If the lifespan is divided into five parts, he remained through four parts and attained Parinibbāna while the fifth part was still remaining. That lifespan, while declining, reached the ten-year span, and then increasing again, it became an incalculable (asaṅkheyya) period. From there, while declining, it stood at the thirty-thousand-year lifespan, at which time Koṇāgamana was born. After he had likewise attained Parinibbāna, that lifespan reached the ten-year span, increased again to an incalculable period, and then declining, stood at the twenty-thousand-year span, at which time the Blessed Kassapa was born. After he had likewise attained Parinibbāna, that lifespan reached the ten-year span, increased again to an incalculable period, and then declining, reached the hundred-year span, at which time our Sammāsambuddha was born. Thus, it should be understood that it declined, increased, and declined again in succession. In that regard, although the Buddhas are born during times when the lifespan is short, the lifespan of those Buddhas is also exactly according to the lifespan of that era. The explanation of the tenth sutta is finished.

## 5. Kassapa Saṃyutta
## 1. Santuṭṭhasutta Vaṇṇanā
In the first sutta of the Kassapa Saṃyutta, 'santuṭṭhāyaṃ' (santuṭṭho ayaṃ) means 'this Kassapa is contented.' 'Itarītarena' does not mean being contented with just any robe among those that are thick, fine, coarse, excellent, strong, or worn out; rather, it means being contented and satisfied with whatever requisites are obtained, whether they be inferior or superior. In detail, there are three kinds of contentment (santuṭṭhi) regarding robes: contentment with whatever is obtained (yathālābhasantuṭṭhi), contentment according to one's strength (yathābalasantuṭṭhi), and contentment with what is appropriate (yathāsāruppasantuṭṭhi). The same method applies to alms-food and so forth.

To explain the distinctions among these types of contentment: In this Dispensation, a monk receives a robe, whether it is good or not. That monk is satisfied with only that robe which he received; he does not long for another, and even if he receives a good one, he does not take it. This is his 'contentment with whatever is obtained' regarding robes. Furthermore, if a monk is naturally weak or overcome by illness and old age, he suffers when wearing a heavy robe. If that monk exchanges that robe with a compatible monk and is satisfied with a light robe, he is still considered contented. This is his 'contentment according to one's strength' (contentment with a robe suitable for one's physical strength) regarding robes. Another monk habitually receives excellent requisites. When he receives an expensive robe or many robes, he gives them away, thinking, 'This is suitable for senior elders, this for those of great learning, this for the sick, and this for those who receive little.' He then makes a double-layered robe (saṅghāṭi) from their old robes or by picking up rags from dust heaps and so forth and wears it, yet he remains contented. This is his 'contentment with what is appropriate' (contentment with a suitable robe) regarding robes.

In this Dispensation, a monk receives alms-food, whether it is coarse or excellent. That monk is satisfied with only that alms-food which he received; he does not long for another, and even if he receives more, he does not take it. This is his 'contentment with whatever is obtained' regarding alms-food. A monk who receives alms-food that is unsuitable for his natural health or for his illness, such that he would be uncomfortable if he consumed it, gives that food to a compatible monk. If he then eats suitable food from that monk's hand and practices the recluse's Dhamma, he is still considered contented. This is his 'contentment according to one's strength' regarding alms-food. Another monk receives much excellent alms-food. Just as with the robes, he gives it to senior monks, those of great learning, those who receive little, and the sick...
151:
...giving it away, he is contented even if he eats the leftovers of those senior monks or wanders for alms and eats mixed food. This is his 'contentment with what is appropriate' (yathāsāruppasantuṭṭhi) regarding alms-food.

In this Dispensation, a monk receives a lodging, whether pleasant or unpleasant. He does not give rise to joy or resentment because of that place; he is satisfied with even a mere grass mat that he has obtained. This is his 'contentment with whatever is obtained' (yathālābhasantuṭṭhi) regarding lodging. A monk who receives a lodging that is unsuitable for his natural health or for his illness, such that he would be uncomfortable living there, gives that place to a compatible monk. If he then lives in a suitable lodging belonging to that monk, he is still considered contented. This is his 'contentment according to one's strength' (yathābalasantuṭṭhi) regarding lodging. Another monk of great merit receives many excellent lodgings such as caves, pavilions, or gabled houses. Just as with the robes and other requisites, he gives them to those who are senior, those of great learning, those who receive little, and the sick, and lives wherever he can; yet he remains contented. This is his 'contentment with what is appropriate' (yathāsāruppasantuṭṭhi) regarding lodging. Also, a monk who reflects, "A noble lodging is a ground for negligence; sloth and torpor overcome one sitting there, and when one is overcome by sleep and wakes up, evil thoughts appear," does not accept such a noble lodging even when it is offered. Rejecting it, he lives in the open air or at the foot of a tree and remains contented. This also is 'contentment with what is appropriate' (yathāsāruppasantuṭṭhi) regarding lodging.

In this Dispensation, a monk receives medicine, whether coarse or excellent. He is satisfied with whatever medicine he receives; he does not long for another, and even if he receives more, he does not take it. This is his 'contentment with whatever is obtained' (yathālābhasantuṭṭhi) regarding medicinal requisites. A monk who needs oil but receives molasses gives that molasses to a compatible monk. If he then takes oil from that monk's hand or seeks other oil to use as medicine, he is still considered contented. This is his 'contentment according to one's strength' (yathābalasantuṭṭhi) regarding medicinal requisites. Another monk of great merit receives many excellent medicinal requisites such as oil, honey, and molasses. Just as with the robes, he gives them to those who are senior, those of great learning, those who receive little, and the sick, and is satisfied with whatever medicine they bring to him. Furthermore, if a monk is offered yellow myrobalan (gallnut) soaked in urine in one vessel and the 'four sweets' (catumadhura) in another, with the words, "Venerable sir, take whichever you wish," and even if his illness could be cured by either, he rejects the 'four sweets' and uses the gallnut as medicine, thinking, "Yellow myrobalan soaked in urine has been praised by the Buddhas and other virtuous ones." Such a monk is one of great contentment. This is his 'contentment with what is appropriate' (yathāsāruppasantuṭṭhi) regarding medicinal requisites.
152:
He is indeed very easily contented. This is his 'contentment with what is appropriate' (yathāsāruppasantosa) regarding medicinal requisites. Thus, referring to these three types of contentment, the Blessed One said: 'Monks, this Kassapa is contented with any kind of robe.'

'One who speaks in praise' (vaṇṇavādī) means: One monk might be contented himself but does not speak in praise of contentment. Another might not be contented himself but speaks in praise of contentment. Another is neither contented himself nor speaks in praise of contentment. Another is both contented himself and speaks in praise of contentment. To show that the Venerable Mahākassapa is like the fourth person, it was said: 'He is one who speaks in praise of contentment with any kind of robe.'

'Improper search' (anesana) refers to various types of improper livelihood, such as acting as a messenger, running errands, and so forth. 'Not obtaining' (aladdhā) means because of not receiving. Some monks, thinking 'How shall I obtain a robe?', associate with meritorious monks and, practicing hypocrisy (kuhana), become agitated and anxious. This Venerable Mahākassapa, even when not obtaining a robe, does not reach a state of alarm through exhaustion. 'Having obtained' (laddhā ca) means receiving in accordance with the Dhamma and fairness. 'Unattached' (agadhita) means being free from the greed of attachment. 'Not infatuated' (amucchita) means not falling into infatuation through excessive craving. 'Not overwhelmed' (anajjhāpanna) means not being covered, enveloped, or entangled by craving. 'Seeing the danger' (ādīnavadassāvī) means seeing the danger both in the offense of improper search and in attached consumption. 'Wise in the way of escape' (nissaraṇapañño) means consuming while knowing only the purpose of escape from the round of suffering, as stated: 'Only for the sake of warding off cold.' This is the meaning.

In phrases such as 'with any kind of almsfood,' the meaning should be understood as contentment with whatever almsfood, whatever lodging, or whatever medicinal requisites for the sick are obtained. In the statement, 'Monks, I will exhort you by Kassapa,' it means 'exhorting by Kassapa' because He says: 'Just as the Elder Mahākassapa is contented with the three types of contentment regarding the four requisites, you too should be like that.' In the statement, 'or by one who is like Kassapa,' it means 'exhorting by one like Kassapa' because He says: 'If there is another who, like the Elder Mahākassapa, is contented with the three types of contentment regarding the four requisites, you too should be like him.'

'One should practice to be like that' means: 'To teach the practice of effacement (sallekha) mentioned in this Santuṭṭhi Sutta is the responsibility of the Buddha; to fulfill this practice is our responsibility; one should carry out the responsibility that has arrived.' Thinking thus, the meaning is: 'You should practice to be like that, just as I have taught.' This concludes the commentary on the first sutta.

In the second sutta, 'one who possesses ardor' (ātāpī) refers to that right effort (sammāvāyāma) which burns away the defilements; with that...
153:
'To fulfill this practice of effacement is also our burden. Indeed, one should take up the burden that has come before one.' Thinking thus, [the Buddha said]: 'You, dear sons, should also practice for such a state to arise, just as I have taught.' The commentary on the first sutta is finished.

## 2. Anottappī Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the second sutta, 'lacking ardor' (anātāpī) refers to one who is devoid of that right effort (sammāvāyāma) which burns away the defilements. 'Lacking dread' (anottappī) refers to one who is without fear regarding the arising of defilements and the non-arising of wholesome states. 'For enlightenment' (sambodhāya) means for the sake of knowing and blossoming through the Noble Path. 'For Nibbāna' (nibbānāya) means for the sake of realizing Nibbāna. 'For the unsurpassed security from bondage' (anuttarassa yogakkhemassa) means for the sake of the fruit of Arahantship. That fruit of Arahantship is both unsurpassed and excellent, and it is secure from the four bondages (yogas).

In the terms beginning with 'unarisen' (anuppannā), they should be understood in the following way. To one who, having obtained a requisite such as a robe not previously obtained, or some pleasant object from a supporter, a fellow-resident, or a pupil, accepts that object unwisely (ayoniso) thinking 'It is beautiful, it is good'; or to one who unwisely adverts to some other previously unexperienced object in whatever way—evil unwholesome states such as greed arise. These states should be known as 'unarisen' (anuppannā) [unwholesome states]. This is because in the beginningless saṃsāra, there is no evil state that has never arisen before. Even regarding an object or base previously experienced, if it arises suddenly due to such an object/base—having not arisen before through natural wisdom, or through recitation and inquiry, or through any of the means of scriptural study, meditative work, or wise reflection—these unwholesome states should also be known as: 'Unarisen unwholesome states, if they should arise, would lead to harm.' Furthermore, those states which arise repeatedly regarding those very objects and bases and are not abandoned should be known as: 'Arisen unwholesome states, if they are not abandoned, would lead to harm.' This is the summary here. As for the detailed distinction between arisen and unarisen, and the entire method of abandoning and not abandoning, I have already stated it in the Visuddhimagga, in the Description of the Purification by Knowledge and Vision (Ñāṇadassanavisuddhiniddesa).

'Unarisen wholesome states in me' (anuppannā me kusalā dhammā) refers to the faultless states known as virtue, concentration, the path, and the fruit, which have not yet been obtained. 'Arisen' (uppannā) refers to the obtaining of those very states. 'If they should cease, they would lead to harm' (nirujjhamānā anatthāya saṃvatteyyuṃ) means it should be understood that if those states such as virtue should cease through decline and not arise again, they would lead to harm. In this sutta, mundane wholesome states decline; there is no decline for supramundane states. The Blessed One made this teaching by the power of this fourth Right Effort (Sammappadhāna): 'For the persistence of arisen wholesome states.' Otherwise, if the second path does not arise quickly, the first path that has ceased would lead to harm—this is how the meaning should be noted in this Pali. In this way, in this second sutta, the Blessed One taught the four Right Efforts by the power of insight (vipassanā) which is the preliminary stage of the Path.

3. In the third sutta, 'simile of the moon' (candūpamā) means like the moon. In what way is it similar? It is not similar in terms of roundness. Rather, when the moon travels through the sky, it does not form an intimacy with anyone...
154:
This teaching is given by the power of these Right Efforts (sammappadhāna). It should be understood here that if the second path does not arise quickly and the first path ceases, it would lead to disadvantage. Thus, in this sutta, these four Right Efforts are taught by the power of insight (vipassanā) which precedes the path. The second sutta is finished.

## 3. Candūpamasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, 'like the moon' (candūpamā) means being like the moon. In what way? Is it by being round? No. Rather, just as the moon, while traversing the sky, does not form intimacy, affection, attachment, liking, longing, or obsession with anyone, yet is not unloved or unpleasing to the multitude (i.e., it is beloved), you too should be like the moon, beloved and pleasing to many by not forming intimacy and so forth, and approach the four classes of families, such as the Khattiyas. Furthermore, just as the moon dispels darkness and spreads light, so too should you be like the moon by dispelling the darkness of defilements and spreading the light of knowledge. In such ways, the meaning should be understood here.

'Withdraws the body, withdraws the mind' means withdrawing or pulling away the body and mind by not forming such intimacy. A monk who does not live in the forest and also thinks sensual thoughts and so forth withdraws neither the body nor the mind. A monk who lives in the forest but thinks sensual thoughts withdraws only the body, not the mind. A monk who lives near a village but does not think sensual thoughts withdraws only the mind, not the body. But a monk who lives in the forest and does not think sensual thoughts withdraws both. Intending to show that one should approach families being of such a nature, he said, 'withdraws the body, withdraws the mind.'

'Always a newcomer' (niccanavaka) means always being like a new arrival or a guest. For example, a guest enters a house reached in order, and when the householders see him, they feel compassion, thinking, 'Our sons and brothers have gone abroad and traveled like this,' and they make him sit and feed him. As soon as he has eaten, [he says,] 'Your...
155:
...take the bowl,' and having requested thus, he gets up and departs. He does not form intimacy with those householders, nor does he manage their affairs. Likewise, you too, when entering a house reached in order, should receive the offerings given by people who are inspired by your deportment, and depart without intimacy with those lay followers and without being concerned with their affairs.

To clarify this state of being 'always a newcomer' (niccanavaka-bhāva), the story of the two brothers should be told. It is heard that two brothers from the village of Vasabha left and ordained. They were known as Elder Cūḷanāga and Elder Mahānāga. Having lived on Cittalapabbata for thirty years and attained Arahantship, they came [back] thinking, 'We will see our mother.' They stayed at the Vasabha Monastery and entered the mother's village for alms the next day. The mother also took out gruel with a ladle and poured it into the bowl of one elder. While looking at that elder, motherly affection for her son arose. Then she said to him, 'Dear, are you my son Mahānāga?' The elder said, 'Laywoman, ask the elder coming behind,' and departed. Having given gruel to the later elder, she asked, 'Dear, are you my son Cūḷanāga?' The elder said, 'Laywoman, why did you not ask the elder who went before?' and departed. Thus, a monk who has cut off intimacy even with his mother is called 'always a newcomer' (niccanavaka).

'Not impudent' (appagabbhā) means not being rude. It means being free from the eight types of physical impudence (kāyapāgabbhiya), the four types of verbal impudence (vacīpāgabbhiya), and the many types of mental impudence (manopāgabbhiya).

The eight types of physical impudence mean performing improper physical actions in the Sangha, a group, towards an individual, in the dining hall, the fire room, the bathing place, on the alms-round path, and when entering a house. For example, some person in the midst of the Sangha sits clasping the knees or with a cloth wrapped around the knees, or sits with legs crossed, and so forth. Likewise in the midst of a group. 'In the midst of a group' means in an assembly of the fourfold community or in an assembly of a group studying the Suttantas and so forth. Likewise towards senior persons.

In the dining hall, it is not giving seats to elders or preventing juniors from taking seats. Likewise in the fire room, it is lighting a fire and so forth without asking the elders. In the bathing place, although it is said, 'One should bathe in the order of arrival without making a distinction between junior and senior,' one who disregards this, comes later, enters the water forcibly, and disturbs or harrasses the seniors and juniors.

On the alms-round path, [it is taking] the best seat...
156:
He goes ahead, jostling with his arms, to obtain the first water and the first alms-food. When entering a house, he enters ahead of the elders. He engages in physical play with the juniors. Such actions are known as (bodily impudence).

Verbal impudence (vacīpagabbhiya), which has four aspects, refers to uttering improper words in the midst of the Saṅgha, a group, or an individual, as well as inside a house. In this regard, a certain person in this Sasana preaches the Dhamma in the midst of the Saṅgha without asking permission. Likewise, in the midst of a group as previously mentioned, or in the presence of an individual, when questioned by people in that same place, he answers without asking permission from the elders. Inside a house, however, he says things such as, "What does such-and-such a person have? Is there gruel, or is there hard food or soft food? What will you give me? What shall we chew today? What shall we eat? What shall we drink?"

Mental impudence (manopagabbhiya), which has many aspects, refers to the thinking of sensual thoughts (kāmavitakka) and so forth in various places, even without committing transgressions through body or speech. Furthermore, the evil desire of one who is immoral, thinking, "Let people know me as one who is virtuous," is also called mental impudence. Thus, He says, "Approach [families] being unimpertinent (appagabbha) due to the absence of all these forms of impudence."

'Jarudapāna' means an old well. 'Pabbatavisama' means an uneven precipice on a mountain. 'Nadīvidugga' means a place with a broken bank at a river. "Without drawing back the body" means that a person who is fond of playing and so forth in such places looks on with affection, without drawing back his body, without making it heavy on one side, without maintaining his balance against the wind, and without drawing back his mind, because he does not see the danger, thinking, "If I fall here, I will suffer broken limbs and so forth," and thus he is not frightened. That person falls and meets with misfortune such as broken limbs. However, a person who desires to look because he wants water or for some other business, looks while drawing back his body, making it heavy on one side, maintaining his balance against the wind, and also drawing back his mind, being frightened by seeing the danger. That person does not fall; having looked as much as he desires, he departs happily wherever he wishes.
157:
In the phrase 'Even so' (evameva kho), there is this comparison between the simile and the subject. The four types of families should be understood as the old well and so forth, and the monk should be understood as the man who looks. Just as the man who looks at the old well, the precipice, and so forth with an unrestrained body and mind falls there, even so, the monk who approaches families with unrestrained body and so forth becomes bound to those families; because of that bondage, he meets with various misfortunes such as the breaking of the feet of virtue (sīla). Just as the man with a restrained body and mind does not fall into that old well or precipice, even so, the monk who approaches families with a restrained body, restrained mind, restrained speech, and well-established mindfulness, having a restrained body and mind, does not become bound to those families.

When he is not so bound, just as the feet of the man who does not fall into the old well or precipice are not broken or destroyed, even so, the feet of virtue are not destroyed. Just as the hands are not broken or destroyed, even so, the hands of faith (saddhā) are not broken or destroyed. Just as the belly is not ruptured or cut, even so, the belly of concentration (samādhi) is not ruptured or cut. Just as the head is not cracked or broken, even so, the head of wisdom (ñāṇa) is not cracked or broken. Just as stumps and thorns do not pierce that man, even so, the thorns of lust (rāga) and so forth do not pierce this monk. Just as that man, being free from danger, looks as much as he desires and departs happily wherever he wishes, even so, the monk, depending on families and making use of requisites such as robes, develops his meditation subject, contemplates conditioned formations (saṅkhāra), reaches Arahatship, and being happy with supramundane bliss, goes to the region of Nibbāna, where he has never been before, as he desires.

Now, a person of low inclination and wrong practice might say, "The Fully Enlightened One, having told us to abandon the three kinds of impudence and approach families being like the moon by being ever-new, places us in an impossible position, imposes an unbearable burden, and makes us do what cannot be done." To cut off the argument of such a person of wrong practice, and to show that "It is possible to do so; there is such a monk," He spoke the words beginning with, "Kassapa, O monks..."

"He moved his hand in the sky" means that he moved his hand in the lower part, the upper part, and on both sides, like one causing a double flash of lightning to move in the midst of the blue sky. This phrase is also known as an 'unbroken word' (asambhinnapada) in the Tipitaka, the Word of the Buddha. 'Attamano' means one with a delighted mind, one with his own mind, not one whose mind is seized by being cut off by dejection. This statement, "Kassapa, O monks," was also spoken in the same manner as before, to cut off the arguments of others and to show that "There is such a monk."
158:
"They should perform acts of devotion" means they should offer requisites such as robes and so forth. "They should practice for such a state" means they should practice for that unchanging state by fulfilling virtue where virtue is concerned, and by perfecting concentration, insight, the path, and the fruit where those respective states are concerned. "Anudaya" means the state of wanting to protect. "Anukampa" means the state of having a tender heart. Both of these are synonyms for compassion (karuṇā). "Monks, Kassapa..." This statement was also spoken, following the previous method, to cut off the arguments of others and to show that "there is such a monk." "Or with Kassapa..." In this context, the meaning should be understood as in the previous method, by connecting it with the simile of the moon and so forth. The third sutta is finished.

## 4. Kulūpaka Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, "Kulūpaka" means one who frequents the houses of families. "Let them give only to me" means let them give to me alone. "Sandīyati" means being weary or oppressed. The rest should be understood according to the method already stated. The fourth sutta is finished.

## 5. Jiṇṇa Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, "Jiṇṇa" refers to the elder who is old. "Garukāni" (heavy) means that those robes, from the time they were received from the Teacher, became heavy due to being sewn with thread and patched in torn places, thus becoming many-layered. "Nibbasanāni" (discarded) is the name given because they were previously worn and then discarded by the Blessed One. "Therefore" means because you are old and have heavy rag-robes. "Robes given by householders" means he says, "Give up the practice of wearing rag-robes (paṃsukūlika-dhutaṅga) and wear robes given by householders." "Invited meals" means he says, "Give up the practice of eating only alms-food (piṇḍapātika-dhutaṅga) and enjoy invited meals such as food distributed by tickets (salāka-bhatta) and so forth." "And near me" means he says, "Give up the practice of forest-dwelling (āraññika-dhutaṅga) and live only in a monastery near a village."

Is it not the case that if a king appoints a general to the position of general, and while that general is pleasing the king with his duties such as serving the king, the king takes back that position and gives it to another, he is said to be doing something improper? In the same way, the Teacher traveled three gāvutas to meet the Elder Mahākassapa, sat at the foot of the Bahuputtaka banyan tree between Rājagaha and Nālandā, and ordained him with three exhortations. Then, did he not exchange his own robes with the elder and make him a forest-dweller and a rag-robe wearer from birth? If the Teacher, while being pleased by the elder's actions, out of a desire to act for the elder's sake, urged him to give up the rag-robe practice and so forth and to accept robes given by householders, would it not be said that the Teacher was doing something improper to the Elder Mahākassapa? This might be questioned. It would not be said that he did something improper. Why? Because he desired his welfare. Indeed, the Teacher had no desire for him to give up the ascetic practices (dhutaṅgas). For example, just as musical instruments like a large drum do not make a sound if they are not struck, so too, the Teacher thought that such persons do not speak words like a lion's roar if they are not requested. With the intention of making him roar a lion's roar, he said, "Therefore, you, Kassapa..." and so forth. The elder also, in accordance with the Teacher's wish, roared a lion's roar by saying, "Venerable Sir, I am old, and I have lived in the forest for a long time," and so forth.
159:
Did not the Blessed One exchange his robes with the Elder Mahākassapa and cause him to undertake the forest-dweller's practice and the rag-robe wearer's practice from birth? If the Blessed One, while being pleased by the elder's actions, out of a desire to act for the elder's sake, urged him to give up the rag-robe practice and so forth and to accept robes given by householders, would it be said that he did something improper? It would not be said that he did something improper. Why? Because it was due to the power of desiring his welfare. In truth, the Blessed One did not wish for him to give up the ascetic practices. For example, just as musical instruments like a large drum do not make a sound if they are not struck, so too, the Blessed One thought that such persons do not roar a lion's roar if they are not requested. With the intention of making him roar a lion's roar, he spoke in this way. The Elder Mahākassapa also, in accordance with the Blessed One's wish, roared a lion's roar in this manner: "Venerable Sir, I am old, and I have lived in the forest for a long time," and so forth.

"Diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra" means dwelling in happiness in the present life. This can only be obtained by one who dwells in the forest, not by one who dwells near a village. This is because one who dwells near a village hears the sounds of children, sees unsuitable sights, and hears unsuitable sounds. Because of seeing and hearing such things, dissatisfaction (anabhirati) arises in that monk. However, a monk dwelling in the forest, having entered the forest after traveling a gāvuta or half a yojana, hears the sounds of leopards, tigers, lions, and so forth. Because of hearing those sounds, a delight in seclusion (viveka) that is superior to human delight arises. With reference to this meaning, it was said:

"For the monk who has entered an empty place, who has a peaceful mind, and who clearly sees the Dhamma with insight, there is a delight that transcends that of humans."
"Whenever he contemplates the rise and fall of the aggregates, he obtains joy and gladness; that is the Deathless for those who know it."
"Whether in front or behind, if no other person is found, there is comfort for one who delights alone in the forest."

Similarly, dwelling in happiness in the present life can only be obtained by a monk who collects alms-food, not by one who does not practice the alms-food eater's ascetic practice. A monk who does not practice the alms-food eater's practice tends to go at improper times, goes hurriedly, is restless, goes with anxiety, and has many doubts regarding that food. However, a monk who collects alms-food does not go at improper times, does not go hurriedly, is not restless, goes without anxiety, and does not have many doubts regarding that food.

How is this? A monk who does not practice the alms-food eater's practice, while dwelling in a monastery far from the village, thinks early in the morning, "Will I get gruel or leftover rice? At the dining hall or..."
160:
Specifically, a monk who does not practice the alms-food eater's ascetic practice (piṇḍapātika-dhutaṅga), thinking, 'I will receive something from the designated meals and so forth,' goes out very early in the morning, breaking spider webs and waking up sleeping herds of cattle (before they rise); when he goes thus, he is one who wanders at an improper time (akālacārī). To catch up with people who have left their homes for field work and such, he goes swiftly like a hunter chasing prey; when he goes thus, he is one who wanders hurriedly (turitacārī). If he sees someone on the way, he asks, 'Is such-and-such a male lay follower or such-and-such a female lay follower at home or not?' If he hears, 'They are not at home,' he thinks, 'Where will I get food now?' and trembles with anxiety like one being burned by fire. Even though he himself wishes to go to the west, if he receives a meal-ticket for the east, he approaches another monk who received a ticket for the west and says, 'Venerable sir, I will go to the west; please take my ticket and give yours to me,' thus exchanging the meal-ticket.

Alternatively, while taking and consuming one meal-ticket food, when people say, 'Give us the bowl for another person's meal-ticket food,' he says, 'Venerable sir, give me your bowl; I will put the food in my bowl and then give you your bowl,' thus having another monk's bowl brought, putting the food into his own bowl when it arrives, and returning the bowl; this is called 'exchanging the bowl.' In the monastery, kings, royal ministers, and others give great offerings. This monk has also received a meal-ticket for a more distant village. If he does not go there, he fears he will not receive a meal-ticket for the next seven days; out of fear of loss (alābhabhaya), he goes. A monk who goes in this way is said to go with worldly concern (palibuddha). When that monk goes for the sake of meal-ticket food and so forth, many doubts arise in him: 'Will they give to me or not? Or will they not give? Will they give fine food or coarse food? Will it be a little or a lot? Will it be cold or hot?'

However, a monk who observes the alms-food eater's ascetic practice (piṇḍapātika) rises early, performs his major and minor duties, attends to his body, enters his dwelling place, applies his mind to the meditation subject (kammaṭṭhāna), notes the time, and goes only when it is the proper time for the people to be able to offer alms with a ladle and so forth; therefore, he is not one who wanders at an improper time (akālacārī). Because he goes practicing insight (vipassanā) by dividing each footstep into six parts, he is not one who wanders hurriedly (turitacārī). Due to his own venerable nature, he does not ask, 'Is such-and-such a person at home or not?' He does not even accept meal-ticket food and the like. Since he does not accept them, what would he have to exchange? He is without worldly concern regarding the wishes of others...
161:
...and applying his mind to the meditation subject, he goes as he pleases. Unlike the other, he does not have many doubts. If he does not receive food in one village or one street, he wanders elsewhere. Even if he does not receive it there, while wandering elsewhere, when he obtains mixed alms-food, he consumes it as if it were nectar (amata) and goes on.

This benefit is obtained only by a rag-robe wearer (paṃsukūlika), not by one who is not a rag-robe wearer. For one who is not a rag-robe wearer wanders seeking rainy-season robes and does not seek a suitable lodging (senāsana). However, a rag-robe wearer does not need to wander seeking rainy-season robes and thus seeks only a suitable lodging. This is obtained only by a triple-robe wearer (tecīvarika), not by others. For one who is not a triple-robe wearer has many goods and requisites, and thus lacks a comfortable dwelling. It is obtained only by those with qualities such as fewness of wishes (appicchatā), not by others. Therefore, it is said: 'Seeing his own pleasant dwelling in this very life.' The fifth sutta ends.

## ၆။ ဩဝါဒသုတ်အဖွင့်

In the commentary on the sixth sutta, why did the Buddha say, 'Either I...'? It was for the purpose of establishing the Elder Mahākassapa in his own position. Was it because Sāriputta and Moggallāna were not there? They were there. However, the Buddha had this thought: 'These two, Sāriputta and Moggallāna, will not remain for long. But Kassapa will live to be one hundred and twenty years old. After I have attained Parinibbāna, he will sit in the Sattapaṇṇi Cave, conduct the Recitation of the Dhamma and Vinaya (Dhamma-vinaya-saṅgaha), and make my Dispensation (Sāsana) endure for a period of five thousand years. I shall establish this Mahākassapa in my place; in this way, the monks will consider that Kassapa's words should be listened to.' Therefore, he spoke thus.

'Dubbacā' means those who are difficult to speak to with words of admonition. 'Dovacassakaraṇehi' means by those qualities that make one difficult to admonish. 'Appadakkhiṇaggāhino' refers to those who, even after hearing words of instruction, do not receive them respectfully and do not practice according to the instruction. He shows that those who do not practice are called 'those who grasp from the left' (vāmaggāhino). 'Accāvadante' means speaking overbearingly, referring to those who engage in excessive debate relying on the scriptures (pariyatti) they have heard. 'Who will speak more?' means when preaching the Dhamma, who will speak more, you or I? 'Who will speak better?' means one person may speak much but in a disconnected and unpleasant way, while another speaks in a connected and sweet way; referring to this, he said, 'Who will speak better?' One person may speak both much and well but does not speak for long and rises quickly; another can continue for a long time; referring to this point, he said, 'Who will speak longer?' The sixth sutta ends.
162:
## 7. Dutiyaovāda Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the seventh sutta, 'faith' (saddhā) refers to the faith of conviction in the Triple Gem. 'Energy' (viriya) refers to both physical and mental energy. 'Wisdom' (paññā) refers to the wisdom that understands wholesome states. The phrase "There are no monks who give exhortation" means that for this person, there are no good friends (kalyāṇamitta) who can admonish and repeatedly instruct him; the Venerable shows that this is a cause of decline. The seventh sutta ends.

## 8. Tatiyaovāda Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, the phrase "tathā hi pana" is a particle used when presenting the reasons for former docility and current difficulty in being admonished. "Tatra" means among those elders. "What is the name of this monk?" is a question asking whether this monk is Tissa Thera or Nāga Thera. "Tatra" [in the second instance] means when such honor and offerings are being made. "Tathattāya" means for that state, specifically for the state of living in the forest and so forth. "Sabrahmacārikāma" refers to one who is called so because of desiring, longing, and praying in this way: "May these monks surround and follow me." "Tathattāya" [in the second instance] means for the purpose of generating gains and honor. "Brahmacārupaddavena" refers to being oppressed by the danger (upaddava), which is the excessive desire and lust for the four requisites of fellow practitioners. "Abhipatthanā" means excessive longing. "Brahmacāri-abhipatthanena" means by way of the four requisites, which is called the excessive longing of fellow practitioners. The eighth sutta ends.

## 9. Jhānābhiñña Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the ninth sutta, "yāvadeva ākaṅkhāမိ" means as much as I wish. Following this, the four fine-material jhanas (rūpāvacara jhāna) are taught by way of "quite secluded from sensual pleasures" and so forth; the four immaterial attainments (arūpa samāpatti) by way of "with the complete surmounting of perceptions of forms" and so forth; the attainment of cessation (nirodha samāpatti) by way of "with the complete surmounting of the base of neither-perception-nor-non-perception, the cessation of perception and feeling"; and the five mundane direct knowledges (lokiya abhiññā) by way of "manifold forms of psychic power" and so forth. Everything that should be said regarding this text, along with the word-by-word commentary and the methods of meditation development, has already been explained in detail in the Visuddhimagga.
