In the eighth sutta, 'siṅgāla' refers to an old jackal (jarasiṅgāla). Just as a body, even if golden-colored, is still called a foul body, and urine, even as it is being voided, is called foul urine, so too a jackal born that very day is still called an 'old jackal'. 'Ukkaṇṭakena nāma' means by the disease of that name. It is said that this disease arises in the winter season. When it occurs, the hair falls out from the entire body; the whole body becomes hairless and cracks all over, and the sores ache when struck by the wind. Just as a man bitten by a rabid dog wanders about unsteadily, so too one must wander when this disease arises, not knowing where relief might be found. The eighth sutta is finished.

## 9. Verambhasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, 'verambhavātā' refers to the great storms of that name. In what kind of place do those winds blow? They blow in a place where, to one standing there, the four great islands appear only as large as lotus leaves. 'Yo pakkhi gacchati' (the bird that goes) refers to the wind-bird (vātasakuṇa) that goes about crying out when the new rains begin; it is in reference to that bird that this was said. In the phrases beginning with 'unprotected body', one is said not to guard the body by fidgeting with hands and feet or by bending the spine. One is said not to guard speech by speaking various kinds of coarse talk. One is said not to guard the mind by thinking thoughts of sensual desire and so forth. 'Anupaṭṭhitāya satiyā' means by not establishing mindfulness of the body (kāyagatāsati). The ninth sutta is finished.

## 10. Sagāthakasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, 'asakkārena cūbhayaṃ' means by lack of honor and by both (honor and lack of honor). 'Samādhi' refers to the concentration of the fruition of Arahantship. Indeed, he does not waver because of those honors or lack of honors. 'Appamāṇavihārino' refers to one who dwells in the immeasurable fruition attainment. 'Sātatikaṃ' refers to one who practices constantly. 'Sukhumadiṭṭhivipassakaṃ' refers to an insight practitioner who has arrived after undertaking insight for the sake of the subtle attainment of the fruition of the path of Arahantship. 'Upādānakkhayārāmaṃ' means delighting in Nibbāna, which is the destruction of clinging. 'Āhu sappuriso iti' means they say he is a good man. The tenth sutta is finished.

## Paṭhamo Vaggo.
193:
## 2. The Second Chapter (Dutiya Vagga)
## 1-2. Commentary on the Suvaṇṇapāti Sutta, etc.
167-168. In the first sutta of the second chapter, "sampajānamusā bhāsantaṃ" means speaking a deliberate lie even for a very slight reason. A monk who is well-established, thinking "I will fulfill the precepts," cannot be moved (from virtue) even by a mass of requisites as large as Mount Sineru. However, when he abandons virtue and becomes dependent on gain, honor, and fame, he speaks a lie even for the sake of a handful of bran, or performs other improper acts. The second sutta is clear in meaning. These are the first and second suttas.

## 3-10. Commentary on the Suvaṇṇanikkha Sutta, etc.
In the third sutta and others, "suvaṇṇanikkhassa" refers to a nikkha (weight/coin) of pure gold. "siṅgīnikkhassa" refers to a nikkha of siṅgī gold. "pathaviyā" refers to the great earth within the universe. "āmisakiñcikkhahetu" means for the sake of some material gain, even as little as a handful of bran. "jīvitahetu" means for the sake of life, such as when being captured and about to be killed by bandits in a forest. "janapadakalyāṇiyā" refers to the most beautiful woman in the land. These are the third sutta and others.

## The Second Chapter is finished.

## 3. The Third Chapter (Tatiya Vagga)
## 1-2. Commentary on the Mātugāma Sutta, etc.
170-171. In the first sutta of the third chapter, "na tassa, bhikkhave, mātugāmo" means that even a woman who desires that practice (sexual intercourse) cannot overwhelm the mind of that monk sitting alone in seclusion; it means that gain, honor, and fame can overwhelm the mind of such a monk (only such a monk's mind is referred to). The second sutta is clear in meaning. These are the first and second suttas.

## 3-6. Commentary on the Ekaputtaka Sutta, etc.
172-175. In the third sutta, "saddhā" refers to a female lay follower who is a Stream-enterer (Sotāpanna). The remaining words in this sutta are clear. Likewise in the fourth, fifth, and sixth suttas. These are the third sutta and others.
194:
## 7. Commentary on the Third Samaṇabrāhmaṇa Sutta
In the seventh sutta, among the words beginning with "samudaya," the existence (attabhāva) along with past karma, such as being of noble birth, beauty of form, eloquence in speech, making known the ascetic qualities (dhutaṅga), wearing the robes, and the accomplishment of a retinue—these are called the origin (samudaya) of gain and honor. One does not know that origin in detail by way of the Truth of Origin (Samudayasacca). Cessation (nirodha) and the practice (paṭipadā) should be understood only by way of the Truth of Cessation (Nirodhasacca) and the Truth of the Path (Maggasacca). The commentary on the seventh sutta ends.

## 8. Commentary on the Chavi Sutta
In the eighth sutta, because gain, honor, and fame cause rebirth in hell and so forth, they destroy this entire existence; and because they bring about death and suffering equal to death even in this life, it is said they "cut the skin" and so on. The commentary on the eighth sutta ends.

## 9. Commentary on the Rajju Sutta
In the ninth sutta, "vāḷarajjuya" means that ropes made of thread and so on are soft, but a rope made of horsehair (vāḷarajju) is harsh and rough. Therefore, only this horsehair rope is taken as a simile. The commentary on the ninth sutta ends.

## 10. Commentary on the Bhikkhu Sutta
In the tenth sutta, "diṭṭhadhammasukhavihāra" means dwelling happily in the attainment of fruition (phalasamāpatti). "tesāhamassa" should be resolved into "tesaṃ ahaṃ assa." Indeed, an Arahant who receives gains and is endowed with merit, while receiving donors who bring gruel, food, and so on, giving thanks (anumodanā), preaching the Dhamma, and answering questions, does not find the opportunity to sit down and enter the attainment of fruition. This is said with reference to that point. The commentary on the tenth sutta ends.

## The Third Chapter (Tatiya Vagga).

## 4. The Fourth Chapter (Catuttha Vagga)

## 1-4. Commentary on the Bhindi Sutta, etc.
180-183. The first sutta of the fourth chapter is clear in meaning. In the second sutta and others, "kusalamūla" refers to the three types of wholesome states such as non-greed. "sukkadhamma" is a synonymous teaching of that same...
195:
This is a teaching by way of figurative expression (pariyāya). However, the summary meaning here is: because the blameless state known as the root of the wholesome (kusalamūla) was not yet completely cut off, Devadatta might have been reborn in heaven or attained the paths and fruits. But that blameless state has come to be completely cut off for that Devadatta; it is completely cut off and destroyed in every way. These are the first sutta and others.

## 5. Commentary on the Acirapakkanta Sutta
In the fifth sutta, "parābhavāya" means for ruin and destruction. "assatarī" is a she-mule born from a donkey in the womb of a mare. "She carries a fetus for her own death" means that when they mate that she-mule with a horse, she conceives, and when the time for birth arrives, she is unable to give birth and stands kicking the ground with her feet. Then, they tie her four legs to four stakes, rip open her belly, and take out the young mule. She dies right there. Therefore, this was said. The fifth sutta ends.

## 6. Commentary on the Pañcarathasata Sutta
In the sixth sutta, "bhattābhiဟာရော" (bhattābhihāro) means food to be brought forward. To show the amount of that food, it is said "five hundred pots of rice" (pañca thālipākasatāni). There, one pot of rice contains enough food for ten men. "They would split the gall in the nose" means they would put either bear's gall or fish's gall into his nostrils. The sixth sutta ends.

## 7-13. Commentary on the Mātu Sutta, etc.
186-187. In the seventh sutta, "even for the sake of one's mother" means: "If you lie, we will release your mother. If you do not lie, we will not release her." When asked thus by bandits in a forest, even for the sake of that mother who has fallen into the hands of bandits, one should not speak a deliberate lie. In the suttas following this, the method is to be understood in the same way. The seventh sutta and others end.

## The Commentary on the Lābhasakkārasaṃyutta is finished.
196:
## 7. Rāhulasaṃyutta
## 1. Paṭhamavagga
## 1-8. Commentary on Cakkhusutta and others
188-195. In the first sutta of the Rāhulasaṃyutta, ‘eko’ means one who dwells alone (ekavihārī) in the four postures. ‘Vūpakaṭṭho’ means secluded from defilements, silent (quiet). ‘Appamatto’ means dwelling without being apart from mindfulness. ‘Ātāpī’ means being endowed with energy. ‘Pahitatto vihareyyaṃ’ means "I shall dwell with a mind sent forth for the sake of attaining the special distinction."

‘Aniccaṃ’ (impermanent) means impermanent in the sense of non-existence after having arisen. Alternatively, it is called impermanent for these reasons: because it has the nature of arising and passing away, because it is temporary (momentary), because it has an end in change, and because it rejects the nature of permanence.

‘Dukkhaṃ’ (suffering) is called suffering due to four reasons: because of the sense of being hard to bear, because of the sense of being the basis of suffering, because of the sense of constant oppression, and because of the sense of rejecting happiness.

‘Kallaṃ’ means suitable. ‘Etaṃ mama’ (this is mine) is the grasping of craving (taṇhāgāha). ‘Esohamasmi’ (this I am) is the grasping of conceit (mānagāha). ‘Eso me attā’ (this is my self) is the grasping of views (diṭṭhigāha). Here, the grasping of craving should be understood by way of the 108 mental wanderings of craving, the grasping of conceit by way of the nine types of conceit, and the grasping of views by way of the sixty-two types of views.

In the passage ‘nibbindaṃ virajjati’ (dispassionate, he becomes detached), the four paths are taught by way of dispassion (virāga). In the passage ‘virāgā vimuccati’ (through dispassion, he is liberated), the four fruits of recluseship are taught by way of liberation (vimutti).

In this first sutta, among the five doors, only the sensitive material (pasādarūpa) is taken. By the word ‘mano’ (mind), the mind of investigative course (sammasanacāracitta) belonging to the three planes is taken. In the second sutta, among the five doors, only the object is taken. In the third sutta, among the five doors, only the mind based on the sensitive material is taken. By the term 'mind-consciousness' (manoviññāṇa), the mind of investigative course belonging to the three planes is taken. In this way, the method should be applied to all suttas. In the sixth sutta, the dhammas belonging to the three planes are taken. In the eighth sutta, ‘taṇhā’ (craving) refers only to the craving that has reached the javana stage at the respective doors. These are the first and subsequent suttas.

## 9. Dhātusuttavaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, name (nāma) is taught by way of the consciousness element, and form (rūpa) is taught by way of the remaining elements; thus, name-and-form (nāmarūpa) is taught. The ninth sutta ends.
197:
## 10. Khandhasuttavaṇṇanā
In the tenth sutta, the form aggregate (rūpakkhandha) is a dhamma of the sense sphere. The remaining four aggregates are dhammas of the four planes by way of all-inclusive delimitation. However, in this sutta, they should be taken as dhammas of the three planes. The tenth sutta ends.

## Paṭhamo Vaggo.

## 2. Dutiyavagga

## 1-10. Commentary on Cakkhusutta and others
198-199. In the second vagga, the ten suttas have clear meanings. These are the first and subsequent suttas.

## 11. Anusayasuttavaṇṇanā
In the eleventh sutta, by the phrase "in this body with consciousness," he shows one's own conscious body. By the phrase "and externally," he shows another's conscious body or an unconscious body. Alternatively, by the former phrase, he shows only the consciousness of oneself and others, and by the latter phrase "externally," he shows non-sentient form (anindriyabaddharūpa). "I-making, mine-making, and the underlying tendency of conceit" refers to the view of I-making, the craving of mine-making, and the underlying tendency of conceit. "Do not occur" is an inquiry: "In what way does one know so that these defilements do not occur in these objects?" "Sees with right wisdom" means seeing well with the wisdom of the path together with insight (vipassanā). The eleventh sutta ends.

## 12. Apagatasuttavaṇṇanā
In the twelfth sutta, "free from I-making, mine-making, and conceit" means being removed from the state of I-making, from the state of mine-making, and from conceit. "Well transcended the categories of conceit" means thoroughly going beyond the portions of conceit. "Peaceful and well liberated" means peaceful through the subsiding of defilements, and well liberated from the defilements themselves. The remaining words are clear. The twelfth sutta ends.

## Dutiyoyo Vaggo.
198:
In both of these vaggas, the stage of the non-learner (asekhabhūmi, i.e., Arahantship) is taught. However, in this Rāhulasaṃyutta, the first vagga was taught upon request, while the second vagga was taught without request. It should be noted that in the entire Rāhulasaṃyutta, the Buddha taught only the dhammas that ripen liberation (vimuttiparipācanīyadhamma) for the sake of the Venerable Rāhula's attainment of the fruit of Arahantship.

## Rāhulasaṃyuttavaṇṇanā Niṭṭhitā.
199:
## 8. Lakkhaṇasaṃyutta
## 1. Paṭhamavagga
## 1. Commentary on the Aṭṭhi Sutta

In the Lakkhaṇasaṃyutta, this Elder Lakkhaṇa, referred to as "Venerable Lakkhaṇa," should be known as one of the great disciples (mahāsāvaka) who entered the Dispensation through the 'Ehi Bhikkhu' ordination among the thousand matted-hair ascetics (jaṭilas) and attained Arahantship at the conclusion of the Ādittapariyāya Sutta. Because this Elder possessed a physical form (attabhāva) that was complete in every aspect and endowed with marks (lakkhaṇa) similar to those of a Brahma, he was known by the name "Lakkhaṇa." Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, however, was the second chief disciple who attained Arahantship on the seventh day after his ordination.

"Sitāṃ pātvākāsī" means he manifested or showed a gentle smile. What did the Elder see that caused him to smile? He saw a being born in the realm of petas (hungry ghosts) who was merely a skeleton (aṭṭhikasaṅkhalika), as mentioned in the Pāli text above. This seeing was done with the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu), not with the physical eye (pasāda-cakkhu). This is because such physical forms (attabhāva) do not come within the range of the physical eye. Why did he smile when he should have felt compassion upon seeing such a physical form? It was because he reflected on his own attainment and the perfection of the Buddha’s knowledge. Upon seeing that peta, the Elder reflected on his own attainment, thinking, "I am free from such a physical form that must be obtained by those who have not seen the Four Noble Truths; what a gain for me, what a great blessing for me!" He also smiled while reflecting on the perfection of the Buddha’s knowledge, thinking, "Oh, how wonderful is the perfection of the Buddha’s knowledge! He taught that 'the result of kamma (kamma-vipāka), O monks, is unthinkable and should not be thought about.' The Buddhas teach having directly witnessed it; the Dhamma-element (dhammadhātu) of the Buddhas is indeed well-penetrated."

If that is so, why did Venerable Lakkhaṇa not see it? Did he not possess the divine eye? It is not that he did not have it; he had it. However, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna saw it because he was reflecting (āvajjanā), while the other (Lakkhaṇa) did not see it because he was not reflecting. Since those who have destroyed the taints (khīṇāsava) do not smile without a reason, Venerable Lakkhaṇa asked, "Friend Moggallāna, what is the cause, what is the reason for your smile?" The Elder...
200:
However, because those who have not personally seen the origin of this peta being would find it difficult to believe, and because he wished to explain it by making the Blessed One a witness, he said, "Friend, it is not the time to answer," and so on. Later, when questioned in the presence of the Blessed One, he explained in the manner beginning with, "Here, friend, I saw this skeleton-peta."

In that context, "aṭṭhikasaṅkhalika" refers to a heap of bones that is white and devoid of flesh and blood. In the phrase "vultures, crows, and hawks also," these birds should be understood as yakkha-vultures, yakkha-crows, and yakkha-hawks. The appearance of that peta does not manifest within the range of ordinary vultures and other birds. "Anupatitvā anupatitvā" means following or pursuing repeatedly. "Vitudenti" means they fly here and there, pecking at it with sharp iron beaks that are like sword blades. In the Pāli "sā sudaṃ aṭṭassaraṃ karoti," "sudaṃ" is a particle (nipāta). It means that the skeleton-peta makes a terrifying cry of distress (aṭṭassara) due to intense pain. It is said that such physical forms (attabhāva), even as large as a league (yojana), arise to experience the results of unwholesome kamma. These forms are as sensitive as a ripe boil. Therefore, that skeleton-peta made such a sound because she was oppressed by powerful pain.

After saying this, Venerable Mahāmoggallāna, wishing to show the spiritual urgency (dhamma-saṃvega) that arose based on compassion for beings, thinking, "Beings wandering in Saṃsāra cannot escape such evil physical forms," said, "Friend, this thought occurred to me: how wonderful it is!" and so on. Then the Blessed One, wishing to manifest the power of the Elder, said, "Monks, my disciples live having become vision (cakkhubhūta)," and so on. In that context, they are called "cakkhubhūta" because they possess the divine eye (dibba-cakkhu) that has arisen. It means they live having produced the divine eye. The same method applies to the second term, "ñāṇabhūta" (having become knowledge). In the phrase "yatra hi nāma," "yatra" is a word denoting a cause. The connection of the meaning is: because a disciple will also know, see, and witness the state of such petas, therefore we said, "Monks, my disciples live having become vision; monks, my disciples live having become knowledge." "Monks, I saw that being long ago" means that while the Buddha was directly witnessing the infinite world-systems, the infinite groups of beings, their realms, destinations, stations of rebirth, and abodes through the penetration of Omniscient Knowledge (sabbaññuta-ñāṇa) at the Bodhi tree, he had already seen that being.
201:
A cattle butcher is a being who makes a living by killing cattle, removing the meat from the bones, and selling it. "By the remnant of the result of that karma" refers to the remnant of that *aparāpariya-vedanīya* karma accumulated through various intentions (*cetanā*). Among those various intentions, the one that produced rebirth in hell has had its result exhausted; then, taking either the remaining karma or the sign of karma (*kamma-nimitta*) as an object, rebirth occurs once again among the *petas* and so forth. Therefore, that rebirth is called "the remnant of the result of that karma" because of the similarity of the karma or the similarity of the object.

This being also came into existence in this manner. Therefore, the Blessed One said, "By the remnant of the result of that karma." For that skeleton *peta*, at the time of passing away from hell, the heap of bones of the cattle that had been stripped of meat became the sign of karma. Although that evil karma was hidden, it became manifest to the wise, and he was born as a skeleton *peta*. This is the first sutta.

## 2. Pesisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the story of the meat-strip, a cattle butcher made a living for many years by making meat strips from beef, drying them, and selling the dried meat. Therefore, at the time of his passing away from hell, the meat strip itself became the sign of karma. He was born as a meat-strip *peta*. This is the second sutta.

## 3. Piṇḍasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the story of the meat-lump, a bird hunter made a living by catching birds and, when selling them, making them into mere lumps of meat with featherless skin. Therefore, at the time of his passing away from hell, the lump of meat itself became the sign of karma. He was born as a meat-lump *peta*. This is the third sutta.

## 4. Nicchavisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the story of the skinless *peta*, that sheep butcher made a living by repeatedly killing sheep and making them skinless; thus, following the previous method, the skinless body of a sheep became the sign of karma. He was born as a skinless *peta*. This is the fourth sutta.
202:
## 5. Asilomasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the story of the sword-hair *peta*, that pig butcher made a living for a long time by killing pigs that had been fed and raised for a long time with a sword. For him, the very act of raising the sword to kill became the sign of karma. Therefore, he was born as a *peta* with swords for hair. This is the fifth sutta.

## 6. Sattisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the story of the spear-hair *peta*, that hunter took a decoy deer and a spear and went to the forest, where he pierced and killed all the deer that approached that decoy deer with his spear. For him, the very act of piercing with a spear became the sign of karma. Therefore, he was born as a *peta* with spears for hair. This is the sixth sutta.

## 7. Usulomasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the story of the arrow-hair *peta*, a 'torturer' (*kāraṇika*) is an executioner who oppresses those guilty of offenses against the king with various methods of torture and finally kills them by shooting them with arrows. He shoots only after knowing, "If I shoot at this particular spot, he will die." Having made a living in this way and fallen into hell, when he was reborn in this realm due to the remnant of the result from that hell, the very act of shooting with arrows became the sign of karma. Therefore, he was born as a *peta* with arrows for hair. This is the seventh sutta.

## 8. Sūcilomasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the story of the needle-hair *peta*, a 'charioteer' (*sūta*) is a horse tamer. Some also say he is an ox tamer. For him, the very act of piercing with a needle-tipped goad became the sign of karma. Therefore, he was born as a *peta* with needles for hair. This is the eighth sutta.

## 9. Dutiyasūcilomasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the second story of the needle-hair *peta*, a 'slanderer' (*sūcaka*) is one who creates discord. He caused people to be divided from one another and, in the royal court, he would repeatedly slander, saying, "This person has such-and-such a thing; this person has done such-and-such an act," leading them to ruin and destruction. Therefore, just as people were divided and ruined by his slandering, so too, by needles...
203:
...to experience the suffering of being pierced by needles, he took his own karma as the object and was born as a needle-hair *peta*. The ninth sutta is finished.

## 10. Kumbhaṇḍasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the story of the *peta* with large testicles, a 'village-cheat' (*gāmakūṭaka*) is a judicial minister (judge). In accordance with his deceitful evil karma, testicles as large as water pots or great jars appeared. Because he took bribes in secret and hidden places and, by giving false judgments, committed manifest offenses, making owners into non-owners, his secret organ became manifest. Because he imposed unbearable burdens on others when inflicting punishment, his secret organ appeared as an unbearable burden. Because he was dishonest (deceitful) while standing in the place where one should stand with uprightness when judging, he had to sit unevenly on his secret organ. The tenth sutta is finished.

## Paṭhamo Vaggo.

## 2. Dutiyavaggo

## 1. Sasīsakasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the story of the *peta* who committed adultery, that being touched the touch of a married woman protected and guarded by others, and delighted his mind with sensual pleasure which is like filth. In accordance with his karma, he was born there to experience suffering while touching the touch of excrement. The first sutta is finished.

## 2. Gūthakhādasutta-vaṇṇanā

The story of the wicked Brahmin is quite well-known. The second sutta is finished.

## 3. Nicchavitthisutta-vaṇṇanā

In the story of the skinless woman *peta*, although a woman is not the master of her own touch, she stole that touch which belonged to her husband and caused delight in others. Therefore, in accordance with her karma, having deviated from pleasant touch, she was born as a skinless woman to experience painful touch. The third sutta is finished.
204:
## 4. Commentary on the Maṅgulitthi Sutta
In the story of the Maṅgulitthi, 'maṅguli' means ugly, unsightly, and loathsome in appearance. That woman, while performing the duties of a servant to a deity (yakkha-dāsī), deceived the people by saying, "If you perform such and such an offering, such and such a benefit will accrue to you." Taking perfumes, flowers, and so forth, she caused the multitude to hold wrong views. Therefore, in accordance with that kamma, because she had stolen the perfumes, flowers, and so forth, she was reborn with a foul-smelling body; and because she had caused the people to hold wrong views, she was reborn in the peta realm with an unsightly, ugly, and loathsome body. The commentary on the fourth sutta is finished.

## 5. Commentary on the Okilinī Sutta
In the story of the Okilinī, 'uppakkaṃ okiliniṃ okiriniṃ' means that the woman lies on a heap of glowing coals, writhing and rolling around as she is cooked. Therefore, she has a body cooked by the hot fire (uppakka), a body that is soiled (okilinī) because impurities constantly flow from it, with pus and foul blood oozing from her body, and she is also covered all around with glowing coals (okirinī). Indeed, coals the color of flame-of-the-forest (kiṃsuka) flowers fall upon her from below, from both sides, and from the sky above. Therefore, it is said, "uppakkaṃ okiliniṃ okiriniṃ."

In a past life, that woman, overcome by jealousy, had poured a brazier of coals over her rival. To elaborate—a certain dancer of the King of Kāsī had placed a brazier of coals nearby and was wiping water and sweat from her body with her hands. The king spoke with that dancer and showed signs of great pleasure. The chief queen, unable to endure this and overcome by jealousy, took that brazier shortly after the king had left and poured the coals over the dancer. Because she had committed that evil kamma, she was reborn in the peta realm to experience the corresponding result. The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.

## 6. Commentary on the Asīsaka Sutta
In the story of the executioner, because he had beheaded thieves for a long time by the king's command, when he was reborn in the peta realm, he became a headless peta (kabandha), possessing only a torso. The commentary on the sixth sutta is finished.
205:
## 7-11. Commentary on the Pāpabhikkhu Sutta and Others
In the story of the monk, 'pāpabhikkhu' refers to a wicked monk. Although he consumed the four requisites donated through the faith of the people, he was unrestrained in body and speech, his livelihood was ruined, and he lived a life of indulgence and negligence. Therefore, after being cooked in hell for the interval between two Buddhas, starting from the dispensation of the Buddha Kassapa, when he was reborn in the peta realm, he was reborn with an appearance resembling that of a monk. The same judgment should be understood for the stories of the nun (bhikkhunī), the female trainee (sikkhamānā), the male novice (sāmaṇera), and the female novice (sāmaṇerī). The commentary on the seventh and following suttas is finished.

## The Commentary on the Lakkhaṇasaṃyutta is finished.
206:
## 9. Opammasaṃyutta
## 1. Commentary on the Kūṭa Sutta
In the first sutta of the Opammasaṃyutta, they are called 'kūṭaṅgama' because they go to the peak. They are called 'kūṭasamosaraṇa' because they converge at the peak. 'Kūṭasamugghāta' means by the destruction of the peak. 'Avijjāsamugghāta' means by the destruction of ignorance (avijjā) through the Path of Arahantship. 'Appamatta' means being established in non-separation from mindfulness (sati). The first sutta (is finished).

## 2. Commentary on the Nakhasikha Sutta
In the second sutta, 'reborn among humans' (manussesu paccājāyanti) means that those who pass away from the human world and are reborn as humans are only this few. 'Other than among humans' (aññatra manussehi) means that those who pass away from the human world and, excluding the human world, are reborn in the four woeful states (apāya) are as numerous as the dust on the great earth. In this sutta, devas are also included together with humans. Therefore, it should be understood that just as those reborn among humans are few, so too are those reborn among devas. The second sutta (is finished).

## 3. Commentary on the Kula Sutta
In the third sutta, 'suppadhaṃsiyāni' means easily harassed. 'Kumbhatthenakehi' refers to thieves who, wishing to take others' property, enter another's house and look around by the light of a lamp, having placed the lamp inside a pot (kumbha); they are harassed by such 'pot-thieves'. 'Amanussehi suppadhaṃsiyo hoti' means that even low spirits (paṃsupisāca) destroy one who is devoid of the development of loving-kindness (mettā-bhāvanā), let alone powerful non-human beings. 'Bhāvita' means developed; 'bahulīkata' means frequently practiced; 'yānīkata' means made into a vehicle that is well-yoked; 'vatthukata' means made into a foundation in the sense of a standing place; 'anuṭṭhita' means established; 'paricita' means consolidated from all sides and well-developed; 'susamāraddha' means well-undertaken by the mind. The third sutta (is finished).

## 4. Commentary on the Okkhā Sutta
In the fourth sutta, 'okkhāsataṃ' refers to a hundred large-mouthed pots. 'Dānaṃ dadeyya' means one might give a hundred large pots filled with choice food as an offering. There is also a Pali reading 'ukkāsataṃ'; the meaning of that word should be understood as a hundred lamps. Filling an area a hundred times larger than the area reached by the light of a single lamp with the seven kinds of jewels...
207:
There is also a Pali reading 'ukkāsataṃ,' the meaning of which should be understood as a hundred torches. It means that one should fill an area a hundred times larger than the area illuminated by a single lamp with the seven kinds of jewels and offer them as a gift. 'Gaddūhanamattaṃ' means the duration of time it takes to pull the teat of a cow and milk it just once. Alternatively, 'gandhaūhanamattaṃ' means the duration of time it takes to pick up a ball of perfume with two fingers and smell it just once. If, even for such a brief moment, a person can develop a mind of loving-kindness (mettācitta) that pervades all beings with welfare—whether within the limit of a room, a courtyard, a monastery, or its precincts, or within the limit of a world system (cakkavāḷa), or throughout immeasurable world elements—this development of loving-kindness is of greater fruit than a gift given three times a day. The fourth sutta is concluded.

## 5. Sattisutta-vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the fifth sutta, regarding the words beginning with 'paṭileṇissaāmi': striking at the tip and making it bend like a roll of cotton or a roll of resin, and joining them together so they adhere, is called 'paṭileṇeti.' Striking in the middle to make it bend, or striking with the edge and making both edges adhere together, is called 'paṭikoṭṭeti.' Rolling it as one would make a roll of cotton, or unrolling a coarse mat that has been rolled up for a long time and then rolling it up again, is called 'paṭivaṭṭeti.' The fifth sutta is concluded.

## 6. Dhanuggahasutta-vaṇṇanā
In the commentary on the sixth sutta, 'daḷhadhammā dhanuggahā' refers to archers who possess exceptionally strong bows. A 'daḷhadhanu' (strong bow) refers to a bow with the strength of two thousand [men]. A 'bow with the strength of two thousand' is one where, when a weight of iron or copper is tied to the strung bowstring and the bow is lifted by the handle to the length of an arrow, the weight is lifted off the ground. 'Susikkhitā' (well-trained) refers to those who have studied the art of archery under a teacher for ten or twelve years. 'Katahatthā' (skilled) does not mean merely having learned the art; these archers are called 'katahatthā' because they have practiced until they attained mastery (vasībhāva). 'Katūpāsanā' (experienced) refers to those who have demonstrated their skill in the presence of royalty and others.

There has never been another man in the past with the speed of that man, except during the time when the Bodhisatta was the King of the Swift Swans (Javanahaṃsa). At that time, the Bodhisatta...
208: The Bodhisatta brought four arrows. At that time, the Bodhisatta's younger brothers said, "Brother, we will race along with the sun." The Bodhisatta said, "The sun is extremely swift; you will not be able to race with it." Although they were told so, they said the same thing a second and third time, and one day, saying "Let us go," they climbed Mount Yugandhara and stayed there. The Bodhisatta asked, "Where are my brothers?" and when told, "They have gone to race with the sun," he thought, "My poor brothers will perish." Out of compassion for them, he went himself and stayed near them. Then, when the sun rose, both brothers flew up into the sky along with the sun, and the Bodhisatta also flew up together with them. Before reaching the time of the mid-morning meal (antara-bhatta), the heat of fire arose between the wings of one of the brothers. That brother called out to his elder brother, the Swan King, saying, "I can go no further." The Bodhisatta Swan King comforted his younger brother, saying, "Brother, do not be afraid," and wrapping him within the cage of his wings, he dispelled the distress and sent him away, saying, "Go now." The second brother raced until the time of the mid-morning meal, and when the heat of fire arose within his wings, he said the same. The Bodhisatta Swan King did the same for him and sent him away, saying, "Go now." As for himself, he raced until midday and, reflecting, "These brothers are indeed foolish; I too should not be foolish," he turned back, thinking, "I shall visit my unseen friend, the King of Bārāṇasī," and proceeded to the city of Bārāṇasī. As he circled above the city, the twelve-yojana-wide city appeared like an alms-bowl covered with a lid. As he circled round and round, gaps appeared here and there. He himself appeared as if he were more than a thousand swans. The Swan King then restrained his speed and headed towards the royal palace. The King looked out and, realizing, "My dear friend, the Javanahaṃsa King, has arrived," he opened the window, prepared a jeweled seat, and stood watching. The Bodhisatta sat upon the jeweled seat. Then the King anointed the inside of the Swan King's wings with oil cooked a thousand times and offered him popped rice mixed with honey and a sweet drink. After the Swan King had partaken of them, the King asked, "Friend, where have you been?" The Swan King related the events and said, "Great King, at that time I raced until midday and, reflecting 'There is no benefit in racing,' I returned." Then the King said, "Lord, I wish to see your speed in racing with the sun." "Great King, it is very difficult for you to see," he replied. "Lord, if that is so, please show even a mere imitation of it," the King requested. "Great King, I shall show you; assemble the archers," he said. The King assembled the archers. Then the Swan King called four archers known as 'piercers of a hair' (akkhaṇavedhī), had a pillar erected in the middle of the city, and having a small bell fastened to his neck, he stood atop the pillar and [addressed] the four archers...
209:
(The King) said, "I wish to see the speed of your flight." "Great King, it is difficult to see; you are not able to see it," (the Swan King) replied. "Lord, if that is so, please show even a mere imitation," he requested. "Great King, very well, assemble the archers," he said. The King assembled the archers. Then the Swan King took four (archers), had a ceremonial arch (toraṇa) erected in the middle of the city, adorned his neck with a bell, and sat atop the arch. He said, "Let four men, supported by the arch, each shoot an arrow towards the four directions." He himself flew up together with the first arrow, and without even catching that arrow yet, he caught the arrow going south when it was about one cubit (ratana) away from the bow. He caught the second when it was about two cubits away, the third at three cubits, and the fourth before it even reached the ground. Then, only when he was sitting on the arch holding all four arrows did the people see him. That Swan King said to the King, "Great King, look, our speed is this swift." Thus, it should be understood that the Bodhisatta, when he was the Javana-haṃsa, brought those arrows.

"They run in front" means they speed ahead. However, these goddesses are not always in front; sometimes they are in front, and sometimes they are behind. For in the celestial mansions situated in the sky, there are also gardens and lotus ponds. When they bathe and play in the water in those ponds, they are also behind. But traveling with great speed, they run in front again. "Āyusaṅkhāra" (life-formations) is said with reference to the physical life-faculty (rūpa-jīvitindriya). For that life-faculty is exhausted even more swiftly (sīghataraṃ) than those (goddesses). The destruction of mental phenomena (arūpa-dhamma), however, cannot be demonstrated (as being so fast). The sixth sutta is finished.

## 7. Āဏိသုတ္တဝဏ္ဏနာ
In the seventh sutta, "Dasārahānaṃ" refers to the kings of this name. It is said that they always took a tenth part (as tax), therefore they were known as "Dasāraha". "Āṇaka" is the name of a drum. It is heard that in the Himālaya, there was a great lake called Mahākuḷīra. In that lake, a giant crab ate every elephant that entered. Then the elephants, being oppressed, cared for a certain female elephant, saying, "Depending on this elephant's son, we shall have safety." She gave birth to a son of great power. They cared for that young son as well. When he reached maturity, he asked his mother, "Mother, why do these elephants care for me?" She told him the story. He said, "What can a crab do to me? Come, let us go."
210: Surrounded by a herd of elephants, that elephant king went to the lake and was the first to descend. The crab, hearing only the sound of the water, came and seized that elephant. The crab's claw was very large; that elephant king, unable to move the crab this way or that, put his trunk in his mouth and cried out in distress. The elephants said, "The elephant king on whom we thought we would depend for safety has been caught first," and they fled in all directions. Then, the mother of that elephant king, standing not far away, spoke to the crab with pleasant words, saying, "We are land-elephants; you lords are water-nāgas (crabs). An elephant king should not be harmed," and she spoke this verse: "Whatever crabs there are in the ocean, in the Ganges, and in the Yamunā, Among those water-born crabs, you are especially noble. Please release this creature (the elephant king) who is weeping and lamenting." The sound of women is known to disturb and agitate men; therefore, that crab loosened its grip on the claw. The young elephant quickly raised both feet and trampled on the crab's back. As soon as he trampled it, the back broke like a clay pot or vessel. Then, piercing it with his tusks, he lifted it up, threw it onto the land, and let out a joyful roar. Then the elephants came from here and there and trampled that crab. One of the crab's claws was severed and fell; Sakka, the king of devas, took that claw and went away. The other claw, however, dried up in the hot wind and sun, and became the color of cooked lac. When it rained, that claw was carried away by the flood of water and got caught in the net of the ten brother kings who were playing in the Ganges, having spread their nets upstream. When they finished playing and lifted the net, they saw it and asked, "What is this?" "Lord, it is a crab's claw-bone," they were told. "This claw is not suitable to be worn as an ornament; let us cover it with parchment and make a drum," they said. Having covered it, they beat it. The sound of the drum pervaded the city of twelve yojanas. Later, they said, "It is not suitable to beat this drum every day; let it be a ceremonial drum for festival days," and they made it a royal ceremonial drum. When that ceremonial drum was beaten, all the people, having bathed and adorned themselves with flowers, would mount elephant-carriages, horse-carriages, and so on, and quickly assemble. Thus, because it brought the people together as if calling them, the drum was named Ānaka.
211:
They fitted other pegs (āṇi) made of gold, silver, and so on. Only a collection of pegs made of gold and so on remained. At that time, the sound of that drum, which had a range of twelve yojanas, could be heard with difficulty even inside the assembly hall.

Gambhīrā means deep by way of the Pali text, similar to the Salla Sutta. Gambhīratthā means deep by way of meaning, similar to the Mahāvedalla Sutta. Lokuttarā means explaining the nine supramundane states. Suññata-paṭisaṃyuttā means explaining only the nature of emptiness of beings, similar to the Saṃkhitta Saṃyutta. 'To be learned and to be mastered' (uggahetabbaṃ pariyāpuṇitabbaṃ). Kavikata refers to literary works made by poets and Dhamma preachers. 'Kapeyya' is also a synonym for that kavikata. Cittakkhara refers to literary works with ornate letters. 'Cittabyañjana' is also a synonym for that cittakkhara. Bāhirakā refers to literary works outside the Dispensation (Sāsana). Sāvakabhāsitā refers to literary works spoken by the disciples of various teachers. Because of the ornateness of letters, phrases, and sentences, and because of the perfection of hearing, novices, young monks, women, and great householders will be delighted and gather, wishing to listen, thinking, 'This person is a Dhamma preacher.' Therefore (tasmā) means: because the discourses (suttantas) spoken by the Tathāgata disappear when they are not learned and practiced, therefore (they should be learned). The seventh sutta is finished.

## 8. Kalingara Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the eighth sutta, kalingarūpadhānā means using a small block of wood as a pillow and as a footrest (for sleeping). Appamattā means being heedful in learning arts and sciences. Ātāpino means being endowed with energetic effort. Upāsanasmiṃ means in the exertion of arts and in attending to teachers. At that time, those princes would rise early in the morning and go to the hall of arts. Having learned the arts there and exerted themselves through recitation and so on, they would wash their faces and go to drink rice gruel. After drinking rice gruel, they would go back to the hall of arts, learn the arts, and while reciting, go for their morning meal. Having finished the morning meal, thinking, 'Let there not be long sleep due to heedlessness,' they would place small blocks of khadirā wood under their heads and feet, sleep for a little while, and then go back to the hall of arts to learn and recite. In the evening, while reciting, they would return home, eat their evening meal, and recite throughout the first watch. When sleeping, in the same manner...
212:
(The princes) sleep using a block of wood as a pillow. Through such exertion, those princes became those who could hit a streak of lightning (akkhaṇavedhino) and those who could split a hair (vālavedhino). This (Kalingarūpadhāna) Sutta was preached with reference to this meaning.

Otāra means an opportunity (an opening). Ārammaṇa means a cause or condition. Padhānasmiṃ means making an effort in the place of meditation. In the early Bodhi period, monks would attend to their meditation subjects immediately after finishing their meal. While they were thus attending, the sun would set. After bathing, they would descend to the cloister and walk in meditation throughout the first watch. Then, reflecting, 'Let me not sleep for long,' they would sleep using a block of wood as a support to relieve physical fatigue. In the last watch, they would rise again and descend to the cloister. This was said with reference to those monks. This island of Sri Lanka, during the time of the three kings, also had the sound of a single bell and was a single ground for meditation. The sound of a bell struck in various places would reach Pilicchikoliya; the sound of a bell struck in Kalyāṇī would reach the island of Nāgadīpa. There was a time when one had to point a finger to show, 'This monk is a worldling (puthujjana), this monk is a worldling.' One day, all the monks were indeed Arahants. Tasmā means: because Māra cannot find an opportunity against monks who use a block of wood as a pillow, therefore (tasmā). The eighth sutta is finished.

## 9. Nāga Sutta Vaṇṇanā
In the ninth sutta, ativelaṃ means a time exceeding the limit, a time exceeding the measure. Kimangaṃ panāhaṃ means 'For what reason should I not approach?' Bhisamuḷālaṃ means lotus stalks and lotus roots. Abbhuhetvā means having pulled out. Bhiṅkacchāpā refers to young elephants. Those young elephants are called bhiṅkacchāpā because they constantly make the sound 'bhiṅkāra'. Pasannākāraṃ karonti means performing the actions of those who are devoted, such as offering the four requisites. Dhammaṃ bhāsanti means preaching the Dhamma with an unbroken voice after learning one or two Jātakas or Suttantas. Pasannākāraṃ karonti means that laypeople, being devoted because of such preaching, offer the four requisites. Neva vaṇṇāya means it is not for the sake of the beauty of qualities, nor for the sake of the strength of wisdom. When the beauty of qualities declines, the physical complexion and physical strength also decline; therefore, it means it is not for the sake of physical complexion and strength. The ninth sutta is finished.
213:
## 10. Commentary on the Biḷāra Sutta

10. In the phrase 'sandhisamalasankaṭīre', 'sandhi' refers to the gaps (junctions) between houses. 'Samala' refers to the path where excrement leaves the village or the place where it flows. 'Sankaṭīra' refers to the place where rubbish is piled up. 'Mudumūsiṃ' refers to a soft-fleshed mouse. 'Vuṭṭhānaṃ paññāyati' means the teaching is evident. The tenth sutta ends.

## 11. Commentary on the Siṅgāla Sutta

11. In the phrase 'yena yena icchati', it is shown that the old jackal obtains relief of mind from time to time by changing his posture in whatever place he desires and by the blowing of cool winds. The phrase 'sakyaputtiyapaṭiñño' (one who claims to be a son of the Sakyans) is spoken in reference to Devadatta. This is because that Devadatta will not obtain even this much relief of mind in a future existence. The eleventh sutta ends.

## 12. Commentary on the Second Siṅgāla Sutta

12. 'Kataññutā' means knowing a favor done. 'Kataveditā' means specifically acknowledging a favor done. In this regard, there is this story concerning the gratitude of the old jackal: It is heard that seven brothers were plowing a field. The youngest brother was guarding the cattle while standing at the edge of the field. Then, a python caught an old jackal. Seeing this, the youth struck the python with a stick and caused it to release the jackal. After releasing the jackal, the python caught the youth instead. The jackal thought, 'This youth has given me my life; I too shall give him his life.' He then gripped in his mouth a billhook that was placed on top of a gruel pot and went near the youth. The other brothers saw this and followed, saying, 'The jackal is carrying away the billhook.' Knowing that the brothers saw him, the jackal dropped the billhook near the youth and fled. When the brothers arrived, they saw their younger brother caught by the python, so they cut the python with the billhook, rescued their brother, and departed. In this way, even in an old jackal, there can be some form of gratitude and acknowledgment of a favor. The phrase 'sakyaputtiyapaṭiñño' is also spoken in reference only to the conduct of Devadatta. The twelfth sutta ends.

## The Commentary on the Opamma Saṃyutta is finished.
214:
## 1. Commentary on the Kolita Sutta

## 10. Bhikkhu Saṃyutta

In the first sutta of the Bhikkhu Saṃyutta, the word 'āvuso' is the form of address used among disciples. When the Blessed Buddhas address disciples, they use the term 'bhikkhave'. However, the disciples, thinking 'Let us not be like the Buddhas,' say 'āvuso' first and then say 'bhikkhave' (to one another). When addressed by the Buddhas, the community of monks (bhikkhusaṅgha) responds with 'bhante'; when addressed by disciples, they respond with 'āvuso'.

'Ayaṃ vuccati' means that because initial thought (vitakka) and sustained thought (vicāra) cease in the second jhāna, and because of their cessation, the sense-base of sound (saddāyatana) does not occur, therefore this second jhāna is called 'the Noble Silence' (ariya-tuṇhībhāva). This is the connection of the meaning here. In the passage 'dhammī vā kathā ariyo vā tuṇhībhāvo', the practice of meditation (kammaṭṭhāna) as well as the first jhāna and so forth also come to be known as Noble Silence.

'Vitakkasahagatā' means having initial thought as an object. 'Saññāmanasikārā' refers to perception and attention. 'Samudācaranti' means they occur. It is said that the Venerable Moggallāna was not yet proficient in the second jhāna. Then, when he emerged from that second jhāna, initial and sustained thoughts appeared to him continuously. Thus, for that elder, the second jhāna as well as perception and attention were part of decline (hānabhāgiya). To show this, the Buddha spoke thus. 'Saṇṭhapehi' means establish well. 'Ekodibhāvaṃ karohi' means make the mind one-pointed. 'Samādaha' means place the mind well on the meditation object. 'Mahābhiññataṃ' refers to the state of having the six higher knowledges. Indeed, by this means, the Teacher developed the elder's concentration, which was prone to decline, for seven days and led the elder to attain the six higher knowledges. The first sutta ends.

## 2. Commentary on the Upatissa Sutta

In the second sutta, the phrase 'atthi nu kho taṃ kiñci lokasmiṃ' is spoken in reference to either a very noble being or to conditioned phenomena (saṅkhāra). Why is the phrase 'satthupi kho' asked? Because the Venerable Ānanda had excessive desire and affection for the Teacher, he asked to know, 'Would grief and so forth not arise for this Venerable Sāriputta even upon the passing (alteration) of the Teacher?' 'Dīgharattaṃ' refers to the time that has passed since the day the Vedanāpariggaha Sutta was preached to the wanderer Dīghanakha at the entrance of the Sūkarakhata cave. On that day, the underlying defilements of the Venerable Sāriputta were completely destroyed.
215:
On that day (when the Vedanāpariggaha Sutta was taught), for the Elder, these defilements following the round of rebirths were completely eradicated. The second sutta (commentary) is finished.

## 3. Ghaṭasutta Vaṇṇanā

In the third sutta, "ekavihāre" means in a single chamber. At that time, many visiting monks had gathered. Then, as lodgings were insufficient according to the precincts or the monastery, a single chamber (cave) fell to the lot of two Elders. During the day, those Elders stayed in separate places, but at night, they spread a robe-curtain between them. Those Elders stayed only in their respective places. Therefore, it is said "ekavihāre" (in one dwelling).

"Oḷārikena" is said with reference to having a distinct (gross) object. The Venerable Moggallāna dwelt with the attainment of the divine eye and the divine ear element. The objects of that divine eye and divine ear, known as the base of forms (rūpāyatana) and the base of sounds (saddāyatana), were distinct objects. Thus, because forms were seen with the divine eye and sounds were heard with the divine ear element, that dwelling is called "oḷārika" (distinct dwelling).

"Dibbacakkhu visujjhi" means it became pure for the purpose of seeing the physical form of the Blessed One. "Dibbā ca sotadhātu" means that divine ear element also became pure for the purpose of hearing the voice of the Blessed One. For the Blessed One too, both the divine eye and the divine ear element were pure for the purpose of seeing the physical form of the Elder and hearing his voice. At that time, the Elder thought, "How does our Teacher, the Blessed One, dwell now?" and having developed the light-kasiṇa, he saw with the divine eye the Blessed One sitting in the Fragrant Chamber (Gandhakuṭi) at the Jetavana monastery, and heard his voice with the divine ear element. The Blessed One did the same. In this way, those two noble ones both saw each other and heard each other's voices.

"Āraddhavīriyo" means having fulfilled energy, having exerted energy. By the phrase "yāvadeva upanikkhepanamattāya", it is meant that a mustard-seed-sized pebble placed near the Himalayas, which is three thousand yojanas in extent, would be for the purpose of merely placing it nearby to compare: "Is the Himalaya mountain great, or is this pebble great?" The same method applies to the subsequent phrase. "Kappaṃ" refers to the life-span (āyukappa). By the phrase "loṇaghaṭāya", he shows the meaning of a great salt jar that is supported by the rim of the universe and stands touching the Brahma world at its mouth.
216:
In bringing forth similes, these two great elders did so by way of similarity and by way of their existing qualities. How? This psychic power (iddhi), because of its exceedingly lofty and extensive nature, is like the Himālaya mountains. Wisdom (paññā), because of its nature of pervading and being established in the four planes of Dhamma, is like the taste of salt that pervades all dishes. Thus, they first brought forth similes by way of similarity.

The characteristic of concentration (samādhi) is very prominent in the Elder Mahāmoggallāna. Although it is not that the Elder Sāriputta lacks psychic power, the Blessed One placed only this Elder Moggallāna in the foremost position (etadagga), saying: "Monks, among my disciple monks who possess psychic power, Mahāmoggallāna is the foremost."

The characteristic of insight (vipassanā) is very prominent in the Elder Sāriputta. Although the Elder Mahāmoggallāna also possesses wisdom, the Blessed One placed only this Elder Sāriputta in the foremost position, saying: "Monks, among my disciple monks of great wisdom, Sāriputta is the foremost."

Therefore, just as these two elders do not overstep each other's duties, they brought forth similes by way of their existing qualities. In the characteristic of concentration, Mahāmoggallāna has reached perfection; in the characteristic of insight, the Elder Sāriputta has reached perfection; but in both of these, the Fully Enlightened Buddha has reached perfection. The commentary on the third sutta is finished.

## 4. Navasuttavaṇṇanā
In the fourth sutta, 'appossukko' means being without effort (unconcerned). 'Saṅkasāyati' means he dwells. 'Veyyāvaccaṃ' refers to the duties to be performed regarding robes. 'Ābhicetasikānaṃ' refers to those states that depend on the exalted mind. 'Nikāmalābhī' means one who obtains at will, due to the ability to attain meditative states at any desired moment. 'Akicchalābhī' means one who obtains without difficulty, due to the ability to attain by easily suppressing the hindrances (nīvaraṇa) which are obstacles to jhāna. 'Akasiralābhī' means one who obtains without trouble, due to the ability to emerge from jhāna according to the predetermined time; it means one who has mastered jhāna. 'Sithilamārabbha' means having initiated lax effort. The commentary on the fourth sutta is finished.

## 5. Sujātasuttavaṇṇanā
In the fifth sutta, 'abhirūpo' means one whose appearance surpasses other appearances. 'Dassanīyo' means worthy of being looked at. 'Pāsādiko' means one capable of inspiring confidence in the mind just by being seen. 'Vaṇṇapokkharatāya' means because of the beauty of one's complexion. The commentary on the fifth sutta is finished.
217:
## 6. Commentary on the Lakuṇṭakabhaddiya Sutta

In the sixth sutta, the term 'dubbaṇṇa' means having an unattractive physical complexion. 'Okoṭimaka' means being dwarfish (short). 'Paribhūtarūpa' means having a nature that is despised or held in contempt due to one's physical proportions. It is said that the monks of the group of six (Chabbaggiya) would touch and stroke Lakuṇṭakabhaddiya in various places such as his head and shoulders, saying, "Friend Bhaddiya, Friend Bhaddiya," and would play with him in various ways, pulling him here and there. Therefore, he is called 'paribhūtarūpa' (one with a despised appearance).

Why did this person come to have such a nature? In the past, it is said that he was a Great King, and to that king, elderly men and elderly women were objects of loathing. If that king saw elderly people, he would have them keep their topknots, make them tuck up their loincloths, and make them play according to his whim. Upon seeing elderly women, he would also make them behave in distorted ways as he desired and make them play according to his whim. Great shame arose for them in the presence of their children and relatives. The king's evil conduct caused a great uproar from the earth up to the six deva realms.

Then Sakka, King of the Devas, thought: "This blind fool is harassing the multitude; I will humble him." Sakka, assuming the form of an elderly villager, placed a pot of buttermilk on a small cart and entered the city driving the cart. As the king was leaving the city riding an elephant, he saw him and said, "Friends, this old man is coming toward us with a buttermilk cart; stop him, stop him!" Although the king's attendants ran here and there, they did not see him. This was because Sakka had resolved: "Let only the king see me, let no others see me." Then, while the attendants were saying, "Where is he, O King? Where is he, O King?", the king, together with his elephant, entered under the cart like a calf approaching a cow. Sakka then smashed the buttermilk pot.

The king's entire body, starting from his head, became drenched with buttermilk. After having his body rubbed and washed, bathing in the garden pond, and adorning himself, the king saw that old man again as he re-entered the city. Upon seeing him, he said, "This is the same old man we saw before; he is seen again. Stop him, stop him!" The attendants ran here and there, saying, "Where is he, O King? Where is he, O King?" The king again met with the same distorted situation as before. At that moment, Sakka made the oxen and the cart disappear, and standing in the sky...
218:
Sakka, standing in the sky, said: "You blind fool, you perceived me as 'this is a buttermilk merchant.' I am Sakka, the King of the Devas. I have come to prevent that evil conduct of yours. Do not perform such an act again," and after threatening him, he departed. Due to that evil kamma, this person became one with an unattractive appearance (ugly).

In the time of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Vipassī, however, this person was a cuckoo with variegated wings named Cittapattakokila. While living in the Khema Deer Park, he went to the Himālaya one day, took a sweet ripe mango in his beak, and while returning, he saw the Teacher surrounded by the community of monks. He thought: "On other days, I see the Tathāgata empty-handed. Today, however, I have this ripe mango; I will offer it to the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala)." He descended from the sky and hovered. The Teacher, knowing the bird's mind, looked at his attendant monk. That monk took out the bowl, paid homage to the Buddha, and placed it in the Teacher's hand. The cuckoo placed the ripe mango in the bowl of the One of Ten Powers. The Teacher sat right there and consumed it. The cuckoo, with a confident mind, repeatedly reflected on the virtues of the One of Ten Powers, paid homage, and returned to his nest, spending seven days in nothing but the bliss of rapture (pītisukha). Due to this wholesome kamma, his voice became sweet and melodious.

In the time of the Perfectly Enlightened Buddha Kassapa, when they began to build a cetiya (stupa), they consulted: "What size shall we make it? Let us make it seven leagues (yojana) in size." Others said, "This size is too great; let us make it six leagues." Others said, "This too is still too great; let us make it five leagues, four leagues, three leagues, two leagues." At that time, this person was a master carpenter and said, "Friends, if done this way, it will be easy to maintain and repair in the future." Taking a measuring line and spreading it out, he stood at a distance of one gāvuta (quarter-league) and said, "Let each face be one gāvuta; the cetiya will be one league in circumference and one league in height." They followed the master carpenter's words. The cetiya was completed in seven years, seven months, and seven days. Thus, he imposed a measure (limit) on the Buddha who is measureless. Due to that kamma, he was born as a dwarf (okoṭimaka).

"Hatthayo pasadā migā" means elephants and spotted deer. "Natthi kāyasmiṃ tulyatā" means there is no such thing as a standard measure in the body; the meaning is that the physical measure of the body is not the cause (of spiritual attainment). The sixth sutta is finished.
219:
## 7. Commentary on the Visākhasutta
In the commentary on the seventh sutta, the Visākhasutta, the phrase *poriyā vācāya* means with speech similar to that of city dwellers or townspeople, which is complete in syllables and words, and is pleasant to hear. *Vissaṭṭhāya* means with speech that is clear, distinct, not hesitant, and not affected by bile or phlegm. *Anelagalāya* means not like the way dull and slow-witted people speak with saliva dripping from their mouths, but rather with speech that is faultless, pure, and clear. *Pariyāpannāya* means with speech that is included within the Four Noble Truths, arising without abandoning the Four Noble Truths. *Anissitāya* means with speech that is not spoken based on attachment to the cycle of rebirth (*vaṭṭa*). "*Dhammo hi isinaṃ dhajo*" means the ninefold supramundane Dhamma is the banner of the Sages (*Isis*), such as the Buddhas and Paccekabuddhas, who seek special qualities such as the morality group (*sīlakkhandha*). The commentary on the seventh sutta ends.

## 8. Commentary on the Nandasutta
In the commentary on the eighth sutta, the Nandasutta, the term *ākoṭitapaccākoṭitāni* refers to alms-bowls that have been beaten and smoothed on one side with the hand or a mallet, and then turned over and beaten again. *Añjetvā* means having filled with eye-salve (applying eye-salve). *Acchaṃ pattan* refers to a clay bowl of exceptionally clear and bright color. Why did the Venerable Nanda do this? It was to know the intention of the Blessed One. It is said that he had this thought: "If the Blessed One says, 'My younger brother Nanda truly looks beautiful,' I will live in this manner for the rest of my life. If he sees fault in this matter, I will discard this manner, take rags from a dust heap to make robes, and live in a remote dwelling at the edge of the forest." *Assasī* means "will be."

*Aññātuñchena* means: seeking fragrant food prepared with spices such as ginger, chili, onion, bay leaf, and cumin at the marked houses of powerful people is called *ñātuñcha* (conspicuous alms-gathering). However, seeking mixed food obtained by standing at doors in the order of houses is called *aññātuñcha* (inconspicuous alms-gathering). This *aññātuñcha* is what is intended here. *Kāmesu anapekkhinan* means (the Venerable Nanda) who is without regard for the objects of sensuality (*vatthu-kāma*) and the defilements of sensuality (*kilesa-kāma*). All the words beginning with "*āraññiko ca*" are spoken solely by way of undertaking (the dhutanga observances). This sutta, "*Kāmesu ca anapekkho*," was spoken later by the Blessed One after returning from showing the celestial nymphs in the deva world. From the day this sutta was taught, the Venerable Nanda, while striving and exerting effort, established himself in the fruit of Arahantship within a few days and became a supreme recipient of offerings in the world including the devas. The commentary on the eighth sutta ends.
220:
## 9. Commentary on the Tissasutta
In the ninth sutta, *dummano* means having an arisen dejection of mind. Why did this Venerable Tissa become so miserable and dejected? He was one who had ordained from the Khattiya (warrior/royal) caste. Therefore, after he was ordained, they made him wear a double-layered undergarment, wrap himself in a fine robe, applied eye-salve to his eyes, and anointed his head with realgar oil (*manosilā-tela*). When the other monks went to their night and day quarters, he, not knowing that a monk should sit in a secluded place, went to the refectory, climbed onto a large bench, and sat there.

Visiting monks who were rag-robe wearers (*paṃsukūlika*) arriving from other regions came and thought, "It is not proper to see the Ten-Powered One (the Buddha) with bodies covered in dust in this manner. Let us first put down our belongings." They then went to the refectory. Even when those elder monks arrived, Venerable Tissa remained sitting motionless. Other monks asked, "May we perform the foot-washing duty? May we fan you with a palmyra fan?" But Tissa, while still sitting, asked, "How many rains (*vassa*) do you have?" When they replied, "We have no rains yet. But how many rains do you have?", he said, "I was ordained only today."

Then the monks said to him, "Friend, you have only just had your topknot cut; even today the smell of lice still lingers at the base of your head. While such senior elders are asking to perform duties for you, you sit silent and motionless. You do not have even a measure of respect. In whose teaching have you been ordained?" Surrounding him and piercing him with the stings of their words, they said, "Have you ordained because you are oppressed by debt, or oppressed by fear, or because you are unable to make a living?" He looked at one elder, and that elder said, "Old man, why do you look at me?" He looked at another, and that one said the same. Then, the royal pride (*khattiya-māna*) arose in him, thinking, "These monks surround me and pierce me with the stings of their words." Tears the color of rubies flowed from his eyes.

Then he said to those monks, "To whom have you come?" The monks replied, "What is this? Do you think we have come to you, you who have discarded the layman's appearance?" and said, "We have come to the Blessed One, the supreme person in the world including the devas." He, becoming angry, said, "If you have come to my elder brother, I will make you go back the very way you came," and he went out. On the way, he thought, "If I go in this manner, the Blessed One will have these monks expelled." Being miserable and dejected, he went along with tears flowing. It was for this reason that Venerable Tissa became thus.
221:
"Vācāsannitodakena" means with the goad of words. "Sañjambharimakaṃsu" means they performed continuous oppression or harassment; it means they pierced from above. "Vattā" refers to one who speaks whatever they wish to others. "No ca vacanakkhamo" refers to one who cannot endure the words of others. "Now, you are pierced by this anger and by these goads of words. In the past, you were even banished from the kingdom," the Buddha said. When this was said, the monks requested the Blessed One, "Venerable Sir, at what time was he banished?"

The Teacher said: In the past, when the King of Bārāṇasī was reigning in Bārāṇasī, two ascetics, one named Jātimanta of noble birth and one named Mātaṅga of the outcaste (Caṇḍāla) class, came to Bārāṇasī. Among them, the ascetic Jātimanta arrived first and stayed in a potter's shed. The ascetic Mātaṅga arrived later and asked for permission to stay there. The potter said, "Venerable Sir, there is another monk who entered and stayed here first; please ask him." That ascetic Mātaṅga took his requisites, stood at the door of the shed, and said, "Teacher, please give us the opportunity to stay for one night as well." "Enter, sir," he replied. To Mātaṅga, who had entered and was sitting, he asked, "Sir, what is your clan?" "Teacher, I am of the Caṇḍāla clan." When he said this, [Jātimanta] said, "I cannot sit in the same place with you, a Caṇḍāla; go to a separate place." 

Mātaṅga then spread a grass mat and lay down right there. Jātimanta lay down near the door. The other, Mātaṅga, when going out to urinate, stepped on Jātimanta's chest. When asked, "Who is this?", he replied, "It is I, Teacher." "You wretched Caṇḍāla, do you not see another path? Why do you come and step on me?" "Teacher, I stepped on you because I did not see; please forgive me," he apologized. When the Bodhisatta Mātaṅga went outside, Jātimanta thought, "When this wretched Caṇḍāla returns, he will surely come by this same path," and so he turned around and lay down with his head where his feet were. The Bodhisatta also thought, "The teacher is lying with his head in this direction; I will go by the side of his feet," but as he entered, he stepped on the chest again. When asked, "Who is this?", he replied, "It is I, Teacher." "At first, it could be said you did it unknowingly, but now you do it to deliberately oppress me. When the sun rises, may your head split into seven pieces!" he cursed. The Bodhisatta, without saying a single word, held back the sun before dawn, so that it could not rise. People and animals such as elephants and horses woke up.
222:
The people went to the royal palace and reported, "Great King, there is no one in the whole city who is still asleep, yet the dawn is not seen; what could this be?" The King said, "In that case, investigate the city." While investigating, they saw the two ascetics in the potter's shed and thought, "This matter must be the work of these ascetics," and reported it to the King. The King said, "Question them," so they went and asked Jātimanta, "Did you create this darkness?" Jātimanta said, "I did not do it; this deceitful, wretched ascetic has infinite trickery, ask him instead." They went to the Bodhisatta and asked, "Venerable Sir, did you create this darkness?" The Bodhisatta replied, "Yes, I did it because this teacher cursed me." They reported this to the King, and the King himself came and asked the Bodhisatta, "Venerable Sir, is it true that you did this?" "Yes, Great King." "Why did you do it, Venerable Sir?" "This teacher has cursed me; if this teacher apologizes to me, I will release the sun." The King said, "Venerable Sir, please apologize to him," but Jātimanta said, "Should one of noble birth like me apologize to such a Caṇḍāla? I will not apologize."

Then the people said, "Will you not apologize of your own will?" and they grabbed his hands and feet, made him prostrate at the Bodhisatta's feet, and said, "Apologize!" The ascetic lay there silently. Again they said, "Apologize!", and then he said, "Teacher, forgive my fault." The Bodhisatta said, "I will first forgive your fault and release the sun, but when the sun rises, your head will split into seven pieces." He then said, "Place a lump of clay the size of this teacher's head on his head, and place him in water as deep as his neck in the river." The people did as instructed. By then, the king's forces along with the people of the country had gathered. The Bodhisatta released the sun. When the sun's rays came and struck the lump of clay, that clay split into seven pieces. At that very moment, Jātimanta dove into the water, emerged at another landing, and fled. The Teacher, having brought forth this story, connected the past to the present to give instruction: "Not only now do you receive reproach from the monks; in the past, too, because of this anger, you were banished from the country." Then he said, "Tissa, such behavior is not suitable for you," and so on. The ninth sutta is finished.

## 10. Theranāmaka Sutta Vaṇṇanā

In the tenth sutta, "Vaṇṇavādī" means one who habitually speaks of the benefits. "Yaṃ atītaṃ taṃ pahīnaṃ" means that the past five aggregates are said to be abandoned by the abandoning of desire and lust for them. "Anāgataṃ" means that the future five aggregates are said to be relinquished by the relinquishing of desire and lust for them.
223:
By abandoning desire and lust for the aggregate of the five components, it is said that the past aggregate of the five components is abandoned. By relinquishing desire and lust for the future aggregate of the five components, it is said that it is completely relinquished. 'Sabbābhibhū' means one who stands having overcome all aggregates (khandha), sense bases (āyatana), and elements (dhātu), as well as the phenomena existing in the three realms of existence. 'Sabbavidū' means one who stands having made clear and known all the aforementioned varieties of aggregates, sense bases, elements, and the three realms. 'Sabbesu dhammesu' means one who is not smeared by the smears of craving and wrong view in those phenomena existing in the three realms. 'Sabbañjaha' means one who stands having abandoned all those aforementioned phenomena of the three realms by abandoning desire and lust for them. 'Taṇhakkhayavimuttaṃ' refers to a person who is liberated by the liberation of the fruit (phala-vimutti) that has Nibbāna—known as the destruction of craving—as its object. The tenth sutta is finished.

## 11. Mahākappinasuttavaṇṇanā

In the eleventh sutta, Mahākappina is the name of a great elder (Mahāthera) who attained the power of higher knowledge (abhiññā) and was among the eighty great disciples. It is said that during his life as a layman, he ruled a kingdom of three hundred leagues in the city of Kukkuṭavatī. Being one in his final birth, he wandered with an ear inclined to hear such news concerning the Buddha's Dispensation. Then one day, surrounded by a thousand ministers, he went to play in the park. At that time, pedestrian merchants from the Middle Country (Majjhimadesa) arrived at that city, and after storing their goods, they went to the palace gate with gifts in hand, thinking, 'We shall see the King.' Hearing that 'The King has gone to the park,' they followed him to the park, stood at the gate, and informed the gatekeeper. Then, when it was reported to the King, the King had them called in. The merchants offered their gifts, paid homage, and stood there. The King asked, 'Friends, where have you come from?' They replied, 'From Sāvatthī, O King.' 'Is your country well-supplied with alms-food? Is the King righteous?' he asked. 'Yes, O King, the country is prosperous and the King is righteous,' they replied. 'Is there any news in your region?' he asked. 'There is, O King, but it is not proper to speak with mouths that have remnants of food,' they replied. The King had water provided from a golden pitcher. They washed their mouths, faced towards where the Ten-Powered One (the Buddha) was, raised their joined palms, and said, 'O King, in our region, the Jewel of the Buddha (Buddharatana) has appeared.' Upon merely hearing the word 'Buddha,' a rapture spread throughout the King's entire body. Then he asked, 'Friends, did you say "Buddha"?' 'We say "Buddha," O King,' they replied. Having made them say it three times in this way, he thought, 'The word "Buddha" is immeasurable; it is not possible to set a limit to this word.' Being thus devoted to the word 'Buddha,' he gave them a hundred thousand coins and asked again, 'What other news is there?' 'O King, the Jewel of the Dhamma (Dhammaratana) has appeared,' they replied. Hearing that as well, he took their confirmation three times in the same way, gave another hundred thousand, and asked again, 'What other news is there?' 'O King, the Jewel of the Saṅgha (Saṅgharatana) has appeared,' they replied. Hearing that as well, he took their confirmation three times in the same way, and another...
224:
...having given a hundred thousand, he wrote the matter of the gift in a letter and sent them, saying, 'Friends, go to the Queen.' When those merchants had gone, he asked the ministers, 'Friends, a Buddha has appeared in the world; what will you do?' They asked, 'O King, what do you wish to do?' 'I shall ordain,' he said. 'We too shall ordain,' they replied. All of them, without regard for home or wealth, departed on the very horses they had come on (to ordain).

The merchants went to Queen Anojā and showed her the letter. After reading the letter, she asked, 'Friends, the King has given you many coins; what deed did you perform?' They replied, 'O Queen, we have brought delightful news.' 'Friends, can you let me hear it too?' she asked. 'O Queen, we can, but it is not proper to speak with mouths that have remnants of food,' they replied. The Queen had water provided from a golden pitcher. After washing their mouths, they reported to her in the same manner they had reported to the King. Upon hearing it, the Queen was filled with joy and, in the same way as the King, took their confirmation three times for each word. For each confirmation, she gave thirty [thousand], totaling nine hundred thousand coins. The merchants received a total of one million two hundred thousand coins. Then she asked them, 'Friends, where is the King?' They replied, 'O Queen, he has departed, saying "I shall ordain".'

'Friends, if that is so, you may go,' she said, and after dismissing the merchants, she summoned the wives of the ministers who had gone with the King and asked, 'Mothers, do you know where your husbands have gone?' They replied, 'O Queen, we know; they went with the King to play in the park.' 'Yes, it is true they went, but upon reaching the park, they heard "A Buddha has appeared, the Dhamma has appeared, the Saṅgha has appeared," and they have gone, saying "We shall ordain in the presence of the Ten-Powered One." What will you do?' she asked. They asked, 'O Queen, what do you wish to do?' 'I shall ordain; I no longer wish to keep on the tip of my tongue the saliva spat out by those kings,' she said. 'If that is so, we too shall ordain,' they said, and all the women had their carriages harnessed and departed.

The King, together with the thousand ministers, reached the bank of the Ganges (Gaṅgā) river. At that time, the Ganges was full of water. Then, seeing the river, he thought, 'This Ganges is full of water and teeming with fierce crocodiles and fish. There are no servants or people with us who could make a boat or a raft for us. However, the virtues of that Teacher, the Buddha, are spread from the Avīci hell below to the highest realm of existence (bhavagga) above. If this Teacher is truly the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), may the hooves of these horses not get wet.' Having made this resolution, [he drove] the horses onto the surface of the water...
225:
They made the horses descend into the water. Not even the hooves of a single horse were wetted, and as if traveling on a royal highway, they reached the other bank and arrived at another great river ahead. In that river, there was no other act of truth; by that same act of truth, they crossed that river, which was half a yojana wide.
