After that, they reached a third great river named Candabhāgā and crossed it as well by that same act of truth.

The Blessed One, having arisen from the attainment of great compassion (mahākaruṇā-samāpatti) at dawn on that day, surveyed the world and saw: "Today, King Mahākappina, having renounced a kingdom of three hundred yojanas, is coming to ordain in my presence accompanied by a thousand ministers." Thinking, "It is proper for me to go and welcome them," he attended to his physical needs early in the morning and, surrounded by the community of monks, wandered for alms in Sāvatthī. After the meal, having returned from the alms round, he himself took his bowl and robes, ascended into the sky, and sat cross-legged under a great banyan tree (nigrodha) at a place facing the landing place where they would cross on the bank of the Candabhāgā river. Establishing mindfulness before him, he emitted the six-colored Buddha-rays.

As they were ascending from that landing place, they saw the six-colored Buddha-rays darting here and there. Upon seeing the face of the One of Ten Powers (Dasabala), which possessed the splendor of the full moon, they concluded just by seeing him: "The teacher for whose sake we have come out to ordain is surely this Noble One." From the place where they saw him, they approached, bowing and paying homage, and worshipped the Teacher. King Mahākappina, holding the Teacher's heels, paid homage and sat in a suitable place along with the thousand ministers. The Teacher preached the Dhamma to them. At the end of the discourse, all of them were established in Arahatship and requested ordination from the Teacher.

The Teacher, knowing that "these people have given gifts of robes in previous lives and thus have come bringing their own robes," stretched out his golden-colored hand and said: "Come, monks (Ehi bhikkhavo), the Dhamma is well-proclaimed; lead the holy life for the complete ending of suffering." That very speech became the going-forth (pabbajjā) and higher ordination (upasampadā) for those venerable ones. They surrounded the Teacher like great elders of sixty years' standing.

Queen Anojā, too, surrounded by a thousand chariots, reached the bank of the Ganges. Not seeing any boat or raft brought for the King, she thought with her wisdom: "The King must have gone by making an act of truth. That Blessed One, indeed..."
226:
...has appeared for their benefit alone. If that Teacher is truly the Perfectly Enlightened One (Sammāsambuddha), may our chariots not sink in the water!" Thus making an act of truth, she drove the chariots onto the surface of the water. Not even the rims of the chariot wheels were wetted. Having crossed the second and third rivers by that same act of truth, she saw the Teacher at the foot of the banyan tree. The Teacher thought, "If these women see their husbands, desire (chandarāga) might arise and create an obstacle to the Paths and Fruits; I shall make it so that this cannot happen." He acted in such a way that they could not see each other. All those women ascended from the riverbank, paid homage to the One of Ten Powers, and sat down. The Teacher preached the Dhamma to them. At the end of the discourse, all the women were established in the Fruit of Stream-entry (Sotāpattiphala) and then saw each other. The Teacher thought, "Let the Theri Uppalavaṇṇā come." The Theri arrived, ordained all the women, and took them to the nunnery. The Teacher, taking the thousand monks, went to Jetavana through the air. Referring to this, it was said: "Mahākappina is the name of this great elder who attained the power of higher knowledge (abhiññā) and is among the eighty great disciples."

'Janetasmim' means among the multitude of beings brought forth. 'Ye gottapaṭisārino' means those who rely on and profess their lineage, saying, "We are Vāseṭṭhas, we are Gotamas"; among them, the Khattiya (warrior-noble) is the best. 'Vijjācaraṇasampanno' means being endowed with the eight types of higher knowledge (vijjā) and the fifteen types of conduct (caraṇa). 'Tapati' means shines. 'Jhāyī tapati brāhmaṇo' means the Arahant Brahmin, meditating with the two types of jhāna, shines and is resplendent. At that moment, the Elder Kāḷudāyī was sitting nearby, meditating with the two types of jhāna. 'Buddho tapati' means the Omniscient Buddha shines and is resplendent. This is said to be a verse of all-encompassing blessing (maṅgala). It is heard that King Bhātika, after performing a ceremony of worship, said to his teacher: "Recite a single verse of victory (jayamangala) that is not separate from the Three Jewels." That teacher, having reflected on the Word of the Buddha in the Tipiṭaka, wishing to recite this verse, said, "The sun shines by day," and paid homage with joined palms to the setting sun. Saying, "The moon glows by night," he paid homage to the rising moon. Saying, "The Khattiya in his armor shines," he paid homage to the King. Saying, "The meditator shines, the Brahmin," he paid homage to the Sangha of monks. Finally, saying, "The Buddha shines with his majesty (tejasā)," he paid homage to the Great Stupa (Mahācetiya). Then the King said, "Do not lower your hands," and placed a thousand coins on those very raised hands. The eleventh sutta is finished.

In the twelfth sutta, the meaning should be understood. 'Cirarattaṃsametikā' means those who have a view that has been united and established for a long time. It is said that they have wandered together for five hundred lives. 'Sameti nesaṃ saddhammo' means now this True Dhamma of the Dispensation is united for them, reaching a state of similarity. 'Dhamme buddhappavedite' means in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Buddha, this Dhamma of the Dispensation is beautiful for them. 'Suvinitā kappinena' means well-disciplined in the Dhamma preached by the Noble Ones by their preceptor, the Elder Mahākappina.
227:
## 12. Sahāyakasutta-vaṇṇanā

In the twelfth sutta (the meaning should be understood). "Cirarattaṃsametikā" refers to those who have views that have stood in harmony, having associated for a long time. It is said that they wandered together for five hundred births. "Sameti nesaṃ saddhammo" means that now, for them, this Dhamma of the Dispensation harmonizes and accords. "Dhamme buddhappavedite" means that in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Buddha, the Dhamma of the Dispensation shines for them. "Suvinītā kappinena" means they are well-disciplined by their preceptor (Mahākappina Thera) in the Dhamma proclaimed by the Noble Ones. In all the remaining Pali, the meaning is clear. The twelfth sutta is finished.
